# Expanded Compendium of Materia Medica
<note>original: "增廣本草綱目" (Zengguang Bencao Gangmu). The "Bencao Gangmu" is the foundational encyclopedia of Chinese medicine and natural history, originally compiled by Li Shizhen in the 16th century. This "Expanded" (Zengguang) version indicates a later edition with additional commentary or updated information.</note>

<image-desc>A light brown paper cover of a traditional stitch-bound Chinese book. On the left side, a vertical rectangular box with a double-line border contains the title in large Traditional Chinese characters. Handwritten notes appear at the top in pencil and on the right side in ink. Four visible binding holes with thread are on the right edge.</image-desc>

<term>Compendium of Materia Medica (Bencao Gangmu): Literally "The Categorized Outline of Roots and Herbs," the most comprehensive medical book in the history of traditional Chinese medicine.</term>

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 15, Herb Section
## Herbs of Damp Ground, Part 1 ->53 Species<-

### Chrysanthemum
<gloss>Ranked in the "Superior" category of the *Shennong’s Classic of Materia Medica*. Also named "Seasonal Flower." In the *Classic*, it is called "Female Virtue." In the *Additional Records*, it is called "Female Flower," "Female Stem," "Essence of the Sun," "Rebirth," "Longevity Prolonger," and "Wall-Healer." In the *Erya*, it is "Golden Stamen." In the *Compendium*, it is "Shade-Completion." In the *Additional Records*, it is "Universal Fullness." Zhen says: According to Lu Dian’s *Piya*, the character for Chrysanthemum (*ju*) was originally written with the radical for "to crouch" or "to exhaust" (*ju*). The *Monthly Ordinances* states that in the ninth month, the chrysanthemum has yellow flowers. The business of flowering...</gloss>

...reaches its exhaustion and end at this point, hence it is called *Ju* <note>The Chinese name *Ju* (菊) sounds like the word for "exhaustion" (鞠), implying it is the last flower of the year</note>. The name of the flower is taken from its correspondence to the seasonal nodes. Cui Shi’s *Monthly Ordinances* says: "Female Virtue" and "Female Flower" are names for the chrysanthemum flower. "Wall-Healer" and "Essence of the Sun" are names for the root. Baopuzi <note>The Daoist philosopher Ge Hong</note> says: What the immortal formulas call "Essence of the Sun," "Rebirth," and "Universal Fullness" are all the same chrysanthemum, but the names for the root, stem, flower, and seed differ. Su Song says: The *Tang Tianbao Single-Remedy Illustrations* records that the White Chrysanthemum originally grew in the valleys and fields of Nanyang. People in Yingchuan call it the "Peak-Returning Chrysanthemum." In Ru’nan, it is called "Tea-Bitter Mugwort." In Shangdang, Jian’an, and Shunzheng prefectures, it is also named.

<margin>Collected Explanations</margin>
Kou Zongshi says: Chrysanthemums grow in the rivers, marshes, and fields of Yongzhou. Collect the roots in the 1st month, leaves in the 3rd, stems in the 5th, flowers in the 9th, and seeds in the 11th. All should be dried in the shade. Tao Hongjing says: There are two kinds of chrysanthemum. One has a purple stem, a fragrant aroma, and a sweet taste; its leaves can be made into soup—this is the True Chrysanthemum. The other has a large green stem, smells like mugwort or wormwood, and tastes too bitter to eat; it is called "Bitter Coix" <note>Wild chrysanthemum, *Chrysanthemum indicum*</note> and is not the true chrysanthemum. The leaves are very similar; distinguish them only by sweetness or bitterness. They are most abundant in Li County, Nanyang. Today they are found everywhere near roads; they are easily grown from seed. There is also a White Chrysanthemum; the leaves and stems are similar, but the flowers are harvested in the 5th month. The *Scriptures of the Immortals* consider it to have wonderful effects. Though many can be obtained, it should be taken regularly. Chen Cangqi says: White Chrysanthemums grow on level marshes; they flower in the 5th month and are purplish-white. Su Song says: They are found everywhere. Those from Nanyang, Jing, Ying, and Tan are best. In early spring, they spread across the ground with fine sprouts. They flourish in summer, flower in autumn, and seed in winter. However, there are many varieties. Only those with purple stems, fragrant aroma, and thick, soft leaves are considered tender and edible. Those with slightly large flowers and a very sweet taste are the "True" ones. Those with large green stems, thin leaves, and a pungent smell like mugwort, with small flowers and a bitter taste, are called "Bitter Coix" and are not true. In Nanyang, there are also two kinds: the White Chrysanthemum has leaves as large as mugwort, green stems/leaves, thin roots, white flowers, and yellow stamens. The Yellow Chrysanthemum has leaves like garland chrysanthemum, and both flowers and stamens are yellow. Today, those who prepare medicinal diets mostly use the white ones. There is another kind with small flowers and petals like small pearls underneath, called the "Pearl Chrysanthemum," which is said to be excellent for medicine. Kou Zongshi says: In recent times there are over twenty kinds. Only the one with single petals, small yellow flowers, deep green leaves that are small and thin, and which blooms in the 9th month, is the correct one. The White Chrysanthemum from Dengzhou with single petals is also used in medicine; others are not used in medical classics. Wang Rui says: Large, fragrant flowers are "Sweet Chrysanthemums"; small yellow ones are "Yellow Chrysanthemums"; small ones with a foul smell are "Wild Chrysanthemums." Li Shizhen says: There are hundreds of varieties of chrysanthemum. The perennial roots grow spontaneously. The stems, leaves, and flower colors differ by variety. Song dynasty authors Liu Meng, Fan Zhineng, and Shi Zhengzhi all wrote *Chrysanthemum Manuals*, yet even they could not include them all. The stems vary between upright, trailing, purple, red, green, or light green. The leaves vary in size, thickness, sharpness, or bluntness. The flowers vary between double-petaled, single-petaled, with centers, without centers, with seeds, or without seeds. Colors include yellow, white, red, purple, variegated, light, and dark. The taste varies between sweet, bitter, and pungent. There are also distinctions between True, Autumn, and Winter chrysanthemums. Generally, only the single-petaled, sweet-tasting ones are used in medicine. The "Sweet Chrysanthemum" of Dengzhou (yellow) and Shuzhou (white) recorded in the manuals are these. Sweet chrysanthemums grow in mountains and wilds, but now everyone cultivates them. The flowers are tiny and the quality is not very high. Those shaped like honeycombs have fine seeds inside and can be planted by pressing them into the soil. Tender leaves and flowers can all be dried and eaten. The White Chrysanthemum has slightly larger flowers and a less sweet taste; it is also harvested in the autumn months. Those without seeds are called "Male Chrysanthemums"; scattering their burnt ashes on the ground can kill a hundred types of insects. Lu Nongshi says this is from the *Rites of Zhou*.

<margin>Flower <gloss>Leaves, roots, stems, and seeds are the same.</gloss></margin>
<margin>Flavor and Nature</margin>
Sweet. Balanced. Non-toxic. <gloss>The *Additional Records* says: Sweet. Sun Simiao says: Sweet, bitter, cold. Used in medicine. Bitter ones are not used in medicine.</gloss> Kou Zongshi says: Bitter, sweet, cold. It can ascend or descend <note>Refers to the movement of Qi in the body</note>; it is the "slight Yang within Yin." Li Shizhen says: The *Classic* says the taste is sweet and bitter. The *Additional Records* says it is sweet. Various masters take the sweet one as the "True Chrysanthemum" and the bitter one as "Bitter Coix," using only the sweet for medicine. I respectfully note: Zhang Hua’s *Treatise on Curiosities* says there are two kinds; the sprouts and flowers look the same, but the taste differs slightly—the bitter is not fit for eating. Fan Zhineng’s *Manual Preface* says only the Sweet Chrysanthemum is edible and used in medicine and tonics. The other yellow and white flowers are bitter; though not for tonics, they can be used in medicine. For treating "Head-Wind" <note>Chronic headaches or migraines</note>, the white ones are especially good. According to these two accounts, there are naturally sweet and bitter types of chrysanthemums. For food, one must use the sweet; for medicine, all chrysanthemums can be used, provided one does not use the "Wild Chrysanthemum" (also called Bitter Coix). Lei Xiao’s *Herdsman’s Chat* says: True Chrysanthemum prolongs life; Wild Chrysanthemum causes purging...

It emphasizes the plant's seasonal significance and its various uses in both medicine and diet.</summary>

<margin>
Just as Yellow Essence <note>Polygonatum sibiricum</note> prolongs life, Gelsemium <note>Gelsemium elegans, a highly toxic plant</note> kills people; such is the nature of things.
</margin>

White Atractylodes, Wolfberry root, and Mulberry root bark serve as its assistants. <insert>Primary Indications:</insert> All types of "wind" disorders <note>In Traditional Chinese Medicine, "wind" refers to conditions involving dizziness, spasms, or sudden onset</note>, dizziness, swelling and pain, a sensation as if the eyes are falling out, excessive tearing, dead skin, aversion to wind, and damp-numbness. Long-term consumption benefits the blood and vital energy <term>Qi (vital life force)</term>, lightens the body, resists aging, and extends years of life. <gloss>Classic of Materia Medica</gloss> It treats recurring lower back pain.

Tao <note>Tao Hongjing, 456–536 AD</note> states: It removes irritability and heat in the chest, settles the intestines and stomach, benefits the five pulses, and regulates the four limbs. <gloss>Additional Records; Tao</gloss> It treats wind-heat in the head and eyes, dizziness that causes one to collapse, pain in the skull, and dissipates all "wandering wind" on the body. It benefits the blood vessels and has no contraindications. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss> It can be used to make pillows.

<margin>
It brightens the eyes. The leaves also brighten the eyes; both raw and cooked are edible. <gloss>Great Materia Medica</gloss> It nourishes the blood of the eyes and removes cataracts. <gloss>Zhu Zhenheng</gloss> It governs insufficiency of Liver Qi. <gloss>Wang Haogu</gloss>
</margin>

# White Chrysanthemum <gloss>Flavor: Bitter and Pungent; Nature: Balanced; Non-toxic</gloss>
Primary indications: Wind-dizziness; prevents hair from turning white. <gloss>Tao Hongjing</gloss> It dyes the beard and hair black. When combined with Giant Sesame <note>Black sesame</note>, Poria mushroom, and honey into pills, it removes wind-dizziness, reverses graying, prevents aging, and improves the complexion. <gloss>Chen Zangqi</gloss> Brightens [the eyes]. <gloss>Zhu Zhenheng</gloss> says: Yellow Chrysanthemum belongs to the Earth element.

It shares the Metal element with Water and the ability to supplement Yin-blood with Fire; thus, it nourishes the eyes. Shizhen <note>Li Shizhen, author of the Compendium of Materia Medica</note> says: The chrysanthemum sprouts in spring, flowers in autumn, and fruits in winter, fully receiving the essence of the four seasons. It endures frost and dew; its leaves wither but do not fall, and its flowers dry but do not drop. Its flavor combines sweet and bitter, and its nature is balanced and harmonious. Ancient people said it could remove wind-heat, benefit the liver, and supplement Yin. They perhaps did not realize it captures the essence of Metal and Water most abundantly, thus benefiting the two "Water" organs <note>The Kidneys and the Liver, in this cosmological context</note>. Supplementing Water controls Fire, and benefiting Metal balances Wood. When Wood is balanced, the "wind" subsides; when Fire descends, the heat is removed. Its use in treating head and eye wind-disorders is profound. The yellow variety enters the Yin division of Metal and Water; the white enters the Yang division of Metal and Water; the red acts on the blood division of women. All can be used as medicine. The "divine understanding" of this depends on the practitioner. Its sprouts are vegetables, its leaves can be steeped as tea, its flowers are edible, and its roots and seeds are medicine. Bagged, it makes a pillow; brewed, it makes wine. From root to tip, there is nothing without merit. It is fitting that former sages compared it to a "Gentleman" <note>Junzi, a person of noble character</note>. Shennong ranked it in the "Superior Class." Recluses gathered it in wine baskets, and poets ate its fallen petals. Fei Changfang said drinking chrysanthemum wine on the ninth day of the ninth month wards off misfortune. The *Biographies of the Immortals* claim Kang Fengzi and Zhu Ruzi both became immortals by consuming chrysanthemums. The *Records of Jingzhou* state that those in Huguang suffering from long-term wind-weakness lived long lives by drinking from the Chrysanthemum Pond. Such is the value of the chrysanthemum; how could it be ranked with common flowers? Zhong Hui’s *Praise of the Five Beauties of the Chrysanthemum* says: Its round flowers hang high, mirroring the celestial pole; its pure yellow is unmixed, the color of the Earth; planting early and flowering late shows the virtue of a gentleman; braving frost to bloom represents a chaste character; light in the cup, it is the food of immortals. ○ The *Miscellaneous Records of the Western Capital* say to gather chrysanthemum stems and leaves, mix them with millet to brew wine, and it is ready by the following September.

### Appendix of Formulas <gloss>Sixteen total</gloss> <insert>Six old, ten new</insert>

**Consumption of Sweet Chrysanthemum** <gloss>The *Jade Casket Formulas* state: Prince Qiao’s formula for reversing gray hair and increasing years. Gather sprouts on the first Yin day of the 3rd month, called "Jade Radiance." Gather leaves on the first Yin day of the 6th month, called "Face Completer." Gather flowers on the first Yin day of the 9th month, called "Golden Essence." Gather roots and stems on the first Yin day of the 12th month, called "Long Life." Dry these four parts in the shade for fifty days. Take equal parts, grind into powder. Take one spoonful with wine, or make pills with honey the size of a firmiana seed and take seven pills with wine, three times a day. In 100 days one becomes light and moist; in one year white hair turns black; in two years lost teeth regrow; in five years an 80-year-old man turns back into a child. Meng Shen says: Gather stems on the 5th day of the 5th month and flowers on the 9th day of the 9th month.</gloss> **Consumption of White Chrysanthemum** <gloss>The *Great Clarity Spiritual Treasure Formulas* cite the 9th day of the 9th month.</gloss> Two pounds of white chrysanthemum flowers, one pound of Poria. Grind and sift into powder. Take two spoonfuls with warm wine, three times a day. Or mix with pine resin that has been frozen and form pills the size of a chicken egg; take one per dose. **Tianbao Single Formula for treating dizziness in men and women; long-term use improves complexion and prevents aging.** Zangqi says: Baopuzi mentions Liu Sheng’s alchemy method using white chrysanthemum juice, lotus juice, "earth blood" juice, and ailanthus juice mixed with alum. **White Chrysanthemum Wine** <gloss>For chronic wind-headache, dizziness, dry falling hair, and phlegm in the chest. Symptoms include sudden dizziness and blurred vision as if about to collapse. First, cauterize both "Wind Pool" <note>Acupuncture point GB20</note> points 14 times each, then take this wine and powder for a permanent cure. Method: In late spring/early summer, collect soft white chrysanthemum sprouts, dry in shade, and grind. Take one square-inch spoonful with "ashless" wine on an empty stomach, twice a day, gradually increasing to three spoonfuls. If one does not drink wine, take with soup or porridge. In the 8th month of autumn, collect flowers and dry in the sun. Take three large pounds in a silk bag and soak in three large measures of wine. After seven days, drink three times a day, keeping a slight "wine energy" <note>a mild buzz</note> constantly for best effect.</gloss> Su Song’s *Illustrated Materia Medica*. **Wind-Heat Headache** <gloss>Chrysanthemum, Gypsum, and Chuanxiong, 3 mace each. Grind to powder. Take 1 mace with green tea.</gloss> *Simple Formulas*. **Knee-Wind Pain** <gloss>Pound chrysanthemums and aged mugwort; heat and apply. Long-term use removes the ailment.</gloss> Wu Min’s *Formulas for Supporting Longevity*. **Smallpox entering the eyes** <gloss>Causing cataracts...</gloss>

## Wild Chrysanthemum
<gloss>From the Supplement to the Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Bitter Yì <gloss>Shizhen says: "Yì" refers to the heart of a lotus seed. This plant's taste is bitter like it, hence the shared name.</gloss>
<gloss>Collection Notes</gloss> Su Song says: Bitter Yì grows by marshes. The stalks are like Aster, and the flowers like Chrysanthemum. The Chrysanthemum is sweet while the Yì is bitter; the saying "bitter as Yì" refers to this. Shizhen says: Bitter Yì is extremely common in fields and wilderness everywhere. It is no different from the Chrysanthemum, but the leaves are thinner, smaller, and more pointed. The flowers are small with many stamens, shaped like a honeycomb. The aroma and taste are bitter, pungent, and harsh.

**Root, Leaf, Stalk, and Flower** Flavor is bitter, pungent, and warm. Slightly toxic. <gloss>Zhenheng says: Consuming Wild Chrysanthemum greatly damages the Stomach Qi.</gloss>
**Primary Treatments** Regulates the center and stops diarrhea. Breaks up blood stasis; suitable for women with retained blood in the abdomen. <gloss>Zangqi</gloss> Treats carbuncles, swellings, "clove-sores" <note>deep-rooted boils</note>, scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note>, and polyps in the eye.
<gloss>Appended Formulas</gloss> <gloss>Four new ones</gloss>

**Carbuncles and Swellings**: For all unnamed toxic swellings, Master Sun’s Collection of Effective Formulas uses Wild Chrysanthemum (including the stalks), crushed and decocted in hot wine. Drink to induce sweating and apply the dregs topically for an immediate cure. <gloss>From Simple Formulas for Health</gloss> Use one handful each of Wild Chrysanthemum stalks/leaves and Cocklebur grass. Crush together and add one bowl of wine. Squeeze out the juice to drink and apply the dregs. Inducing sweat brings recovery. Alternatively, harvest Cocklebur leaves on the 6th day of the 6th month and Wild Chrysanthemum on the 9th day of the 9th month; grind to powder and take three <term>qian</term> with wine.

**Blistering Skin Sores**: Boil Wild Chrysanthemum roots in water and wash the area. <gloss>From Collected Medical Works</gloss> **Unbroken Scrofula**: Decoct Wild Chrysanthemum in wine and drink; apply the dregs to the site. It will dissipate naturally; if not, it will break and drain on its own. <gloss>From Proven Formulas of the Hall of Auspicious Bamboo</gloss>

## Anlü
<gloss>Pronounced Yan-Lü</gloss> <gloss>Top Grade of the Divine Farmer's Classic</gloss>
<gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Anlü <gloss>Shizhen says: "An" means a thatched hut, and "Lü" means a village gate. This herb has old stalks like mugwort or rushes that can be used to thatch huts and gates, hence the name. The Zhenyuan Formulas call it Anlü-mugwort. Historical notes say "Anlü" refers to the temporary quarters of an army on the march, so "Lü" (gate) should perhaps be "Lu" (hut).</gloss>
<gloss>Collection Notes</gloss> <gloss>From the Miscellaneous Records:</gloss> Anlü seeds grow in the valleys of Yongzhou, as well as in Shangdang and by roadsides. Harvest the fruit in the tenth month and dry in the shade.

Hongjing says: It looks like mugwort or wormwood. It is found everywhere near roads. It is occasionally used in Daoist alchemical texts. People plant it to ward off snakes. Su Song says: Today it is found in the Yangtze and Huai regions. In spring, it grows sprouts and leaves like mugwort, two to three feet high. Flowers in the seventh month, fruits in the eighth, and seeds are harvested in the ninth. Shizhen says: The leaves do not resemble mugwort but are like Chrysanthemum leaves, though thinner with many fine serrations. Both sides are green. It grows four to five feet high. The stalk is white like mugwort. The fruit contains tiny seeds and propagates very easily. Those who heat-dry it use it to graft Chrysanthemums.

### Seeds
**Aroma and Flavor** Bitter, slightly cold, non-toxic. <gloss>The Miscellaneous Records say: Slightly warm. In the past, Shennong, Leigong, Tongjun, and Qibo said it was bitter and slightly warm, non-toxic. Li Dangzhi said it was warm. Yaoyuan said it was pungent. Shizhen says: It has a descending nature. It is "minor Yang within Yin." It enters the Blood portion of the Foot Absolute Yin (Liver) Meridian. Cai says: Use Plum seeds as an assistant.</gloss>
**Primary Treatments** Stagnant blood in the five internal organs, water retention in the abdomen, bloating of the skin, lingering heat, and numbness/pain from Wind, Cold, or Dampness.

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 15

For various bodily pains; taken over a long period, it lightens the body, extends life, and prevents aging. <gloss>From the Classic of Materia Medica</gloss> <note>original: "Benjing"</note>.
It treats hardness below the ribs, cold and heat in the diaphragm, generalized numbness <term>Zhoubi: a condition of wandering pain or numbness throughout the body</term>, and menstrual blockage in women. It aids digestion, brightens the eyes, and is said to be eaten by the "divine immortals" of the Quda <note>A mythical or obscure beast; see the description below</note>. <gloss>From the Miscellaneous Records</gloss> <note>original: "Bielu"</note>.
It supplements the vital energy <term>Qi</term> and promotes courage. It treats impotence in men, abdominal bloating and fullness, weakness and heaviness in the waist and legs, vaginal discharge, and aching joints with irritability that prevents eating. <gloss>From Daming</gloss>.
Ground and mixed with wine, it treats lower back pain from strains and postpartum blood-related pain in women. <gloss>Li Shizhen’s Invention</gloss>.
<gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> The *Classic* says long-term use lightens the body and prevents aging. In ancient formulas, it was used in large prescriptions like the "Leopard Bone Pill" to treat fright and malevolent influences.
Sun Simiao’s *Supplement to the Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold* contains "General Leijun’s Solo Formula" for treating fractures and blood stasis; it uses the juice of boiled Anlü, or it can be taken as a powder. People today frequently use this method for traumatic injuries.
Whether drunk or applied topically, the effect is extremely rapid. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Wu Pu’s *Materia Medica* and the *Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians* both mention that the Quda beast eats Anlü to become an immortal; this likely refers to the plant's potent properties.
The Quda is a beast's name. It resembles a mule but is smaller. Its front legs are long and its hind legs are short. It cannot feed itself. When a mule or a donkey travels, the Quda must be carried on its back to move. Thus it is so named.

# Yarrow <gloss>Pronounced: Shi</gloss>
<gloss>Top Grade of the Classic</term>

<insert>Explanation of Names</insert> 
<gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> According to Ban Gu’s *White Tiger Hall Discussions*, Confucius said: "The word *Shi* (Yarrow) means *Qi* (Elderly/Venerable)." An elderly person has lived many years and experienced much; they are capable of knowing all things.
<gloss>Lu Dian’s *Piya* says:</gloss> Among plants, this one has the longest life, hence the character contains the radical for "elderly." The *Treatise on Curiosities* <note>original: "Bowu Zhi"</note> says that yarrow lives a thousand years, and at that age, it produces three hundred stalks. Because its root is ancient, it can know good and bad fortune <note>referring to its use in I Ching divination</note>.

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> 
<gloss>The Miscellaneous Records say:</gloss> Yarrow seeds grow in the valleys of Mount Shaoshi. Harvest the seeds in the eighth and ninth months.
<gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> This plant is found everywhere. Its stalks can be used as divination sticks. Master Tao mistakenly identified it as the fruit of the paper mulberry. Paper mulberry fruit tastes sweet, while this tastes bitter. I am now correcting this.
<gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Today it is found in Taizhou and Shangcai County, near the Temple of the White Tortoise. It grows like wormwood in clumps, five or six feet high. One root produces twenty stalks, or up to fifty in some cases. The stalks grow straight like silk threads, which distinguishes it from other wormwoods. After autumn, it flowers at the tips of the branches; the flowers are reddish-purple and shaped like chrysanthemums, followed by seeds.
<gloss>As recorded in the "Biographies of Tortoise and Divination" in the Records of the Grand Historian:</gloss> When yarrow is a thousand years old, it grows atop lotus leaves. A hundred stalks share a single root. In places where it grows, there are no tigers or wolves among the beasts, and no venomous stings among the insects. Xu Guang’s commentary notes: Liu Xiang said that a tortoise is spiritual at a thousand years, and yarrow at a hundred years produces a single root with a hundred stalks. Master Chu said: Where yarrow reaches a hundred stalks, a divine tortoise will surely guard it from below, and azure clouds will constantly cover it from above. Tradition says: When the world is at peace and the King’s Way is perfected, the yarrow stalks grow long and large, and the clumps reach a hundred stalks. Nowadays, finding eighty stalks or more, or stalks eight feet long, is very difficult. If one finds sixty stalks over six feet long, they are usable. The specimens currently sent from Caizhou do not match these descriptions; perhaps such divine objects are not commonly found.
<gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Yarrow belongs to the wormwood family but is a "divine herb." Thus the *Book of Changes* says: "The virtue of the yarrow is round and divine." The Emperor’s yarrow sticks were nine feet long, feudal lords' seven feet, high officials' five feet, and scholars' three feet. Zhang Hua’s *Treatise on Curiosities* says that if the tip is larger than the base, it is preferred. If yarrow is unavailable, wormwood or chasteberry stalks may be used as substitutes for divination.

## The Seed <gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss> Bitter and sour. Balanced. Non-toxic.

<insert>Primary Indications</insert> 
Supplements vital energy, fills the flesh and skin. Brightens the eyes and increases intelligence and wisdom, allowing for "foreknowledge." Long-term use prevents hunger, stops aging, and lightens the body. <gloss>From the Classic</gloss>

## The Leaf <gloss>Primary Indications</gloss> Masses and accumulations in the abdomen <term>Piji: chronic abdominal lumps</term>. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

<insert>Appended Formula</insert> <gloss>One new entry</gloss>

<margin>Abdominal masses</margin> 
Yarrow leaves, a single-clove garlic, pangolin scale powder, and table salt. Pound with good vinegar into a cake. Size it to the mass and apply. Leave for the duration of two incense sticks. The mass will dissolve into pus and blood and be expelled through the stool. <gloss>From Liu Songshi’s Formulas for Preserving Longevity</gloss>

# Mugwort (Ai) <gloss>Classified as a Medium-grade drug in the *Supplementary Records*</gloss>

### Explanation of Names
Moxibustion Grass <gloss>from the *Erya*</gloss>; Medical Grass <gloss>from the *Supplementary Records*</gloss>; Yellow Grass <gloss>from the *Piya*</gloss>; Mugwort-Artemisia <gloss>Shizhen states: Wang Anshi’s *Explanation of Characters* says that Mugwort (Ai 艾) can govern or cure (yi 乂) diseases, and its quality improves with age, hence the character contains the component for "to govern." Lu Dian’s *Piya* notes that the *Treatise on Curiosities* claims if you carve ice into a round shape and hold it toward the sun, placing mugwort where the shadow falls will catch fire <note>This describes a lens made of ice used to focus sunlight</note>. Thus, it is also called "Ice Terrace." Doctors use it to cauterize a hundred diseases, so it is called Moxibustion Grass. One burning is called a "unit" (zhuang), modeled after the strength of a robust man.</gloss>

### Collected Explanations
<gloss>The *Supplementary Records* state: Mugwort leaves grow in fields and wilderness. Collect them on the third day of the third lunar month and dry them in the sun. Tao Hongjing says: It is found everywhere; those from Fudao and Siming are superior. This variety is excellent for treating all diseases via moxibustion. When young, it spreads on the ground; the stalks resemble artemisia, and the leaf backs are white. Short seedlings are best. Collect on the third day of the third month or the fifth day of the fifth month. Dry in the sun; it must be aged before use. Li Shizhen states: The *Classic of Materia Medica* does not specify a local origin, only that it grows in fields. In the Song Dynasty, those from Tangyin and Fudao were best, and those from Siming were illustrated. Recently, the Tangyin variety is called "Northern Mugwort" and the Siming variety "Sea Mugwort." Since the Chenghua era (1465–1487), the variety from Qizhou has been considered superior and is called "Qi Mugwort." Legend says that while the heat of other mugwort cannot penetrate one's alcohol tolerance, a single moxibustion with Qi Mugwort penetrates directly through. This herb grows mostly on mountains and plains. In the second month, the perennial roots sprout seedlings in clumps. The stalks grow straight and white, four to five feet high. The leaves spread in four directions like artemisia, divided into five points, with smaller points at the tips. The surface is green, the back is white, downy, soft, and thick. In the seventh or eighth month, spikes emerge between the leaves like plantain spikes, with tiny flowers and abundant seeds. It withers after the frost. It is harvested on the fifth day of the fifth month, stalks and all. My late father, Yuechizi (whose taboo name was Yanwen), once wrote the *Treatise on Qi Mugwort* in one volume, praising it: "Produced on the sunny side of the mountains, harvested at the Dragon Boat Festival; its merit in curing disease and moxibustion is no small help." Zong Lin’s *Record of Seasonal Splendor of Jing-Chu* says: On the fifth day of the fifth month, before the cock crows, collect mugwort shaped like a human; these are very effective for moxibustion. On that day, mugwort is fashioned into human shapes and hung over doors to ward off toxic energy. The dried stalks can be soaked in sesame oil to lead fire for moxibustion, which moistens the sores until they heal. It can also be used as fuel or as a candle wick.</gloss>

---

### Preparation of the Leaves
<gloss>Kou Zongshi states: Grind dry mugwort leaves and remove the green residue to get the white fibers. Add a little powdered stone sulfur; this is called "Sulfur Mugwort," used by physicians. Add a little rice flour when grinding for internal medicine. Li Shizhen states: For all mugwort use, it must be aged. Process it until fine and soft; this is called "processed mugwort." Using fresh mugwort for fire will damage the muscles and meridians. Mencius said: "For a seven-year illness, seek three-year-old mugwort." Pick out dust and debris, select clean leaves, place in a stone mortar, and pound with a wooden pestle. Sieve out the dregs to get the white fibers, then pound again until soft as cotton. Dry it by heat before use so the fire is effective. For women’s pills or powders, use processed mugwort boiled with vinegar until dry, pound into cakes, dry by heat, and grind to powder. Using glutinous rice paste to make cakes or frying with wine is not ideal. Hong Mai’s *Chatter from the Rong Garden* says: Mugwort is hard to grind fine; if you put three or five pieces of Poria (Kuailing) into the mortar with it, it can be turned into fine powder instantly—a truly strange phenomenon.</gloss>

### Flavor and Nature
Bitter, slightly warm, non-toxic. <gloss>Su Gong says: Raw it is cold, processed it is hot. Li Yuansu says: Bitter and warm, the "Yang within Yin." Shizhen says: Bitter and pungent; raw it is warm, processed it is hot.</gloss>

### Primary Indications
Moxibustion for a hundred diseases. Can be made into a decoction to stop vomiting of blood, dysentery, and sores of the lower parts, and uterine bleeding in women.
Benefits the "Yin energy," grows muscle, dispels wind and cold, and helps people conceive. When making a decoction, do not let it be exposed to wind. <gloss>from *Supplementary Records*</gloss>
Drink the expressed juice to stop bleeding from injuries and kill intestinal worms. <gloss>Tao Hongjing</gloss>
Mainly for nosebleeds, bloody dysentery; used in water decoctions or pills/powders. <gloss>Su Gong</gloss>
For heavy uterine bleeding (red or white), hemorrhoids, and blood in the stool.
Apply to metal wounds (cuts), stops abdominal pain, stabilizes pregnancy. A decoction made with bitter wine (vinegar) treats ringworm very well. Drink the juice to treat all "cold energy" or "ghostly energy" in the heart and abdomen. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>
Treats vaginal discharge, stops cholera-like vomiting and cramps, and treats chills and fever after dysentery. <gloss>Daming</gloss>
Treats disorders of the Girdle Vessel where the abdomen feels full and the waist feels as if sitting in water. <gloss>Wang Haogu</gloss>
Warms the center, expels cold, and removes dampness. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

### Discoveries
<gloss>Meng Shen says: In spring, pick tender mugwort to eat as a vegetable, or mix with flour to make dumplings. Swallowing three to five the size of marbles followed by rice treats all "evil ghostly energy." Long-term use stops cold dysentery. Making dry cakes of tender mugwort and taking them with ginger decoction is excellent for diarrhea and postpartum blood in the stool. Su Song says: Recently, some people take mugwort alone, or mix it with steamed papaya for pills, or drink it as a soup on an empty stomach to supplement weakness. However, it can be toxic; if the "poison" breaks out, heat energy rushes upward, causing uncontrollable mania. During the Zhenghe era (1111–1117), there were cases of people losing their voices or bleeding; truly, it should not be taken recklessly. Zhu Zhenheng says: Infertility in women is often due to blood deficiency being unable to retain essence. Common doctors call the uterus "deficient and cold" and prescribe pungent, hot mugwort. They do not realize that mugwort’s nature is extremely hot. When used in moxibustion, the energy moves downward; when taken as medicine, the energy moves upward. The *Materia Medica* only says its nature is warm, not mentioning its heat...</gloss>

<keywords>Mugwort, Ai, Moxibustion, Qi Mugwort, Li Shizhen, Traditional Chinese Medicine, Gynecology, Cauterization</keywords>

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 15
<note>Original: Bencao Gangmu, Juan 15</note>

->**Mugwort Leaf**<-
<note>Original: Aiye (Artemisia argyi)</note>

People enjoy its warming properties and often take it for long periods; when toxicity eventually manifests, how can one blame the Mugwort? I have examined Su Song’s *Illustrated Classic* <note>Tujing Bencao, an 11th-century pharmaceutical work</note> and feel moved by his insights on processed mugwort. Shizhen <note>The author, Li Shizhen</note> states: Raw mugwort leaf is slightly bitter and very pungent; when processed <note>aged or charred</note>, it becomes slightly pungent and very bitter. Its nature is warming, and when processed, it is hot. It is pure *Yang* <note>the active, heating principle in Chinese cosmology</note>. It can capture the true fire of the Sun and restore the original *Yang* energy when it is nearly exhausted. When ingested, it travels through the three *Yin* meridians <note>Spleen, Liver, and Kidney channels</note> to expel all cold and dampness, transforming a harsh, killing atmosphere into a harmonious warmth. When used for moxibustion <note>burning the herb on or near the skin</note>, it penetrates all meridians to treat a hundred types of pathogenic diseases, restoring those with chronic, stubborn ailments to health. Its merit is indeed great! Su Gong claimed it is cold in nature, while Su Song claimed it is hot. One observed its ability to stop bleeding <note>often a cooling function</note>, while the other observed its hot energy rising to the defensive levels of the body. To simply say its nature is "cold and toxic" is an error. This is because they did not realize that blood follows the *Qi* (vital energy); when *Qi* moves, blood disperses. The "heat" occurs because long-term consumption causes the energy to rise to the defensive level. Medicine is for treating illness; once the illness is cured, one should stop. If a woman suffering from deficiency-cold, chronic chills, damp-stagnation, or vaginal discharge uses Mugwort alongside Angelica and Aconite to treat her illness, how could that be wrong? Yet, those who recklessly seek to conceive children take Mugwort without ceasing, supplementing it with other pungent and hot herbs. This creates a long-term imbalance of nature, leading to "fire-agitation" <note>overheating of the body's systems</note>. Whose fault is this? Why blame the herb? Furthermore, Mugwort pills are profoundly effective for treating various pains in the heart and abdomen and regulating women's disorders. "Gelatin and Mugwort Decoction" is particularly miraculous for treating deficiency-dysentery and bleeding during pregnancy or after childbirth. For elderly people with weak energy in the "Cinnabar Field" <note>Dantian, the lower abdomen energy center</note> who fear cold in the navel and abdomen, placing processed mugwort in a cloth bag to cover the area is wonderfully effective beyond words. It is also suitable to insert into socks for cold-damp beriberi.

# Appendix of Formulas
<margin>24 Old, 27 New</margin>

## Cold Damage and Seasonal Qi
<note>Infectious febrile diseases</note>
For epidemic headaches, high fever, and a surging pulse: Use three *sheng* <note>approx. 3 liters</note> of dried mugwort leaves, chopped and wrapped in silk <gloss>One version in *Leiyao*</gloss>. For high fever with red spots turning black and blood in the urine: Use a piece of mugwort the size of a chicken egg <insert>from *Shanghan Leiyao*</insert>, boil in one *dou* of water until one *sheng* remains. Drink at once to induce sweating. From *Zhouhou Fang* <note>Handbook of Formulas for Emergencies</note>. For cold damage during pregnancy: Boil three *sheng* of wine until two and a half *sheng* remain; divide into two doses.

## Stroke with Locked Jaw
Take a five-inch piece [of mugwort], insert one end into the ear, seal the area with dough so no air escapes, and perform moxibustion on the other end for seven "streaks" <note>units of burning herb</note>. If the right side is affected, treat the left; if the left is affected, treat the right. This formula is found in *Shengjin Fang*. 
Also, moxibustion on the *Chengjiang* point <note>on the chin</note> <gloss>five streaks per point</gloss>.

## Stroke with Pulling Pain
For numbness or paralysis: Take about one *hu* <note>a large volume</note> of dried mugwort, rub into clumps, and place in a ceramic steamer. Plug all holes except one; place the painful area against that hole and burn the mugwort to steam/smoke it.

## Shrunken Tongue and Locked Jaw
Crush raw mugwort to extract the juice. For throat swelling and pain: *Yifang Dacheng* suggests crushing tender mugwort for juice and swallowing slowly <note>*Jingyan Fang* suggests using a handful of green mugwort including stems and leaves</note>.

## Epilepsy and Wind Disorders
One will know when the time comes. See the formulas appended later. Soaking the herb is also acceptable. From *Shengji Lu*: Crush a handful to extract three *he* <note>approx. 300ml</note> of juice, add a little salt, and drink for an immediate cure. Chewing dry mugwort also works. This formula was passed down by Master Li Chen.

## Ghost-Strike and Evil Influence
<note>Sudden, unexplained collapse or sharp pain</note>
Apply moxibustion with processed mugwort to the area between the scrotum and the anus <note>the perineum</note>, with the number of streaks matching the patient's age. From *Doumen Fang*. For sudden stabbing pain in the chest, ribs, or abdomen that cannot be pressed, or sudden vomiting/nasal bleeding.

## Infant Umbilical Wind
<note>Tetanus neonatorum</note>
Burn mugwort leaves to ash and fill the navel; secure with a cloth. Or perform moxibustion over a slice of garlic; once the smell of mugwort is detected in the child's mouth, they are cured. From *Jianbian Fang*.

## Fox-Bewitchment and Intestinal Worms
<note>A condition involving emotional distress and physical erosion</note>
The patient's teeth lose color, the tongue turns white, or they are lethargic and indifferent to pain or itching. If they have dysentery, treat the lower body immediately. If the physician ignores this and only treats the upper body, the worms will eat the anus and rot the internal organs, leading to death. Burn mugwort in a tube to smoke the lower parts, letting the smoke enter; adding a little realgar is even better. From *Zhouhou Fang*.

## Chronic Head-Wind Pain
Rub fresh mugwort into pills and sniff them frequently.

## Facial Sores
For itching with yellow discharge: Boil two *liang* <note>approx. 75g</note> of mugwort in one *sheng* of vinegar in a sand pot to get a juice. Apply to thin paper and stick to the sores two or three times a day. From *Yuyao Yuan Fang*.

## Evil Qi in Heart and Abdomen
Drink the juice of crushed mugwort leaves. <insert>from *Yaoxing Lun*</insert>

## Cold Pain of Spleen and Stomach
Boil white mugwort powder in water and take two *qian* <note>approx. 7.5g</note>. <insert>from *Weisheng Yi*</insert>

## Heart Pain from Demonic Worms
Stabbing pain with vomiting of clear water: Boil one *sheng* of white processed mugwort in three *sheng* of water until one remains. Drink to vomit out the worms. Or take raw mugwort juice at dawn after eating a piece of fragrant dried meat; the worms will be expelled. See *Zhouhou Fang*.

## Vomiting Clear Water
Boil dried new mugwort into a soup and sip it. <insert>from *Guaizheng Qifang*</insert>

## Cholera with Vomiting and Diarrhea
If it does not stop: Boil one handful of mugwort in three *sheng* of water until one remains; drink at once. <insert>from *Waitai Miyao*</insert>

## Chronic Dysentery
Mugwort leaves (5 *liang*), aged tangerine peel (2 *liang*), and prepared ginger (3 *liang*). Grind to powder and make pills the size of a parasol tree seed using a paste of vinegar and rice. Alternatively, boil equal parts mugwort and tangerine peel into a soup. Take 20-30 pills with salt water. From *Shengji Zonglu*.

## Chronic White Dysentery in Elderly or Young
Boil mugwort and take on an empty stomach with rice water. This has miraculous effects and has been tested many times. See *Yonglei Fang*.

## Blood in Stool
One handful of aged mugwort and one piece of ginger; decoct in water and drink hot. <insert>from *Sheng Bian*</insert>. Or decoct mugwort and ginger into a thick juice and mix with three egg whites. From *Shengji Lu*.

## Sudden Unstoppable Diarrhea
Take three *he* of the decoction. <insert>from *Qianjin Fang*</insert>

## "Wild Chicken" Disease (Hemorrhoids)
First wash with a decoction of pagoda tree and willow, then apply seven streaks of moxibustion. This was effective for Official Wang, who took several doses while traveling to Xichuan. It is said that for large hemorrhoids like cucumbers protruding from the rectum with burning heat, this is the only remedy when one collapses in pain.

### Bleeding During Pregnancy
Zhang Zhongjing <note>The "Sage of Medicine," c. 150–219 CE</note> states: For women suffering from uterine leakage, persistent bleeding after a miscarriage, or bleeding during pregnancy, the Ass-hide Glue and Mugwort Decoction <note>Jiao Ai Tang</note> is the primary treatment. Use two ounces of Ass-hide Glue <note>Ejiao</note>, three ounces of Mugwort leaf, two ounces each of Sichuan Lovage <note>Chuanxiong</note> and Licorice, and three ounces each of Angelica <note>Danggui</note> and Rehmannia. Add four ounces of Peony. Boil in five pints of water and five pints of clear wine until three pints remain. Add the glue to melt it completely. Take one pint with warm wine per dose, three times a day. <margin>From: Essentials from the Golden Cabinet (Jinkui Yaolue)</margin>
<margin>For fetal movement during pregnancy, waist pain, "rushing at the heart," persistent bleeding, or cases where the fetus has died in the womb: use moxibustion. For fetal movement with severe nausea: boil one chicken-egg-sized piece of mugwort in four pints of strong vinegar and four pints of wine until two pints remain; divide into two doses. <note>From: Emergency Formulas to Keep up One’s Sleeve (Zhouhou Fang)</note></margin>

### Postpartum Abdominal Pain
For those on the verge of death due to pain caused by catching a cold after childbirth: take two pounds of aged Qizhou Mugwort <note>Artemisia argyi from Qizhou, the highest quality variety</note>, dry it by a fire, and crush it. Spread it upon a mattress and cover it with a layer of silk. Use a warming iron over it. Once the scent of the mugwort emerges from the patient's mouth, the "cold energy" will depart along with the mugwort's essence, and the abdominal pain will naturally cease. This merit should not be viewed lightly. <margin>From: Yang Cheng’s Proven Formulas</margin>
<margin>From: Secret Records of Mother and Child. ### Persistent Nosebleeds

### Persistent Night Sweats
Take two mace of processed mugwort, three mace of White Spirit-of-Poria <note>Fushen, a fungus grown on pine roots</note>, and three smoked plums. Boil in one cup of water until eighty percent remains. Take warm before bed. <margin>From: Formulas of the Perfected Immortal Tongmiao</margin>

### Red, Swollen, and Painful Eyes
Burn mugwort to create smoke and cover it with a basin. Once the smoke is exhausted, scrape the soot from the basin and mix it with warm water to wash the eyes; it heals immediately. Adding Coptis <note>Huanglian</note> makes it even more effective. <margin>From: Doumen Formulas</margin>

### Facial Discoloration and Tattoos
Take three pints each of mugwort ash and mulberry ash. Leach them with water to obtain a lye, repeating three times. Tie a five-colored cloth in the middle as before. Apply a small amount to the area; the skin will naturally soften and peel away. This is very effective. <margin>From: Arcane Essentials from the Imperial Library (Waitai Miyao)</margin>

### Women's Facial Sores
Known as "Powder-Flower Sores." Use five mace of lead powder <note>Dingfen</note> mixed with rapeseed oil on a clay plate. Use one or two clumps of mugwort to smoke it. When the smoke is gone, place the plate on the ground overnight. Remove it the next morning and apply the mixture. It leaves no scars and is excellent for regenerating flesh. <margin>From: Tan Yeweng’s Tested Formulas</margin>

### Facial Warts
Perform three sessions of moxibustion with mugwort fire and they will be removed immediately. <margin>From: Formulas of Divine Assistance (Shenghui Fang)</margin>

### Fungal Infection of the Palms
Take four or five ounces of high-quality fresh mugwort. Boil in four or five pans of water for six or seven vigorous boils. Pour into a wide-mouthed jar and tie two layers of hemp cloth over the top. Place the palm over the jar to steam it. If it cools, reheat it. The effect is miraculous. <margin>From: Lu’s Hall of Accumulated Virtue Formulas</margin>

### Boils and Toxic Swelling
Take one ounce of processed Qizhou mugwort, three mace of Wood-turtle seeds <note>Mubiezi/Momordica</note>, two mace of Realgar, and one mace of Sulfur. Grind into a powder and knead it into the mugwort. Divide into four strips. Place each strip between "Yin and Yang" tiles <note>curved roof tiles</note> to smoke the affected area, then follow with an oral dose of Sage-Communicating Powder <note>Tongsheng San</note>. <margin>Medical Formulas Summary</margin>

Take one ounce of mugwort leaf and boil in one pint of water until four-tenths remain. Administer orally. <margin>From: Formulas for Emergencies (Beiji Fang)</margin>

### Boils and Toxic Swelling
Take a large load of mugwort and wormwood, burn to ash, and place in a bamboo tube. Leach with water to obtain the juice. Mix two portions with lime until it reaches the consistency of paste. First, prick the sore with a needle until it is painful, then apply the medicine three times. The root of the boil will be pulled out naturally. Han Guang of Yushan used this to treat people with miraculous success. In the early Zhenguan era <note>627–649 CE</note>, Governor Xu of Quzhou sought out this formula and successfully treated over thirty people. <margin>From: Master Sun’s Thousand Golden Proven Formulas</margin>

### Early-Stage Hemorrhoids
For those not yet formed and for various heat-swells: apply wet paper to the area. The first spot to dry is the "head" of the swelling. Apply moxibustion there. Regardless of the number of cones, if it is painful, continue until it is not; if it is not painful, continue until it is. The toxin will naturally disperse. If it does not disperse, it will at least be prevented from attacking the internal organs. This is truly a divine formula. <margin>From: Li Jiang’s Ministry of War Collection</margin>

### Persistent Ulcers
If the mouth of the sore is cold and stagnant, wash it with a decoction of Northern Mugwort. <margin>For a bone stuck in the throat: take raw mugwort and wormwood, extract the juice, and boil one gallon of the liquid mixed with wine until four pints remain. ### Accidental Swallowing of Copper or Iron
Take a handful of mugwort and wormwood. Boil in five pints of water until one pint remains. Drink it all at once to induce passage. <margin>From: Lord Qian’s Casket Formulas</margin>

### Insects in the Ear
Performing several sessions of moxibustion is very effective. <margin>From: Collection of Simplified Formulas</margin>

### Wind-Toothache
Melt a little wax and spread it on paper. Layer mugwort on top and roll it with a bamboo shoot sheath into a tube. Light it and use the smoke to fumigate the nostrils and cheeks according to the side of the pain. Fill the mouth with the smoke and then exhale. This stops the pain and eliminates the swelling. Si Jiqian suffered from this for over a month; he tried this once and was cured. <margin>From: Formulas for Universal Relief (Puji Fang)</margin>

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 15

## Seeds <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Bitter, pungent, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Primary Indications</gloss> Brightens the eyes and treats all forms of "ghost qi" <note>Ancient term for malignant environmental pathogens or sudden, unexplained illnesses</note>. Zhen <note>Zhen Quan, a Tang-era physician</note> notes: It strengthens the *yang* energy, assists the "water treasury" <note>The Kidneys</note>, benefits the waist and knees, and warms the uterus. It is as effective as the Great Mallow. 

### Tao Hongjing <note>Famous alchemist and physician, 456–536 CE</note> states: 
Take equal parts Mugwort seeds and dried ginger. Grind them into a fine powder and mix with honey to form pills the size of a parasol tree seed. On an empty stomach, take thirty to ninety pills per dose. Swallow with three to five spoonfuls of rice to help the medicine down. Take twice daily. This treats a hundred types of "evil qi" <note>Pathogenic factors</note>; it causes those spiritual disturbances to flee immediately.

### <gloss>Appendix</gloss> Summer Platform <note>Xiatai</note>
The *Supplementary Records* <note>Mingyi Bielu</note> lists this as a name with no known use, stating: "The flavor is sweet. It treats a hundred diseases and clears 'exhausted qi'." Hongjing says: "For a medicine to be described as this miraculous, yet no longer be recognized or used, is truly a pity." Shizhen states: "The name 'Mugwort Person' <note>Airem</note> is very similar to this. 

### Water Platform <note>Shuitai</note>
This is another name for Summer Platform Mugwort. It is also said that it 'can bring back exhausted qi from a hundred diseases.' Since it is primarily for 'stagnant and exhausted qi,' I suspect these are the same substance listed twice. Therefore, I have appended it here after Mugwort."

## Thousand-Year Mugwort <gloss>Category</gloss> <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss>
Shizhen states: Thousand-Year Mugwort comes from the Small Wudang Mountains <note>Taihe Mountains</note>. Its stem is short, reaching only about a foot in height. Its root is like that of fleabane. Its leaves are over an inch long, lacking a sharp point; the face of the leaf is blue-green and the back is white. In autumn, it blooms with small yellow flowers resembling wild chrysanthemums. Its fruit is like blue pearls or cinnabar beads. Harvest the leaves during the "Three Volt" days <note>The hottest days of mid-summer</note> and dry them in the sun. The leaves do not look like common mugwort, but they possess its fragrance. When rubbed, they crumble immediately; they do not form the lint-like wool <note>moxa</note> that common mugwort leaves do. Taoist practitioners often present this as a local tribute.

## Leaves <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Bitter, slightly warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Primary Indications</gloss> Treats various ailments involving "deficiency-cold" in men and "blood and qi" disorders in women. To be taken as a water decoction. —Shizhen.

## Capillary Wormwood <note>Artemisia capillaris; Yinchenhao</note> <gloss>Top Grade of the Classic</gloss> <gloss>Explanations of Names</gloss>
Su Gong <note>Tang dynasty official and physician</note> states: Although this belongs to the wormwood family, it does not die during the winter. Because it grows "due to" <note>Yin</note> the "old" <note>Chen</note> stalks of the previous year, it is named *Yinchen*. The word for "wormwood" (*Hao*) was added later.

<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss>
The *Supplementary Records* say: Capillary Wormwood grows on Mount Tai and on the high banks of hills and mounds. Harvest in the fifth month and at the beginning of autumn, then dry in the shade. 
Hongjing says: Today it is found everywhere. It resembles common fleabane, but the leaves are tight and fine. After autumn, the stems wither, but it survives the winter and sprouts again in spring. It is valued for its fine sprouts, which distinguish it from other wormwoods.
Shizhen states: According to Zhang Yi’s *Guangya* and Wu Pu’s *Materia Medica*, it is written as "Dust-Due" <note>Yinchen using the character for 'dust'</note>, though the meaning of that is unknown.
Tao Hongjing states: The leaves look like Blue Wormwood <note>Qinghao</note> but are white on the back.
Tianming states: Capillary Wormwood comes from the southern ridges of Hezhou. One name for it is "Stone Capillary Wormwood."
Su Song <note>1020–1101 CE</note> states: It grows everywhere nearby, but none is as good as that from Mount Tai. In early spring, the sprouts grow three to five inches high, looking like fleabane with tight, fine leaves. It has no flowers or fruit. Harvest the stems and leaves in the fifth or seventh month and dry in the shade. Today it is called "Mountain Capillary Wormwood." 
In Jiangning Prefecture, there is a type with large leaves and thick, yellowish-white roots; it flowers and fruits in summer. In Jiezhou, there is a type called "Wormwood" which looks exactly like Blue Wormwood but has a white back. The *Materia Medica* classics all consider these to be the medicinal Yinchen. 
Modern doctors in the South use several kinds of "Mountain Capillary Wormwood." Master Jiao explains: The variety used in the capital <note>Kaifeng</note> and the North has leaves like Mugwort, fine, with white backs. Its scent is like Mugwort and the flavor is bitter; when dried, it turns black. The variety used south of the Yangtze has stems and leaves looking like domestic Yinchen but grows much taller (three to four feet). Its scent is extremely fragrant, and its flavor is sweet and pungent; locals call it "Dragon-Brain Mint." The variety used in Yan is actually "Stone Fragrant Elsholtzia" <note>Shixiangru</note>; its leaves are very fine, yellow in color, and the flavor is pungent and highly aromatic. It is warm in nature. If mistakenly used as a spleen-clearing medicine, it causes great agitation in the patient.
According to the *Materia Medica*, there is only "Capillary Wormwood" (Yinchenhao), not "Mountain Capillary Wormwood." The notes say it "resembles fleabane but is tight and fine," which describes the variety currently used in the capital and the North. Generally, worldly formulas use Mountain Capillary Wormwood as a sweat-inducing medicine for the muscles, but it is rarely effective. However, the Southern variety is excellent for treating heat and brain-pain in "Cold Damage" <note>febrile diseases</note>. Many doctors argue that domestic Yinchen can also release the muscles and clear "stagnation in the chest," but it is rarely used in formulas. It can be ground into a drink. The medicinal properties are detailed in popular formulas and its efficacy is well-attested.

Su Song states: When using it, one must use the leaves. Master Jiao says those with eight corners are best. Dry in the shade, remove the roots, and chop finely. Do not let it come into contact with fire.
Shizhen states: In the past, people often wrote poems about Yinchen as a vegetable. It is called "Mountain Capillary Wormwood" to distinguish it from the domestic variety. Hong Shunyu’s "Rhapsody on the Old Garden" mentions "threads of green Yinchen soaked in vinegar," referring to this. Even today, people in the Huai and Yang regions harvest wild Yinchen sprouts on the second day of the second month, mixing them with flour to make "Yinchen Pancakes" for food. Later authors relied on local varieties, leading to confusion. Now, the Mountain variety sprouts in the second month; its leaves are like Mugwort or light-colored Blue Wormwood, white on the back, finely divided and flat. In the ninth month, it blooms with tiny yellow flowers and bears seeds the size of Mugwort seeds. Both flowers and fruit resemble those of *Anlü* <note>Artemisia keiskeana</note>. Some varieties lack flowers and fruit entirely.

## Stems and Leaves <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic. <gloss>Primary Indications</gloss> Wind-dampness, cold and heat, "evil qi" knots, and jaundice. Long-term use [promotes health]. 
Wu Pu states: Shennong, Qibo, and Lei Gong say it is non-toxic. The Yellow Emperor says it is balanced and non-toxic. 
Zhen Quan states: Bitter and pungent; slightly toxic. 
Tianming states: Stone Yinchen is bitter, cooling, and non-toxic. It can "subdue" sal ammoniac. 
Zhang Yuansu <note>c. 1118–1231 CE</note> states: It is bitter and sweet, a "slight yang within yin" medicine. It enters the Foot Taiyang <note>Bladder</note> Meridian.

# Sweet Wormwood (Qinghao)
<gloss>Lower Class of the Divine Husbandman’s Classic</gloss>

### Explanation of Names
Fragrant Wormwood <gloss>Divine Husbandman’s Classic</gloss>, *Zhang-fan-shu-shu* <gloss>Botanical Names of Shu</gloss>, *Fang-li-shu*, Scented Wormwood <gloss>Explication of Meanings. Baosheng states: This is called "Pig Wormwood" in the regions east of the Yangtze because its scent resembles a pig. Others call it Green Wormwood. The Erya <note>ancient dictionary</note> calls it "Qi." Sun Yan notes: In the Jing and Chu regions, wormwood is called "Qi." Guo Pu notes: Today, people call the fragrant wormwood that is roasted and eaten "Qi." Shizhen states: According to Baosheng, it is the tallest of the wormwoods. According to the Erya, only this variety is granted the simple name "Hao" <note>Wormwood</note>.</gloss>

### Collected Explanations
<gloss>The Supplementary Records state: Sweet Wormwood grows in the rivers and marshes of Huayin. Hongjing states: It is found everywhere. Today, people take Sweet Wormwood and mix it with fragrant vegetables to eat. Baosheng states: The leaves are extremely fine and edible. By summer, it grows four to five feet tall. After autumn, it opens small, pale yellow flowers. Below the flowers, seeds form, about the size of millet. In the eighth or ninth month, the clusters ripen. The roots then dry out. The seeds and leaves are both used in medicine. If dried for a long time, it makes an excellent fragrant drink. Zongshi states: Sweet Wormwood is the first to sprout in spring. People pick it as a vegetable. The roots are red and also fragrant. Shen Kuo’s *Dream Pool Essays* says: There are two kinds, one yellow and one green. The Materia Medica calls it "Green" Wormwood (Qinghao) to distinguish it. Between Yin and Sui in Shaanxi, among the wormwood thickets, there are occasionally one or two plants that are a strikingly deep green. Locals call this "Fragrant Wormwood." The stems and leaves look like common wormwood, but while common wormwood is pale green, this is a deep green, like the color of pine or cypress. In late autumn, while other wormwoods turn yellow, this one alone stays green and its scent is fragrant. I suspect the ancients used the deep green variety as the superior one. Otherwise, why would they specify "Green" when all wormwoods are green? Shizhen states: Sweet Wormwood is everywhere. The seedlings emerge in the second month. The stem is as thick as a finger, fat and soft. Both stem and leaves are deep green. The leaves slightly resemble Capillary Wormwood but are green on both the front and back. The root is white. The fruit is small. <gloss>Processing: When using it, the middle of the plant is best. From the knees to the waist. Use the seeds but not the leaves, or the roots but not the stems. In the seventh or eighth month, it opens tiny flowers which are quite fragrant. The fruit is the size of a hemp seed and contains tiny seeds.</gloss> Method: If all parts are used together, it may cause chronic illness. To prepare the leaves, use the urine of a seven-year-old child; soak them for seven days and nights, then remove and sun-dry.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the botanical entries in the Materia Medica (Bencao Gangmu), moving from Capillary Wormwood (Yinchen) to the detailed properties and medical applications of Sweet Wormwood (Artemisia annua), specifically its leaves, roots, and seeds.</meta>

### Leaves, Roots, and Seeds
<gloss>Flavor and Scent: Bitter, Cold, Non-toxic. <note>Shizhen says: It subdues sulfur <note>original: "fu liuhuang," an alchemical property believed to stabilize or alter sulfur during processing</note>.</note></gloss>
<margin>Main Indications</margin> Scabies and itching, crusted sores, and malignant ulcers. It kills lice and treats jaundice caused by heat or miasmic vapors. It opens the stomach <note>improves appetite</note> and brightens the eyes.
<gloss>Classic of Materia Medica</gloss>: Treats <term>searching</term> <note>a type of parasitic or abdominal mass</note>, malaria, chronic "dwelling" illnesses <note>original: "zhu," referring to stubborn, lingering infections</note>, blood-and-qi disorders in women, abdominal fullness, and chronic dysentery caused by cold or heat. Use the seeds in autumn and winter, and the sprouts in spring and summer; in both cases, pound them for their juice to drink. They may also be sun-dried and ground into powder to be taken with wine.
<gloss>Zangqi</gloss>: Supplements the "middle" <note>the digestive system</note> and benefits the <term>qi</term> <note>vital energy</note>. It lightens the body, treats exhaustion, maintains a youthful complexion, and makes hair grow long and black to prevent aging. It also removes heat, helps the hair, and dispels wind and toxins. For heart pain caused by heat: pound the yellowed leaves to extract juice for drinking and apply externally as a poultice.
<gloss>Da Ming</gloss>: Treats the alternating chills and fever of malaria.
<gloss>Shizhen</gloss>: Pounded fresh and applied to metal wounds <note>cuts from blades</note>, it stops bleeding and relieves pain. It is highly effective.
<gloss>Su Song</gloss>: For inflammation that spreads, urinary blockages, and internal or external abscesses: decoct the juice with lime.
<note>Wang Yaojian: Su Song stated that Sweet Wormwood is the premier herb for treating "bone heat" <note>chronic low-grade fever associated with consumption</note> and exhaustion. Ancient formulas often used it on its own.</note>
<gloss>Shizhen says</gloss>: Sweet Wormwood is the earliest to receive the <term>qi</term> of the <term>Spring Wood</term> <note>the elemental energy of growth and the liver/gallbladder system</note>. Therefore, the conditions it treats are all related to the "Minor Yang" and "Terminal Yin" blood systems. According to the *Comprehensive Collection of Monthly Ordinances*: On the first "Geng" day of the mid-summer heat, if one picks Sweet Wormwood and hangs it inside the gateway or courtyard, it can ward off evil spirits. Drying it in the shade and grinding it to a powder to take two <term>qian</term> <note>approx. 7.5 grams</note> on the Winter Solstice and New Year’s Day is also beneficial. Observing this, we see the herb’s power to treat "ghost-dwelling" diseases <note>likely tuberculosis or contagious wasting diseases</note> and "hidden corpses" <note>lingering toxins</note> is well-founded.
<margin>Attached Formulas</margin><gloss>4 old, 13 new</gloss>

**Wasting and Thinness:** Finely chop Sweet Wormwood. Take three <term>sheng</term> <note>approx. 600ml</note> of water and five <term>sheng</term> of child's urine. Decoct together until only one and a half <term>sheng</term> remains. Strain, place in a vessel, and simmer into a thick paste. Form into pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take 20 pills with warm wine on an empty stomach and before bed. <gloss>From Doumen's Formulas</gloss>

**Consumption with Chills and Fever:** For limb fatigue and pain in men or women. In the ninth month, when the seeds have formed, pick the plant, remove the stems, and soak in child's urine for three days. Sun-dry and grind into powder. For each dose, use two <term>qian</term> with one smoked plum, decocted into a soup. <gloss>From Lingyuan Formulas</gloss>

**Bone-steaming and Ghost-qi:** <note>Refers to chronic consumptive heat/tuberculosis</note>. Take five large <term>dou</term> <note>approx. 50 liters</note> of clarified child's urine. Take five <term>dou</term> of Sweet Wormwood (the kind with seeds picked in the 8th or 9th month is best), chop finely, and combine in a large cauldron. Boil over a fierce fire until reduced to three large <term>dou</term>. Strain the residue until perfectly clean. Simmer again over a low fire until reduced to two <term>dou</term>. Add one pig’s gall. Simmer together until reduced to one and a half <term>dou</term>. Remove from heat and let cool. Store in a ceramic vessel. When ready to use, take three <term>liang</term> <note>approx. 110g</note> of licorice, roast it, and grind to powder. Mix with the prepared paste and pound. Form into pills. Take 20 pills on an empty stomach with rice water. Gradually increase to 30 pills. <gloss>From Cui Yuanliang's Highly Effective Sea Formulas</gloss>

**Bone-steaming with Irritability and Heat:** One handful of Sweet Wormwood. One pig’s gall. Forty apricot kernels (peeled and blanched). One large cup of child's urine. Decoct until half remains and take warm on an empty stomach. <gloss>From Shiben's Reliable Formulas</gloss>

**Excessive Sweating from Deficiency:** For irritability and dry mouth. Use one pound of Sweet Wormwood, extract the juice, and simmer into a paste. Add one <term>liang</term> each of powdered Ginseng and Ophiopogon. Simmer until it can be formed into pills the size of parasol tree seeds. Take 20 pills after meals with rice water. This is called "Sweet Wormwood Decoction." <gloss>From General Records of Holy Benefaction</gloss>

**Malaria with Chills and Fever:** <gloss>From the Handbook of Formulas for Emergencies</gloss>: Use one handful of Sweet Wormwood and two <term>sheng</term> of water; pound for juice and drink. <gloss>From Cunren Formulas</gloss>: Pick on the 5th day of the 5th month before dawn. Dry in the shade. Use four <term>liang</term> with one <term>liang</term> of cinnamon heart. Grind to powder. Take two <term>qian</term> with wine before the onset of symptoms. <gloss>From Tested Formulas</gloss>: Pick leaves on the Dragon Boat Festival, dry in the shade, and mix with cinnamon heart. Grind to powder. Take one <term>qian</term> per dose. If chills come first, use hot wine; if heat comes first, use cold wine. Take at the fifth watch <note>dawn</note> on the day of onset. Strictly avoid "trigger foods" <note>foods thought to worsen illness, like shellfish or heavy meats</note>.

**Severe Warm Malaria:** Heat without chills. Use two <term>liang</term> of Sweet Wormwood soaked in child's urine and roasted. Add half a <term>liang</term> of red lead <note>original: "huangdan," lead tetroxide, used cautiously in ancient medicine</note>. Grind to powder. Take two <term>qian</term> stirred into plain hot water. <gloss>From Cunren Formulas</gloss>

**Red and White Dysentery:** On the 5th day of the 5th month, pick equal parts Sweet Wormwood and Mugwort. Pound together with fermented black beans to make cakes. Dry in the sun. **Nosebleed:** Pound Sweet Wormwood for juice and drink it. Also, plug the nostrils with the herb. <gloss>From Western Formulas</gloss>

**Hemorrhoids with Blood in Stool:** Use the leaves without the stems, or the stems without the leaves. Grind to powder. Before a bowel movement, take with cold water; after a bowel movement, take with a mixture of water and wine. <gloss>From Yonglei's Collected Formulas</gloss>

**Metal Wounds and Falls:** <gloss>From the Handbook of Formulas for Emergencies</gloss>: Pound Sweet Wormwood and apply as a seal. It heals once the bleeding stops. **Nasal Polyps:** Sweet Wormwood ash and lime in equal parts. Boil with water into a paste and apply to the spot. <gloss>From General Records of Holy Benefaction</gloss>

# Yellow Flower Wormwood
<gloss>From the *Compendium* <note>referring to the *Bencao Gangmu*</note></gloss>
**Other Names** Stinking Wormwood. **Collection of Explanations** Da Ming says: Stinking Wormwood is also called Straw Wormwood. Shizhen says: Fragrant Wormwood and Stinking Wormwood are both generally called Straw Wormwood. This variety is similar to Sweet Wormwood, but its color is green tinged with pale yellow. Its scent is pungent and stinking, making it inedible. It is the kind people gather to use as a toxic starter for fermenting yellow rice wine.

**Properties** Bitter, Slightly Cold, Non-toxic. **Main Indications** Pediatric wind-cold and seasonal heat.

# White Wormwood
<gloss>From the *Classic of Materia Medica*</gloss>
**Other Names** Bushy Wormwood <gloss>from the *Erya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note></gloss>, Youhu <gloss>from the *Erya*</gloss>, Fluffy Wormwood <gloss>from *Dietary Therapy*</gloss> <gloss>pronounced "shang"</gloss>
Shizhen says: There are two types of White Wormwood: the water variety and the land variety. The *Erya* generally calls them "Fan" <note>original: "繁", meaning bushy or luxuriant</note> because they propagate so easily. "Fan" or "Bushy Wormwood" refers to the land-grown Mugwort; it is pungent and smoky, not pleasant. "Fan" or "Youhu" refers to the water-grown Fragrant Wormwood; it is pungent, aromatic, and pleasant. "Fan" or "Zhi Chou" becomes "Hao" <note>wormwood</note> in the autumn. This refers to both the water and land varieties generally. It means they each have specific names in the spring, but as they grow old in the autumn, they are all simply called "Hao." White "Fan" is called "Fan."

**Collection of Explanations** The *Supplementary Records* <note>original: "Bielu"</note> say: White Wormwood grows in the rivers and marshes of Zhongshan. Gather it in the second month. Hongjing says: There are many types of wormwood, but one rarely hears the common people call anything "White Wormwood." Since pharmacists do not use it, they mostly ignore it. The general name for "old wormwood" reflects the atmosphere of autumn—the sound of whistling, desolate wind.
**Collection of Explanatory Notes** [Pharmacists] no longer recognize it.
Gong says: The *Erya* states that "Fan" is indeed White Wormwood. It is found everywhere. The leaves look much like fine Mugwort, covered in white hairs, rough to the touch, and coarser than Sweet Wormwood. From its first growth until autumn, it is whiter than all other wormwoods. Zongshi says: Fluffy Wormwood can be eaten as a vegetable. Therefore, the *Poetry Commentaries* say: "Offer 'Fan' in the sacrificial bowls," referring to its use as food. Lu Ji’s poem says: All types of Mugwort that are white are called "Fan." Today, White Wormwood sprouts before other grasses; it is fragrant and delicious to eat.
<gloss>It is suitable both steamed or boiled</gloss>
Song says: The ancients used this herb as food. Today, people only eat Reed Wormwood and no longer eat this. Some suspect White Wormwood is actually Reed Wormwood, but Meng Shen’s *Dietary Therapy* lists Reed Wormwood as a separate entry with a different description, so they are clearly two different things. This shows how food preferences have changed from ancient to modern times. Also, in Jiezhou today, White Wormwood is used as a substrate for fungi; its sprouts and leaves look similar, but for use in medicine, I fear it cannot be used this way.

Shizhen says: White Wormwood is everywhere. There are two kinds: water and land. When the *Classic* mentions its use, it likely refers to the water-grown kind. This is why it says it "grows in rivers and marshes" rather than "mountain valleys or flat lands." The two kinds look similar, but the land variety is pungent and smoky, lacking the fragrance and flavor of the water variety. The *Book of Songs* says: "The deer cry out 'yo-yo,' eating the 'ping' in the fields." This "ping" <note>original: "苹"</note> is the land-grown Bushy Wormwood, commonly called Mugwort. The deer eats nine types of detoxifying herbs, and White Wormwood is one of them. The *Book of Songs* also says: "Gathering 'fan' by the marshes and islands." The *Zuo Zhuan* <note>An ancient narrative history</note> says: "Plants like 'ping,' 'fan,' and 'yunzao' <note>water weeds</note> can be offered to the ghosts and gods and served to princes." These all refer to the water-grown White Wormwood. Thus, there is no doubt that the White Wormwood of the *Materia Medica* is the Fragrant Wormwood <note>original: "Qihao"</note>. Zheng Qiao’s *General Treatises* claimed "ping" was Reed Wormwood, but he was wrong. The deer is a mountain animal, but "Qi" is a water wormwood. Lu Ji’s *Poetry Commentary* claimed "ping" was Ox-tail Wormwood, but he was also wrong. Ox-tail Wormwood is green, not white, with fine leaves that grow straight up like a cow's tail. Fragrant Wormwood grows in marshes; it sprouts in the second month with leaves like tender Mugwort but more finely divided. The tops are green and the undersides white. The stems can be red or white, and the roots are white and brittle. Both the roots and stems can be eaten raw or cooked, pickled, or sun-dried. This is likely Reed Wormwood. Jing Cha’s *Great Summons* <note>An ancient poem</note> says: "The sour-dressed 'Qi' wormwood of Wu is neither too thick nor too thin." This means the people of Wu were skilled at seasoning pickled fish, and their wormwood pickles were perfectly balanced and sweet. This clearly refers to the water-grown variety.

<margin>
The *Materia Medica* notes that pickling it in vinegar is very beneficial to people. Drinking the pounded juice treats "Heat Jaundice" and stops "evil heart pain" <note>severe chest pain</note>. Sun-dry it and grind into powder; take one spoonful with rice water on an empty stomach to treat sudden watery dysentery in the summer. Burning it to ash, soaking it, and decocting the liquid treats urinary dribbling disorders.
<gloss>Meng Shen</gloss>
<gloss>Meng Shen</gloss>
Benefits the intestines and stomach; counteracts Pufferfish poisoning.
</margin>

# Sprouts and Roots
**Properties** Sweet, Neutral, Non-toxic. <gloss>Simiao says: Pungent, Neutral, Non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: It may trigger sores and scabies.</gloss>
**Main Indications** It treats sudden pathogenic "evils," wind-related illnesses, and damp-numbness <note>joint pain and stiffness</note>. It supplements the "middle" <note>the digestive system</note>, benefits the <term>qi</term>, and makes hair grow long, black, and thick. It treats "heart suspension" <note>anxiety or a fluttering sensation in the chest</note>, low appetite, and constant hunger. Long-term use lightens the body <note>suggests health and agility</note>, sharpens the hearing and vision, and prevents aging. <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss>

# Horned Wormwood <gloss>From the Tang Materia Medica</gloss>

### Explanations of Names
<gloss>Su Gong says: Horned Wormwood looks like White Wormwood. Its flowers resemble the Fringed Pink <note>Qu Mai</note>, appearing a lovely reddish-crimson. The seeds look like Cowherb seeds <note>Wangbuliuheng</note>, black in color, and they form "horns" <note>seed pods</note>. Gathered in the seventh and eighth months. Su Song says: It looks like Cnidium <note>Shechuang</note> and Sweet Wormwood. The seeds are in horns like those of a turnip, black and fine, ripening in autumn. It is found everywhere. Zongshi says: The stems and leaves are like Sweet Wormwood, and it bears pale reddish-purple flowers about three or four-tenths of an inch in diameter. After the flowers fade, it forms horns about two inches long that are slightly curved. Lei Xiao says: When using this, do not use "Red Wormwood" or "Evil Wormwood," as these two types look very similar to Horned Wormwood but are toxic and have shorter horns. Once gathered, chop it finely on a block of scholar-tree wood <note>Huai</note> before use.</gloss>

### Seeds
#### Properties
<gloss>Bitter, slightly cold, non-toxic.</gloss>
#### Main Indications
Treats "ghostly qi" <note>a traditional category for sudden, unexplained, or infectious illnesses attributed to malevolent influences</note>. Grind into powder and take with wine. From the *Sichuan Edition* <note>Shuben</note>.

### Properties
<gloss>Bitter and acrid, slightly toxic.</gloss>

### Main Indications
Treats dry or wet scabies and various malignant sores containing parasites. From the *Materia Medica*. It is also exceptionally effective for treating rotting gums and dental disease. According to Zongshi and Lei Xiao.

### Attached Prescriptions <gloss>One old, one new</gloss>
