<gloss>Mostly due to "gan" <note>a childhood wasting disease or chronic inflammation</note>.</gloss> <insert>Burn Horned Wormwood into ash</insert> and apply to the area at night. Strictly avoid greasy foods and granulated sugar.

->Non-healing Mouth Sores<-
<gloss>Whether the sores reach the chest or are fresh, regardless of whether the patient is an adult or a child: apply Horned Wormwood ash.</gloss> If fluid builds up, spit it out. Effective after one night. From the *Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold*.

->Scrofula<-
<note>Swelling of the lymph nodes, typically in the neck.</note> From the *Collection of Simple Formulas*.

Sprinkle the area with Horned Wormwood ash. From the *Collection of Simple Formulas*.

->Dry Skin Ailments<-
From the *Secret Essentials from the Outer Terrace*.

# Fragrant Wormwood <gloss>From the Supplement</gloss>

### Explanations of Names
Righteous Wormwood <gloss>from the *Erya* dictionary</gloss>; Zhi <gloss>also from the *Erya*</gloss>; Mother-hugging Wormwood <gloss>from the records</gloss>.
<gloss>Master Lei Xiao says: The word "Xun" <note>fumigation/fragrance</note> refers to its lofty nature; it is also called "Yi" <note>righteous</note>.</gloss>

### Collection of Explanations
<gloss>Shizhen says: Fragrant Wormwood grows on high ridges and resembles the Small Thistle. Its perennial roots sprout before all other grasses. The commentary says it is the "Righteous Wormwood." It grows in marshy areas that are gradually rising. Its leaves resemble Slanted Wormwood <note>Xiehao</note> but are finer. In the second month, the stems grow. The leaves are edible and can also be steamed for their beautiful fragrance. It is similar to Vine Wormwood <note>Manhao</note>, but the taste is slightly numbing and not as sweet or fragrant as the vine variety.</gloss>

### Properties
<gloss>Bitter, warm, non-toxic.</gloss>

### Main Indications
Breaks up stagnant blood and lowers <term>qi</term> <note>vital energy</note>. Boil and eat it. According to Zangqi.

# Lousewort <gloss>Middle Class of the Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>

### Explanations of Names
Horse-New Wormwood <gloss>from the Tang version</gloss>; Horse-Fragrance Wormwood <gloss>from the Classic</gloss>; Jinggang; Shiye; Lan-shi-cao <gloss>also from the Miscellaneous Records</gloss>; Tiger Hemp.
<gloss>Shizhen says: The smell of this wormwood is like horse droppings <note>original: "Mashi"</note>, hence the name "Ma-xian" <note>Horse-First</note>, which is a corruption of the characters for horse droppings. "Ma-xin" <note>Horse-New</note> is another variation of this name.</gloss>

### Collection of Explanations
<gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* say: Lousewort and Lan-shi-cao both grow in the rivers and marshes of Nanyang. Ma Cheng says: The leaves are as large as Shepherd's Purse. The flowers are red and white. Gathered in the second and eighth months. Dry the stems and leaves in the shade. In the eighth and ninth months, the seeds ripen. It is commonly called "Tiger Hemp" and is found everywhere. When the sprouts first emerge, they are short and small; the seeds ripen in mid-summer. The seedlings of these plants are extremely similar when they first grow. Yu Xi says: According to the *Erya*, "Wei" is the "Male Wormwood" <note>Muhao</note>. The note says this refers to the wormwood that produces no seeds. The *Book of Odes* also mentions this. Lu Ji says: The Male Wormwood begins growing in the second month and flowers in the seventh month. Its flowers resemble those of Sesame <note>Huma</note> and are purple. In the eighth month, it produces pods like small beans that are sharp and long. It is also called Horse-New Wormwood. Song says: Guo Pu claimed the Male variety has no seeds, but Lu Ji claimed it does. These two accounts differ slightly; we should follow the one that identifies it as having seeds. Shizhen says: In the *Miscellaneous Records*, Male Wormwood and Lousewort were originally the same entry. What Lu Ji described as having seeds is actually Lousewort, but he mistakenly cited the seedless Male Wormwood to explain it. Details on the Male Wormwood can be found in its own section of this Materia Medica.</gloss>

### Properties
<gloss>Bitter, level, non-toxic. The *Miscellaneous Records* say: Bitter and slightly cold.</gloss>

### Main Indications
Treats chills and fevers, "ghost infusion" <note>chronic or wasting disease attributed to spiritual pathogens</note>, stroke, damp-numbness, and female vaginal discharge or infertility. From the *Classic*. It also treats five types of abdominal masses <note>jia</note>, breaks up urinary stones, clears stagnation in the bladder, and aids urination, especially when urine is red. From the *Records*.

# Motherwort <gloss>Divine Husbandman's Classic, Superior Class <note>Herbs in the "Superior Class" were considered non-toxic and capable of promoting longevity when taken over long periods.</note></gloss>

<gloss>Explanations of Names</gloss>
**Mother’s Benefit** <gloss>Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>
**Tui** <gloss>Er Ya Dictionary</gloss>
**Zhenwei** <gloss>Miscellaneous Records</gloss>
**Tui** <gloss>In the Er Ya, the pronunciation is "Tui"</gloss>
**Wild Gastrodia** <gloss>Collected Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>
**Pig’s Hemp** <gloss>Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>
**Fire Ash** <gloss>Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>
**Stinking Depression** <gloss>Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>
**Bitter Low Herb** <gloss>Illustrated Materia Medica</gloss>
**Summer-Wither Herb** <gloss>Supplement to the Illustrated Materia Medica</gloss>
**Local Zhihan** <gloss>Compendium of Materia Medica</gloss>

<gloss>Shizhen says: This herb and its seeds are highly effective for women's health, brightening the eyes, and nourishing the essence <note>referring to "Jing," a fundamental life force in Chinese medicine</note>; hence the name "Mother’s Benefit." Its stem is square and resembles hemp, which is why it is called "Wild Gastrodia." It is colloquially known as "Pig’s Hemp" because pigs enjoy eating it. It withers after the Summer Solstice, giving it the name "Summer-Wither." The *Formulas of Recent Efficacy* call it "Local Zhihan." Lin Yi noted: "Zhihan" <note>likely a phonetic transcription of a Persian or Central Asian medicinal extract, possibly "Zat-al-han"</note> comes from the Western regions; it is made by boiling the blood of warm-blooded animals with various medicines and is used to treat puncture wounds and fractures. Since Motherwort can be made into a syrup to treat similar injuries, it was named "Local Zhihan." Yusuo says: The commentaries for the *Er Ya* and *Huainanzi* state this is the modern Motherwort. It is also called "Tui-chou." Lu Ji says that "Tui" is Motherwort. When the philosopher Zengzi saw this plant, he was often moved to think of his mother.</gloss>

<gloss>Collected Notes</gloss> <gloss>The Divine Husbandman's Classic says: Motherwort grows near seashores and marshes. Harvest in the fifth month. Tao Hongjing says: It is found everywhere now. The leaves resemble those of perilla, and the seeds are small, elongated, and have three ridges. It is rarely used in common prescriptions. Su Song says: It is extremely common today in the countryside and fields. Guo Pu’s commentary on the Er Ya says: The leaves resemble hemp, the stem is square, and the flowers are white.</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the detailed botanical description and medicinal applications of Motherwort (Chongwei), specifically focusing on distinguishing its varieties, its nomenclature in ancient texts like the Er Ya, and the specific therapeutic uses of its seeds and stems.</meta>

Flowers grow between the nodes, and every node produces flowers. The seeds resemble those of the cockscomb, but are black. The stem is square-edged. It is harvested in the fifth month. Others say the seeds are harvested in the ninth month. Medical formulas rarely use the seeds. Su Xu said: When Motherwort first sprouts in early spring, it can be soaked and washed to remove the bitter juice, then boiled and eaten as a vegetable. It does not wither in the winter <note>This "evergreen" claim is later disputed by Li Shizhen</note>.

Shizhen says: Motherwort is very abundant in damp areas near water. In early spring, the sprouts emerge like tender wormwood. By the start of summer, it grows three to four feet tall. The stem is square, similar to a yellow hemp stem. Its leaves resemble mugwort leaves, but the undersides are green; one stalk has three leaves, and the leaves have pointed lobes about an inch long. Spikes of flowers grow at every node, encircling the stem in clusters. In the fourth and fifth months, small red-purple flowers bloom within the spikes; some are slightly white. Each calyx contains four tiny seeds, about the size of wormwood seeds, triangular and brown. Pharmacopoeias often mistakenly sell these as "Giant Sesame" <note>original: "Jushengzi," usually referring to black sesame or flax</note>. The plant has a pungent odor when growing and withers after the Summer Solstice. Its roots are white. Su Song’s *Illustrated Materia Medica* says the leaves resemble perilla and the seeds are black like cockscomb seeds, harvested in the ninth month. Kou Zongshi’s *Augmented Materia Medica* says it does not wither in the cold. These are all incorrect traditions. There are two varieties of this herb—white-flowered and purple-flowered—but the stems, leaves, seeds, and spikes are identical. However, the white variety enters the **Qi** division <term>Qi: the body's vital energy and functional activity</term>, while the red variety enters the **Blood** division; they should be used accordingly. According to the *Manual of Palace Affairs*, the white-flowered version is Motherwort (Yimucao), while the purple-flowered one is Wild Gastrodia. Yet, the notes for the "Spirit-Returning Pill" say the purple-flowered one is Motherwort and the white one is not. Chen Cangqi’s *Materia Medica* says Motherwort grows in fields and is called "Stinking Vine," while Gastrodia grows in level marshes and resembles Vervain, with purple flowers at every node and seeds like Green Box seeds. Sun Simiao’s *Essential Formulas* says Gastrodia has a stem like hemp and its summer flowers resemble Rat-tail Sage. These authors treat Motherwort and Gastrodia as two different things, failing to realize they are one species with two varieties. It is common for plants to have both red and white flowers, such as the Tree Peony, Herbaceous Peony, and Chrysanthemum. Furthermore, Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Er Ya* dictionary states that *Tui* (pronounced "Tui") is Motherwort, also called Mother’s Benefit, with leaves like perilla and white flowers at the nodes. It also mentions *Xu* (pronounced "Tui"), which has square stems and sharp leaves with spikes; between the spikes are pale blue flowers that can be made into a drink, called "Ox Water-Chestnut" in the Jiangdong region. Based on this, the names *Tui* and *Xu* originally referred to the same plant, distinguished only by flower color. There is no doubt they are one thing. The Song Dynasty revisions of the *Materia Medica* mistakenly identified "Gastrodia Herb" as the medicinal "Gastrodia Root" <note>Tianma, *Gastrodia elata*, a parasitic orchid</note>, which is a grave error. Chen Cangqi’s *Materia Medica* also lists a plant called "Gathered Overgrowth" that grows in shady spots south of the Yangtze, resembling Motherwort with square stems and white flowers, used for postpartum blood disorders. This is simply the white-flowered variety of Motherwort; thus, its efficacy in treating blood diseases is the same.

### **The Seeds**

Postpartum abdominal bloating <margin>Daming</margin>. For health cultivation, it supplements the center, benefits the **Qi**, clears the blood vessels, fills the marrow, stops thirst, and moistens the lungs <margin>Wu Rui</margin>. Treats "Wind" <note>sudden illnesses like tremors or strokes</note>, clears heat, regulates Qi, activates blood, nourishes the Liver and benefits the Heart, calms the soul, and regulates women’s menses, including flooding, spotting, and issues before or after childbirth. Long-term use makes a woman fertile.

<gloss>Insight: Zhenheng says: Motherwort seeds activate blood and circulate Qi; they have the effect of supplementing **Yin** <term>Yin: the cooling, moistening, and nourishing aspects of the body</term>, hence the name "Mother’s Benefit." In prenatal and postpartum care, the primary concerns are Blood and Qi. Before birth there should be no stagnation; after birth there should be no deficiency. This herb treats irregular menses and all prenatal/postpartum blood and Qi disorders; it is a magnificent remedy. Yet doctors rarely know to use it. Li Dongyuan stated that those with dilated pupils should not use Motherwort seeds because their pungent warmth scatters energy and fans "Fire." While Angelica is also pungent and warm, it is also bitter and sweet and can harmonize the blood, so it is not forbidden. My humble opinion is that the eyes see when they receive blood. Motherwort moves blood very quickly. Dilated pupils result from blood deficiency; therefore, it is forbidden not because it "fans fire," but because it might further deplete the blood. However, if the eyes are diseased due to blood stagnation, then it is appropriate; thus, it is said to "brighten the eyes."</gloss>

<gloss>Ideally take with warm wine.</gloss> This is a divine formula for pain. In the third month, harvest Motherwort (also called "The Burden" or "Summer-Withered Herb"). **Blood in the Urine** Pound Motherwort to extract one liter of juice and drink it; recovery will be immediate. <gloss>From: Arcane Essentials from the Imperial Library</gloss>

**Red and White Dysentery** <note>A term for bloody or mucus-filled stools, often associated with bacterial or amoebic infections</note> For severe cases, use Motherwort dried in the sun, aged vinegar, and plums charred while retaining their properties. **Childhood Malnutrition and Dysentery** For children near death, use the tender leaves of Motherwort boiled with rice to make a porridge. Eat until cured; this is highly effective.

**Hemorrhoids with Bleeding** Drink the juice of pounded Motherwort leaves. <gloss>From: Mirror of Dietary Medicine</gloss>

**All Ulcers and Fistulas** For women’s mastitis <note>inflammation of the breast</note>, childhood head sores, and oozing, yellow, inflammatory heat-sores, scabies, or leprosy: use the extracted juice for drinking or topical application. <gloss>See: Greatly Beneficial and Divinely Effective Formulas</gloss> Cut five liters of "Heavenly Hemp" <note>another name for Motherwort here</note>, boil in fifteen liters of water until ten liters remain. **Acute and Chronic Boils** The *Taiping Holy Prescriptions* suggest pounding Motherwort and sealing the wound with it, while also drinking five ounces of the expressed juice to dissolve the boil. The *Great Compendium of Medical Formulas* suggests harvesting Motherwort with its flowers in the fourth lunar month. Burn it to a char (retaining its properties). First, use a small sharp knife to make a cross-cut at the root of the boil to draw blood. Wipe it dry, then use a straw core to dip into the medicine and twist it deep into the wound. After a while, purple blood will emerge. Twist and squeeze until the blood is clean, then apply more medicine until red blood appears, at which point you stop. Repeat this three to five times a day and night. For severe cases, the root will rot away in two days; for mild cases, one day. If the root of the sore swells up, it is working.

**Ruptured Boils** Applying pounded Motherwort is very effective. Grind the herb into a powder, mix with water, and apply it to the breast overnight; the root of the boil will emerge and can be picked out with a needle. After removal, continue applying the medicine to promote skin growth and easy healing. Avoid wind, cold, sexual activity, alcohol, meat, and all "toxic" foods. <gloss>From: Taiping Holy Prescriptions</gloss>

**Throat Blockage and Swelling** Pound Motherwort and mix with a bowl of freshly drawn well water. Squeeze out the thick juice and drink it all at once. <gloss>From: Taiping Holy Prescriptions</gloss>

**Malignant Sores and Boils** The method is to harvest the roots and shoots on the fifth day of the fifth lunar month. Do not use fire to dry them; let them dry in the shade. Pound and sift the herb, mix with yeast water to form balls the size of a hen's egg, and sun-dry again. Construct a small kiln with openings on four sides. Place fire above and below, and the medicine in the center. Use a strong fire for the duration of a meal, then remove the heavy fire but keep a small fire to maintain the heat for one full day and night. Store the result in a porcelain vessel. Grind, sift, and regrind for three days. Use it as a washing powder <note>ancient soap substitute</note> daily.

**Ear Discharge** <gloss>Drip the juice of Motherwort stems and leaves into the ear</gloss>. The *Essentials of Management* states that on the fifth day of the fifth month, harvest the "Heavenly Hemp" plant with roots and flowers. Sun-dry and burn it to heal the condition. In the third month, use the roots. <gloss>From: Simple and Easy Formulas for Health</gloss> Mix the ash with the natural juice of Pokeweed root and sour vinegar to make a cake. Calcine it over a charcoal fire. Store for half a year before use. Added to facial medicines, it is very good at moisturizing the skin. <gloss>From: Su Song</gloss>

**Items: Empress Wu’s Facial Whitening Method** <note>Referring to the Tang Dynasty Empress Wu Zetian</note> On the fifth day of the fifth month, harvest the whole Motherwort plant (roots and shoots). Do not let it touch fire while drying; dry it in the sun. Pound and sift, mixing with yeast water into balls the size of a hen’s egg. Sun-dry again. Build a kiln with four openings; place fire above and below with the medicine in the center. After a strong fire for one meal’s time, reduce to a small "nurturing" fire for one full day and night. Take it out and store in porcelain. Grind and sift for three days. Use as a washing powder daily. For every ten ounces, add one ounce of talcum and one drachm of rouge. <gloss>From: Formula of the Realized Man Sun Simiao</gloss>

**Horse Bites** If a horse bite becomes a sore, finely cut "Low Grass" <note>likely a synonym for Motherwort</note>, stir-fry it with vinegar, and apply.

**Bathing Method for Children** Boil five ounces of Motherwort in water to bathe the child. The flavor is acrid. This prevents the growth of sores and scabies. <gloss>From: Simple Formulas for the Masses</gloss>

# Small-flowered Motherwort
<gloss>Pronounced: Jìn</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> This herb grows in the south. The plant resembles Motherwort with a square stem and opposite nodes. Shizhen says: This is simply the white-flowered variety of Motherwort, which the *Erya* <note>ancient dictionary</note> calls *Tui*. The purple-flowered one is what the *Erya* calls *Shiyi*. Both names refer to the same thing. One plant, two varieties; therefore, this entry also treats blood diseases and has the same efficacy as Motherwort. Guo Pu specifically identified the white-flowered one as Motherwort, while others argued it was not. Upon careful examination, the tender shoots are edible, which is why it is called a "vegetable" (Cai). Kou Zongshi's remark that the tender shoots of Motherwort can be boiled and eaten confirms this.

> **Properties of the Shoots** Acrid, non-toxic. Primary uses: Breaking up stagnant blood and treating postpartum abdominal pain. Drink the boiled juice. <gloss>From: Zangqi</gloss>

# Deer-ear Herb
<gloss>Pronounced: Méi</gloss>
<gloss>Explanations of Names</gloss> Mi <gloss>From: Materia Medica</gloss>. People in Wu and Shu call it "Wu Wind Herb," also known as "Deer-ear Herb." It is said that when deer are ill, they seek this herb.
<gloss>Commentary</gloss> Li Daoyuan's *Commentary on the Water Classic* states: Mount Xishan in Weixing has much "Mi-xian" grass. It does not bend in the wind, but shakes when there is no wind. The *Additional Records* say: It grows in the marshes of Hanzhong. Harvest the stems and leaves in the seventh month and dry in the shade. "Wind" should be understood as "windless movement." Zangqi says: Another name is "Heartless Grass." It is rarely used in formulas. It grows in clumps and resembles Motherwort or Pasque-flower. Its leaves are hairy and it has a stem. There are large and small varieties.

It also distinguishes between the purple and white-flowered varieties of the plant and introduces Deer-ear herb.</summary>

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of Motherwort (Yimucao) by detailing its seeds (Chongweizi) and related plants like Heartless Grass (Wuxincao), then transitions into a major entry on Self-heal (Xiakucao). Catchword on border: Herbal Section.</meta>

The varieties of this plant are known among the people of Chu as the "Big Wu-feng Grass" for the larger variety and "Small Wu-feng Grass" for the smaller. Jiesheng notes: the leaves resemble Motherwort, growing in clusters with a hairy texture. Its flowers are yellow and its roots are a reddish-black.

# Motherwort Seeds
<note>Latin: Leonuri Semen; Chinese: Chongweizi</note>

### Energy and Taste: Bitter, Acrid, and Non-toxic
The *Supplementary Records* <gloss>Bielu</gloss> state they are slightly cold. Zhicai notes: they work well when combined with Ash Bark <term>Qinpi</term>.

They are used to dispel wind-dampness, treat joint pain throughout the body, and manage seizures or epilepsy. They address the vomiting of bitter fluids, palpitations, and "thieving winds" <note>a term for sudden, harmful environmental influences</note>, as well as abscesses and swellings. The *Divine Husbandman's Classic* <gloss>Benjing</gloss> notes their use for scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes, usually in the neck</note> and for expelling excess fluids in damp-numbness. Long-term consumption "lightens the body" <note>a Daoist term for achieving health and longevity</note> and brightens the eyes.

# Consumption Causes Infertility
<note>Warning: Prolonged or improper use was believed to prevent pregnancy</note>

To prevent pregnancy, Zangqi suggests boiling the seeds in water. They are also used to wash and purify malignant sores. The *Essential Meaning of Surgery* quotes the Yellow Emperor: "If a patient has a fever, feels lethargic, sweats as if bathing, and fears the wind with shortness of breath, what is this illness?" Qibo replied: "This is called 'Wine-Wind' <note>illness caused by drinking alcohol then being exposed to wind</note>. Treat it with Water Plantain <term>Zexie</term>, Atractylodes <term>Zhu</term>, and Deer’s Mane <term>Mixian</term>."

### Appended Formulas
**For chronic, malignant sores (three years old or more):** Use the root of "Heartless Grass," Wolfsbane <term>Langdu</term>, and sparrow droppings <term>Baidingxiang</term> (five drachms each), and one drachm of resin. Grind into a powder and apply to the area.
**For childhood lockjaw caused by wind:** Use half an ounce of "Heartless Grass" and two and a half drachms of prepared White Aconite <term>Baifuzi</term>. Grind into a powder; for each dose, take one drachm mixed with mint wine. <gloss>From: Sage-like Benefit Records</gloss>

# Heartless Grass
<note>Chinese: Wuxincao</note>

The *Song Illustrated Classic Supplement* states it grows in Qinzhou, Shangzhou, and various counties of Fengxiang. It flowers in the third month, fruits in the fifth, and the roots and sprouts are harvested in the sixth or seventh months. This herb’s medicinal properties and appearance are very similar to Motherwort; it is suspected they may be the same plant. I record this here for future investigation. Note that "Mouse-ear Grass" is also called "Heartless," but it is a different species.

---

# Self-heal
<note>Latin: Prunella vulgaris; Chinese: Xiakucao. Listed as a "Lower Grade" herb in the Divine Husbandman's Classic.</note>

### Explanation of Names
One name is "Winter-surviving" <term>Naidong</term>. Zhenheng explains: This herb withers <term>ku</term> immediately after the Summer Solstice <term>Xiazhi</term>. Because it is imbued with the "Pure Yang" energy of spring, it withers when it encounters the first "Yin" energy of summer—hence the name "Summer-Wither Grass" (Self-heal).

**Collection:** The *Supplementary Records* say it grows in the valleys of Sichuan. Gathered in the fourth month. Su Gong says: it is found everywhere in marshy lowlands. After the Winter Solstice, it sprouts leaves resembling Inula. In the third or fourth month, it blooms in spikes of purple or white, looking like Salvia flowers. It produces seeds in spikes and withers by the fifth month.
**Shizhen’s Note:** It is very common in the wild, growing one to two feet high. The leaves are slightly fragrant, growing opposite each other. The spikes are one to two inches long, containing small light-purple flowers. Each spike has four tiny seeds. Danxi previously claimed it had no seeds, but he was unobservant. The tender sprouts can be soaked to remove bitterness and eaten with oil and salt. Zongshi says "True Motherwort" survives winter, but Zhenheng clarifies that Motherwort and Self-heal are two distinct plants: one withers early and has no seeds (according to some), while the other (Motherwort) withers later and bears fruit.

### Energy and Taste
Bitter, acrid, cold, and non-toxic. Zhicai notes: Snake Gourd <term>Tugua</term> serves as its assistant. It has the power to subdue mercury.

### Primary Governance
Used for alternating chills and fever, scrofula, "rat-fistulas" <note>chronic draining sores on the neck</note>, head sores, and for breaking up goiters and tumors. It disperses "bound energy," treats swollen feet and damp-numbness, and lightens the body.
**Zhenheng notes:** While the classics say it treats scrofula and disperses energy, it also tonifies the blood vessels of the Liver Meridian <term>Jueyin</term>. For "deficient" patients, it is excellent; for "excessive" patients, use it alongside dispersing medicines. 
**Shizhen notes:** Master Li’s *Simple Formulas* uses Self-heal for eye pain, soaking it overnight in sugar water. It resolves internal heat and calms "Liver Fire." Lou Quanshan says it is miraculously effective for eyeball pain that worsens at night. Since the eye is linked to the Liver Meridian, and night belongs to "Yin," the "Pure Yang" energy of Self-heal treats this perfectly by balancing Yin with Yang. He recounts a man with severe eye and head pain whom no medicine could help; a powder of two ounces of Self-heal, two ounces of Nutgrass <term>Xiangfu</term>, and half an ounce of Licorice cured him when taken with green tea.

Four mace <term>mace: a traditional unit of weight, roughly 3.75 grams</term> ground into powder. Take one and a half mace per dose, mixed with clear tea. <insert>Attached Prescriptions</insert> 1 old, 6 new.

**To Brighten the Eyes** To supplement Liver deficiency, treat eye pain, constant cold tearing, painful blood vessels in the eyes, and sensitivity to light. Use half an ounce of Self-heal and one ounce of Nut-grass <term>Xiangfuzi: the rhizome of Cyperus rotundus</term>. Grind into powder. Take one mace per dose, mixed with "wax tea" <note>a high-quality compressed tea</note> broth. <gloss>Simple and Convenient Formulas</gloss>

**Red and White Vaginal Discharge** Collect Self-heal flowers when they bloom, dry them in the shade, and grind into powder. Take two mace per dose with rice water before meals. <gloss>Mr. Xu’s Family Prescriptions</gloss>

**Incessant Uterine Bleeding** Grind Self-heal into powder. Take one square-inch spoonful <term>an ancient measurement for powder</term> per dose, mixed with rice water. <gloss>Sacred Benevolence Formulas</gloss>

**Postpartum Blood Fainting** For cases where the heart-energy seems exhausted: crush Self-heal to extract one cup of juice. Drinking it is miraculous. <gloss>Mr. Xu’s Family Prescriptions</gloss>

**Bruises and Blade Wounds** Chew fresh Self-heal into a pulp and apply it to the wound; it heals immediately. <gloss>Easy and Simple Formulas for Health</gloss>

**Vitiligo (White Patches on Skin)** Boil a concentrated decoction of Self-heal and wash the affected area daily. <gloss>The Business of Heaven and Earth</gloss>

**Scrofula and "Horse-Knife" Sores** <note>Scrofula refers to swollen lymph nodes in the neck; "horse-knife" refers to hard, elongated swellings</note> Regardless of whether they have burst or not, or if they have become chronic fistulas: use six ounces of Self-heal and two cups of water. Boil down to 70% and drink away from mealtimes. For those with severe blood deficiency, boil the juice into a thick paste to consume and apply topically. It is even better when combined with "Ten Complete Great Supplementing Decoction" <note>Shiquan Dabu Tang</note> plus Nut-grass, Sichuan Fritillary, and Polygala. This plant generates blood and is a "sage medicine" for treating scrofula; it is easy to find and highly effective. <gloss>Xue Yi’s Surgical Experiences</gloss>

# Liu Jinu’s Herb <gloss>Tang Materia Medica</gloss>
<note>Latin: Artemisiae anomalae Herba</note>

## Names
Golden Jinu <gloss>Big Bird</gloss>, Wuceng <gloss>Compendium</gloss>. Shizhen says: According to Li Yanshou’s *History of the Southern Dynasties*, Liu Yu (the Emperor Gaozu of the Song dynasty), whose childhood name was Jinu, was out hunting in Xinzhou during his humble years. He encountered a giant dragon and shot it with an arrow. The next day, he went back and heard the sound of a mortar and pestle. Following the sound, he found several boys dressed in green in a thicket, grinding medicine. When asked why, they replied: "Our master was shot by Liu Jinu, and we are preparing medicine to apply to the wound." Yu said: "You are spirits, why not just kill him?" They replied: "Jinu is a future king; he cannot be killed." Yu shouted at them, and the boys vanished. He took the medicine and returned home. Whenever he encountered blade wounds, applying this medicine healed them instantly. Because of this story, people call the plant "Liu Jinu’s Herb." The *Records of Southern Yue* <gloss>Nanyue Zhi</gloss> says that people in the Jiangnan region, because the surname Liu is composed of the characters for "Mao," "Jin" (Gold), and "Dao" (Knife), call it "Golden戎" (Golden Warrior), or "Golden Qinu." People east of the river also call it "Black Vine Vegetable."

## Collection and Identification
Gong says: Liu Jinu’s herb resembles Mugwort. It grows three to four feet tall. The leaves are like Mountain Orchid but pointed and long. A single stalk grows straight up with a seed spike at the top. The leaves grow alternately, and the seeds are tiny and fragmented. <gloss>Lei Xiao says</gloss>: It now comes from Yuezhou. It is a type of wormwood, four to five feet high. Leaves resemble chrysanthemum, flowers are white, and the fruit is yellowish-white, forming a spike. Collect the shoots in summer and dry them. <gloss>Song says</gloss>: Today it is also found in Hezhong, Mengzhou, Hanzhong, and Chuzhou. In spring, the shoots emerge with stalks like Mugwort but with four ridges, reaching two to three feet. The green leaves resemble willow. In the fourth month, tiny yellowish-white flowers bloom, shaped like "Tile Pine" <note>Orostachys fimbriata</note>. In the seventh month, it bears seeds like millet but finer. The root is pale purple like wild lettuce. The shoots, flowers, and seeds are all used, collected in the sixth and seventh months. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss>: Liu Jinu grows on a single straight stalk. The leaves are like Atractylodes <term>Cangzhu</term>, pointed, long, rough, and dark on top, pale on the back. In the ninth month, the top of the stalk divides into several branches, each cluster holding ten small flowers with white petals and yellow centers, resembling small chrysanthemums. After the flowers fade, there is white fluff like Sow-thistle fluff. The seeds are long and thin, also like Sow-thistle. The description of the fruit being like millet or weeds seems to refer to a different plant. Its leaves are also not of the wormwood variety.

# The Seeds

<gloss>Lei Xiao says</gloss>: When collecting, discard the stems and leaves and use only the fruit. Rub them with a cloth to remove the thin husks until clean.

## Energy and Taste
Bitter, warm, and non-toxic.

## Primary Uses
Breaks up blood stasis and reduces abdominal swelling. Excessive consumption causes diarrhea. <gloss>Su Gong</gloss> Stops bleeding and relieves pain; treats postpartum ailments. <gloss>Rihua</gloss> Steam with wine from the hour of the Snake to the hour of the Monkey <note>9 AM to 5 PM</note> and dry in the sun. Shizhen says: The stems, leaves, flowers, and seeds can all be used.

## Primary Uses
Extremely effective for blade wounds. Breaks up pain in the heart and abdomen. Directs energy downward and treats water bloating. Opens the blood circulation. Treats menstrual blockages and masses in women. Stops cholera <note>acute vomiting and diarrhea</note> and watery diarrhea. Treats blood in the urine of adults and children. For fresh use, grind into powder for consumption. <insert>Attached Prescriptions</insert> 1 old, 7 new.

**Blood in Urine or Stool** Grind Liu Jinu into powder. Take two mace mixed with tea on an empty stomach; it will stop immediately.

**Internal Bruising and Blood Stasis** For blood trapped in the abdomen: use one ounce each of Liu Jinu, Drynaria <term>Gusuibu</term>, and Corydalis <term>Yanhusuo</term>. Boil in two liters of water down to one liter and drink.

**Gaseous Bloating and Fullness** Grind the seed spikes of Liu Jinu into powder. Take three mace per dose, boiled with wine. Do not exceed this dose. <gloss>Zuancheng</gloss>

**Acute Injury Stasis** <gloss>Simple Collection of Formulas</gloss> Use seven parts [of the herb] mixed with one part wine and one part "boy's urine" <note>a traditional adjunct believed to enhance blood-moving properties</note>. Warm and drink immediately.

**Incessant Nosebleeds** <gloss>Thousand Golden Formulas</gloss> People today use this for vomiting and diarrhea as well; it is a "divine medicine" for breaking blood stasis. <gloss>Easy and Simple Formulas for Health</gloss>

**Liu Jinu Herb Decoction** For scalds and burns: Grind Liu Jinu into powder. First, brush glutinous rice starch onto the burn with a chicken feather, then sprinkle the powder over it. It relieves pain and leaves no scars—highly proven. <gloss>Comprehensive Recording of Divine Assistance</gloss>

**Formula for Scalds and Burns** For any burn or scald, first sprinkle salt powder on it to protect the flesh from rotting, then sprinkle the medicinal powder. It is wonderful. <gloss>Proved Prescriptions</gloss>

**Scrofula with Wind-Heat** For swelling and pain: grind Liu Jinu into a very fine powder. <gloss>Sacred Benevolence Formulas</gloss>

**Boils and Carbuncles** From the *Comprehensive Recording of Divine Assistance*; application stops them immediately.

## Crooked Joint Herb
<gloss>From the Song Dynasty's Illustrated Classic of Materia Medica</gloss>
**Names:** June Ice <gloss>Li Shizhen’s contemporary name</gloss>, June Frost <gloss>from the Systematic Materia Medica</gloss>, Twin-Green <gloss>from the Illustrated Classic</gloss>.
<note>Shizhen says:</note> This herb is cold in nature and has a dispersing effect. <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> Su Song <note>a famous Song dynasty scholar</note> says: Crooked Joint Herb <note>likely a species of Polygonum or similar knotted herb</note> grows in Junzhou. In the fourth month, it sprouts square stems that are green in color. Every node has leaves.
The leaves are like

*Illustrated Classic of Materia Medica*: June Frost <gloss>from the Systematic Materia Medica</gloss>, Twin-Green <gloss>from the Illustrated Classic</gloss>.

## Beautiful Spring Herb
<gloss>From the Song Dynasty's Illustrated Classic of Materia Medica</gloss>
**Names:** Fairy Mugwort <gloss>from the Illustrated Classic</gloss>, Fixed Ginseng Herb.
<note>Su Song says:</note> Beautiful Spring Herb grows in the valleys and mountains of Tanshan. Tanshan is located on the borders of Gaomi. In Henan, Huaiyang Prefecture, Yingchuan, and Qiao Prefecture, the locals call it "Dragon-Ram Herb." In the northern mountain prefectures and Naqi Prefecture, it is called "Clumping Orchid." Additionally, on Zituanyuan Mountain in Shangdang, it is known as Fixed Ginseng Herb or Fairy Mugwort. It is currently found in many places and is very effective at treating scrofulous sores <term>scrofula: swollen lymph nodes, often on the neck</term>, though many people do not recognize it. Shizhen says: This herb has extraordinary merit, yet its physical description is not well-documented. Today’s physicians also call it 
Beautiful Spring Herb or "Nine Immortals." Since "Fairy Mugwort" shares a name with another plant, I fear they may not be the same thing. This requires further investigation.

## Stems and Leaves
**Flavor and Nature:** Sweet, neutral, and non-toxic. **Primary Uses:** For sores on the back, carbuncles, reducing swelling, and scrofula. Take together with Licorice, ground into a powder and mixed with juice. <gloss>Su Song</gloss>

## Flowers and Roots
**Flavor and Nature:** Sweet <gloss>one source says slightly bitter</gloss>. **Primary Uses:** Swelling, carbuncles, and "Yellow Ferment" <gloss>Su Song</gloss> <note>referring to jaundice or yellowing of the skin</note>.
<note>Su Song says:</note> During the Tianbao era of the Tang Dynasty, Yang Zhengjian of Yingchuan Prefecture recorded a formula that famous doctors found effective. The formula states: Beautiful Spring Herb treats severe cases of cold-damage fever that has knotted into scrofulous sores. If there are openings in the neck that pass through the body, intense fever, yellow-red urine, golden color in the eyes, a dark or bluish face, stabbing pains near the heart, dizziness, and sores below the abdomen or jaundice, this medicine is proven to work. For the medicine: collect the flowers in the third month of spring, dry them in the shade. Take one liter and grind into powder. Every morning on an empty stomach, take three square-inch spoonfuls mixed with one cup of raw sesame oil. Take it all at once, once a day. After five days, take it again until you feel a change. The roots treat scrofulous sores; crush them for a cup of juice and drink on an empty stomach to induce several bowel movements, which will immediately remove the illness. If one dose does not fully cure it, take another after seven days for a permanent cure. Avoid alcohol, wheat noodles, pork, fish, garlic, and dairy.

## Inula Flower
<gloss>Top Grade in the Divine Farmer’s Classic</gloss>
**Names:** Golden Boiling Herb <gloss>from the Classic</gloss>, Golden Coin Flower <gloss>from the Systematic Materia Medica</gloss>, Dipping Gold <gloss>from the Illustrated Classic</gloss>, Summer Chrysanthemum <gloss>or</gloss> Yue-bie.
<note>Shizhen says:</note> Its flowers have lush green leaves and are round, facing downwards, hence the name "Xuanfu" <note>meaning "Revolving Cover"</note>. Shizhen says: All these names are based on 
its appearance. The *Erya* <note>the oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> says: it "steals the Geng." "Geng" represents the element of Metal. This means its yellow flowers bloom by "stealing" the energy of Metal. The *Miscellany of the West Yang* says: Golden Coin Flower is also called "Carrying and Lifting." <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> The *Supplementary Records* say: Inula grows in flat marshes and river valleys. Collect the flowers in the fifth month and dry in the sun; they will be ready in twenty days. <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> It grows in nearby damp lowlands. It looks like a chrysanthemum but is larger... 
<gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> The roots come from Henan. The northern regions also have it. It looks like Sow-thistle. Only the herb itself should be used for Inula preparations; the roots of similar-looking plants are not the true Inula flower roots. Su Baosheng says: The leaves look like water mint, and it is yellow like a chrysanthemum. Collect the flowers from the sixth to the ninth month. Kou Zongshi says: It is found everywhere now. After the second month, it sprouts near water. It greatly resembles safflower but lacks thorns, growing one to two feet tall. Its stems are thin like willow. In the sixth month, it blooms like a chrysanthemum, the size of a copper coin, and deep yellow. People in the fields call it Golden Coin Flower. Collect the flowers in the seventh and eighth months. Nowadays, people plant it in their gardens; the flowers and leaves are identical and it spreads very easily. I suspect this is indeed the Inula. <gloss>Kou Zongshi says:</gloss> Inula leaves 
are like large chrysanthemums or mugwort. In autumn, it blooms with pale yellow flowers like the seeds of the Firmiana tree. Its fragrance is stronger than the chrysanthemum. There is another "Revolving Flower" <note>Xuanhua</note> which is the Bindweed flower; it is not this flower. See that entry. Shizhen says: The flower looks like 
a Golden Coin Chrysanthemum. Those growing by the water have small, single-petaled flowers. Those cultivated by people have larger flowers and stems. People say it grows wherever dewdrops fall, which is why it spreads so easily, <gloss>but this is not actually true</gloss>.

# Inula Flower
<gloss>(Collected Explanations) Collect the flowers over a period of several days. Remove the stems, the husks, and any stray wood. To prepare them for medicinal use: Steam the flowers from the hour of the Snake <term>the hour of the Snake: 9:00 AM to 11:00 AM</term> until the hour of the Horse <term>the hour of the Horse: 11:00 AM to 1:00 PM</term>. Hang them up to dry before use.</gloss>

### Nature and Flavor
Salty, warm, and slightly toxic. <insert>The *Bielu* <note>original: "Mingyi Bielu," an ancient pharmacological text</note> states: Sweet, slightly warm, cooling, and aids flow. [Lei] Nan says: Sweet and non-toxic. Daming says: Non-toxic. [Kou] Zongshi says: Pungent and bitter; pungent.</insert>

### Main Indications
Resolves stagnant Qi <term>Qi: the vital energy or "breath" of the body</term>, fullness beneath the ribs, and palpitations caused by fright; eliminates excess water, clears cold and heat between the five internal organs, tonifies the center, and descends Qi. <gloss>(From the *Benjing* <note>original: "Shennong Bencao Jing," the foundational Classic of Materia Medica</note>)</gloss> Treats phlegm accumulation in the chest where saliva is as thick as glue or lacquer, fluid accumulation in the heart and flanks, lingering fluids in the bladder, wind-damp numbness, withered skin and flesh, and discharge in the eyes; it benefits the large intestine, clears the blood vessels, and improves the complexion. <gloss>(From the *Bielu*)</gloss> Primarily treats edema, expels abdominal swelling, opens the stomach, stops vomiting and hiccups, and treats the inability to keep food down. <gloss>(According to Zhen Quan)</gloss> Dissolves phlegm and water, and eliminates "wind" affecting the head and eyes. It also treats coughing with rebellious Qi and sensations of fullness or blockage. <gloss>(According to Daming)</gloss> Heals edema, dry belching, and the inability to eat. <gloss>(According to Su Song)</gloss>

### Elucidations
> <gloss>(Kou Zongshi says)</gloss> Inula flower <note>original: "Xuanfuhua," likely *Inula japonica*</note> moves water and descends Qi. Zhang Zhongjing <note>a famous Han dynasty physician</note> treated cases of "fullness below the heart" and persistent belching after sweating or purging in cold-damage disorders with "Inula and Red Ochre Decoction." This herb is used frequently in various miscellaneous formulas.
> <gloss>(Cheng Wu-yi says)</gloss> When the Qi is hardened, it becomes stagnant. Therefore, use this to soften and resolve the hardness of stagnant masses.
> <gloss>(Zhu Zhenheng says)</gloss> Kou Zongshi mentioned its ability to move phlegm and water; it is also a medicine that disperses "wind" from the head and eyes. Patients suffering from deficiency should not take it in large quantities, as it cools and clears the large intestine.
> <gloss>(Li Shizhen says)</gloss> Furthermore, Inula acts on the Lung channel of Hand-Taiyin and the Large Intestine channel of Hand-Yangming. In treating various diseases, its efficacy lies solely in its power to move water, descend Qi, and clear the blood vessels. Li Weigong said that the flowers can damage the eyes. Tang Shenwei's *Bencao* mistakenly included the root's functions under the flower's entry; I have now corrected this.

# Celosia Seed <gloss>(From the *Benjing*, Top Grade)</gloss>
### Explanation of Names
<insert>Grass Wormwood, Cockscomb Seed, Sack Herb, Grass Jue Ming <note>original: "Cao Jueming," often confused with Cassia seeds</note></insert>

### Collected Explanations
<gloss>(Su Song says)</gloss> <insert>The names are similar, but why? Its seeds brighten the eyes, sharing the same efficacy as Cassia seed <note>Juemingzi</note>, hence the name "Grass Jueming." Furthermore, the *Bielu* says Celosia grows by roadsides in flat valleys. Collect the stems and leaves in the third month and dry them in the sun; collect the seeds in the fifth and sixth months. The seeds look like those of the Ginger Lily. The tender sprouts resemble the Cockscomb and Amaranth, hence it is called "Cockscomb Amaranth." The *Tongzhi* states the common name is "Ox-tail Wormwood," which is correct.</insert>
<gloss>(Su Song says)</gloss> It is found everywhere. It resembles a wheat spike flower with very fine seeds. There is another "Grass Wormwood" <note>Caohao</note> or "Grass Hall" herb which has very similar therapeutic properties. Their forms and names are so similar it causes doubt, but they are actually two different species. This herb grows over a man’s height, with soft, thin leaves and purple-white flowers. The fruit is a pod with black, flat seeds, even more like Amaranth seeds but larger. It grows in low, damp ground. In the fourth and fifth months, herbalists call it "Amaranth Wormwood." <gloss>(Su Song continues)</gloss> Today it is found in the Jiang-Huai regions. In the second month, it produces green sprouts, growing three to four feet tall. The leaves resemble willow but are softer. The stem is like wormwood, bluish-red. Flowers bloom in the sixth and seventh months, red at the top and white at the bottom. The seeds are black, shiny, and flat like Amaranth seeds. The root resembles wormwood root, white and growing as a single straight stalk. Collect the seeds in the sixth and eighth months.
<gloss>(Li Shizhen says)</gloss> Celosia <note>original: "Qingxiangzi," *Celosia argentea*</note> has many names. it grows mostly in fields. Its tender sprouts resemble Amaranth and are edible. When mature, it stands three to four feet tall. The sprouts, leaves, flowers, and fruits are identical to the Cockscomb flower <note>original: "Jiguanhua"</note>, with no difference except that Cockscomb flower heads are large and flat or rounded, whereas this herb produces pointed flower spikes at the tip, four to five inches long, shaped like a rabbit's tail. They are pale red (water-red), though some are yellow-white. The seeds are within the spike, identical to Cockscomb seeds.

## Feather Cockscomb
<gloss>Commonly known as "Grass Celosia" or "Wild Cockscomb"</gloss>

The seeds of Feather Cockscomb and Amaranth look exactly the same. Su Gong <note>a Tang dynasty pharmacologist</note> claimed they grew in pods, but this was an error. Xiao Bing noted that the variety with yellow flowers is named <margin>Appendix: The Technique of Tao Zhu</margin> "Tao Zhu's Herb." <note>Tao Zhu refers to Fan Li, a famous scholar-merchant; this name suggests the plant's use in alchemical "techniques."</note> [Lei] Xiao says: There is a type of Feather Cockscomb with yellow flowers called Tao Zhu Shu; the seedlings look similar. [Chen] Zangqi says: Tao Zhu Shu is different from what Tao Hongjing and Chen Zangqi described. There is also "Celestial Spirit Herb," which belongs to this category; both are appended below.

On the fifth day of the month, collect the seeds and carry them with you. <margin>Celestial Spirit Herb</margin> [Li] Shizhen says: The stems, leaves, spikes, and seeds are all the same as the Cockscomb. In the ninth month, the leaves turn a vibrant, fresh red; when viewed from a distance, they look like
a woman being celebrated by her husband, hence it is called "Silk Flower." The people of Wu <note>modern-day Jiangsu/Zhejiang region</note> call it "The Old Youth" <note>likely because it retains its vibrant color late into the season</note>. A variety with red leaves in the sixth month is called "Ten-Variety Brocade."
In the fifth month, one can extract the juice to "subdue" <term>subdue: an alchemical term for stabilizing a volatile mineral</term> realgar. <margin>Black Seeds</margin> [Lei] Xiao says: There are two types of "Simeng" seeds and "Scattered Fine" seeds that truly resemble Feather Cockscomb seeds.
One uses sulfur and arsenic to refine cinnabar. However, the flavors are different; Simeng seeds are bitter and produce a sticky saliva when chewed.

---

**The Leaves** <gloss>Preparation: [Lei] Xiao says: For all uses, first heat iron until red and quench it in water. Use this water to pound the herb into a paste for application.</gloss> <gloss>Properties: Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic.</gloss> **Main Indications:** Treats "evil Qi" <term>evil Qi: external pathogens like wind or heat</term> and heat within the skin, wind-related itching, and body rashes. It kills the "three worms" <note>various internal parasites</note>. <gloss>Su Gong</gloss> Treats malnutrition-related sores, fistulas, hemorrhoids, and "gnawing" ulcers of the lower regions. <gloss>From the *Bielu*</gloss> Boiled into a juice or decocted into a liquid, it is highly effective for treating
<gloss>Damp-Hidden sores</gloss> Su Gong [states it] is excellent for treating bleeding from metal wounds <note>wounds from blades or tools</note>.
<gloss>[Su] Gong</gloss> Stops [bleeding] and clears [vision].

**The Seeds** <gloss>Properties: Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic. [Zhen] Quan says: Sweet.</gloss> **Main Indications:** Treats lips and mouth turning blue or green. <gloss>From the *Benjing*</gloss> Treats "evil Qi" in the five internal organs, benefits the brain marrow, strengthens the tendons and bones, moistens the liver, improves hearing and vision, and expels wind, cold, and damp-related numbness or "jaundice." <gloss>Daming</gloss> Treats liver heat and toxins that attack the eyes, causing redness, obstructions, "green blindness" <term>green blindness: likely referring to glaucoma or optic nerve atrophy</term>, and swollen membranes.
<gloss>Evil scrofula <note>swelling of the lymph nodes</note></gloss> <gloss>[Zhen] Quan says:</gloss> [Xiao] Bing says: For treating the eyes, there is the "Feather Cockscomb Seed Pill." [Kou] Zongshi says: The classic texts do not explicitly mention treating the eyes. Only the *Treatise on Nature* and [the works of] Rihua Zi began to say it treats the liver and brightens the eyes. Many people now commonly use it for eye ailments, which seems slightly at odds with the original intent of the classics.
<gloss>[Zhen] Quan says:</gloss> [Li] Shizhen says: The efficacy of Feather Cockscomb seeds in treating the eyes is comparable to that of Cassia seeds (*Jue Ming Zi*). Although the *Benjing* does not explicitly mention "treating eyes," it lists the name "Grass Cassia" and notes it treats "blue lips." From this, its power to brighten the eyes can be inferred.
The eyes are the "aperture" <term>aperture: the external opening associated with an internal organ</term> of the liver. Blue/green lips are a symptom of the Liver Meridian (Foot Jueyin). Ancient formulas often used this herb to clear heat; thus, it is clear that Feather Cockscomb is a medicine for the Liver Meridian. Furthermore, its use
in treating eyes often shows proven results, which provides further evidence. The *Records of Observation* mention that during the Chuping era, a certain "Master Blue Ox" regularly took Feather Cockscomb pills; he lived for over a hundred years but appeared to be only fifty or sixty.

**1. To stop a nosebleed:** <gloss>Old formula</gloss> When a nosebleed is so severe that the patient feels they might die, pound Feather Cockscomb seeds to extract three *ge* <note>roughly 300ml</note> of juice and pour it into the nose.

*Guangli Formula*

**Cockscomb** <gloss>From the *Jiayou Bencao* of the Song Dynasty</gloss>
<margin>Shizhen says: Named for the flower's shape.</margin>
<gloss>Explanations of Names</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> [Li] Shizhen says: Cockscomb flowers grow everywhere. The seedlings sprout in the third month. By summer, the tall ones reach five or six feet. The stems are thick. The leaves are green, similar to White Amaranth but narrower, with slight red veins.
The plant is reddish. Some flowers are round, others flat and wrinkled. In the sixth or seventh month, flowers bloom at the tips in red, white, or yellow colors. The spikes that are round and pointed resemble the Feather Cockscomb; those that are flat, curled, and level
resemble the comb of a rooster. The flowers are large, some measuring one to two feet around, curling out in beautiful layers. The seeds are inside the spikes,
black, fine, and smooth, identical to Amaranth seeds. The spikes look like withered millet. The flowers are extremely durable, withering only after the frost.

<meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal entries from the previous section. ### Seeds
The flavor is sweet, the nature is cool, and they are non-toxic. They treat "intestinal wind" <note>bleeding from the rectum often attributed to "wind" heat</note>, bloody stools, both red and white dysentery, and internal abscesses. <insert>They also treat flooding [heavy uterine bleeding] and vaginal discharge.</insert> For use in medicine, the seeds should be large and stir-fried.

### Flower
The nature and flavor are the same as the seeds. It is primarily used to treat bleeding from hemorrhoids, bloody stools, red and white dysentery, abdominal pain, and red or white vaginal discharge (the color of the flower used should match the color of the discharge).

<gloss>[Li] Shizhen says: <insert>For persistent vomiting of blood</insert>, take white Cockscomb flowers, soak them in vinegar, and boil them seven times. Grind into a powder. Each dose is two qian <note>a traditional unit of weight, roughly 3.75 grams</note>, taken with hot wine. From the *Collection of Proven Recipes*.</gloss>

<gloss>Alternatively, grind into a powder and mix with refined honey to form pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take thirty pills per dose with an Astragalus decoction twice a day. From the *General Records of Holy Benevolence*.</gloss>

**Blood in the stool:** <gloss>Stir-fry both the Cockscomb flowers and seeds, then decoct and ingest. From the *Sage's Benevolence Formulas*.</gloss>

**The five types of hemorrhoids and anal swelling:** If the condition persists for a long time and turns into a fistula, take one liang <note>roughly 37.5 grams</note> each of Cockscomb flower and "Phoenix-Eye" grass. Decoct in two cups of water and wash the area frequently. From the *Precious Mirror of Health*.</gloss>

**Blood in the stool:** <gloss>Use Cockscomb flower and the white inner bark of the Ailanthus (Tree of Heaven) root, in equal parts.</gloss>

**Bloody stools and rectal prolapse:** <gloss>Use white Cockscomb flower and Ledebouriella root (Fangfeng) in equal parts. Grind into a powder and mix with paste to form pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take 70 to 91 pills on an empty stomach with rice water. Another method: stir-fry white Cockscomb flower and mix with one liang of Notopterygium root (Qianghuo) powder. Take two qian per dose with rice water. From the *Mysterious Formulas of the Water-type Bell*.</gloss>

<insert>Incessant urinary blockage:</insert> <gloss>Use red Cockscomb flower as a single ingredient. Sun-dry it and grind into a powder. Take two qian on an empty stomach mixed with wine. Avoid fishy smells and pork. From *Sun’s Collection of Effective Formulas*.</gloss>

**Postpartum blood pain:** <gloss>Decoct white Cockscomb flowers in wine and ingest. From *Li Lou’s Extraordinary Formulas*.</gloss>

**White vaginal discharge in women:** <gloss>Sun-dry white Cockscomb flowers and grind into a powder. Every morning on an empty stomach, take three qian with wine. For red discharge, use the red flowers. From *Sun’s Collection of Effective Formulas*.</gloss>

**White discharge and "sand-dribbling" urinary stones:** <gloss>Take white Cockscomb flower, sow-thistle, and calcined silkworm in equal parts. Burn them but preserve their medicinal nature <note>a process called "carbonizing" to enhance blood-stopping properties</note>, then take with strong liquor on an empty stomach. From *Picking the Mysteries*.</gloss>

**Red and white dysentery:** <gloss>Decoct Cockscomb flowers in wine. Use red flowers for the red variety and white flowers for the white variety. From the *Collection of Simple Formulas*.</gloss>

## Safflower <gloss>From the Song Dynasty's Kaibao Era Materia Medica</gloss>
### Nomenclature: Safflower <gloss>The Seed</gloss>, Yellow-Blue
<gloss>[Su] Song says: The flower is red but the plant is named "Yellow-Blue." [Ma] Zhi says: "Yellow-Blue" is simply the Safflower. It grows in the Liang and Han regions as well as the Western Regions <note>Central Asia</note>. The *Record of Natural History* states that Zhang Qian <note>the famous Han dynasty diplomat</note> obtained the seeds from the Western Regions. It is now also planted in the Wei region. The flowers grow on spiked heads. People in Fujian collect them when the dew is present. After picking, more flowers emerge until the plant is exhausted. In the forest, it produces white seeds the size of small beans. The flowers are dried to dye things a true red or to make rouge. [Li] Shizhen says: Safflower can be planted in the second, eighth, or twelfth months. After rain, scatter the seeds like hemp. The young sprouts and leaves are edible. The leaves resemble those of the small thistle. By the fifth month, it blooms with flowers like the large thistle but red. Pick the flowers at dawn, pound them thoroughly, and rinse with water in a cloth bag to squeeze out the yellow juice. Pound again with the sour liquid from fermented millet, rinse, and squeeze again. Cover with wormwood overnight and sun-dry. Alternatively, pound into thin cakes and dry in the shade before storing. When using as medicine, crush them. The seeds are harvested in the fifth month, washed clean, crushed, and decocted. The juice can be mixed with vinegar for a delicious vegetable dressing; it can also be used for axle grease or in candles.</gloss>

### Flower
<gloss>Flavor and Nature:</gloss> Pungent, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>[Zhu] Yuansu says: It enters the Heart meridian to nourish the blood. Its bitter and warm nature makes it "Yang within Yin." Therefore, it enters the Heart and assists Dang Gui (Angelica sinensis).</gloss>

**Primary Indications:** Postpartum blood-fainting, locked jaw, persistent retained blood <note>lochia</note> in the abdomen causing stabbing pain, and fetal death in the womb. Decoct with wine for administration. It also treats "Gu" poisoning <note>illness caused by dark magic or toxins</note>.

<gloss>In large doses, it breaks up stagnant blood; in small doses, it nourishes the blood. [Zhu] Zhenheng says: It moistens dryness in the blood, stops pain, disperses swelling, and regulates menstruation. [Li] Shizhen says: Blood is produced in the pericardium and stored in the liver; it belongs to the Chong and Ren vessels. Safflower juice is of the same "category" as blood, so it can move the blood circulation in men and regulate menses in women. In high doses it moves blood, in low doses it nourishes it. According to the *Casual Notes on Cultivating the Curious*, the wife of Mr. Xu from Xinchang fell ill after childbirth and appeared dead, though her chest remained slightly warm. A famous physician named Lu said, "This is blood-fainting." He claimed she could be saved with dozens of catties of safflower. They quickly bought it and boiled it in large pots. They placed three tubs under a slatted window and laid the woman on the bed above it to steam her. As the water cooled, they added more. After a short time, her fingers moved, and after half a day, she regained consciousness. This follows the same method used by Xu Yinzong of the Tang Dynasty, who used Astragalus decoction steam to treat Empress Dowager Liu's stroke.</gloss>

**Sixty-two types of "Wind" disorders:** <gloss>Zhang Zhongjing <note>the Sage of Medicine</note> treated sixty-two types of wind combined with internal abdominal blood-and-qi pain using one large liang of safflower, divided into three doses. From the *Illustrated Materia Medica*.</gloss>

**All types of toxic swellings:** <gloss>Pound fresh safflowers to extract the juice and drink it.</gloss>
<margin>From the *Secret Essentials from the Exterior*</margin>

**Swollen and blocked throat:** <gloss>When the throat is impassable, pound safflower to extract one sheng <note>about 200ml</note> of juice and drink it.</gloss>

## Saffron
<gloss>Compendium</gloss> <term>Explanatory Name</term> Bofulan <note>a transliteration of the Persian *za'faran*</note>. <gloss>Compendium</gloss> <term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>[Li] Shizhen says: Saffron comes from the Western Regions, the Muslim territories, and Arabia <note>original: "Tianfang Guo"</note>. ## Rouge
<gloss>Compendium</gloss> <term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Shizhen says: According to Fu Hou’s *Notes on Ancient and Modern China*, rouge originated with King Zhou of the Shang Dynasty. He made it by condensing the juice of safflowers to decorate the faces of women. Because it was produced in the land of Yan, it was named Yanzhi <note>literally "Yan Fat/Paste"</note>.</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: There are four types of rouge. One is made by dyeing white lead powder with safflower juice; this is what Su E's *Interpretations* describes as having leaves like a thistle and flowers like a chrysanthemum, originating in the West. In China, it is called Safflower (Honglan) and is used to color women's faces. The second type is made from the juice of the Mountain Rouge flower. Duan Gonglu’s *Records of the Northern Households* says this flower grows in the mountains of Duanzhou, with leaves like indigo. It blooms in the first lunar month, resembling knotweed. Locals harvest the buds to make rouge powder, which can also dye silk. The third type is made from the juice of the Mountain Pomegranate flower, as recorded in Zheng Qian’s *Foreign Materia Medica*. The fourth type is made by dyeing cotton with "Purple Mineral" <note>Lac or shellac resin</note>, called "Foreign Rouge." Li Xun’s *Pharmacopoeia of the Southern Seas* records this. Today, Southerners mostly use this Purple Mineral rouge, commonly called "Purple Stalk." Generally, all of these can be used in medicines for blood diseases. Additionally, the seeds of the Malabar spinach (Luokui) can provide juice to be mixed with powder for the face, also called Foreign Rouge; this is found in the Vegetable Section.</gloss>

# Greater Thistle and Lesser Thistle <gloss>Middle Grade in the Miscellaneous Records</gloss>
<insert>Correction</insert> Moved here from its own entry in the *名醫別錄* (Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians).

<margin>Shizhen says: The name for Thistle (Jì) sounds like the word for a hair knot (jì), because its flower resembles a top-knot. It is called "Tiger Thistle" because its sprouts appear fierce and prickly. The prefix "Horse" implies it is large. It is called "Mountain Burdock" because its root resembles the burdock root. It is called "Chicken Neck" because its stem looks like the neck of a chicken.</margin>
<margin>Zongshi says: Although the leaves of the Greater and Lesser thistles are similar, their medicinal powers differ. The Greater Thistle grows in mountain valleys; its root treats abscesses and swellings. The Lesser Thistle grows on flat plains; it cannot dissipate swellings, but both are capable of breaking up stagnant blood.</margin>
<margin>Song says: Lesser Thistle is found everywhere, commonly known as "Green Prickly Thistle." In the second month, the sprouts grow two or three inches; the roots and sprouts are eaten together as a delicious vegetable. In the fourth month, it grows over a foot tall with many prickles. From the center, a flower head emerges, resembling a safflower but purplish-blue. Northerners call it "Thousand Needle Grass." Harvest the sprouts in the fourth month and the roots in the ninth month; dry both in the shade. The sprouts and roots of the Greater Thistle are similar to this, but simply larger and more robust.</margin>

<insert>Collection of Explanations</insert> <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* says:</gloss> Greater Thistle grows in mountain valleys.
<gloss>Hongjing says:</gloss> It is also called Mountain Burdock. <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> gives it the names Tiger Thistle and "Lone Broom."
<gloss>Gong says:</gloss> Greater Thistle is the "Tiger Thistle," and Lesser Thistle is the "Cat Thistle."
<gloss>Baosheng says:</gloss> Greater Thistle grows in mountain valleys to a height of three or four feet. The leaves resemble Lesser Thistle, which only grows about a foot tall. The Greater Thistle's leaves are not wrinkled, which is the distinction. It is difficult to prepare as a vegetable because it has tiny bristles, though they are not harmful to humans.

# Teasel Root <term>Xuduan; Dipsacus asperoides</term>
<gloss>Superior Grade in the *Classic* <note>referring to the *Divine Husbandman’s Classic of Materia Medica*</note></gloss>
<gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Shuzhe <insert>From the *Materia Medica*</insert>, Bone-knitter <insert>From the *Miscellaneous Records*</insert>, Dragon Bean <insert>From the *Miscellaneous Records*</insert>, Southern Herb. <insert>Shizhen says:</insert> The name *Xuduan* (meaning "reconnecting the broken") comes from its medicinal merit in treating injuries and knitting bones back together.
<gloss>Collection and Explanation</gloss> <insert>The *Miscellaneous Records* state:</insert> Teasel grows in the valleys of Mount Chang. Harvest the roots in the seventh or eighth month and dry in the shade. <insert>Su Gong says:</insert> It comes from Hua Prefecture; harvest on the eighth day of the seventh month. <insert>Tao Hongjing says:</insert> Jing Prefecture also has a Teasel that grows as a vine with thin leaves and stems as thick as a lampwick. The root is large, yellowish-white, and contains juice. Harvest in the seventh or eighth month. Nowadays, people use the stems and leaves where the nodes are broken and the skin is yellow and wrinkled like a chicken’s foot; this is also called "Searching the Trees for Parasites." Others have a "Bone-knitting Tree" which grows over ten feet tall with leaves like a bottle gourd; its bark is used for metal wounds. In Guangzhou, there is a "Teasel Vine," also called "Various Vines"; one cuts the stem to collect the juice for drinking to treat deficiency and exhaustion. If a branch is broken and stuck in the ground, it lives. I fear these are not the true Teasel. Li Dangzhi says it is the Tiger Thistle, but this is a great error, though the Tiger Thistle is also a medicine. <insert>Han Baosheng says:</insert> It is found in all mountain valleys. What is commonly used now has leaves like Taro but with a square stem. The root is like the Greater Thistle, yellowish-white. Tao Hongjing’s description was incorrect. <insert>Su Song says:</insert> It is also found in the prefectures of Wu, Shaanxi, Hezhong, Xingyuan, Shu, and Yue. The sprouts emerge after the third month. The stalks have four ridges like ramie. The leaves grow in opposite pairs. In the fourth month, it blooms with reddish-white flowers similar to Motherwort. The root is like the Greater Thistle but reddish-yellow. <insert>Careful Examination:</insert> Wang Ying says Teasel is the Horse Thistle, which has leaves similar to the Lesser Thistle but larger. The leaves resemble "Old Man’s Vegetable" <note>likely a species of Cirsium</note> but are smaller and thicker with prickles on both sides. The flowers are purple. This matches the illustrations from Yue Prefecture, but the goods in the markets are of several varieties, and few can distinguish the true herb. Good doctors often use the roots of "Thatch-Grass" because they look similar, but if taken by mistake, they make the tendons soft. Shizhen says: The accounts of Teasel are inconsistent. Su Gong says it is a vine, while Li Dangzhi and others say that which has yellow, wrinkled skin and breaks at the nodes is genuine. Su Gong says whenever using it, do not be confused; those are all Tiger Thistles. Rihua says it is the Greater Thistle, also called Mountain Burdock. Su Gong and Su Song both say the leaves resemble Taro. Su Song further listed it under the section for Thistles, making it hard to follow. However, since the Han dynasty, the Greater Thistle has been accepted as Teasel for a long time. Upon investigating the reality, what the two Sus (Su Gong and Su Song) described seems to match and should be considered correct. What people use today comes from Sichuan; it is red, thin, and releases a dust-like smoke when broken. This is considered the best quality.
<margin>Zheng Qiao’s *General Treatises* mentions that what the commentaries describe is "Southern Teasel," but I do not know on what basis he says this, other than to distinguish it from the Sichuan Teasel.</margin>

Avoid using it with Thunder-ball <term>Leiwan; Omphalia lapidescens</term>.

Prolonged consumption increases energy and strength. <insert>From the *Materia Medica*</insert>. For women with uterine flooding and spotting, metal wounds, internal leakage, to stop pain, generate flesh, and for traumatic injuries, stagnant blood, abdominal pain, and stiff joints. <insert>From the *Miscellaneous Records*</insert>. It removes all toxins and opens the blood vessels. <insert>From Daming</insert>.

# Rhapontic Root <gloss>Listed in the Upper Class of the Classic</gloss>
<gloss>Also known in the *Materia Medica* as Wild Orchid</gloss> <gloss>The *Classic* calls it Ying</gloss> <gloss>Also called Thistle-Hao</gloss> <gloss>Gong calls it Ghost Sesame</gloss> <gloss>Daming gives another name</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: The northwest corner of a house is called "Lou." Anything black is called "Lu." Since this herb turns black after autumn and its base is dark, it is named "Loulu" <note>Leak-Rush</note>. The *Tang Rhymes* pronounce it like "Ge." Its leaves resemble hemp, so the common folk call it "Ghost Sesame."</gloss>

<margin>Jinghong notes: For skin infections like erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection</note>, decoct into a wash for hemorrhoids; it is very effective. Shizhen notes: It lowers Qi and clears heat.</margin>

## Seedlings <gloss>Flavor is bitter; property is slightly cold; non-toxic</gloss>

Mainly used for "lacquer sores" <note>contact dermatitis from lacquer trees</note> on the face or entire body. Burn to ash and apply to the skin; it may also be eaten raw. <gloss>From the *Additional Records*</gloss>. Burned to ash, it is extremely effective for treating metal wounds <note>cuts from blades</note>. <gloss>According to Hongjing</gloss>

> Hongjing says: Mount Qiao is supposedly the burial place of the Yellow Emperor, located in Shang Commandery. This herb grows along the roadsides there. Merchants harvest the seedlings for sale. In common practice, the root is called "Deer-Li Root"; it is rubbed with bitter vinegar to treat sores and scabies.
> 
> Gong says: This medicine is commonly called "Thistle-Hao." Its stems and leaves resemble white mugwort, and it has yellow flowers. The stems grow long like fine hemp, reaching the size of an arrow shaft, with four or five petals. After the seventh or eighth month, it turns entirely black, which distinguishes it from other herbs of the mugwort family. The stems, leaves, and seeds are commonly used; I have not seen the root used.
> 
> Su Song says: In the Shannan region, it is called "Wood Veratrum," which is toxic and not the true Rhapontic Root. People today mistake the Horse Thistle—which looks like Bitter Hibiscus—for Rhapontic Root, but that is also incorrect.
> 
> Zhi says: Other versions state the leaves of Rhapontic Root are as large as thistles, growing four to five feet tall. The seed pod resembles a sesame pod but is smaller. People east of the Yangtze River use the seedlings, which are more effective than the roots. Those from Jiangning and Shangjing are of the best quality.
> 
> Tao calls it "Deer-Li" and Su calls it "Wood Veratrum," but both are wrong. Rhapontic Root is distinct. Zhangqi says: Southerners use the seedlings, while Northerners use the root. It grows like a tree, similar to the medicinal Evodia, reaching two to three feet. It is toxic and kills parasites. Mountain dwellers use it to wash sores and scabies.
> 
> Baosheng says: The leaves resemble Horn-Hao. It is most abundant in the damp lowlands of Cao and Yan provinces. Harvest the stems in the sixth and seventh months; they dry to a color blacker than other herbs.
> 
> Daming says: Both the flowers and seedlings can be used. It looks like a radish and tastes like dried burdock. It has white flowers and seeds on top.
> 
> Song says: Today it is found in the prefectures east of the capital and in the Xiang and Hai regions. Old accounts say the leaves resemble white mugwort with yellow-white flowers. The stems are like arrows and the pods resemble sesame. Among current illustrations, only the one from Shan Prefecture is somewhat accurate.

<meta>This page continues the botanical description of Rhapontic Root (Loulu), moving from its physical varieties in different regions to its pharmacological properties and specific medicinal recipes. It also introduces the related plant, Winged Thistle (Feilian).</meta>

<page-num>Fourteen</page-num>
<header>Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 15, Herb Category</header>

Those varieties from Yizhou have flowers and leaves quite similar to the peony. Those from Qinzhou have flowers like the single-petaled "Cold Chrysanthemum" <note>a late-blooming chrysanthemum variety</note> and are purple in color, with five to seven branches sharing a single stalk. Those from Haizhou have purple-green flowers and leaves resembling a single-petaled lotus; below the calyx and beside the root, there is a white downy fuzz. The base of the leaf is like a turnip but finer, also resembling an onion, and is purple at the base. People in the Huaidian region call it the "Old Man Flower." Although the flowers produced in these three regions differ, their leaves and roots are similar. However, the leaves of the varieties from Qin and Haizhou are more silver-toothed <note>serrated</note> in shape. 

Since one substance can have such varied forms, which one should physicians follow? One should follow the old saying that those produced in Danzhou are superior. Furthermore, the *Materia Medica* states that *Feilian* <note>Winged Thistle</note> is also called *Loulu*, and is said to be similar to "Bitter Hibiscus." Its root is white-fleshed with black skin when fresh, and when dry, it is as black as *Scrophularia* <note>Figwort root, a dark medicinal root</note>. The flowers are gathered in the seventh or eighth month and dried in the shade. This description closely matches the flowers, leaves, and roots of the *Loulu* illustrated in Qinzhou and Haizhou; however, the locals there only call it *Loulu* and do not call it *Feilian*. 

Zhen says: There is a variety that truly resembles *Loulu* but has a bitter and sour taste; if taken by mistake, it causes persistent vomiting. 

Shizhen says: According to Shen Kuo's *Dream Pool Essays*, the *Loulu* used by current physicians is actually the true *Feilian*. *Feilian* is another name for *Loulu*; its seedlings resemble Bitter Hibiscus, and its root is like Burdock with a cottony head. It is the root that is recorded for use. Now, what is called *Loulu* in pharmacies is like oil-steamed garlic; in late autumn, it becomes withered and black like "pickled vegetables." At that time, using the seedlings is the true *Loulu*. The rest is discussed under the *Feilian* entry.

## Preparation of Roots and Seedlings <gloss>Zhen says: In all cases where Rhapontic Root is obtained, chop it finely and boil it with Raw Licorice for three to five boils, then remove the Licorice before use.</gloss>

Flavor and Nature <gloss>Salty and cold, non-toxic. The *Additional Records* say: Extremely cold. Zangqi says: It is toxic, yet also says it is non-toxic. It is a medicine for the Foot Yangming <note>Stomach</note> Channel. Fang Cai says: Forsythia serves as its messenger <note>an assistant herb that guides the effect</note>.</gloss>

<margin>Main Indications</margin>

# Treating itching and promoting the flow of breast milk. Long-term use lightens the body <note>a sign of health and longevity</note>, augments the Qi, sharpens hearing and vision, prevents aging, and extends life. <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss>. It stops bed-wetting, clears "heat-qi," and treats skin sores and itching that look like hemp seeds or beans. <gloss>From the *Additional Records*</gloss>. It clears the small intestine, treats seminal emission and blood in the urine, overcomes "wind" <note>pathogenic influences causing sudden illness</note>, treats red eyes from wind-heat, and high fever in children. It heals crush injuries, reconnects sinews and bones, treats breast abscesses and scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes</note>, treats metal wounds, stops bleeding, drains pus, tonifies the blood, promotes tissue growth, and opens the menstrual pathways. <gloss>According to Daming</gloss>

Hongjing says: This medicine is very beneficial to people when taken for a long time, yet it is rarely seen in formulas for consumption. The varieties found near the capital are only used to treat fistulas and scabies. People in the markets mostly treat it as a medicine for the Stomach Channel, and ancient formulas for treating carbuncles, abscesses, and fistulous tracts often list "Loulu Decoction" as the primary treatment. Pang Anchang's *Treatise on Cold Damage* used *Loulu* leaves to treat carbuncles and as a preventative measure for seasonal smallpox. 

For epidemic fevers, he used *Loulu* leaves; if unavailable, he substituted them with Gardenia fruit, also utilizing its cold nature to clear heat, perhaps unaware that it specifically enters the Foot Yangming <note>Stomach</note> channel. <gloss>Attached Prescriptions</gloss>: 2 old, 6 new.
