# Winged Thistle (Feilian) <gloss>Listed in the Upper Class of the *Classic*. Also known as Rhapontic Root (*Loulu*). The *Additional Records* call it "Small Rhapontic Root." The *Additional Records* also write it as Flying Pheasant, Flying Path, Crouching Rabbit, Crouching Pig, and Heavenly Perilla. Shizhen says: "Feilian" is the name of a divine bird. It has the body of a deer with leopard patterns, the head of a sparrow, the tail of a snake, and has horns; it can summon the wind. This herb has skin along its stem like the feathers of an arrow, and since it later treats "wind" disorders, it was given the names Winged Thistle (Feilian) and Flying Pheasant (Feizhi).</gloss>

<term>Loulu (漏蘆)</term>: Rhapontic Root (Rhaponticum uniflorum).
<term>Feilian (飛廉)</term>: Winged Thistle (Carduus crispus).
<term>Yongju (癰疽)</term>: Carbuncles and abscesses; severe skin infections.
<term>Wugu (無辜)</term>: A traditional pediatric diagnosis involving malnutrition, bloating, and sometimes parasitic infection.

<insert>Collected</insert> <gloss>(The *Separate Records* say)</gloss> **Winged Thistle** <note>original: "Feilian"; likely *Carduus crispus*</note> grows in the river valleys and marshes of Henei. The roots are harvested in the first month, and the flowers in the seventh and eighth months, then dried in the shade. <gloss>Hongjing says</gloss> It is found everywhere and closely resembles bitter sowthistle, but the leaves have many thorns and gaps. Below the leaf, it attaches to the stem with a soft skin that rises up like the feathers of an arrow. Its 
<insert>individual</insert> flowers are purple-white. Common medical formulas rarely use it, but Daoists consume its seeds and stems to achieve longevity. It is also included in the "Divine Pillow" formulas. Since **Rhapontic Root** <note>original: "Loulu"</note> is now listed separately, this name "Loulu" is merely an alias for this plant. <gloss>Gong says</gloss> There are two types. One grows in flat marshes, which is the one described by Master Tao [Hongjing]. The other grows on mountain ridges; its leaves are quite similar but lack the deep serrations and are very hairy. Its stem also lacks the "feathers" [wings]. The root grows straight down without side branches; when fresh, the flesh is white and the skin is black with black veins inside. When dried in the sun, it turns as black as **Figwort** <note>original: "Xuanshen"; a dark-colored medicinal root</note>. Both the leaves, flowers, and roots are used to treat "gnawing" sores <note>likely parasitic or gangrenous ulcers</note> and to kill parasites; both the marsh and mountain varieties are effective. Nowadays, common people mistake **Horse Thistle** <note>original: "Majian"</note>, which resembles bitter sowthistle, for Rhapontic Root, but this is incorrect. <gloss>Baosheng says</gloss> The leaves resemble bitter sowthistle, the flowers resemble soft feathers and are purple-yellow, and the seed down is white. It grows in marshes everywhere. It is harvested in the fifth and sixth months and dried in the sun. <gloss>Hui says</gloss> When using it, do not use the "Red Fat Vine" <note>original: "Chizhiwan"</note>, which looks like Winged Thistle. However, Red Fat Vine turns the color of blood when it comes into contact with wine; this is how it can be identified. <gloss>Song says</gloss> The Winged Thistle illustrated today in Taizhou has flowers like the single-petaled late chrysanthemum, purple in color, with five to seven flowers on a single stalk. The variety from Haizhou has purple-blue flowers like a single-petaled lotus; the lower stem and the area near the root are covered in white fuzz. The root is black, like a small turnip but finer, resembling an onion base. This is close to the Winged Thistle described by Tao [Hongjing]. However, they simply call it Rhapontic Root. Modern physicians rarely use Winged Thistle and cannot identify it accurately. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss> Winged Thistle is a type of mugwort. Su Song's *Illustrated Classic* suspected the Rhapontic Root from Haizhou was actually Winged Thistle. Shen Kuo's *Dream Pool Essays* also states that the root of Winged Thistle is like Greater Burdock but with fibrous tips. Under the ancient formula for "Rhapontic Root Powder," it says to "use the one with white fuzz," which proves the white-fuzzed one is undoubtedly Winged Thistle. Upon examination, these three substances are similar in qi, flavor, and function, and seem interchangeable. Perhaps one species has several varieties, or the names have differed across time and region.

It stops coughing caused by wind-evil and promotes the flow of breast milk. Long-term consumption improves the qi, brightens the eyes, and prevents aging. ### Ramie

<gloss>(*Separate Records*)</gloss> <insert>Name</insert> <gloss>(Shizhen says) Ramie <note>original: "Zhuma"</note> is used to make hempen cloth <note>original: "Zhu"</note>, hence the name. Generally, fine hemp fibers are called *Rui*, while coarse ones are called *Zhu*.</gloss> <gloss>Tao Hong[jing]</gloss>
<insert>Lower</insert> <insert>Grade</insert> <gloss>(Jing) Upon investigation, this is the modern "Continuous Ramie." The character for hemp (麻) consists of "shelter" (广) and "forest" (林); it is a pictograph of hemp being processed under a roof.</gloss> <insert>Collected</insert> <gloss>(Baosheng)</gloss> <gloss>(Song says) In the past, the origin of Ramie was not recorded. Today, it is found in many places across Shu [Sichuan] and the Jiangnan/Zhejiang regions. One can peel its bark to spin cloth. The sprouts grow seven to eight</gloss>
feet high. The leaves are like those of the **Paper Mulberry** <note>original: "Chu"</note> but without the deep lobes; the face is green and the back is white with short hairs. Between summer and autumn, it produces fine spikes of green flowers. The root is yellowish-white, soft, and hollow. Harvest in the second and eighth months. According to Lu Ji's *Commentary on the Classic of Poetry*, a single cluster of Ramie has dozens of stems; the perennial roots remain in the soil and sprout naturally in spring without needing replanting. It is planted in the various regions of Jing and Yang. It is harvested twice a year, the bark is peeled, and the thick outer surface is scraped off with bamboo to obtain the inner fiber, which is like sinew. This is boiled and used to weave cloth. This practice is still followed in the Jiangnan and Zhejiang regions. <gloss>Zongshi says</gloss> Ramie is like the stinging nettle; its flowers are like the White Poplar, forming long spikes. Each cluster has dozens of spikes, greenish-white in color. <gloss>(Shizhen says)</gloss> There is domestic ramie and also mountain or wild ramie. There is also "Purple Ramie" with purple-faced leaves. The "White Ramie" leaf has a green face; both have white backs. The roots can be scraped, washed, and boiled for food during famines; the taste is sweet and pleasant. The seeds are brown; they are collected in the ninth month and can be planted in the second month. Perennial roots also sprout on their own.

# Root
<gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Sweet, cold, and non-toxic. <gloss>Quan says: Sweet and balanced. Daming says: Sweet, cold, slippery, and non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Main indications</gloss> Stabilizing the fetus <note>used to prevent miscarriage or ease pregnancy complications</note>. Treats "heat-toxin" rashes <note>likely erysipelas, a bacterial skin infection</note>, clears heat in the heart and diaphragm to relieve thirst, treats vaginal bleeding during pregnancy, and eases restlessness before and after childbirth. It also treats seasonal epidemic fevers, extreme thirst, and mania. For those who have suffered heat-poisoning from mineral drugs <note>referring to "Jinshi" drugs, often toxic alchemical tonics containing lead or mercury</note>, as well as for arrow wounds and snake or insect bites. The extracted juice stops "wasting-thirst" <note>a condition often associated with diabetes in modern medicine</note>. <gloss>From the Separate Records</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss>: Ramie root is highly effective at tonifying *Yin* <note>the cooling, fluid-balancing aspect of the body</note> and moving stagnation. However, some professional pharmacists might ignore it because it is cheap and common, as if it were never used. <gloss>Zangqi says</gloss>: The nature of Ramie is to "break the blood" <note>disperse stasis</note>. If Ramie fiber is kept near a woman who has recently given birth, her silkworms will not survive <note>a folk belief suggesting the plant's potent "breaking" nature is harmful to delicate life-cycles</note>.

<insert>Appended Formulas</insert> <gloss>4 old, 7 new.</gloss>

> **Cough with Phlegm:** Char Ramie root until its medicinal nature is retained, then grind into powder. Dip three to five mace <note>a traditional unit of weight, roughly 3.7 grams</note> of raw tofu into the powder and eat it. It is effective and the condition will not return. <gloss>From Orthodox Manual of Medicine</gloss>
> **Cold Pain in the Stomach Duct:** Use half a tael <note>about 15-20 grams</note> each of Ramie root and clam shell powder. Grind into powder. Take two mace per dose with freshly drawn water on an empty stomach. 
> **Urinary Blockage (Strangury):** <gloss>From Selection of Mysterious Formulas</gloss> Wash and grind Ramie root, spread it on silk, and apply it to the lower abdomen. The urine will flow once the medicine is removed.
> <margin>Urinary Strangury</margin> This also treats various types of urinary blockages. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss>: Boiling Ramie root as a tea and drinking it frequently is excellent.
> <margin>Five Types of Strangury</margin>**Five Types of Urinary Blockage:** Take two stalks of Bitter Ramie root and crush them. Use one and a half basins of water and boil until seven-tenths remain. Drink it immediately. A yellow, glue-like juice (or juice like small red beans) will be passed. Even if the abdominal pain is unbearable, the blockage in the private parts will be cleared. Also treats all types of strangury. <gloss>From Sage-like Benefit Formulas</gloss>
> **Cessation of Menstruation in Women:** Pound raw Ramie root into a pulp and sit on it <note>a sitz bath or topical application</note>.
> **Sudden Deafness:** Pound Ramie root into a pulp, steam it, and grind it. Place it on a thin cloth. Boil four liters [of water/wine]. For each dose, use eighteen liters of water and half a liter of wine, boiling for one or two days. Effective for severe pain. <gloss>From Master Mei’s Formulas</gloss> 
> **Abscesses and Back Sores:** Boil Ramie root into a thick decoction and wash the area. Also, divide the decoction into two doses to drink. One version does not use silver. <gloss>From Binhu’s Collection of Simplified Formulas</gloss> <gloss>For early-stage swellings that have not yet formed a head, pound cooked Ramie root and apply it. Change the dressing day and night; the swelling will subside and heal.</gloss> <gloss>From Illustrated Classic</gloss>
> **Bone Stuck in Throat:** Boil Ramie root into a thick juice and gargle/swallow three times a day. This is for bones accidentally swallowed. A previously tested formula: Use the juice of pounded Ramie root and drip it in with a spoon; it works instantly. <gloss>From Great Medical Formulas</gloss>
> **Chicken Bone Stuck in Throat:** <gloss>From Secret Essentials from the Outer Terrace</gloss> Pound Wild Ramie root into juice and form into pills the size of a longan fruit. Swallow with fish bone soup or chicken bone soup.

# Leaf
<gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Same as the root. <gloss>Main indications</gloss> Bleeding from metal wounds <note>cuts from blades</note>, injuries, and fractures. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss>: Ramie leaves are very effective at dispersing blood stasis. Collect them on the fifth day of the fifth month <note>the Dragon Boat Festival, a traditional day for harvesting potent herbs</note>. Mix with lime, pound into balls, and dry in the sun for storage. When someone has a cut or injury, grind a ball into powder and apply it. The bleeding will stop immediately, and a scab will form easily. Note: Li Zhongnan’s *Classified Formulas* says: For all injuries where blood does not disperse, collect Wild Ramie and Perilla <note>Su</note> leaves in the fifth or sixth month. Pound them and apply to the wound. If blood remains in the abdomen causing distress, wring out the juice and drink it to dissolve the stasis.

# Ramie <gloss>Also pronounced "xiang"</gloss>

### Explanation of Names
<gloss>Shizhen says: The character for Ramie (Zhu) is sometimes written as Xie or Xie.</gloss>

### Collected Explanations
<gloss>Gong says:</gloss> This is the Ramie plant. People today harvest the bark to make cloth or soak it [to extract fibers]. The seeds resemble hemp seeds. Harvest in the ninth or tenth month and dry in the shade.
<gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is found everywhere. People in the north plant it to weave cloth and make ropes. The stalks grow four to five feet, sometimes six to seven feet high. The leaves resemble taro but are thinner, with yellow serrated flowers. The young seeds are flat and black, resembling the seeds of the Yellow Mallow. The stems are light, hollow, and pure white. Northerners take the bark to make "hemp" and use the reeds dipped in sulfur to make fire-starters <note>a primitive match</note>, as they catch fire very quickly. Children also eat the young seeds. When planting, the roots must be connected in clusters, which is why it is called "Zhu" <note>implying a clustering nature</note>.

# Great Blue
<term>Da Qing</term> <note>Likely *Isatis tinctoria* (Woad) or *Clerodendrum cyrtophyllum*, plants historically used both for blue dye and for clearing "heat-toxins" in the blood</note>
<gloss>Listed in the Middle Grade of the Separate Records</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: Its name comes from its deep blue leaves.</gloss>

<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>The Separate Records says: Harvest the leaves in the third or fourth month and dry them in the shade. Hongjing says: It is now produced in the eastern territories and border regions; it has purple stems about a foot long, and both the stems and leaves are used. Su Song says: Today, the stems and leaves are collected and shade-dried in the prefectures of Jiangdong. Shizhen says: It grows everywhere, reaching two to three feet in height. The stems are round, and the leaves are three to four inches long, green on the surface and pale on the underside, growing in opposite pairs. In the eighth month, it bears small red flowers in clusters. The blue fruit is the size of a Sichuan pepper; by the ninth month, the fruit turns red.</gloss>

### Stems and Leaves
<gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Bitter, "Great Cold" <note>extremely cooling</note>, non-toxic. <gloss>Zhen Quan says: Sweet. Shizhen says: Sweet and slightly salty, not bitter.</gloss>

# Main Indications
Treats seasonal headaches, intense heat <note>high fever</note>, and mouth sores <gloss>Separate Records</gloss>. Highly effective for seasonal epidemic "heat-toxins" <gloss>Tao Hongjing</gloss>. Treats "cold and heat" associated with pestilence <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>. Treats "Heat-Toxin Wind," irritability, thirst, dry mouth, fever in children, epidemic diseases, "Wind-Rash" <note>hives or rubella</note>, and poisoning from mineral drugs <note>toxic alchemical elixirs containing lead or mercury</note>. It neutralizes toxins, treats severe heat-poisoning causing skin peeling, jaundice, miasmas, and "Cinnabar Toxin" <note>erysipelas, a red skin infection</note> <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>. <gloss>Su Song says: Ancient formulas for treating "Cold Damage" (typhoid), "Yellow Sweat," and jaundice include "Great Blue Decoction." It is also used in "Root Decoctions" for typhoid headaches. It is widely used for seasonal diseases. # Fenugreek
<term>Hu Lu Ba</term> <note>*Trigonella foenum-graecum*. Known today as a culinary spice, but valued here as a powerful warming medicine.</note>
<gloss>Added during the Jiayou era of the Song Dynasty</gloss>

<gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Bitter Bean. <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> Yu Xi says: Fenugreek comes from Guangzhou and Qianzhou. It sprouts in spring, produces seeds in thin pods in summer, and is harvested in autumn. Most people today use the variety from Lingnan <note>Southern China</note>. Some say it is actually "Foreign Radish Seed," though this has not been fully verified. Su Song says: It currently comes from Guangzhou; some say the seeds come from various foreign lands in the South Seas, and are essentially the radish seeds of those countries. When merchants plant them here, they do sprout and grow, but they are not as high-quality as those brought from abroad. Today’s physicians consider it a vital medicine for treating "Cold-Deficiency of the Original Organ" <note>referring to the Kidneys and the body's foundational vitality</note>. Shizhen says: To use it as medicine, wash it clean, soak it in wine overnight, dry it in the sun, and then steam it until cooked or fry it.

**Qi and Flavor** Bitter, Greatly Warm, Non-toxic. <gloss>Jing says: It is Pure Yang <note>highly warming and activating</note></gloss>

**Main Indications** For Cold-Deficiency of the Original Organ. When the Qi is weak, combine it with Aconite and Sulfur. Within a year, after feeling a slight crawling sensation in the eye, the vision cleared. # Malin Seed
<term>Li Shi</term> <note>The seeds of *Iris lactea* var. *chinensis*. Used to stop bleeding and treat throat issues.</note>
<gloss>Listed in the Superior Grade of the Divine Husbandman's Classic</gloss>

<gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Li Shi <gloss>Separate Records</gloss>, Ma Lan Zi <gloss>Tang Materia Medica</gloss>, Ma Lian Zi <gloss>Illustrated Classic</gloss>. The "Monthly Ordinances" says the "Li" plant emerges in mid-winter; Zheng Xuan noted that "Li" is Malin. The *Tongsu Wen* says its name is Malin, and the Materia Medica calls it Li Shi. Su Song says: People mistakenly call it Ma Lian Zi. The *Guangya* says Malin is Li. Gao You says the phrase "Li sprouts" refers to this grass. Scholars who didn't recognize it called it "Li Ting," which is incorrect. Malin is also called "Pig's Ear," which is the same as Purslane. Shizhen says: The *Erya* says Wan (pronounced 'ping') is the Ma Wan. This is the Li grass...</gloss>

The leaves of Malan are already hard when they emerge from the soil and have no flavor; even horses and cattle refuse them, so how could humans eat them? For now, I dare not equate these seeds with Malan and will wait for a more learned scholar to decide. Li Shizhen counters: The *Bielu* notes that these seeds are also called *Li* <note>荔</note> seeds, which is simply a scribal error for the character *Li* <note>蠡</note>. Sun Bian’s *Guangya* clearly states that *Li* is another name for Malan. Furthermore, Prince Zhou Xian’s *Materia Medica for Relief of Famine* mentions that the tender shoots are bitter and "dry-hot" in nature; if soaked in water to remove the bitterness and seasoned with salt, they can indeed be eaten. Master Tao’s doubts were based only on hearsay; he was unfamiliar with many medicines, and I am now correcting this error.

# Great Burdock
<margin>Middle Grade in the *Records of Famous Physicians*</margin>
<gloss>Explanatory Names: Rat Stick <note>Bielu</note>, Burdock <note>Bielu</note>, Great Strength Seed <note>Gangmu</note>, Old Burdock Vegetable <note>Gangmu</note>, Leaning Ox <note>Gangmu</note>, Bat <note>Gangmu</note>, Insect-Ant <note>Gangmu</note>. Shizhen says: Its fruit is "ugly" <note>original: "E"</note> and has many prickly hooks, hence the name "Ugly Fruit" <note>E Shi</note>. Its roots and leaves are both edible. People call it "Ox Vegetable," and since the seeds catch on things like a "Rat Stick," it is compared to a sheep carrying things.</gloss>

The seed husks are very prickly; if a rat passes by, they cling to it and cannot be detached. **Collected Explanations** <gloss>The *Records of Famous Physicians* says: Great Burdock grows in the plains and marshes of Lushan. Su Gong states: Lushan is northeast of Dengzhou. This herb has leaves as large as taro; the flower heads resemble chestnuts. The seeds are small and long, like those of the common hedge-parsley. Wu Jie says: Great Burdock is indeed the seed of the Burdock plant. It is found everywhere. The leaves are like burdock leaves but longer. The seeds resemble grape pits but are brown. The outer husk is like a chestnut's but as small as a fingertip and very prickly. Some roots are extremely large and are prepared as a vegetable. People harvest the seeds for medicine after autumn. Shizhen says: Ancient people grew Burdock from seeds in fertile soil. They would cut the shoots and wash them to use as greens, and boil the roots to make preserves, saying it was very beneficial to health. Today, people rarely eat it. In the third month, the shoots emerge. The stems can reach three or four feet high. In the fourth month, it blooms in clusters of pale purple flowers. The fruit resembles maple pods but smaller. The calyx is covered in over a hundred fine prickles. One pod contains dozens of seeds. The largest roots are as thick as an arm and nearly a foot long, grey-black in color. Harvest the seeds in the seventh month and the roots in the tenth month.</gloss>

Meng Shen: Moistens the lungs, disperses qi, benefits the throat, removes wind from the skin, and opens the twelve meridians. Wang Haogu: Dissipates the toxins of rashes and spots. Shizhen.</gloss> <gloss>Li Gao says: Rat Stick Seed has four uses: it treats wind-dampness, hives, and throat wind.</gloss> <margin>Attached Formulas <gloss>Five old, eleven new</gloss></margin> **Wind-edema and body swelling** <gloss>Prepare two ounces of Rat Stick seeds, stir-fry and grind into powder. ## Cocklebur
<term>Cang'er</term> <note>Xanthium strumarium. Known for its prickly burrs that cling to fur and clothing.</note>
<gloss>Listed in the Middle Grade of the Classic</gloss> <gloss>Explanations of Names</gloss> **Barbarian Cocklebur** <gloss>from the Classic</gloss> **Constant Thought** <gloss>from Master Kong</gloss> **Grey Ear** <gloss>from the Erya</gloss> **Noble’s Ear** <gloss>from the Book of Songs</gloss> **Various Ears** <gloss>from the Outline</gloss> **Earrings** <gloss>from the Annotations to the Songs</gloss> **Earth Mallow** <gloss>from the Classic</gloss> **Sheep-borne** <gloss>from Tao Hongjing</gloss> **Priest’s Head** <gloss>from the Illustrated Classic</gloss> **Bright Roast** <gloss>from the Records</gloss> **Drink-up Herb** <gloss>from the Compendium</gloss> **Wild Eggplant** <gloss>from the Compendium</gloss>

**Collected Explanations**
> <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> The poets called it *Juan’er*, the *Erya* calls it *Cang’er* (Grey Ear), and the *Guangya* calls it *Zheng’er*. These names all refer to the shape of the fruit. Lu Ji’s *Annotations to the Songs* states that the fruit looks exactly like a woman’s earrings, which is why it is sometimes called "Earring Herb." Zheng Kangcheng identifies it as the "White Barbarian Flower." People in Youzhou call it "Noble’s Ear." The *Treatise on Curiosities* says: "In the city of Luoyang, a man once drove sheep into the region of Shu. The 'Barbarian Vegetable' seeds had many prickles that stuck to the sheep’s wool and thus reached China." This is why it is called "Sheep-borne." Locally, it is also called "Priest’s Head."
>
> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> Sojourners all eat it and call it the "Constant Thought" vegetable. It is used when the leaves are covered in yellow powder, though it is used very rarely in medical formulas.
>
> <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The leaves are shaped like hemp leaves and also like eggplant, hence the names "Wild Eggplant" and others. Its texture is slippery like a mallow, so it is called "Earth Mallow." This is the same plant mentioned by poets in the "Juan’er" chapter of the *Book of Songs*. The name "Constant Vegetable" appears in Zhang Yi’s *Guangya* and is also acceptable.
>
> <gloss>From the *Additional Records*:</gloss> Cocklebur grows in the wilds of Anding and Longchuan.
>
> <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is found everywhere today. Lu Ji’s *Annotations* says the leaves are a bluish-white similar to coriander. It has white flowers and thin stems that grow as a creeper; it can be boiled and eaten as a potherb, though it is slippery and has little flavor. In the fourth month, it produces seeds that look exactly like a woman’s earrings. Guo Pu says it is shaped like a mouse's ear and grows in clusters like a tray. What we see today is mostly like this and does not grow as a creeper.
>
> <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> According to Prince Zhou’s *Materia Medica for Famine Relief*, the Cocklebur's leaves are bluish-white and resemble "Sticky-Paste Vegetable." The fruit ripens in autumn and is smaller than a mulberry but covered in prickles. The tender shoots can be blanched in hot water, soaked, and seasoned to eat during famines. Its seeds can be roasted, peeled, and ground into flour to make flatbreads; they can also be pressed for oil to burn in lamps.

# The Stems and Leaves
<gloss>Preparation <gloss>Master Zhen says: Whenever gathered, remove the heart of the plant. Take Siberian Solomon's Seal (Huangjing) and slice it finely with a bamboo knife. Mix it with the Cocklebur and steam from the hour of the Snake to the hour of the Pig <note>approx. 9:00 AM to 11:00 PM</note>. Afterward, remove the Solomon’s Seal and dry the Cocklebur in the shade for use.</gloss></gloss>

<gloss>Nature and Flavor <gloss>Bitter, acrid, slightly cold, and slightly toxic. <margin>Master Su Gong says: Avoid pork, horse meat, rice-wash water, and ground cinnabar.</margin></gloss></gloss>

<gloss>Primary Indications <gloss><gloss>According to the Collected Records:</gloss> Wind-stroke, damage by cold, and headache. <gloss>The *Vegetable Materia Medica* states:</gloss> It treats "Great Wind" (leprosy), epilepsy, head-wind, and wind-dampness where the toxin is in the bone marrow or knee-cap. In summer, gather and sun-dry to grind into powder; take one or two spoonfuls with water. In winter, take with wine or make into pills (thirty pills, three times a day). After a hundred doses, the illness will exit the body like "gushing mustard seeds," or through sweating, or the skin will become mottled and scaly; once the old skin rises and falls away, the new muscle will be smooth as "congealed fat." It also makes one sleep less. <insert>It treats various other toxins and kills lice in rice-wash water.</insert> Long-term use sharpens the ears and eyes, lightens the body, and strengthens the will. <gloss>Master Su Gong notes:</gloss> The leaves receive the essence from below; they remove "saliva" (mucus), treat yellowing of the eyes, and excessive sleepiness. The ash, mixed with iron-filings and pig fat, can be applied to boils to draw them out. The root, boiled in wine, treats rabid dog bites. <gloss>Master Chen Zangqi says:</gloss> Gather in the eighth month. Master Li Shizhen says: Cocklebur is effective for dispelling "Wind-Qi" when taken over a long period. One must strictly avoid pork; if "Wind-Evil" attacks while taking it, red rashes will break out all over the body. According to the *Good Formulas of Su and Shen*: The roots, sprouts, leaves, and fruit should all be washed, dried, and burned to ash. Use hot water to leach the ash and collect the concentrated juice. Simmer this over a double-stove. As the liquid evaporates, add more juice from a nearby golden vessel. Keep the fire going day and night until it forms a "frost" (crystalline extract). Store in a dry bottle. Every morning and evening, take two *qian* with wine. It warms and supplements, dispels wind, and preserves a youthful complexion. It is especially good for "skin-wind," leaving the skin clean and clear. Adding a little to bathwater is also excellent. The official Chang Tongjian of Yizhou took this for over ten years; even in his late seventies, his skin was rosy and he was vigorous—all due to the power of this medicine. The *Formulas of the Slit Gate* say: For women where "Blood-Wind" attacks the brain, causing dizziness, fainting, or sudden collapse, use the tender hearts of Cocklebur (Xi-Xian grass), dry in the shade, grind to powder, and take one large spoonful with wine. Its effect is divine. <insert>Appended Formulas</insert> <gloss>Twelve old ones, sixteen new ones.</gloss></gloss></gloss>

*   **The All-Purpose Salve (Ten-Thousand Responses Salve):** <gloss>Treats all carbuncles, back-abscesses, "headless" malignant sores, swollen toxins, boils, wind-itch, leprosy, warts, hemorrhoids, toothaches, and throat blockages. It is extremely effective. This substance excels at clearing the "Nape Gate" and connecting to the skull—this is the Cocklebur.</gloss>
<margin>Gather the roots and leaves of Cocklebur on the fifth day of the fifth month. Gather several shoulder-loads, wash clean, let them wither in the sun, then chop finely. Boil in five large pots of water until soft and rotten. Strain through a sieve.</margin>
Remove the coarse dregs, filter again through silk cloth, and return to a clean pot. Boil over a fierce fire, then simmer over a low fire until it thickens into a paste. Store in a new jar and seal. Apply to the affected area for immediate recovery.

*   **For All Wind-Toxins:** <gloss>Also kills the "three worms" <note>parasites</note>, treats intestinal hemorrhoids, and improves appetite. Taking one spoonful daily with wine is extremely effective. From the *Collection of Simple Formulas*.</gloss>

<header>Treats all types of Wind-Qi, blood-wind leg sores, sudden water poisoning, "Gu" sorcery poisoning, venomous snake bites, chronic skin diseases, black facial spots, red nose, "Great Wind" leprosy, everted malignant sores, all types of carbuncles and boils, red and white dysentery, dental pain from "Wind," red and white eye pain, uncontrollable nosebleeds, bleeding from five types of hemorrhoids, and various types of postpartum dysentery. Harvest the leaves, wash them, dry them in the sun, then pound and sieve them. Each dose consists of a square-inch spoonful <note>An ancient measurement approximately equal to a modern tablespoon</note> taken with wine or rice water, two times during the day and three times at night. If you feel nauseous, mix the powder with honey to make pills, following the same dosage. For mild "Wind" conditions, take twice a day. If the body develops spots like millet or hemp seeds, this is the "Wind-toxin" exiting the body; you may use a needle to prick them and release the yellow fluid to stop the irritation. Harvesting is best in July or September.

**All types of "Wind-Qi"** <note>In traditional medicine, "Wind" refers to pathogens that move quickly through the body, causing symptoms like itching, dizziness, or paralysis.</note> Take one *dan* <note>a large volume measurement</note> of tender Cocklebur leaves, chop them, and mix with five *sheng* <note>pints</note> of wheat malt. Form into blocks and ferment within wormwood for twenty days until it becomes medicinal leaven <note>a fermented starter used in brewing medicinal ales</note>. Take one *dou* <note>decaliter</note> of the powder. Steam rice and, while still warm, mix in three *sheng* of the leaven to brew. Seal for seven days. Once matured, if you experience dizziness from "Wind," use sun-dried Cocklebur leaves ground into powder. Take one *qian* <note>approx. 3.75 grams</note> mixed with wine on an empty stomach. This is divinely effective. While sealing this wine, cover it with two layers of cloth to keep out "polluted" air. While taking this, avoid horse meat and pork.
<margin>From Meng Shen’s *Dietary Materia Medica*</margin>
If vomiting occurs, make pills with honey the size of a parasol tree seed. Take twenty pills per dose; you will be fully recovered in ten days.

# Common Carpesium (Tianmingjing) <gloss><insert>Originally in the Supreme Class of the *Divine Husbandman's Classic of Materia Medica*</insert> <insert>Revised</insert> Li Shizhen says: According to the accounts of Su Song and Shen Kuo, this entry now incorporates the plant known as "Crane-louse" (*Heshi*) from the *Tang Dynasty Materia Medica*. Other names from the *Miscellaneous Records* (*Bielu*) include: Heavenly Turnip (*Tianmanjing*), Heavenly Gate Essence (*Tianmenjing*), Ground Cabbage (*Disong*), Ground Pine (*Disong*), Ground-is-the-Same (*Yudidong*), Three Turnips (*Sanjing*), and Wheat-Stalk Ginger (*Maogujiang*). One name in the *Classic* is Toad Orchid (*Chanchulan*). Other names in the *Miscellaneous Records* include: Frog Indigo (*Xiamalan*). One name in the *Classic* is Pig's Head (*Shishou*). Also called Live Deer Herb (*Huolu cao*), Liu Peng's Herb (*Liupeng cao*), Centipede Herb (*Youyan cao*), Mother Pig's Mustard (*Muzhujie*), Crane-louse (*Heshi*), and Wild Ox-Knee (*Duniuxi*).</gloss>

<gloss>Su Gong <note>A Tang Dynasty pharmacologist</note> says: Common Carpesium is the "Live Deer Herb." The *Miscellaneous Records* also call it Heavenly Turnip. People in the south call it Ground Cabbage Leaf.</gloss>

The leaves resemble those of the turnip (*manjing*) and cabbage (*song*), which is why it bears these names. Its flavor is sweet and pungent, hence the name "Ginger." In appearance, it resembles indigo (*lan*), with very fine stems and leaves. Because it grows in damp, lowly places, it is called "Pig’s Stink" (*Xixian*) or "Pig’s Indigo" (*Xilan*). However, because its fragrance is similar to an orchid, it is also named "Toad Orchid." Li Shizhen says: "Common Carpesium" is a record of the "Heavenly Turnip." Its smell is like a pig (*shi* or *xi*), hence the names "Pig’s Head" and "Pig’s Stink." Ancient people called it "Live Deer Herb." Common folk, due to its fishy smell, mistakenly called it "Fox’s Waist." The *Erya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> calls it *Jilei* or "Pig’s Head." Guo Pu’s commentary notes that in the regions south of the Yangtze, it is called "Pig’s Head" and can be used to boil silkworm pupae for food. Chen Cangqi says: Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* claiming it is the same as "Wheat-Stalk Ginger" is incorrect. Tao Hongjing, in his notes on the "Fishing Camphor" entry, says there is an herb resembling "Wolf’s Teeth" with a pungent, foul smell called "Ground Cabbage," which people call "Liu Huan’s Herb," used to heal metal wounds. It is said that during the Yuanjia era of the Song Dynasty, Liu Huan of Qingzhou shot a deer and removed its five internal organs. He stuffed this herb into the cavity, and the deer suddenly stood up and ran. Liu, amazed, pulled the herb out, and the deer collapsed. This happened three times. Liu then secretly recorded the herb and planted it. It proved highly effective for healing fractures and wounds, which is why it bears his name, as well as the name "Live Deer."

---

### Collected Explanations <gloss><insert>Correcting Errors</insert> Tao Hongjing says: Common Carpesium is what is now called "Pig’s Stink" (*Xixian*), also named "Pig’s Head." During the summer months, one should drink its juice to remove heat-related illnesses. The flavor is very bitter, though some say it is sweet, which may be incorrect. Su Gong says: Pig’s Head is bitter and foul-smelling, while Carpesium is pungent and fragrant; they are entirely different species. Ma Yuxi says: Su Gong identifies Common Carpesium as what Southerners call "Ground Cabbage." Chen Cangqi's *Supplement to the Materia Medica* also states that Common Carpesium is "Ground Cabbage." The *Kaibao Materia Medica* should not have listed "Ground Cabbage" as a separate entry; it should have been combined here. Li Shizhen says: According to Shen Kuo’s *Dream Pool Essays*, people neither recognize Common Carpesium nor realize that Ground Cabbage is actually *Huoqi*. Furthermore, the *Materia Medica* includes a separate entry for "Crane-louse" (*Heshi*), creating total confusion. They do not realize that Ground Cabbage is simply Common Carpesium. Its leaves resemble pine and also turnips, hence the two names. "Crane-louse" is specifically its fruit. Additionally, the "Ground Cabbage" listed under "Medicinal Cabbages" in the *Miscellaneous Records* is an error and is merged here. The plant looks somewhat like peppermint, with purple-white flowers and a pungent, fragrant taste. Ri Hua says: Ground Cabbage grows everywhere, near homes and in shaded areas by roadsides. It stands two to three inches tall. The leaves resemble cabbage leaves but are smaller. He also says: Crane-louse from Persia is superior, though it is currently produced in Shangdang, where the leaves are thinner than the Persian variety. Da Ming says: Crane-louse grows in the Northwest; the seeds resemble those of lotus-wormwood but are finer. The stems and leaves are used together. Su Song says: Common Carpesium is found throughout the rivers and lakes. Its appearance matches Han Baosheng’s description. He also says: Crane-louse is found in the Jiang-Huai and Heng-Xiang regions. In spring, it sprouts wrinkled leaves like purple perilla, but larger, pointed, long, and not shiny. The stem is about two feet tall. In the seventh month, it produces yellow-white flowers like chrysanthemums. In the eighth month, it bears fruit. The seeds are extremely sharp and fine, turning yellowish-black when dry. Southerners call the leaves *Huoqi*. Note: *Huoqi* is actually *Xixian* (Siegesbeckia); although the flowers and fruit are similar, they are different species and cannot be used interchangeably. Shizhen says: The young shoots of Common Carpesium are green and resemble wrinkled cabbage leaves, with a slight "fox-like" odor. They can be eaten if washed and blanched. As they grow, they produce stems and small yellow flowers like wild chrysanthemums. The seeds resemble those of fennel or wormwood and are very sticky to clothing. The "fox odor" becomes very strong, but it becomes fragrant when roasted. This is why various authors call it "pungent and fragrant." It is similar to how people in the south eat "Mountain Cress" (*Shanjia*). Its roots are white, resembling short Ox-Knee (*Niuxi*). This plant is very common and cheap. Why then did the *Tang Materia Medica* say Crane-louse comes from the Western Regions and the *Song Materia Medica* say it comes from Persia? It is likely because, at that time, its use was unknown in China, and only the Western Rong and Persian peoples knew how to use it as medicine. It was also suited to their climate. This is similar to the saying that it comes from the Western Regions, while failing to realize that the herb used to feed horses in China is the very same plant. Further details can be found under the entry for *Xixian*.</gloss>

# Siegesbeckia
<note>original: 豨薟, *Xixian*</note>

The **Mother of Pig Lard** <note>original: 豬膏母, *Zhugaomu*</note> grows in flat marshes and low, damp places everywhere. It has several names: **Tiger Lard** <note>original: 虎膏, *Hugao*</note> and **Dog Lard** <note>original: 狗膏, *Gougao*</note>. Its leaves resemble the **Cocklebur** <note>original: 蒼耳, *Canger*</note>, and its stems are round and covered in fine hairs. **Su Song** <note>A famous Song Dynasty scholar</note> states: Siegesbeckia is found in all regions. In spring, it produces seedlings with leaves that look like mustard greens but are narrower and longer. The stems are thick, and the plant grows two to three feet high. In early autumn, it produces flowers resembling sesame, and its seeds are much like **Crane-louse** <note>original: 鶴蝨, *Heshi*, the seeds of Common Carpesium</note>. The leaves are collected in summer and dried in the sun. **Chen Zangqi** <note>A Tang Dynasty pharmacologist</note> says: The "Pig Lard Herb" has leaves like the **Perilla** <note>original: 荏, *Ren*</note> and is covered in hairs. **Sun Sheng** says: The leaves resemble Cocklebur; two branches grow opposite each other, and both stems and leaves have yellowish-white hairs. The seedlings are harvested and sun-dried between the third and sixth lunar months.

**Li Shizhen** states: According to Su Gong’s *Tang Materia Medica*, Siegesbeckia was said to taste like **Winter Cherry** <note>original: 酸漿, *Suanjiang*</note>, while "Mother of Pig Lard" was said to resemble Cocklebur, treating them as two separate species. However, Cheng Dao’s memorial on "Siegesbeckia Pills" states that this medicine differs from earlier descriptions: it grows mostly in fertile soil, stands about three feet tall, and has opposite leaves and nodes. Zhang Yong’s memorial on the same pills describes the herb as having "golden edges and silver threads, a plain stem and purple leaves growing from opposite nodes." In the **Sichuan** <note>original: 蜀, *Shu*</note> region, it is called **Fire Paulownia** <note>original: 火楸, *Huoqiu*</note>, and its wide leaves are quite similar to Cocklebur. Furthermore, **Shen Kuo** notes in his *Dream Pool Essays* that people mistakenly identify "Ground Cabbage" as Fire Paulownia. He argues that those following the method of taking "Fire Paulownia" are actually using Ground Cabbage, and that Siegesbeckia (Mother of Pig Lard) was mistakenly listed as a duplicate entry by later generations who did not recognize it.

Faced with these differing opinions, how should one choose the correct herb for treating **Wind-Paralysis** <note>original: 風痺, *Fengbi*, a condition involving numbness and loss of motor function</note>? I, Shizhen, have gathered these various herbs to examine them closely. The "Pig Lard Herb" has ridges on its stems and spots at the tips of its leaves. The leaves resemble Cocklebur but are slightly longer; they resemble Ground Cabbage but are thinner. They grow from opposite nodes, and the stems and leaves are covered in fine hairs. In rich soil, a single plant can branch out significantly. In the eighth or ninth month, it opens small, deep-yellow flowers. The centers contain long seeds similar to **Artemisia** seeds, and the outer calyx has fine prickles that stick to clothing. 

In contrast, **Ground Cabbage** <note>original: 地菘, *Disong*</note> has a green, round stem without ridges, spots, or hair. Its leaves are wrinkled like **Loose-leaf Tea**, and they do not grow from opposite nodes. Observing this, the descriptions by Cheng and Zhang appear more accurate. Today, in **Chenzhou, Henan**, Siegesbeckia is collected as a local tribute, and its appearance matches the "Pig Lard Herb." Therefore, Shen Kuo’s claim that Siegesbeckia is the same as Mother of Pig Lard is not unfounded. Su Gong’s description of it tasting like Winter Cherry was likely a mistake, confusing it with **Black Nightshade** <note>original: 龍葵, *Longkui*</note>. 

However, Shen Kuo’s statement that people should use Ground Cabbage instead of Mother of Pig Lard contradicts Cheng and Zhang. Upon review, while the original entries for Siegesbeckia and Mother of Pig Lard do not specifically mention treating "Wind," the entry for Ground Cabbage in the *Divine Husbandman’s Classic* <note>original: 本經, *Benjing*</note> does mention "removing paralysis and heat; long-term consumption makes the body light and resistant to aging." This suggests Ground Cabbage might be the intended treatment. Yet, the formulas submitted by Cheng and Zhang to the Emperor could not have been erroneous. Perhaps both herbs possess the power to treat Wind? Since modern patients using the Mother of Pig Lard variety of Siegesbeckia often see results, and I see no one using Ground Cabbage for this purpose, there is no need to doubt that Siegesbeckia is the correct ingredient for the "Pig Lard Pills."

# Siegesbeckia is bitter, cold, and slightly toxic. Others say "Mother of Pig Lard" is bitter, neutral, and non-toxic.
<gloss>Chen Zangqi says: It is slightly toxic. It is an error to say it is non-toxic like the other herb "Pig Lard."</gloss>

# It is also said that Mother of Pig Lard primarily treats incised wounds, stops pain, halts bleeding, and promotes the growth of new flesh. It eliminates various malignant sores, dissolves scrofula and goiters. It is effective when used as a wash, a steamed poultice, or applied as a powder.
<gloss>Su Gong</gloss>

# Primary Treatments
<gloss>Su Gong</gloss>
Treats chronic and phlegm-based malaria (consume the juice to induce vomiting); pound and apply to tiger wounds, dog bites, spider bites, bee stings, and scorpion stings. It treats **Wind-Qi** <note>term: A pathological force in traditional medicine associated with sudden onset and movement, often causing numbness or tremors</note> in the hands and feet, paralysis of the four limbs, bone pain, knee weakness, and various sores caused by Wind-Dampness. <gloss>Li Shizhen’s elaboration</gloss>

**Su Song** states: The people of Sichuan have a method for taking Siegesbeckia alone. On the 5th day of the 5th month, the 6th day of the 6th month, or the 9th day of the 9th month, collect the leaves and discard the roots, stems, flowers, and fruit. Wash them clean and dry them in the sun. Place them in a steamer, sprinkling each layer with wine and honey. Steam and then sun-dry; repeat this process **nine times** <note>term: *Jiu Zheng Jiu Bao*, a traditional "Nine Steams and Nine Suns" processing method to transform a herb's properties</note>. The aroma and taste will become extremely fragrant and pleasant. Grind this into a fine powder and form into pills with honey. It is said to greatly benefit the **Original Qi** <note>term: The foundational energy of the body</note>. It treats Wind-Qi in the Liver and Kidneys, numbness in the limbs, coldness in the bones, and weakness in the waist and knees. It also helps move Qi in the large intestine. 

While most regions agree it is cold and slightly toxic, the prefectures of Wenzhou and Gaoying claim it is hot and non-toxic, and that taking it supplements the five internal organs, promotes hair growth, and treats Wind-Dampness sores and muscle paralysis. It is especially suitable for women with chronic "cold" conditions. They use the stems, leaves, flowers, and fruits together for the steaming and drying process. These two accounts differ—perhaps using only the leaves makes it cold and toxic, while including the branches and seeds makes it hot and non-toxic? Or perhaps the properties differ based on the land where it grows? 

**Li Shizhen** clarifies: If the fresh juice is consumed, it causes vomiting, which is why it is called "slightly toxic." If it is processed through the "nine steams and nine suns" method, it becomes a supplement that removes paralysis, which is why it is called "non-toxic." Its nature is cold when raw and warm when cooked; it is not for clearing heat. 

**Tang Shenwei** <note>A Song Dynasty physician</note> notes: According to the memorial for the "Siegesbeckia Pill Formula" submitted by Zhang Yong, the Military Governor of Jiangling: "I have a younger brother, Zhang Song, who at age twenty-one suffered a stroke and was bedridden for five years. A hundred doctors could not cure him. There was a Daoist named Zhong Zhen who, out of concern for my brother's suffering, said: 'If he takes Siegesbeckia pills, he will surely recover.' This herb grows in fertile soil, about three feet tall, with opposite nodes and leaves. Harvest it from the fifth month onward. Cut it five inches above the ground, wash away the mud with warm water, and pluck the leaves and branch tips. Steam and sun-dry nine times—it does not need to be excessively dry, just sufficiently processed. Grind it thoroughly into a powder and mix with refined honey to make pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take twenty pills on an empty stomach with warm wine or water..."

It details the herb's use for paralysis and skin conditions, emphasizing that the "nine steams and nine suns" processing method removes its toxicity and transforms it into a warming tonic.</summary>

# Reed
<gloss>Listed in the Lower Class of the *Additional Records*.</gloss> Standard Name <gloss>Also called *Wei*, *Tan*, or *Jia*.</gloss>

<gloss>Collected Explanations:</gloss> Su Gong says: Reed roots grow in low, damp places. The stems and leaves resemble bamboo. The flowers are like those of the silvergrass and are called *Pengbu*. Harvest the roots in the second and eighth lunar months and dry them in the sun. <gloss>Su Song says: Today they are found everywhere, growing in low, damp marshes and ponds. Their appearance is much like bamboo, with leaves wrapping around the stem, no branches, and white flowers forming spikes like cogon grass. The roots also resemble bamboo roots but with wider-spaced nodes. For medicinal use, take the sweet and pungent roots from underwater; those that are exposed or floating are unusable. According to Guo Pu’s notes on the *Erya* dictionary: *Jia* is the young reed; *Wei* is the mature reed. *Tan* resembles the *Wei* but is smaller and solid-hearted; in the Jiangdong region, it is called *Quchu* or *Xi*, which is the silvergrass. By autumn, when it hardens, it is called *Huan*. *Jian* is similar to *Huan* but thinner and taller, reaching several feet; Jiangdong calls it *Jian*. Their flowers are all called *Tiao*. Their sprouts are all called *Shao* and are edible like bamboo shoots. If this is so, then *Lu* and *Wei* are the same plant. They are what people use today to make mats, though few can distinguish between *Jian*, *Tan*, *Lu*, and *Wei*. Northern people consider *Wei* and *Lu* to be two species. The tall, hollow ones with thin, white skin are *Jia*, *Lu*, and *Wei*. Those shorter than the *Wei* with hollow centers but thick, bluish-green skin are *Tan*, *Wan*, or *Shan*. The shortest ones with solid centers are *Jian* and *Lian*. These names are based on their stages of growth. Their bodies are all bamboo-like, and their leaves are long like chopsticks. Their medicinal properties are the same. Those that have not yet sprouted were called "purple sheaths" in ancient times. When selecting reed roots, they must be from a place where the water flows against the current, and they should be yellow, thick, and fleshy. Remove the hair-like fibers, nodes, and reddish-yellow skin before use.</gloss>

# Sweet Banana
<gloss>From the *Supplementary Records*; Middle Grade</gloss>

## Also named "Bashao"
<gloss>From the *Extension of Meanings*</gloss> **Tianju** <gloss>From the *Records of the Grand Historian*</gloss> **Baju** <gloss>Li Shizhen says: According to Lu Dian’s *Pi Ya*, the banana tree does not shed its leaves; as one leaf unfolds, another withers (scorches), hence it is called "Jiao" <note>sounds like the word for "scorched" or "dried"</note>. Commonly, dry things are called "Ba"; "Ba" is also a synonym for "Jiao." Ji Sheng's "Rhapsody on the Banana" says: The bamboo bears fruit but its root is bitter; the banana unfolds flowers while the stalk withers. "Baju" is a phonetic shift from "Bajiao." People of Shu (Sichuan) call it "Tianju." Cao Shuya's *Record of Extraordinary Things* says: The banana bears fruit, its skin is red as fire and its flesh sweet as honey; eating four or five is enough.</gloss>

### Collected Explanations
Tao Hongjing says: The sweet banana originally came from Guangzhou. Now they are found throughout the region east of the Yangtze. The roots and leaves are identical, but only the fruit of certain types is unfit to eat. Su Gong says: Those from Lingnan (the south) have large fruit with a flavor that can satisfy one's hunger, and the sweet taste lingers between the teeth, hence the name "Sweet Banana." Kou Zongshi says: In the north, they only produce flowers and no fruit. Su Song says: Today, they are found in the two Guang provinces, Fujian, and Sichuan. Those from Fujian and Guangxi are extremely sweet and delicious to eat. In other places, the fibers are used to make rope, and they rarely flower. Recently, they have been planted extensively in the Central Provinces; these are all "Bashao" <note>ornamental plantains</note>. There are many varieties. Those with fruit are called "Sweet Bananas." A stalk emerges from the center of the heart to form a flower. Initially, it produces a large bud resembling a hanging lotus. It has over a dozen layers, each forming a petal. When the petals open, the flowers emerge from within, becoming very lush. Red ones are like torches and are called "Red Bananas." White ones are the color of wax and are called "Water Bananas." The flowers look much like ivory, so they are called "Ivory Bananas." The fruit also differs between green and yellow. There are many varieties, the sweetest of which can be dried and sent to distant places. In the north, they are considered precious fruits. The stalks can be broken down into silk-like fibers; people treat them with lye to spin and weave into a cloth called "Jiao-Ge" <note>banana-fiber cloth</note>. Kou Zongshi says: After three years, the banana tree flowers. A stalk emerges from the center, bearing a single flower that looks exactly like a lotus. The petals are similar, but the color is a pale yellowish-green. There is no stamen in the center; it is entirely made of flower-leaves. The flower head always hangs downward. A single blossom opens in mid-summer and does not finish until after mid-autumn. Usually, for every three leaves that open, three flowers follow.

...leaves fall away. <gloss>Li Shizhen states: According to Wan Zhen's *Records of Extraordinary Things from the Southern Regions*, the "Sweet Banana" <note>original: 甘蕉 (*Ganjiao*); here referring to the edible banana/plantain family</note> is actually the *Bajiao*. It is a type of herb, though its stalk resembles a tree trunk. Large specimens reach over a "span" <note>approx. 5-6 feet</note> in circumference. The leaves are about ten feet long and one to two feet wide. The stalks are hollow and soft like those of a taro plant, consisting of layers of overlapping skin. The root resembles a taro bulb, blue-green in color, with the largest being the size of a wagon hub. The flowers bloom at the end of the stalk, shaped like wine cups and colored like lotus flowers. The fruits form within "rooms" <note>clusters or hands</note> as the flower grows. Each flower cluster contains six fruits that develop in succession; they do not grow or fall all at once. There are three main types of banana: when unripe they are bitter and astringent, but when ripe they are sweet and brittle, tasting like grapes, and can satisfy hunger. One type is as thick as a thumb and six to seven inches long, pointed like a goat’s horn; these grow in pairs and are called "Goat Horn Bananas." Their skin peels to reveal a yellowish-white flesh that is exceptionally sweet. Another type is the size of a chicken egg, resembling a cow's udder; these are called "Cow Milk Bananas" and have a slightly lesser flavor. A third type is the size of a lotus seed, four to five inches long and square-shaped; these have the weakest flavor. All can be preserved in honey as a fruit. Furthermore, Gu Jie’s *Records of Sea Voyages* notes that in the South Seas, bananas flower and fruit year-round. He mentions two types: the "Board Banana," which is large and bland, and the "Buddha Hand Banana," which is small and sweet. In those regions, they are simply called "bananas," unlike in the Jiangnan region where they flower but rarely bear fruit. Fan Chengda’s *Treatise on the Gui Sea* mentions several southern varieties; the large ones do not wither in winter. A central stalk several feet long produces flowers at every joint. After the flowers fade, the fruits appear at the base of the leaves. Once peeled, the flesh is soft and creamy like a green persimmon, with a very sweet and cooling flavor. They fruit in all four seasons. Locals feed them to children to "remove guest heat" <note>temporary fevers or inflammations caused by external factors</note>. The fruit is also called the "Ox Banana." Its juice is used to clear the eyes and relieve pain. A variety with a sweet-sour taste and a light coating of frost is called the "Dried Banana." The "Chicken Egg Banana" is smaller than the Ox type and also fruits year-round. The "Tooth Banana" is smaller than the Chicken type and is particularly fragrant, tender, and delicious, though it only fruits in early autumn. The "Red Banana" has slender leaves like a reed; its flowers are deep red like pomegranate blossoms. If one or two leaves are broken off daily, a spot of bright green appears inside, which is quite lovely. It blooms from spring to late autumn and is commonly known as the "Beauty Banana" <note>often identified as *Canna indica*</note>. The "Eaves-Front Banana" has roots that resemble a saturated gallbladder flask when the soil is fertile. Additionally, Fei Xin’s *Overall Survey of the Starry Raft* notes that many southern countries lack cereal grains and instead plant bananas and coconuts, using their fruit as a staple food.</note>

<insert>Properties:</insert> Sweet, very cold, and non-toxic. <gloss>Zongshi says: Its nature is cold and not beneficial to health; eating too much will disturb one's "cold qi" <note>the body's internal thermal balance</note>.</gloss>

# Wild Ginger (Ranghe)
<gloss>Middle Grade entry from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> <gloss>Revised: moved here from the Vegetable Department and combined with "Veil Grass" (*Micao*)</gloss>

It also grows in the north. In early spring, the leaves emerge looking like small banana leaves. The roots and shoots are thick and fleshy. The leaves wither in winter. The roots are suitable for pickling. It loves shade; those growing under water are particularly excellent. Pan Yue’s *Poetic Exposition on Idle Living* says: "Wild Ginger clings to the shade, while seasonal vegetables face the sun." Kou Zongshi's *Record of Seasons in Jing and Chu* notes that in mid-winter, Wild Ginger is preserved with salt for winter storage. It is also used to treat *Gu* toxins <note>a form of sorcery-based poisoning</note>. The *Lexicon of Urgent Tasks* mentions that Wild Ginger is stored in winter; its use goes back a long time. There are red and white varieties. The white is used in medicine, while the red is edible and often used to make plum-glazes. Before the flower decays, it is edible; after a long time, it rots. It resembles ginger and thrives in shaded, damp earth. One planting lasts forever without needing weeding, just add manure. In early August, tread down the seedlings.</gloss> <gloss>Processing: When using, do not use "Leathery Ox Grass," which looks very similar but is fishy and astringent.</gloss> If the seedlings are killed <note>by treading</note>, the roots will grow more vigorously. In the ninth month, take the side-growing roots for pickling or preserving in soy paste. In mid-October, cover the roots with chaff so they do not freeze to death during winter. When using White Wild Ginger, use a copper knife to scrape off one layer of thick skin. Slice it finely, grind it into a paste in a mortar, and extract the natural juice. Simmer it down and spread it on a new vessel to cool until it looks like dry glue, then scrape it off for use.

## Ephedra (Mahuang)
<gloss>Middle Grade entry from the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss> <insert>Also named</insert> Dragon Sand (*Longsha*) <gloss>from the *Compendium of Materia Medica*</gloss>; Black Salt (*Heiyan*) <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* and Li Shizhen state: these names are quite difficult to explain; some say the name Mahuang comes from its numbing ("ma") taste and yellow ("huang") color, but it is uncertain if this is correct.</gloss>

<gloss>Collection of Notes</gloss> The *Miscellaneous Records* state: Ephedra grows in the lands of Jin and Hedong.
Today, that which comes from Qingzhou, Pengcheng, and Lanyang is considered superior. The stalks should be blue-green and produce much foam. It also grows in Sichuan, but that variety is not as good. <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> It is most abundant in Yingtai of Zhengzhou, Langzhong, and on the sandy islands in the rivers of Shayuan. spring, and by the fifth month of summer, they grow to over a foot long. The tips have yellow flowers and bear fruit that looks like small joined petals, somewhat resembling soap pod seeds. The taste is sweet with a slight numbing Ephedra-like quality. The outer skin is red, the inner kernel is black, and the root is purplish-red. <gloss>Common lore says</gloss> there are male and female types. The female flowers in the third or fourth month and bears fruit in the sixth month. The male has no flowers and bears no fruit. Harvest the stems after the Beginning of Autumn and dry them in the shade. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The skin of the root is yellowish-red; the longer roots are those that grew closer to people.

### The Category of Herbs

Decoctions such as Ephedra Decoction, Pueraria Decoction, and both the Major and Minor Blue Dragon Decoctions all utilize Ephedra to treat Lung-related disorders and "rebellious Qi" <note>original: "上氣" (shangqi); a condition where breath or energy moves upward inappropriately, causing coughing or wheezing</note>. Formulas like Blackberry Lily and Ephedra Decoction or Magnolia Bark and Ephedra Decoction are considered "Major Formulas." The *Jing* <note>The Classic of Materia Medica</note> states: "Light substances can remove excess," and Ephedra and Pueraria belong to this category. When the "Six Excesses" <note>the six environmental pathogens: Wind, Cold, Summer-heat, Damp, Dryness, and Fire</note> invade the "striae" <term>腠理 (couli); the microscopic spaces between the skin and muscles where Qi flows</term> and the pores, the skin becomes blocked. This prevents the "Nutritive and Guard Qi" <note>the body's internal nourishment and external defense systems</note> and the blood from circulating, which is called a state of "Excess." Because Ephedra is a "light and clear" herb in its nature, it can remove this blockage.

Ephedra is slightly bitter, and its stem is hollow. It possesses "Yang within Yin" properties and enters the Foot Greater Yang <note>Taiyang</note> Cold Water Channel <note>the Bladder Meridian</note>. Its thin stems are even capable of directing energy downward. Being cold in its original nature but having been exposed to external cold, it is suitable for inducing sweating to expel cold pathogens from the "Qi level" of the skin and hair, thereby venting the "excess" of the exterior. However, if over-prescribed, it causes excessive sweating which "exhausts the Yang" <note>a dangerous state of collapse where the body's warming energy is lost</note>. It must be strictly avoided for those with fatigue from diet or labor, or those recovering from illness with spontaneous sweating—cases of "Exterior Deficiency"—as it will deplete the person's Primal Qi <note>Yuan Qi</note>.

The scholar Wang Haogu said: "Ephedra is the medicine for 'Excess in the Guard Qi,' while Cinnamon Twig is for 'Deficiency in the Guard Qi.'" Although both are used for Greater Yang <note>Taiyang</note> disorders, they are actually medicines for the Nutritive and Guard systems. The Heart governs the Nutritive Qi (Blood), and the Lung governs the Guard Qi. Therefore, Ephedra is the agent for the Hand Greater Yin Lung Meridian, and Cinnamon Twig is the agent for the Hand Lesser Yin Heart Meridian. Using Ephedra and Cinnamon Twig for coughs caused by "Cold Damage" or "Wind Damage" is the very source of medicinal decoctions.

Li Shizhen notes: Ephedra is the specific medicine for the Lung Meridian; thus, it is frequently used to treat Lung diseases. When Zhang Zhongjing treated "Cold Damage," he used Ephedra if there was no sweating and Cinnamon Twig if there was sweating. Famous physicians of subsequent generations have explained this, but most followed the text literally without investigating its subtle essence. I have researched this and reached a conclusion different from the ancients. 

It is said that "fluids become sweat," and sweat is essentially blood. When blood is in the Nutritive level, it is blood; when it reaches the Guard level, it is sweat. In "Great Cold Damage," the Nutritive level is blocked by blood internally and cannot communicate with the Guard level externally. The Guard Qi is tightly closed, and fluids cannot flow, resulting in fever without sweat and a hatred of cold. In "Wind Damage," the Guard Qi leaks outward and cannot protect the Nutritive level internally. The Nutritive Qi becomes weak and fluids are not held firm, resulting in fever with sweating and a hatred of wind. Both Wind and Cold pathogens enter through the skin and hair. The skin is the "correlative" of the Lungs; the Lungs govern the Guard Qi and envelop the entire body like the heavens. Although these symptoms belong to the Greater Yang <note>Taiyang/Bladder</note> stage, the Lungs actually receive the pathogenic Qi. If the symptoms include a red face, a feeling of being stifled, coughing with phlegm, panting, and chest fullness, are these not Lung diseases? 

When the skin and hair are closed externally, pathogenic heat attacks internally, causing the Lung Qi to become pent-up and congested. Therefore, Ephedra and Licorice are used alongside Cinnamon Twig to lead the pathogen out from the Nutritive level to the surface. Apricot Kernel is added to drain the Lungs and facilitate Qi. If there is no major heat after sweating but panting remains, Gypsum is added. Zhu Gong’s *Book of Living People* suggests adding Gypsum and Anemarrhena in the summer; these are all medicines to drain "Lung Fire." Thus, although Ephedra Decoction is a heavy formula for inducing sweat in the Greater Yang stage, it is actually a medicine for dispersing "Fire Stagnation" in the Lung Meridian. 

If the striae are not tight, fluids leak out and the Lung Qi becomes deficient. When "Deficiency" occurs, one should "tonify the Mother" <note>a Five Elements principle where the Spleen/Earth is the mother of the Lung/Metal</note>. Therefore, Cinnamon Twig and Licorice are used to disperse the "Wind Pathogen" externally to stabilize the surface, while internally "subduing the Wood" <note>the Liver</note> to protect the "Earth" <note>the Spleen</note>. Peony is added to "drain the Water" and stabilize the Spleen—this is "draining the East to tonify the West." Ginger and Jujube are used to move the Spleen's fluids and harmonize the Nutritive and Guard levels. If there is slight panting after purging, Magnolia Bark and Apricot Kernel are added to benefit the Lung Qi. If the pulse is deep and slow after sweating, Ginseng is added to augment the Lung Qi. Zhu Gong’s addition of Scutellaria for "Yang-Dawn Decoction" is to drain Lung Heat. All of these are Spleen and Lung medicines. Thus, while Cinnamon Twig is a light formula for "releasing the muscles" in the Greater Yang stage, it is actually a medicine for regulating the Spleen and rescuing the Lungs. This is a secret that has not been revealed for a thousand years. 

Because of this "Exterior" relationship, I have compared them. Furthermore, for Lesser Yin <note>Shaoyin</note> disease with fever and a deep pulse, there are Ephedra, Aconite, and Asarum Decoction, and Ephedra, Aconite, and Licorice Decoction. Since Lesser Yin and Greater Yang are in an "Interior-Exterior" relationship, the medicine moves toward the exterior. The use of Aconite paired with Ephedra represents "releasing [the pathogen] from within a tonifying [formula]."

A certain "Brocade-Clad Guard" <note>Jin Yi; a high-ranking military official</note> had been drinking wine until dawn during the summer months. He fell ill with "Water and Grain" diarrhea <note>diarrhea containing undigested food</note> that did not stop for several days. The food went straight through him. When Shizhen examined him, his pulse was floating and relaxed, his large intestine was prolapsed, and he had developed bleeding hemorrhoids. This was because the mixed intake of meat and cold tea had suppressed the Yang Qi in the lower body. It was a case of "Wood flourishing and Earth weakening" <note>Liver overacting on the Spleen</note>, described in medical classics as "Long-standing wind becoming grain-diarrhea." The correct method was to "raise and scatter" the energy. I administered "Minor Continuation of Life Decoction" (Xiao Xuming Tang). After one dose, he was cured. Formerly, when Zhang Zhongjing treated Cold Damage on the sixth or seventh day after heavy purging—where the pulse was deep and slow, limbs were cold, and the throat was <insert>Supplementary Formulas</insert> <gloss>5 old, 7 new</gloss> ...not [sore], or for those spitting pus and blood with unstoppable diarrhea—he used Ephedra Decoction to balance the Liver and Lungs while simultaneously "raising and releasing" the energy. This follows the same logic. If one can understand this divinely, many such cases can be solved.

Boil in four *sheng* <note>liters</note> of water until it reduces to two *sheng*, removing the foam. Add one spoonful of glutinous rice and some fermented soy <insert>Cold Damage Dew Decoction</insert>. First, use five *shi* four *dou* <note>large volume measures</note> of snow water... take a bath in the decoction, then eat thin porridge and cover up warmly to induce sweat, and you will recover. <gloss>A proven formula.</gloss> Clean the Ephedra and place it in a cauldron on a stove facing east for three nights. ### Clinical Applications

**Edema:** If the pulse is deep, the condition belongs to the Lesser Yin <note>original: "少陰" (Shaoyin); referring to the Kidney and Heart systems</note>. If the pulse is floating, it indicates Qi deficiency. If there is abdominal distension, it is caused by stagnant Qi and is not a "water" disorder. Use **Ephedra and Prepared Aconite Decoction** to induce sweating: Take three *liang* of Ephedra, boil in seven *sheng* of water and skim off the foam. Add two *liang* of Licorice and one piece of prepared Aconite <note>Aconite (Fuzi) is a potent warming herb used to revive depleted Yang energy</note>. Boil until two and a half *sheng* remain. Take eight *fen* per dose, three times a day, to induce sweating. — *From Zhang Zhongjing’s Essential Prescriptions from the Golden Cabinet (Jingui Yaolue)*

**Wind-Damp Pain (Wind Bi):** <gloss>Take five *liang* of Ephedra (roots removed) and two *liang* of Cinnamon Heart. Grind into a powder. Add two *sheng* of wine and simmer over a slow fire until it thickens like melted tin. Take one spoonful mixed with warm wine until sweating occurs. — From the Formulas of Divine Beneficence (Shenghui Fang)</gloss>

**Chronic Infantile Convulsions (Spleen-Wind):** <gloss>Occurs after vomiting and diarrhea. Take a five-inch piece of Ephedra (nodes removed) and two pieces of White Atractylodes (each the size of a thumb). Use two whole Scorpions. Place them inside a chimney to be "smoked" by the rising soot until ready. Avoid exposure to wind during treatment. — From the Formulas of Divine Beneficence</gloss>
<margin>A common proverb says: "A year should not pass without the use of Ephedra."</margin>

**Sore Throat and Obstruction:** <gloss>Wrap the throat with a blue cloth and burn [the herb]. — From the Formulas of Divine Beneficence</gloss>

**Postpartum Abdominal Pain:** <gloss>Where the lochia (post-birth discharge) is not fully expelled. Grind Ephedra (nodes removed) into a powder. Take one square-inch spoonful with wine, two to three times a day. Stop once the discharge is complete. — From Secret Records of Mother and Child and Formulas of Divine Beneficence</gloss>

**Palpitations Below the Heart:** <gloss>Use equal parts of Pinellia and Ephedra. Grind them into powder and form pills with refined honey the size of a small bean. Take three pills with water, three times a day. — From the Golden Cabinet</gloss>

**Recessed Smallpox (Inverted Pox):** <gloss>Kou Zongshuang’s method: Take half a *liang* of Ephedra (nodes removed) and stir-fry it with a spoonful of honey for a long time. Add half a *sheng* of water, boil several times, and skim the foam. Continue boiling until one-third has evaporated. Remove the dregs and drink while hot. Avoid wind. This causes the recessed rash to reappear on the surface. Another method uses un-aged wine to decoct the herb, which is even faster. Li Yong, a brush-maker in Xianyuan County, had a son suffering from smallpox that had "sunk" due to cold wind. The child was exhausted, but after one dose of this, the rash reappeared miraculously.</gloss>

**Various Wind-Stroke Disorders:** <gloss>Take one *cheng* <note>a large unit of weight, roughly 15-30 lbs</note> of Ephedra (roots removed). On a "Prosperous Day" or a "Yimao" day <note>auspicious days in the traditional sexagenary calendar</note>, take three *shi* <note>approx. 30 liters</note> of "east-flowing water" <note>water from a stream flowing eastward, traditionally thought to possess "living" Yang energy</note>. Using a clean cauldron, boil the water until five to seven *dou* remain. Skim the foam. Gradually add more water until three to five *dou* remain. Filter out the Ephedra and dregs to obtain a clear liquid. Simmer again until only one *dou* remains. Filter once more, then simmer until only one and a half *sheng* of thick juice remains. Seal it in a container; it will keep for one to two years. For each dose, take one to two spoonfuls dissolved in hot water to induce sweat. When simmering, stir constantly so it does not burn or stick to the bottom. Avoid letting chickens, dogs, or "yin persons" <note>likely referring to menstruating women or those with "cold" constitutions, common in traditional alchemical taboos</note> see the process. This is the secret formula of Liu Shouzhen. — From the Formulas for Clarifying Mysteries (Xuanming Fang)</gloss>

# Scouring Rush (Muzei)
<gloss>From the Jiayou era of the Song Dynasty</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen says: This herb has joints and a rough, astringent surface. Those who work with wood use it to rub and polish the grain until it is smooth; thus, it is called the "thief of wood." <note>The name "Muzei" (木賊) literally means "Wood Thief" or "Wood Bandit," referring to how the plant's abrasive silica-rich skin "steals" the roughness from wooden surfaces.</note></gloss>

<insert>Collection of Explanations</insert> Yuxi says: Scouring rush grows in the Qin, Long, Hua, and Cheng prefectures, typically near water. The seedlings grow to about a foot tall and grow in clumps. Each root produces a single stalk without flowers or leaves. It has joints every inch and is green in color. It does not wither even in the depths of winter. It should be harvested in the fourth month. Su Song says: It is found wherever there is water. It can be harvested at any time and is widely used today. Shizhen says: It grows in upright clumps, reaching two to three feet in height. It looks like the teeth of a fine-toothed comb or the center of a palm leaf. It is hollow and jointed, resembling Ephedra but slightly thicker and without branches or leaves.

# Flavor and Nature: Sweet, Slightly Bitter, Non-toxic
<gloss>Shizhen says: Its nature is warm.</gloss>

<insert>Indications</insert> For eye pain, removing "veils" <note>refers to cataracts or pterygium</note>, dissolving accumulated masses, and benefiting the liver and gallbladder. It treats "intestinal wind" <note>bloody stools or hemorrhoids</note>, stops dysentery, and treats continuous menstruation or uterine bleeding with red or white discharge. <gloss>Jiayou era</gloss> Shizhen says: It releases the muscle layer <note>a method of inducing mild sweating to treat early-stage illness</note>, stops tearing, stops bleeding, and dispels "wind-damp" scrotal pain and rectal prolapse. <gloss>Shizhen says: Combined with charred ox horn and musk, it treats chronic recurring dysentery. Combined with tortoise shell, rehmannia, and peony, it treats uterine bleeding. Combined with pagoda tree pods and mulberry ear fungus, it treats bloody stools. Combined with hackberry seeds and bitter orange, it treats menstrual irregularities.</gloss> Upon examination: It treats various bleeding disorders. Zhu Zhenheng says: When the joints are removed and the herb is roasted, it induces sweating very easily; the earlier herbals did not mention this. Shizhen says: The nature of scouring rush is warm, and its flavor is slightly sweet and bitter. Being hollow and light, it is the "Yin within Yang," possessing a rising and floating quality. Because it shares the same form and nature as Ephedra, it is also able to induce sweating and release the muscle layer.

### Accidentally Swallowing a Copper Coin

# Common Rush (Shilongchu) <gloss>Top Grade of the Classic</gloss>
<insert>Explanations of Names</insert> Dragon’s Whiskers <gloss>Classic</gloss>, Dragon’s Ginseng <gloss>Classic of Mountains and Seas</gloss>, Separate Dragon <gloss>Materia Medica</gloss>, Rulie <gloss>Erya</gloss>, Dragon’s Flower <gloss>Record of Notable Physicians</gloss>, Dragon’s Pearl <gloss>Classic</gloss>, Hanging Grass <gloss>Famous Physicians</gloss>, Liao <gloss>Erya</gloss>, Arrow Grass <gloss>Materia Medica</gloss>.

<insert>Correcting Errors</insert> Shizhen says: This is a grass that is mowed; the original text calls it *chu* <note>meaning fodder or hay</note>. It grows by the water. The *Record of Wonders* states that when King Mu of Zhou raised his eight legendary steeds on an island in the Eastern Sea, there was a grass called "Dragon’s Fodder" (Longchu). This is it. Thus, the old saying goes: "A bundle of Dragon’s Fodder can transform into a dragon colt." This follows the logic of Mencius’s "gatherers of fuel and fodder." The name is derived from its appearance. The *Continued Records of Su Qi* mentions a county in Xiandu Mountain (modern-day Chuzhou) that produces this grass, hence the name. Cui Bao’s *Notes on Things Ancient and Modern* says that people claim when the Yellow Emperor ascended to heaven on a dragon, his ministers clutched the dragon’s whiskers, which fell to the ground and turned into this grass; this is a myth. In the Jiangdong region, it is used to weave mats.

In the summer months, the tip of the stem produces small spiked flowers and bears tiny fruits. It has no branches or leaves.
