# Pith Grass (Common Rush) <gloss>From the *Song Dynasty Kaibao*</gloss> <gloss>Compendium</gloss>
<gloss>Alternative name: Tiger Whisker Grass</gloss> <gloss>Compendium</gloss> <gloss>Jasper Grass</gloss> <gloss>Compendium</gloss>
<gloss>Collection of Explanations: Zhi says: Pith grass grows in the marshy lands of Jiangnan. It grows in clumps. The stems are round, thin, and long. People weave them into mats. It is also found in Shaanxi. One must steam it and wait for it to dry, then cut out the white pith from the center to use for lamp wicks. This is called "processed grass." There is also a version that is not steamed, but simply dried raw; this is "raw grass." For medicine, the raw grass is preferred. Shizhen says: This is of the same category as Dragon Whisker. However, Dragon Whisker is tight, small, and solid, while this grass is slightly thicker and hollow in the middle. The people of Wu cultivate it, using the pith for lamp wicks and the grass for weaving mats and rain-cloaks. It is not common in the wild. Alchemists use it to stabilize sulfur and sal ammoniac. The *Canon of Preparation* says: Sal ammoniac meets "Red Whisker Water" in the crucible. "Red Whisker" is also called "Tiger Whisker Grass"; I am certain this refers to the plant, though I do not know if it is specifically this Tiger Whisker.</gloss>

**Stems and Roots** <gloss>Preparation: Shizhen says: Pith grass is difficult to grind. It should be dyed with rice flour paste, sun-dried, and then ground into powder. Put it in water and let it settle; the part that floats is the pith. Sun-dry before use.</gloss> <gloss>Flavor and Nature: Sweet, cold, non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Yuansu says: Pungent, sweet, and Yang in nature. Wu Shou says: Bland and neutral.</gloss>
**Indications** <gloss>For the five types of strangury <note>painful urinary blockages</note>, the raw form should be taken. Taking an infusion of old mats is even better.</gloss> <gloss>Kaibao</gloss> <gloss>Strengthens the lungs, clears the orifices, promotes water circulation, and treats edema and urinary retention.</gloss> <gloss>Yuanrong</gloss> <gloss>Treats acute throat blockage; blowing the powder into the throat is very fast-acting. Burn it to ashes and apply to stop night crying in infants.</gloss> <gloss>Zhenheng</gloss> <gloss>Reduces fire, stops bleeding, circulates Qi, disperses swelling, and quenches thirst. The ashes can be combined with calomel...</gloss>

# Herbs: Part Five <gloss>73 species of Wetland Herbs, Part 2</gloss>

# Rehmannia 
<gloss>Top Grade in the Divine Husbandman’s Classic</gloss> <gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Qi <gloss>pronounced "qǐ"</gloss>, Earth Marrow <gloss>pronounced "suǐ"</gloss>

The *Divine Husbandman's Classic* and Daming state: When testing the raw root in water, those that float are called "Heavenly Yellow," those that half-sink are "Human Yellow," and those that sink completely are "Earth Yellow" <note>original: "Dihuang" (地黃). The name literally means "Earth Yellow."</note>. For medicinal use, those that sink are best, those that half-sink are second, and those that float are not used. Shizhen notes: The *Erya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary.</note> calls it "Qian." Guo Pu noted that in the region east of the Yangtze, it is called "Qianluo." Su Song noted that the sinking variety is the most prized; thus, the character's etymology is related to "sinking" or "being below." <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss>

<margin>The Miscellaneous Records state:</margin> Rehmannia grows in the rivers and marshes of Xianyang. Those grown in yellow soil are best. Collect the roots in the second and eighth months and dry them in the shade. <gloss>Tao Hongjing notes:</gloss> Xianyang is modern-day Chang'an. Those grown in Weicheng have seeds like small wheat. Currently, the "Dried Rehmannia" from Pengcheng is considered the best, followed by Liyang. Recently, the "Plank Bridge" variety from south of the Yangtze has been preferred. There is a specific method for making the dried version involving pounding the juice and steaming it multiple times with great care. The text's mention of "drying in the shade" makes me fear the steaming method might be lost. Some people try to pass off Ox-knee or Solomon's Seal as Rehmannia, but people cannot always tell the difference. It now grows everywhere, with the variety from Tongzhou being superior. In the first month, the leaves sprout and spread across the ground, appearing like Plantain leaves but with wrinkled patterns and no luster. High ones reach over a foot, low ones three or four inches. The flowers resemble sesame flowers but are reddish-purple; some are yellow. The fruit forms a pod like Forsythia, containing very fine, sandy, brownish seeds. The root resembles a human finger, entirely yellow, though its thickness and length vary. It is very easy to plant; any root piece put into the soil will grow. Some say ancient people preferred yellow soil, but now it is grown in rich, dark soil to ensure the roots are large and juicy. The method involves using reed mats to create a circular enclosure over ten feet wide, filled with rich soil to form a mound. Another mat is placed on top with more soil to create a tiered level, reducing the diameter by one foot at each level. This continues for several levels until it looks like a pagoda. Rehmannia roots with many nodes are cut into inch-long pieces and planted on these tiers, filled to the brim. They are watered daily to keep them lush. During the spring or autumn equinox, they are harvested from the top down; this ensures the roots grow large without breaking or being damaged. Roots from Tongzhou are glossy and sweet. <gloss>Kou Zongshi notes:</gloss> The leaves are like those of the Chinese Artichoke, and the flowers are like sesame flowers but with fine spots. Northerners call them "Cow's Milk Flowers." Both leaves and flowers have fine, short white hairs. <gloss>Li Shizhen notes:</gloss> Today, people only consider Rehmannia from Huaiqing to be superior, though the popularity of different regions changes over time. When the shoots first sprout, they spread on the ground; the leaves resemble mountain bok choy but are hairy and rough. The leaf surface is deep green, resembling small tobacco leaves but thicker. A stalk rises from the center of the leaves covered in fine hair. The tip of the stalk opens into small tubular flowers of a reddish-yellow color. The fruit is like a grain of wheat. The roots are four to five inches long, thin as a finger, with reddish-yellow skin like Sheep-hoof root or a carrot. When dried in the sun, they turn black. Raw, they taste of earth. Locals call the shoots "Grandmother's Milk." Ancients planted them from seed, but now only the roots are planted. Wang Man’s *Records of Living in the Mountains* states that the tender shoots can be picked and eaten as a vegetable, which is very beneficial. The *Materia Medica* suggests harvesting in the second and eighth months, but this does not fully account for the plant's nature. In the eighth month, the withered leaves still contain essence that hasn't fully returned to the root; in the second month, new shoots have already begun to draw essence from the root into the leaves. It is much better to harvest in the first or ninth months. This also suits the steaming and sun-drying process. Tan Daoji noted that since ancient times, it has been eaten as a vegetable. <gloss>Chen Jiamo notes:</gloss> Rehmannia grown in the soil of Zhejiang and Jiangsu receives the Yang energy of the South; while the texture is glossy, its medicinal power is weak. Rehmannia from the mountains of Huaiqing receives the pure Yin energy of the North; the skin is bumpy, but its medicinal power is great.

---

# Dried Rehmannia <gloss>Preparation</gloss>

<margin>Chen Zangqi states:</margin> The *Classic* does not distinguish between "raw-dried" and "steamed-dried." Practitioners use them differently: the steamed version is for tonifying moisture, while the raw-dried version is for balancing. One should follow this method. <gloss>Li Shizhen states:</gloss> What the *Classic* calls "Dried Rehmannia" is simply the dried form of raw Rehmannia. While they treat similar conditions, their abilities to "cool blood" versus "supplement blood" differ slightly. Therefore, I have listed "Prepared Rehmannia" as a separate entry below.

### Prepared Rehmannia
<gloss>Commonly called such in the Jin and Song dynasties.</gloss> <gloss>Song says: The method for making Prepared Rehmannia is to take 30 catties of fat Rehmannia, wash them clean, then take another 30 catties of thin or small ones, pound them to extract the juice. Place the fat roots in a stone vessel, soak them in the juice with wine, and let them sit. Steam them, then sun-dry them until the juice is exhausted. The Rehmannia should then be black and shiny like lacquer and taste as sweet as maltose. It must be stored in a ceramic vessel to maintain its oily and moist quality.</gloss>

Remove the skin. Steam it in a willow-wood steamer over a silver pot. Spread it out to let the steam dissipate, mix with wine, and steam again. Remove and dry. Do not let it touch copper or iron tools, as these can damage the kidneys, turn hair white, and harm the vital energy of both men and women. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss> says: The modern method is to select large roots that sink in water. Mix them with good wine and powdered Amomum seeds <note>original: "Sharen"</note>. Steam them in a willow steamer inside a clay pot until the steam penetrates thoroughly. Sun-dry them, then mix again with Amomum wine and steam. Repeat this "nine steamings and nine sun-dryings" until finished. Because Rehmannia is "cloying" or "muddy" in nature, it requires the aromatic and penetrating quality of Amomum to harmonize the five internal organs and allow the energy to return to the Dan-tien <note>The "Cinnabar Field," a vital energy center in the lower abdomen</note>. The "Prepared" Rehmannia sold in markets today is often merely boiled in wine and should not be used. <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Sweet, slightly bitter, slightly fatty, slightly warm, non-toxic. <gloss>Yuan Su</gloss> says: It is sweet, slightly bitter, and cold. Borrowing the power of wine and the process of sun-drying and steaming, it becomes slightly warm and highly restorative. Its flavor is thick and its energy thin. It is "Yang within Yin" and heavy. It enters the Kidney and Liver channels. To treat the exterior or the upper body, it must be prepared with wine. Avoid radishes, onions, garlic chives, and various types of blood. When paired with Peony bark and Angelica <note>original: "Mudanpi" and "Danggui"</note>, it harmonizes and generates blood. <gloss>Primary Indications</gloss> It fills the bones, flesh, and marrow, grows muscle, generates essence and blood, and supplements internal damage or deficiencies of the five organs. It clears the blood vessels, benefits the ears and eyes, and blackens the beard and hair. It treats the "Five Taxations and Seven Injuries" in men, and uterine leakage or irregular menstruation in women. It is used for blood cooling in pregnancy and childbirth, nourishing Yin, and supplementing marrow. <gloss>Yuan Su</gloss> says: While Raw Rehmannia primarily cools the blood, Prepared Rehmannia supplements the blood and energy, nourishes the Kidney Water, and benefits the True Yin. It removes acute pain in the umbilical region and abdomen, and treats dizziness, blurred vision, and aching after illness. <gloss>Hao Gu</gloss> says: It must be used in its prepared state to be slightly warm and supplementing. Those with withered kidney blood must use it.

# Achyranthes (Ox Knee)
<gloss>Listed as a "Superior Grade" herb in the *Classic of Herbal Medicine*. <margin>Collected Commentaries</margin> The *Guangya* dictionary calls it "Hundredfold" (Baibei). <margin>Guangya</margin> The *Classic of Herbal Medicine* also calls it "Mountain Amaranth." <margin>Wild Vegetables for Relief of Famine</margin> Its name "Ox Knee" refers to its power to tonify the body, giving one the strength of an ox. Its leaves resemble amaranth and its stem nodes grow in opposite pairs; hence, it is colloquially known as "Mountain Amaranth" or "Matching Nodes."</gloss>

<insert>Collective Notes</insert>
<gloss>Achyranthes grows in the valleys of Henei <note>modern Henan province</note> and Linqu. The roots are harvested in the second, eighth, and tenth months and dried in the shade. <margin>Additional Records</margin> It is said the leaves resemble amaranth and the stems have nodes, hence the name. <margin>Li Shizhen</margin> says that "Hundredfold," a name from the *Classic of Herbal Medicine*, is a cryptic term for its potency. <margin>Additional Records</margin> states that old illustrations show leaves like amaranth, stems two to three feet high with nodes like a crane’s knee or an ox’s knee. The leaves are purple and round, growing in opposite pairs. Flowers bloom on spikes in autumn, producing very fine seeds. Roots that are exceptionally long and large—up to three feet—and remain soft and moist are of the highest quality. <margin>Su Gong</margin> notes it can also be used by the military. <margin>Li Shizhen</margin> adds: Achyranthes grows everywhere; the wild variety is called "Earth Achyranthes" (Tu Niuxi) and is unfit for medicinal use. Only those cultivated by households in the North and Sichuan are superior. Sow seeds in autumn and plant in spring. The seedlings have square stems and clustered nodes. The leaves are opposite, quite like amaranth but longer and pointed. In autumn, it produces spikes of seeds that look like small louse-insects with soft hairs that cling to the stem and point downward. In late September, harvest the roots and soak them in water for two nights. Remove the skin and the inner silk, then sun-dry. Although white and straight roots are prized, if the white juice is pressed out, they are less potent than those with the skin left on. The tender seedlings can be eaten as a cooked vegetable.</gloss>

<insert>The Root</insert>
<insert>Preparation</insert>
<gloss><margin>Lei Xiao <note>Author of a famous manual on herb processing</note></margin> says: Always remove the crown (head) and reed-like top. Soak the root in the natural juice of Solomon’s Seal (Huangjing) overnight, then filter it out, chop it, and roast until dry. <margin>Li Shizhen</margin> says: Today, we only soak it in wine for medicinal use. If you want the medicine to act on the lower body, use it raw. If you want it to tonify and nourish, use it roasted or steamed with wine.</gloss>

<insert>Properties</insert>
<gloss>Bitter, sour, neutral, and non-toxic. <margin>Zeng</margin> says: Shennong identifies it as sweet, and Lei Gong as sour. Non-toxic, acts as a warming agent.</gloss>

<insert>Main Indications</insert>
Treats "Cold-Dampness Wilting" (wei) and paralysis, contractions and spasms of the four limbs, and knee pain that prevents bending or stretching. It expels stagnant blood and "qi," treats injuries from heat and fire burns, and can induce abortion. Taken over a long period, it makes the body feel light and resists aging. <gloss>From the *Classic of Herbal Medicine*.</gloss> Treats internal damage and shortness of breath, impotence in men, and urinary incontinence in the elderly. It tonifies the "center," reconnects severed tissues, increases essence (semen), aids the "upright qi," and fills the bone marrow. It removes pain in the brain, lower back, and spine. It regulates irregular menstruation and blood stasis in women. <gloss>From the *Additional Records*.</gloss> Treats impotence, tonifies the kidneys, assists the twelve meridians, and expels "malignant blood." <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss> Treats weakness and frailty in the lower back and knees, breaks up abdominal masses (strangury), drains pus, and stops pain. Useful for postpartum abdominal pain and dizziness, and for expelling a dead fetus. <gloss>Daming</gloss> Strengthens tendons and tonifies the liver against "wind-deficiency" <note>a type of neurological or joint weakness</note>. <gloss>Wang Haogu</gloss> It is best when soaked in wine with Cistanche (Congrong). If bamboo or wood splinters enter the flesh, chew this herb into a pulp and apply it as a poultice; the splinter will come out. <gloss>Kou Zongshi</gloss> Treats chronic malaria with alternating chills and fever, five types of painful urination (strangury), blood in the urine, pain in the urethra, diarrhea, throat blockage (tonsillitis), mouth sores, toothache, abscesses, malignant sores, and physical trauma. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss> Whenever you need to lead medicine to the lower parts of the body, use it raw. Whenever you need to tonify the Liver and Kidneys, use it cooked. When cooked, it tonifies; when raw, it expels "bad blood." These are its two main functions. Its ability to treat bone pain in the lower back/knees, leg weakness, impotence, incontinence, chronic malaria, and shortness of breath stems from its power to tonify the Liver and Kidneys. Its ability to soothe abdominal pain, swellings, sores, metal wounds, fractures, throat issues, and menstrual/childbirth disorders stems from its power to expel "bad blood." According to Chen Rihua's commentary on the formulas collected at Linting...

While in Ezhu <note>modern-day Wuchang, Hubei</note>, I received a letter from Wang Nanqiang, the governor of Jiujiang, which stated: "An old man had long suffered from painful urinary blockage <note>strangury</note>, and a hundred medicines proved ineffective. By chance, I saw a recipe in the *Essential Formulas of Linting* using **Achyranthes root**. He took it and was cured." Furthermore, Ye, a Consultant in the Court of Judicial Review, said: "When the blood from urinary blockage flows out and the urine sits in a basin, it congeals like konjac jelly. Over time, it changes into a shape resembling a mouse’s nipple, but without feet. A hundred treatments failed. A village doctor then used a decoction of **Achyranthes root**, having the patient drink five doses a day. It was called 'Earth Marrow Decoction.' Although it did not cure him immediately, the color of the blood gradually faded, and after a long time, he returned to health. Ten years later, the illness recurred; he took the medicine again and was cured." Upon checking the *Materia Medica*, I found the formula listed in the appendix: to treat inability to urinate with pain in the urethra so severe it feels like death, take **Achyranthes** along with its leaves, boil in wine, and consume. I have recorded this here again to demonstrate its miraculous power. Additionally, Yang Shiying's *Direct Guide to Formulas* states: "For painful urinary blockage, bloody urine, or the swelling pain caused by sand and stones <note>kidney or bladder stones</note>, use one tael <note>approx. 37 grams</note> of **Sichuan Achyranthes**, boil in two cups of water until one cup remains, and take while warm. A woman who had suffered this for ten years found success with this remedy. **Local Achyranthes** may also be used; adding musk or frankincense makes it even more effective."

**Wind-dampness and numbness**: For pain, take one catty <note>approx. 500g</note> of **Achyranthes leaves**, chop them, and cook as a porridge with three small measures of rice in fermented bean juice. Eat on an empty stomach. <gloss>From *Formulas of Imperial Benevolence*</gloss>

**Persistent malaria**: Chop a handful of **Achyranthes stems and leaves** and soak in three pints of wine. Drink until slightly tipsy. If it does not stop immediately, repeat. It should stop within three doses. <gloss>From *Formulas Behind the Elbow*</gloss>

**Stream toxins and heat**: In the mountains and valleys, there is a "stream toxin" that strikes people like a sand-flea <note>referring to a waterborne parasite or infection</note>, but no insect is seen. Initial symptoms include chills, fever, irritability, and stiffness/pain in the joints. If not treated urgently, the "insect poison" enters the heart and causes death. Take a handful of **"Male" Achyranthes stems and leaves** (those with purple nodes and large joints), crush with one cup each of wine and water, and drink the warm juice.

# Purple Aster
<term>Ziwan (Aster tataricus)</term>

<gloss>Listed in the Middle Category of the *Classic of Materia Medica*</gloss>
<insert>Names</insert> **Wan** <gloss>from the *Additional Records*</gloss>; **Soul-Returning Herb** <gloss>from the *Compendium*</gloss>; **Night Morning-Glory**. <gloss>Shizhen says: The name comes from the root being purple (*zi*) and soft/pliable (*wan*). Xu Shen’s *Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters* writes it as 'Wan.' The *Doumen Formulas* call it 'Soul-Returning Herb.'</gloss>

<insert>Collection</insert> <gloss>The *Additional Records* say: **Purple Aster** grows in the valleys of Hanzhong and Fangling, and in Zhending and Handan. Collect the roots in the second and third months and dry them in the shade.</gloss> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says: It is found everywhere near roads. It grows along the ground with purple flowers. The roots are very soft and fine with white hairs. There is a white variety called **White Aster**, but it is no longer used.</gloss> <gloss>Da Ming says: It looks like a tiered tower; the roots are jointed, purple, moist, and soft—these are the best.</gloss> <gloss>Su Song says: Today it is found in Yao, Cheng, Si, Shou, Tai, Meng, and Xingguo prefectures. In the third month, it spreads across the ground; the leaves are connected in groups of three or four. In the fifth and sixth months, it blooms with yellow, white, or purple flowers and bears black seeds. Other details match Tao’s description.</gloss> <gloss>Su Gong says: **White Aster** is actually **Female Aster**. Its healing properties are similar to **Purple Aster**, and it may be used as a substitute when the purple variety is unavailable.</gloss> <gloss>Li Ying says: Collect the **Purple Aster** with its roots and leaves, soak them in vinegar with a little salt, and preserve them as a vegetable. It has a pungent fragrance and is known as "Immortal’s Vegetable."</gloss> <gloss>Do not use too much salt, or it will rot.</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: According to Chen Ziming, the *Medical Discussions* claim that roots from Mount Lao resembling **Northern Asarum** are best. It is found throughout the regions east of Yan and Yan. Nowadays, people often use the roots of **Plantain** or **Inula**, dyed purple, to counterfeit it. This is a vital medicine for lung disease. Since lung disease itself depletes fluids, taking counterfeit medicines that further drain fluids is extremely harmful and must be avoided.</gloss>

### The Root

<insert>Preparation</insert> <gloss>Lei Xiao says: Whenever using it, first remove the hair-like fibers. There is a variety with fibers as white as refined silk called "White Sheep-Beard Herb," which is naturally different. Remove the "head" (crown) and any soil.</gloss>

<insert>Properties</insert> Bitter, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>The *Additional Records* say: Pungent.</gloss> <gloss>Zhen Quan says: Bitter and flat.</gloss> <gloss>Xu Zhicai says: **Coltsfoot** serves as its messenger. It dislikes **Tianxiong**, **Dianthus**, **Gaoben**, **Omphalia**, and **Polygala**. It fears **Artemisia capillaris**.</gloss>

<insert>Indications</insert> Reversal of upward Qi <note>A condition where energy or breath moves upward abnormally, causing coughing or gasping</note>, cold and heat in the chest, bound Qi, coughing with rebellious Qi, and ailments of the Five Viscera. <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss> Coughing and spitting of pus and blood; stops asthma and palpitations; relaxes the limbs; supplements deficiencies. Pediatric seizures and epilepsy. <gloss>From the *Additional Records*</gloss> Treats "corpse infusion" <note>An ancient term for wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note>; supplements emptiness and directs Qi downward; treats "labor Qi" <note>exhaustion</note> and deficiency heat; wards off various evils, ghosts, and "Gu" poisoning <note>sorcery-related toxins</note>; harmonizes the center, dissolves phlegm, and stops thirst; moistens the skin, supplements bone marrow, brightens the eyes, and benefits the Lung Qi. It is highly valued.

<insert>Appendix of Formulas</insert> <gloss>3 old, 4 new</gloss>

**Coughing from lung injury:** Use five mace <note>approx. 18.5g</note> of **Purple Aster**. Decoct in one cup of water until 70% remains. Drink warm three times a day. <gloss>From *Easy and Simple Formulas for Health*</gloss>

<insert>Formula</insert> **Persistent cough:** One tael each of **Purple Aster** and **Coltsfoot**, half a tael of **Stemona**. Grind and sift into a powder. For each dose, use three mace of powder with three slices of ginger and one smoked plum. Decoct into a soup and take twice daily; very effective. <gloss>From the *Illustrated Materia Medica*</gloss>

<insert>Formula</insert> **Pediatric cough with loss of voice:** Equal parts **Purple Aster** powder and **Apricot Kernel** (bitter almond). Grind together with honey and form into pills the size of a Gordon Euryale seed <note>about the size of a large pea</note>. For each dose, dissolve one pill in a decoction of **Schisandra** berry. <gloss>From *Mirror of Pediatric Health*</gloss>

<insert>Formula</insert> **Spitting blood and phlegm-cough:** After spitting blood, take **Coltsfoot** and **Purple Aster** (five parts each, stir-fried) and grind into powder. Form into pills the size of a Gordon Euryale seed. Dissolve one pill in the mouth as needed. <gloss>From *Formulas for Guidance*</gloss>

<insert>Formula</insert> **Postpartum hemorrhage:** Take five mace of **Purple Aster** powder with water. <gloss>From *Formulas of Holy Benevolence*</gloss>

<insert>Formula</insert> **Scrofula and "Wind Paralysis":** <gloss>Also called "Calling Wind."</gloss> For cases where the throat is blocked and the patient feels they are dying, take one stalk of **Soul-Returning Herb** root, wash it clean, and insert it into the throat. Once the "evil phlegm" is discharged, the patient will recover. Miraculous effect. <gloss>Note: This is **Purple Aster**, called "Night Morning-Glory" by Southerners.</gloss> <gloss>From *Doumen Formulas*</gloss>

<insert>Formula</insert> **Sudden urinary blockage in women:** Grind **Purple Aster** into powder. Take three pinches with "first-drawn well water" <note>the very first water taken from a well at dawn</note> to clear the passage. If there is blood in the urine, take five pinches for immediate relief. <gloss>From *Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold*</gloss>

# Female Aster
<term>Nuwan (Aster fastigiatus)</term>

<gloss>Listed in the Middle Category of the *Classic of Materia Medica*</gloss>
<insert>Names</insert> **White Aster** <gloss>from the *Additional Records*</gloss>; **Weaver Girl Aster** <gloss>from the *Additional Records*</gloss>; **Nüfu** <gloss>from the *Guangya* dictionary</gloss>. <gloss>Shizhen says: Its root is white, and as the *Guangya* notes, it resembles a woman’s body in its delicate and graceful form, hence the name.</gloss>

<insert>Collection</insert> <gloss>The *Additional Records* say: **Female Aster** grows in the valleys of Hanzhong or Shanyang. Collect in the first and second months and dry in the shade.</gloss> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says: Recently, doctors no longer use it. There is a 'White Aster' similar to **Purple Aster**, but I fear it is not this same plant.</gloss> <gloss>Su Gong says: **White Aster** is indeed **Female Aster**; it is already well-known.</gloss>

<summary>This page describes the medicinal properties and historical lore of Purple Aster (Ziwan) and Female Aster (Nuwan). Because it was listed as a duplicate entry, Tao [Hongjing] expressed doubts. Its efficacy is similar to **Purple Aster**, but this is the variety with white color. <gloss>Lei Xiao says that a variety of White Aster that is as white as silk is called "Sheep's Beard Grass"; I suspect this is the same substance.</gloss>

### Root

**Aroma and Flavor** Acrid, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Zhicai says: It reacts poorly to saltiness.</gloss>

**Primary Vitality and Healing** Wind-cold, "washing" sensations <note>refers to the feeling of cold water being poured over the body, a sign of chills</note>, sudden turbulence with vomiting and diarrhea, loose stools, intestinal rumbling, shifting pains in the upper and lower body, fright-induced seizures, and the "hundred illnesses" caused by alternating cold and fever. <gloss>From the *Classic of Materia Medica*</gloss>. It treats injuries to the lungs, coughing with upward-rushing breath, coldness in the bladder with a feeling of fullness, and the effects of drinking alcohol at night.

<margin>Dietary Restrictions</margin>
<gloss>The *Additional Records* state:</gloss> According to Ge Hong's *Emergency Formulas to Keep Up One's Sleeve*, there is a recipe for turning a dark face white. Use three parts genuine **Female Aster** and one part **Lead Red** <note>original: "qiandan" (lead tetroxide), an ancient cosmetic pigment</note>. Grind into a powder and take "one dagger-spoon" <note>an ancient measurement, roughly 1-2 grams</note> mixed with vinegar. Take three times a day. After ten days, the stool will turn black; after eighteen days, the face will be as dark as lacquer; after twenty-one days, it will become entirely white, and one should stop. If taken beyond this point, it will become too white. This should not be taken by those over thirty years of age. Avoid the "five pungent vegetables" <note>typically onions, garlic, leeks, etc.</note>. Sun Simiao’s *Essential Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold* suggests taking it with wine; for both men and women, the "blackness" will be expelled through the bowels after twenty days. Furthermore, the *Record of Famous Physicians* tells of a Miss Ren during the Xingguo era of the Song Dynasty. She was a great beauty betrothed to a scholar named Wang Gongfu, but the match was unhappy. Due to her depression, her complexion gradually turned black. Her mother sought a physician, and a Taoist gave her "Virgin Powder" to be taken with wine—two mace <note>approx. 7.5 grams</note> twice a day. Within a few days, her face lightened; in a month, she was restored to her original beauty. When the formula was requested, it was found to be simply equal parts **Lead Red** and **Female Aster**. Based on this, Ge Hong’s formula has indeed been proven effective. In the *Collected Explanations*, it is noted: **Purple Aster** treats the blood portion of the Hand-Taiyin <note>Lung</note> channel, while **White Aster** (Female Aster) is a medicine for the Qi portion of that same channel. When there is heat in the lungs, the face becomes dark; when the lungs are clear, the face becomes white. After age thirty, the Lung Qi gradually diminishes and should not be further dispersed, which is why the text warns against taking it at that age.

## Ophiopogon
<term>Maimendong (Ophiopogon japonicus or Lilyturf)</term>

<gloss>Explanation of Names: **Mendong** <gloss>pronounced 'men'</gloss>; **Qin Bird**; **Leek Leaf**; **Enduring the Chill**; **Leek Dew**; also named **Horse Leek**; the people of Yue call it **Sheep Leek** <gloss>all from the *Additional Records*</gloss>; **Yu's Leek** <gloss>Wu Pu</gloss>; **Yu's Leftover Grain** <gloss>Additional Records</gloss>; **Honeysuckle** <note>original: "rendong", though usually refers to Lonicera, here a synonym for its hardiness</note> <gloss>from the *Mirror of the Heart*</gloss>; **Leek-Lover** <gloss>Wu Pu</gloss>; **Undying Herb** <gloss>Wu Pu</gloss>; **Staircase Grass** <gloss>Hongjing says: because the root resembles wheat [mai]</gloss></gloss>

It is called **Maimendong**. <gloss>Shizhen says: The awns [beards] of wheat are called "men." This herb's root resembles wheat and has small hairs or beards; its leaves are like leeks and do not wither even in the depths of winter, hence the names "Wheat-Men-Winter" and the various names involving "Leek."</gloss>

<insert>Collected Explanations</insert>
<gloss>The *Additional Records* say: **Ophiopogon** grows in the valleys of Hangu, as well as on embankments, in fertile soil, among rocks, and in abandoned places. Collect the roots in the second, eighth, and tenth months and dry them in the shade.</gloss>
<gloss>Su Gong says: It grows in fertile valley soil in clusters. The leaves are like leeks, greenish-yellow. The roots can be harvested at any time. Hongjing says: It comes from the Qin Pass area and is found everywhere. In winter it bears fruit like blue pearls. Roots harvested in the fourth month that are plump and large are best. The *Storehouse of Materia Medica* says: Those from Jiangning are small and moist; those from Xin'an are large and white. The large seedlings look like "Deer Onions" <note>Hemerocallis</note>, while the small ones look like leek leaves. There are three or four varieties, but their medicinal functions are similar. The seeds are round and green. It is found everywhere; the leaves are green like sedge grass, over a foot long, and do not wither through the four seasons. The roots are yellowish-white with fine hairs, shaped like a string of beads. In the fourth month, it opens pale red flowers like red threads. The fruit is blue-green and round like a bead. Those from south of the Yangtze have larger leaves, and some say those from the Wu region are superior.</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen says: The ancients used only the wild-grown variety, but in later generations, most of what is used is cultivated. The method is to harvest the roots in early April and plant them in black, fertile sandy soil. Fertilize and water them three times—in the sixth, ninth, and eleventh months. Harvest, wash, and sun-dry the roots on the day before the Summer Solstice. The seeds can also be planted, but they grow slowly. Those from Shanzhong are very good. The leaves are like leeks but have many longitudinal veins and are notably tough and firm.</gloss>

### Root

<gloss>Preparation</gloss>
<gloss>Hongjing says: Generally, use the plump ones. Soak in warm water to soften and pull out the core [heart]. If this is not done, it causes the patient to feel irritable. Typically, one pound of root will be reduced by four or five ounces after removing the cores.</gloss> Shizhen says: For use in decoctions, moisten with boiling water for a short time and pull out the core. Or, roast on a tile until soft and remove the core while hot. If using in pills or powders, soak in wine and roast until ripe, then let it cool in the wind; repeating this three or four times makes it easy to dry without damaging the medicinal potency. Alternatively, it can be soaked in liquid and pounded into a paste to be mixed with other medicines. For tonifying formulas, soak it in wine. <gloss>soaked</gloss>

### Aroma and Flavor

Sweet, balanced, and non-toxic. <gloss>The *Additional Records* say: Slightly cold. Wu Pu says: According to Shennong and Qibo, it is sweet and balanced. According to the Yellow Emperor, Tong Jun, and Lei Gong, it is sweet and non-toxic. Li Dangzhi says it is sweet and slightly warm. Hongjing says: Sweet and slightly cold. It is "Slightly Yang within Yang," but its nature is to descend into Yin. It enters the Qi portion of the Hand-Taiyin <note>Lung</note> channel.</gloss> Zhicai says: Rehmannia and Plantain serve as its "messengers" <note>herbs that guide its action</note>. It dislikes Coltsfoot and Bitter Gourd. It fears Bupleurum, Poria, Radish, and Wood Ear fungi. It subdues Stone and Bell Inflorescence <note>Stalactite</note>.

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 12

[Treats] injuries to the Qi of the middle burner, injuries from overeating, and cases where the stomach network-vessels are severed. It treats emaciation, shortness of breath, and if taken for a long time, it lightens the body, prevents aging, and wards off hunger. <gloss>From the Divine Farmer’s Herbology Classic</gloss>. It treats heaviness in the body, yellowing of the eyes, a feeling of fullness below the heart, guest heat <note>heat from an external source or a temporary imbalance</note> from deficiency-exhaustion, dryness in the mouth and parched thirst. It stops vomiting, heals withered or weak limbs, strengthens the Yin, benefits the Essence, aids digestion, regulates the middle burner, and maintains the stability of Lung Qi. It calms the five internal organs, makes a person robust and healthy, improves the complexion, and aids in fertility. <gloss>From the Additional Records</gloss>. It removes heat from the Heart, stops vexing heat, fever and chills, and physical exhaustion. It brings down phlegm-rheum, cures the "five exhaustions and seven injuries" <note>traditional categories of physical and emotional overstrain</note>, settles the soul and spirit, stops coughing, stabilizes lung atrophy with the spitting of pus, and treats seasonal epidemic fevers, mania, and headaches. It is a major treatment for heat toxins and various types of edema in the face, eyes, and limbs, and it promotes the discharge of water. It is primarily used for seminal emission. <gloss>According to Zhen [Quan]</gloss>. It treats "hidden fire" within the Lungs and supplements insufficient Heart Qi. It governs "reckless movement of blood" <note>internal bleeding</note>, as well as the drying up of menstrual flow and the failure of breast milk to descend. <gloss>From the Materia Medica of Daming</gloss>. If taken for a long time, it lightens the body, brightens the eyes, and when combined with **Plantain**, **Rehmannia**, and **Asparagus**, it removes "damp-bi" <note>joint pain caused by moisture</note>; it can turn gray hair black and make the vision radiant. <gloss>Zangqi says it is an essential medicine. [Tao] Hongjing says:</gloss> Tao Hongjing says: The merit of Ophiopogon in treating Lung heat is great. Its flavor is bitter, but it specializes in "draining" <note>clearing heat/fluids</note> rather than "astringing" <note>holding fluids in</note>, so those with excessive Cold are forbidden from taking it. 

The seeds are the same as **Goji berries** and are used in "Pulse-Generating" formulas. [Li] Yuansu says: Ophiopogon treats hidden fire in the Lungs; when the pulse-Qi is about to fail, add **Schisandra** and **Ginseng**. These three ingredients together form **Pulse-Generating Powder** <note>Shengmai San</note>, which supplements the insufficient Original Qi within the Lungs. [Li] Gao <note>the physician Li Dongyuan</note> says: In the sixth and seventh lunar months, when damp-heat is at its peak, people suffer from bone-weariness, lack of strength, heavy bodies, shortness of breath, dizziness, and darkening vision—sometimes even producing soft phlegm. Therefore, the Perfected Sun <note>the famous physician Sun Simiao</note> used Pulse-Generating Powder to supplement the "Original Heavenly Vitality." The "Pulse" represents a person's Original Qi. The sweetness and coldness of **Ginseng** drains the "ministerial fire" and benefits the Original Qi; the bitterness and coldness of **Ophiopogon** nourishes the "Dry Gold" <note>the Lungs</note> and clears the water source; the sourness and warmth of **Schisandra** drains "Bing fire" <note>excessive heat</note> and supplements "Geng gold" <note>the Lungs</note> while also benefiting the Qi of the five internal organs. [Li] Shizhen says: According to Zhao Jizong’s *Essential for Scholar-Physicians*, Ophiopogon uses **Rehmannia** as its "envoy" <note>an assistant herb that guides the main herb's action</note>. When taken, it prevents hair from turning white, supplements the marrow and Kidney Qi, stabilizes panting and shortness of breath, makes the skin smooth and lustrous, and removes all "evil Qi" and unclean diseases from the body. This is because there is both a "sovereign" and an "envoy." If there is a sovereign without an envoy, the herb acts alone without success. This formula is only suitable for those with flourishing fire and strong Qi; if one has weak Qi and a cold stomach, it must absolutely not be ingested. <gloss>Attached Formulas</gloss> <insert>3 old, 9 new</insert>

**Ophiopogon Decoction** <gloss>Supplements the middle burner, benefits the Heart, improves the complexion, calms the spirit, and benefits the Qi, making a person robust. Its effects are very rapid. Take fresh Ophiopogon roots, remove the core, pound until soft, and squeeze out the juice. Mix with white honey in a silver vessel and boil it in a water bath, stirring without stopping until it reaches the consistency of maltose. **Wasting and Thirsting** <note>resembling symptoms of diabetes</note> with excessive water drinking: Use 2 large *liang* <note>about 75g</note> of fresh, fat Ophiopogon from Yuanbanqiao; and 2 large *liang* of **Coptis** (*Huanglian*) from Xuanzhou that has nine segments. Remove the ends of the Coptis and 3 to 5 segments; use a small knife to trim away the skin and fibers, blow away the dust, and rub clean with a raw cloth before weighing. Grind into a powder. Soak the Ophiopogon in the juice of a large bitter gourd overnight, then remove the core. Pound it into a pulp in a mortar and mix with the Coptis powder. Roll by hand into pills the size of a paulownia seed. After meals, swallow 50 pills with water, twice a day. After only two days, the thirst will surely stop. If the condition is severe: take 150 pills on the first day, 120 on the second, 190 on the third, 80 on the fourth, and 50 on the fifth. To prepare the medicine, the night must have clear and bright weather. Soak the medicine in a clean place; women, chickens, and dogs must be forbidden from seeing it. If you feel better, take 25 pills at a time. After taking them, if you feel empty, take one white sheep’s head, clean it, and boil it in 3 *dou* of water until it falls apart. Take 1 *dou* of the broth and drink it slowly. Do not eat the meat and do not add salt. In no more than three doses, you will recover. <gloss>From Cui Yuanliang's Maritime Tested Formulas</gloss>.

**Exhaustion of Qi** and feeling as though one is about to expire: 1 *liang* Ophiopogon, 2 *liang* toasted **Licorice**, half a measure of glutinous rice, 2 **Jujubes**, and **Bamboo leaves** <gloss>21 pieces</gloss>. Boil in 2 *sheng* of water until reduced to 1 *sheng*. Divide into three doses. <gloss>From the Nanyang Manual for Saving Lives</gloss>.

**Guest heat from deficiency-exhaustion**: Drink Ophiopogon decoction frequently. <gloss>From the Extension of the Materia Medica</gloss>.

**Vomiting blood or nosebleeds** when other formulas fail: Take 1 *jin* <note>approx. 500g</note> of Ophiopogon (core removed), pound to extract the natural juice. **Bleeding from a blade wound** that will not stop: Ophiopogon (core removed) and **Raw Rehmannia**, 5 *qian* <note>approx. 18g</note> each. Decocted in water and taken, the bleeding stops immediately. <gloss>From the Collection for Protecting Life</gloss>.

# Chuihugen <note>Literally "Hammer-Pestle Root"; likely a species of Ophiopogon or a related lily</note> <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss>

<gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It grows in the shady areas of mountain valleys in the Jiangnan region. Its sprouts resemble those of the Daylily. <gloss>Flavor and Nature:</gloss> Sweet, cold, and non-toxic. <gloss>Primary Indications:</gloss> It lubricates the five internal organs <note>the Heart, Liver, Spleen, Lungs, and Kidneys</note>, benefits those suffering from "wasting and thirsting" <note>a condition often associated with diabetes</note>, eliminates irritability, clears heat-qi, and brightens the eyes. Its efficacy is similar to Ophiopogon. <insert>Zangqi</insert>

<margin>
The herb's root resembles Chinese Asparagus Root. Whenever it is used, the central core should be removed.
</margin>

# Daylily (Xuancao) <gloss>Song Dynasty Su Song, Compendium, Kou Zongshi</gloss>

<gloss>Explanation of Names:</gloss> <insert>From the Illustrated Classic</insert> Forget-Worry (Wangyou). <gloss>From the Shuowen Lexicon:</gloss> Xuan <note>meaning to protect or dissipate</note>. <gloss>From the Erya:</gloss> Red-Thorn (Danjie). <gloss>From the Notes on Past and Present:</gloss> Deer Onion (Lucong). <gloss>From the Jiayou Era Materia Medica:</gloss> Deer Sword (Lujian). <gloss>Local name:</gloss> Earth Vermillion (Tuzhu). Wu Zhun. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The word *Xuan* (Daylily) was originally written as *Xuan* (to protect). *The Classic of Poetry* says: "Where can I get the herb of forgetfulness, to plant it on the north side of the house?" This refers to the inability to ease one's worries.
<margin>
Because one presents "Red-Thorns" to someone in sorrow, it is called "Forget-Worry." Its sprouts are cooked and eaten; the flavor is like an onion, but it causes the person to feel intoxicated or dazed, hence the name Deer Onion. The *Record of Customs* by Zhou Chu says: "If a pregnant woman wears its flowers, she will give birth to a boy," hence it is called "Boy-Favoring Herb." The *Book of Hua Ting Shou* from Jiuhua says: "The tender sprouts are used as a vegetable; eating them stirs the 'wind' and makes one dazed as if drunk," which is another explanation for the name "Forget-Worry." Xi Kang's *Treatise on Nourishing Life* states that among herbs, Daylily "nourishes the nature" and allows one to forget worries. It is also called the herb that favors the birth of boys. Guo Pu's *Universal Treatise* identifies it as...
</margin>
<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Daylilies are found in fields and wilds everywhere. Formally known as Deer Onion. Collect the flowers in the fifth month and the roots in the eighth month. People today often collect the tender sprouts and flower buds to make pickles.
To say that Daylily is the same as the Silk Tree (Hehuan) is an error. The Silk Tree is found in the Trees section. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The Daylily prefers low, damp ground. In the sixth month, it grows in clusters with leaves like those of bullrushes or garlic, soft and weak. New leaves replace old ones, remaining green through the four seasons. In the fifth month, stalks emerge and
flowers bloom with six petals that hang down. They open in the morning and wither by evening, continuing until late autumn. The flowers come in red, yellow, and purple. It produces three-sided fruits containing seeds as large as firmiana seeds, black and shiny. Its roots are similar to Ophiopogon and propagate very easily. The *Account of the Plants and Trees of the South* says: "There is a Water Daylily in Guangdong that looks like Deer Onion, with purple or yellow flowers." This belongs to the same category. Some say Deer Onion has spotted patterns on the flowers and is different from the Daylily, but this is a matter of observation. When grown in rich soil, the flowers are thick, deep-colored, spotted, and double-layered, blooming for months. In poor soil, the flowers are thin, pale, and do not last. Xi Han's *Preface to the Boy-Favoring Flower* also mentions that in the Jing-Chu region, it is called Deer Onion and is used in Daoist arts, though this is not a reliable basis. People in the east today dry the flower buds and store them, calling them "Yellow-Flower Vegetable" <note>Lily buds</note>.

# Common Lophatherum
<gloss>From the Compendium</gloss> Explaining the Name: **Bone-Crusher** <note>original: "Sui Gu Zi"</note>
<gloss>Li Shizhen says: The name "Bamboo Leaf" is descriptive of its shape. The name "Bone-Crusher" refers to its ability to induce labor or expel a fetus.</gloss>
It has a long spike. Rural people harvest the roots and sprouts, mash them for their juice, and mix this with rice to make a wine starter that is extremely fragrant.
**Flavor and Nature:** Sweet, cold, and non-toxic.
**Primary Indications:** It removes irritability and heat, benefits urination, and clears the Heart. The root is capable of inducing abortion. <gloss>Noted by Li Shizhen from contemporary use</gloss>

# Common Dayflower
<gloss>The character "Zhi" is pronounced like "Zhi" (to step). From the Compendium. Explaining the Name: **Chicken-Tongue Herb** (Ji She Cao). From the Supplement: **Jade Cicada Flower** (Bi Chan Hua). Also called **Jade Butterfly Flower** (Bi Die Hua). Chen Zangqi says: The Dayflower grows in the regions of Jiangdong and Huainan.</gloss>
Added during the Jiayou period of the Song Dynasty <note>1056–1063 CE</note>.
<gloss>Also known as **Bamboo Leaf Vegetable** (Zhu Ye Cai), **Earring Herb** (Er Huan Cao), and **Basket-Lady Herb** (Lan Gu Cao).</gloss>
<gloss>It grows on flat ground; its leaves resemble bamboo. It reaches a height of one to two feet. The flowers are a deep jade green, excellent for use as a pigment. It has seed pods shaped like a bird's beak. Shizhen says: This plant is found everywhere on level ground. In the third or fourth month, it sprouts leaves that look like bamboo; these are edible when tender. In the fourth or fifth month, it blossoms with flowers shaped like moths—the two petals look like wings, and their jade-green color is lovely. It forms seed pods that are pointed and curved like a bird's beak. The seeds inside are the size of small beans, grey-black and wrinkled, resembling silkworm droppings. Skilled craftsmen harvest the flowers to extract juice for painting and for coloring sheepskin lanterns a blue-green shade like eyebrow pigment.</gloss>
**Sprouts — Flavor and Nature:** Bitter, greatly cold, and non-toxic.
**Primary Indications:** Chills and fever, miasmatic malaria, throat obstruction <note>severe sore throat</note>, pediatric "cinnabar toxin" <note>erysipelas or skin rashes</note>, feverish madness and epilepsy, abdominal masses and fullness, generalized swelling, carbuncles, and bites from snakes or dogs.

**Attached Formulas** <gloss>Newly added</gloss>
**Urination Blockage:** Take one ounce of "Bamboo-Chicken Herb" <note>Dayflower</note> and one ounce of Plantain herb. Mash to extract the juice, add a little honey, and consume on an empty stomach. <gloss>From the Collection of Simple Formulas</gloss>
**Red and White Dysentery:** Take "Basket-Lady Herb," which is the Dayflower vegetable, and decoct it into a soup. Drink daily. <gloss>From the Complete Book of Childcare</gloss>
**Swollen and Painful Throat Obstruction:** Apply the juice of the Dayflower to the affected area. <gloss>From the Sleeve-sized Formulas</gloss>
**Five Types of Painful Hemorrhoids:** Use "Earring Herb" (the Jade Cicada Flower). Press the softened herb into the affected area for immediate effect. <gloss>From Wei Yilin's Proven Formulas</gloss>

# Mallow
<gloss>Listed as Top Grade in the Classic of Materia Medica. Revised: Moved here from the Vegetable section.</gloss>
Explaining the Name: **Dew Mallow** <note>original: "Lu Kui"</note> <gloss>From the Compendium</gloss> **Slippery Vegetable** <note>original: "Hua Cai"</note> <gloss>Li Shizhen says: According to the "Erya Yi," the name "Mallow" (Kui) implies "to calculate" (Kui). The leaves tilt toward the sun; by preventing the sun from shining directly on its roots, the plant shows the "wisdom" to calculate the sun's position. In ancient times, people harvested mallow only after the dew had dissolved, hence it was called "Dew Mallow." Today, people call it "Slippery Vegetable," referring to its mucilaginous nature. Anciently, the Mallow was the primary of the "Five Vegetables," but as it is no longer commonly eaten, it has been moved to this Herbal section.</gloss>
<gloss>The "Bielu" says: It grows on Mount Shaoshi. Tao Hongjing says: If planted in autumn and subjected to frost and dew through the winter, the seeds produced in spring are called "Winter Mallow." These are used in medicine and are extremely "slippery" (lubricating) in nature. Spring mallow seeds are also slippery but are not suitable for medicine. To plant it, the seeds are lightly stir-fried, then scattered on damp ground; they sprout overnight. Su Gong says: This is the common edible mallow; there are several varieties, but they are not used in medicine.</gloss>
<gloss>Su Song says: Mallow is found everywhere. The sprouts and leaves make a delicious vegetable. Winter mallow seeds are used most frequently in medicine throughout history. There are several types: Hollyhock, Musk Mallow, Yellow Mallow, etc. Shizhen says: The ancients grew Mallow as a staple food, but such varieties are now rare. There are three types with purple or white stalks; the white-stalked variety is superior. It has large leaves and small yellow flowers. The smallest variety is called "Duck-Foot Mallow." The seed pod is as large as a fingertip, with thin, flat skin. The seeds inside are light and hollow. Those planted in the 4th or 5th month are kept for seed; those in the 6th or 7th are "Autumn Mallow"; those in the 8th or 9th are "Winter Mallow." It can be harvested year-round. Wang Zhen's "Book of Agriculture" states: Mallow is a "Yang" plant. It grows easily and is found in the wild regardless of soil quality. It was once the leader of all vegetables, providing food for all four seasons. It is drought-resistant, sweet, and non-toxic—a safeguard against famine. It can be pickled or dried. Its roots and seeds treat illness. It is truly a vital product of the medicinal garden and a benefit to people's livelihood, yet people no longer eat it or plant it.</gloss>

<summary>This page details three plants: Common Lophatherum (used for clearing heat and inducing labor), the Common Dayflower (used for throat ailments and toxins), and the Mallow (an ancient staple vegetable now used primarily for its lubricating medicinal properties).</summary>

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 16, Herbs Section

## **Shoots**
<gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Their nature is cold and slippery; they are non-toxic. They are considered the primary of all vegetables. However, their "heart" <note>the central bud or inner leaves</note> can be harmful to a person. <gloss>From the *Record of Distinguished Physicians* (Bielu). Tao Hongjing says: Mallow leaves are particularly cold in nature and should not be eaten in large quantities. Wang Ying says: When prepared as a cooked vegetable, they are very delicious; however, their nature is slippery and sharp, which is not always beneficial to the body. Meng Shen says: Although its nature is cold, if eaten hot, it causes a person to feel feverish, restless, and stirs up the "wind" within the body. Eating it in the fourth lunar month can trigger the recurrence of old illnesses. Eating it after recovering from an epidemic disease can cause a person to lose their sight. Eating the frost-purple variety of mallow can trigger "five kinds of illnesses."</gloss>
It causes one to desire to vomit water. Whenever taking any medicinal drugs, avoid eating the heart of the mallow. The heart is toxic. Yellowed shoots will always trigger chronic illnesses, so do not eat them. It must not be eaten together with carp, crab-apple fruits, or pheasant meat. It also subdues the toxicity of sulfur.

### **Primary Indications**
This is the vegetable of the Spleen. It is beneficial to the Spleen. It benefits the Stomach's *qi* and lubricates the Large Intestine. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> It promotes the passage and removal of accumulated stagnation.
It can be harmful to people. <gloss>Li Shizhen says: Anyone bitten by a rabid dog must never eat this. Eating it will cause the rabies to flare up immediately. When cooking mallow, one must use garlic; if there is no garlic, do not eat it. It also subdues sulfur.</gloss>
If a pregnant woman eats it, the fetus will become slippery and be easily born. <gloss>From the *Record*</gloss> Boiling the juice and drinking it benefits the Small Intestine. It treats seasonal jaundice. The dried leaves, ground into powder or burned into ash and taken, treat bleeding from "gold wounds" <note>wounds caused by metal blades or tools</note>. <gloss>Zhen says</gloss> It removes "guest heat" <note>external feverish symptoms</note>. It treats malignant sores and disperses pus and blood. It treats vaginal discharge in women and heat-toxins in children. It is suitable for those suffering from dysentery or erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection</note>. <gloss>Wang Ying says</gloss> It is suitable for those who have taken mineral-based alchemical drugs. <gloss>Meng Shen says</gloss> Its ability to clear and lubricate the body's orifices is the same as that of the seeds. <gloss>Same as above</gloss> <gloss>Elaboration</gloss> Zhang Congzheng says: For any long-term illness where the stool is obstructed and sluggish, one should eat mallow. It will naturally clear the passage. This is the principle of using "slippery" substances to nourish the orifices. <gloss>Li Shizhen says</gloss> According to Wang Shou's *Medical Secrets from the Royal Library* (Waitai Miyao) of the Tang Dynasty: During an epidemic of "spotted sores" <note>likely smallpox</note>, the sores quickly cover the body and develop white heads. This is a malignant toxic *qi*. In the fourth year of the Yonghui era of Emperor Gaozong <note>653 CE</note>, these sores spread from the Western Regions eastward into China. Simply boiling mallow leaves and eating them with a garlic sauce will stop them. Also, the *Imperial Grace Formulary* (Shenghui Fang) states: For children with fever and "spots" <note>pox or rashes</note>, squeeze a little juice from raw mallow leaves and administer it. This disperses the malignant toxins and "strange *qi*." Note that this refers to what we now call smallpox. Modern practitioners fear that frequent urination or bowel movements will deplete the patient's "primordial *qi*" and prevent the pox from "rising" <note>maturing and healing</note>. Since mallow lubricates the orifices and promotes both stool and urine, it might seem unsuitable. Yet the ancients relied on it. Could it be that the "environmental *qi*" of ancient and modern times differs, and thus treatment methods must change with the times? <gloss>Appended Prescriptions</gloss> <gloss>Four old, three new</gloss> Epidemic spotted sores. <gloss>The formula is found above.</gloss> Hemorrhoids resembling "meat cones." <gloss>If someone suddenly develops flesh-colored spikes on their hands or feet that grow backward like cones and cause unbearable pain, they will be cured by eating mallow. From Xia Ziyi's *Formulas for Strange Diseases*.</gloss> Various fistulas that will not close. <gloss>First wash the area clean with rice water. Take a mallow leaf, warm it slightly over a fire, and apply it. Do this for no more than three days. The leaf will draw out the pus, and then new flesh will grow.</gloss> <gloss>Avoid all fish, garlic, and sexual activity.</gloss> Grind mallow into a powder and apply it. <gloss>Zhai You</gloss> Scalds and burns. <gloss>From the *Dietary Materia Medica*.</gloss> Stings from insects or scorpions. <gloss>Pound the mallow to extract juice and drink it. From the *Formulary of Universal Relief* (Puji Fang).</gloss> Flare-ups from mineral drugs. <gloss>For those with dry mouth and coughing: after every meal, drink one cup of winter mallow juice. Lie down immediately. After a short while, the "scrofula" <note>swollen lymph nodes</note> will be cured.</gloss>

# **Winter Mallow Seeds**
<gloss>The *Record of Distinguished Physicians* (Bielu) says to collect them in the 12th lunar month. (Ji says): Since the seeds are born in the spring, it is illogical to say they can be collected in the 12th month.</gloss>

**Flavor and Nature** They are sweet, cold, and slippery <term>slippery (hua): a property in Chinese medicine that promotes movement and lubrication, helpful for urination and childbirth</term>, and are non-toxic. <gloss>The yellow-flowered variety serves as their "assistant" drug.</gloss>

**Primary Indications** They treat cold and heat imbalances in the five viscera and six bowels <note>the fundamental organ systems in traditional Chinese medicine</note>, and address physical wasting or emaciation. They resolve the "five types of urinary blockage" (strangury) and promote urination. Long-term consumption strengthens the bones, lightens the body's weight, and extends the lifespan. <gloss>From the *Materia Medica* (Bencao).</gloss> For women, they treat internal blockages of the breast with swelling and pain. <gloss>From the *Record of Distinguished Physicians* (Bielu).</gloss> They draw out the "head" or core of carbuncles and abscesses. <gloss>According to Meng Shen.</gloss> They counteract toxicity from alchemical mineral drugs (like cinnabar), promote the flow of breast milk, clear the bowels, and resolve fluid retention. <gloss>From the *Materia Medica of the Jiayou Era* (Jiayou Bencao).</gloss>

They ease labor <note>literally "making the fetus slippery"</note> and treat dysentery. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The flavor and nature of the mallow are thin, bland, and slippery. Because it belongs to the *Yang* <note>active/moving</note> category, it is able to open the bodily orifices, promote lactation, reduce swelling, and ease the passage of the fetus during birth. Its roots, leaves, and seeds share the same medicinal functions. According to Chen Ziming's *Good Formulas for Women*, for a nursing mother whose *qi* (energy) and blood circulation are blocked, these are extremely effective at restoring the flow of fluids. This leads to the ->**Appendix of Formulas**<- <gloss>8 old formulas, 12 new ones</gloss>. Boil until one *sheng* remains. For cases where the abdomen is full, urination and defecation are blocked, and the patient feels they are near death: use the method by Zhang Buyu. <gloss>From the *Imperial Benevolence Formulas* (Shenghui Fang):</gloss> Mix mallow seed powder with breast milk in equal parts and ingest for immediate relief. <gloss>Also from the same source:</gloss> Take two *sheng* of mallow seeds and four *sheng* of water. <meta>This page continues the botanical and medicinal survey of the Mallow family in Volume 16, moving from the common Winter Mallow to the more ornamental and physically distinct Hollyhock (Shukui). It provides detailed descriptions of the plant's growth cycle and morphological differences before cataloging the specific therapeutic uses of its various parts.</meta>

When first planted from seeds, the roots remain in the ground during the winter months and will sprout new shoots on their own. When the shoots are tender, they can be eaten; the leaves resemble those of the Mallow but are larger, also looking somewhat like Luffa leaves with lobes. After the "Grain Fills" <note>the 8th solar term, roughly late May</note>, the stems grow five or six feet high. The flowers resemble those of the Rose of Sharon but are larger, appearing in deep red, pale red, purple, black, and white. There are both single-petaled and multi-petaled varieties. Ancient writers described it well, noting its "sparse stems and dense leaves, single calyx and beautiful flowers, with golden pollen pressed into the center." Only the red and white varieties are used in medicine. Its fruit is as large as a thumb; the skin is thin and flat, and the inner kernels resemble those of the Birthwort <term>Birthwort (Ma Dou Ling): Aristolochia, often used in TCM for respiratory issues</term>. They are light and hollow, making them easy to plant. The bark of the stalk can be peeled and woven into cloth or made into rope. A smaller variety is called the "Common Mallow" <note>original: *Jinkui* (Malva sylvestris)</note>, also known as the "Thorny Mallow." The *Erya* <note>the oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> calls it the "Sun-flower" <note>original: *Shun*</note>.
Its flowers are as large as a five-zhu coin, pink with purple-threaded patterns. The *Supplement to the Materia Medica* by [Chen] Yuxi says this is the same as the "Barbarian Mallow" <note>original: *Rongkui*</note>, but this is incorrect, though their medicinal effects are similar.

# Hare’s Mallow <gloss>From the Tang Materia Medica</gloss>

<insert>Explanatory Names</insert> Heaven’s Mallow <gloss>from the Classic</gloss>; Xi <gloss>pronunciation</gloss>; Thunder-Pellet Grass <gloss>from the Materia Medica</gloss>.

<gloss>Li Shizhen states: The sprouts of the Hare’s Mallow resemble those of the Little-Leaf Buttercup but are purple and glossy. Its flowers are white and look like Plum blossoms. The leaves are clustered, fleshy, and extremely slippery. They grow in low-lying marshlands and fields, and many people recognize them. In the sixth or seventh lunar month, the stems and leaves are harvested and dried in the sun for medicinal use. [Chen] Yuxi says: Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* <note>the oldest Chinese dictionary</note> notes that Hare’s Mallow resembles the common Mallow but is smaller. The leaves look like Goosefoot <note>Chenopodium</note> and have fine hairs. When scorched or cooked, they are edible and slippery to the taste. [Kou] Zongshi says: The stem of the Hare’s Mallow is like a silk thread, similar to the Yellow Hollyhock. Its flower is like a torch in the frost, and its form is tiny, like a single-petaled Hollyhock just beginning to bloom. It has a sandalwood-colored center and a hue like a peony mixed with yellow, though its leaves are those of a Hollyhock. This is the plant Liu Mengde <note>the poet Liu Yuxi</note> referred to when he wrote, "Hare’s Mallow and wild oats sway in the spring breeze." Shizhen continues: According to Guo Pu’s supplementary commentary on the *Erya*, the Hare’s Mallow is also called "Heaven’s Mallow." It has leaves like a common Mallow, as large as a coin and thick, with a green surface and a slightly purple underside. It grows on rocky cliffs. All alchemical minerals <term>Dan Shi: refers to "Cinnabar and Stones," the materials of Chinese alchemy</term> only achieve their "divine" transformations when combined with this plant. Thus, the *Lei Gong Treatise on Food and Preparation* states that if one wishes to make a substance firm and "forget" its nature, one uses the "Purple-backed" variety, meaning it can solidify lead. This knowledge was obtained from a monk at Tiantai Mountain. Furthermore, the *Divine Book of the Bo-Yi* by Nangong Cong says that the Purple-backed Heaven's Mallow grows in the Shu region <note>modern Sichuan</note> and is a spiritual herb. It grows at the water's edge. Using its natural juice to boil mercury will solidify it; it can also boil the "Eight Minerals" to make them resist fire. Additionally, Chu Yushi’s *Record of Ancient and Modern Experiences* says: Before the fifth day of the fifth lunar month, fast and observe a mulberry tree that has Hare’s Mallow growing beneath it. At noon on the fifth day, go beneath the tree and chant: "Mallow, Mallow, you shall all be revived, Svaha!" <note>original: "Su-han-he," a phonetic transliteration of the Buddhist/Sanskrit "Svaha," meaning "so be it."</note> After chanting, stroke the shade of the mulberry tree once with your hand, then bite the Hare’s Mallow and the Five-Leaf Grass with your teeth. Chew them and apply the saliva to your hands and fingers. Repeat this over the whole body. Fast again for seven days without washing your hands. Thereafter, if anyone is bitten or stung by snakes, insects, or scorpions, simply rubbing them with these hands will heal them instantly. I, Shizhen, personally believe that the ancients had a category of "healing by incantation," and this belongs to that tradition. However, it is not strictly necessary to use Hare’s Mallow—what specific meaning it holds here is unclear. If it is meant to counteract poisons, there are many other herbs for treating toxic insects.</gloss>

## Shoots

It stops the toxins of tigers and snakes and treats various sores. Crush for the juice and drink it, or apply to sores to detoxify and relieve pain. <gloss>From the Tang Materia Medica</gloss>.

# Yellow Hollyhock <gloss>From the Song Dynasty Jiayou Materia Medica</gloss>

<insert>Correction</insert> <gloss>Moved here from the Vegetable section.</gloss>
<insert>Explanatory Names</insert> <gloss>Shizhen says: The Yellow Hollyhock (Abelmosk) is a single species. It was originally entered into the Herb section [of older texts], but the *Jiayou Materia Medica* placed it in the Vegetable section because it shares a name with the Hollyhock and has similar medicinal properties. I have now moved it here [to the Herb section].</gloss>

<gloss>[Chen] Yuxi says: The Yellow Hollyhock flower is found everywhere near roadsides. In spring, it sprouts shoots and leaves similar to the Hollyhock, but the leaf tips are narrow and have many deep lobes. In late summer, it blooms with deep yellow flowers. Harvest in the sixth or seventh month and dry in the shade. [Kou] Zongshi says: The Yellow Hollyhock is a distinct species from the common Hollyhock; it is not simply a yellow-colored variety of the latter. Below the center of the leaf, it has a purple-sandalwood color. Pluck the flowers and spread them out to dry in the sun; otherwise, they will rot and soak through. Shizhen says: Sow the seeds in the second month, or let the seeds from the previous year grow naturally from the soil. By summer, it begins to grow. The leaves are as large as castor bean leaves, deep green, and divided into five points like a human hand, with smaller points on the sides. In the sixth month, it blooms with flowers as large as a bowl, goose-yellow with a purple heart. The six petals are slightly tilted and open at noon, falling by dusk. People also call it the "Side-Tilt Golden Goblet Flower." It immediately forms seed pods as large as a thumb and about two inches long, thick at the base and pointed at the tip, with six ribbed sides covered in hairs. When old, they turn black and the ribs burst open. Inside are six chambers like those of a sesame pod, containing numerous black seeds shaped like those of the Birthwort. The stems grow six or seven feet long; the bark can be peeled to make rope.</gloss>

When soaked in oil and applied, it treats scalds and burns. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>.

# Black Nightshade
<gloss>From the Tang Materia Medica</gloss> <gloss>Corrected</gloss> <gloss>Incorporating the Crow’s Eye Herb from the Illustrated Classic</gloss> <gloss>From the Shu Materia Medica and the Illustrated Classic</gloss> <gloss>Also called Bitter Herb</gloss>

->Tang Materia Medica<- ->Materia Medica<- ->Illustrated Classic<- ->Compendium<- ->Heavenly Eggplant<- ->Illustrated Classic<- ->Water Eggplant<- ->Compendium<- ->Heaven Bubble Herb<- ->Compendium<- ->Crow’s Ground Cherry<- ->Compendium<- ->Crow’s Eye Herb<-

The names "Heaven Bubble" and "Crow’s Eye" refer to the shape of the fruit. It resembles the Ground Cherry, so "Crow" is added to distinguish it. <gloss>Li Shizhen states:</gloss> <gloss>Note:</gloss> Jing Huan’s *Manual of Herbs* says: Every province has "Bitter Herb," which is actually Bitter Sowthistle. Another name is Bitter Sowthistle. It says: Bitter Sowthistle is indeed Black Nightshade. In common parlance, it is also called Bitter Herb. The "Five-clawed Dragon" is also called Crow’s Eye Herb. Though "Bitter Moss" and "Bitter Herb" share names, they are different plants. <gloss>Collective Explanations</gloss> <gloss>This is not the tea plant</gloss> Black Nightshade grows everywhere. In the regions of Guan and He, it is called "Bitter Herb." The stems are round, the flowers are white, and the seeds resemble those of the "Ox Plum" <note>Buckthorn</note>; they are green when raw and black when ripe. They are fit only for boiling and eating, and cannot be eaten raw. <gloss>Su Song states:</gloss> Black Nightshade is rare in nearby areas and is mostly found in the North. People call it "Bitter Mallow." The leaves resemble those of the "Wind-Dispelling Herb" <note>Solanum lyratum</note> but lack hairs. The flowers are white and the seeds also resemble those of the "Wind-Dispelling Herb." They are green when raw and black when ripe. It is also called "Red Pearl" and can be used in medicine. Others call it "Crow’s Eye Herb," which grows near rivers and lakes; its leaves are like those of an eggplant, hence the name "Heavenly Eggplant." Some say it is the "Lacquer-Binder Herb." The Lacquer-Binder is actually the "Shu Sheep Spring" already listed in the Herb Section of this Classic. People are often unable to distinguish between them. <gloss>Li Shizhen states:</gloss> Black Nightshade and Lacquer-Binder are two species of the same category. Both grow everywhere. The sprouts emerge in the fourth lunar month; when tender, they are edible, being soft and slippery. The plant gradually grows to two or three feet. The stem is as thick as a chopstick and resembles the Lantern Herb but is hairless. The leaves resemble eggplant leaves but are smaller. After the fifth month, it opens small white flowers with five petals and yellow stamens. It bears perfectly round seeds as large as Schisandra berries. They have small stalks and several grow together in a cluster. The taste is sour. Inside are fine seeds, similar to eggplant seeds. Those that are green when raw and black when ripe are Black Nightshade; those that are green when raw and red when ripe are also a form of Black Nightshade. Their functions are similar and not far apart. Su Gong and the *Illustrated Classic* registered Black Nightshade in the medicinal section but then recorded "Crow’s Eye Herb" separately in the external categories, likely not realizing they are the same thing. They also claimed Crow’s Eye Herb is "Shu Sheep Spring," which is an error. The leaves of Shu Sheep Spring resemble Vitex and it has purple flowers. Its seeds cluster like Goji berries. Details can be found in the specific entry in the Herb Section. Yang Shen’s *Danyuan Records* claims Black Nightshade is the "Wu Mallow," and conversely points to the *Materia Medica* as being in error. He cites the *Basic Questions* and *Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold*. But the "Wu Mallow" of the fourth month is clearly the Hollyhock. I have corrected both points here.

It should be eaten. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>

# Dragon Pearl <gloss>From the Supplement</gloss>

**Name:** Plain Pearl. Su Song says: This refers to the red-berried variety of Black Nightshade.

**Collection and Identification:** Zhen Quan states: There is a variety of Black Nightshade with red berries called Dragon Pearl. The juice can be expressed and eaten; it can turn white hair black. Chen Cangqi <note>author of the *Supplement to the Materia Medica*</note> states: Dragon Pearl grows by the roadside; the seeds are round like Nightshade seeds, hanging from the stems and leaves like a string of beads. It is the same as the sprout, only the fruit turns red when ripe. Shizhen notes: Although Black Nightshade and Dragon Pearl are distinguished by the black or red color of their fruit, they are actually one plant with two colors. They have been forced into two separate categories.

According to Chen Cangqi. Li Ming states: Taking Dragon Pearl turns white hair black and allows one to endure old age. If eaten raw, the bitter ones are also used in medicine.
