# Winter Cherry
<gloss>Middle grade of the Classic</gloss> <gloss>Verified</gloss> <gloss>Medicinal Section</gloss> Bitter Dallying, Grass Category, Winter Cherry <gloss>Herbal</gloss> <gloss>Vinegar Sauce, Classic</gloss> Bitter Dallying <gloss>Jiayou Era</gloss> Lantern Grass <gloss>Tang Herbal</gloss> Leather Cap Grass <gloss>Dietary Therapy</gloss> Heavenly Bubble Grass <gloss>Compendium</gloss> Queen Mother’s Pearl <gloss>Jiayou Era</gloss> Goddess of the River Luo’s Pearl <gloss>Same as above</gloss> The small one is named Bitter Husk <gloss>Illustrated Classic</gloss>

The elegant name is "Chilled Sauce." Guo Pu <note>a famous Jin Dynasty commentator</note> noted that this is the modern Winter Cherry. People of the Jiangdong region call it Bitter Husk. The smaller variety is called "Little Bitter Dallying." According to the *Notes on Ancient and Modern*, the name "Husk" comes from the fruit’s shape, which resembles a "Leather Cap" <note>a ceremonial headpiece shaped like a triangle</note>, and its seeds are round like pearls. Shizhen says: The name "Winter Cherry" <note>original: "Suanjiang" or Sour Sauce</note> comes from the flavor of the fruit. "Bitter Husk" and "Bitter Dallying" come from the flavor of the sprouts. "Lantern" and "Leather Cap" come from the shape of the outer husk. "Queen Mother’s Pearl" and "Goddess's Pearl" come from the shape of the fruit inside. <gloss>According to Yang Shen’s *Miscellaneous Sayings*: "Lantern Grass," "Bitter Dallying," and "Winter Cherry" are all the same plant. The people who transcribed the herbals lived at different times, so the entries were repeated. In the capital of Beijing, the wild fruit is called the "Red Maiden" <note>Hong Guniang</note>; a crimson bag hangs on the outside, containing a red pearl-like seed that is sweet-sour and edible. It is quite lovely as it grows alongside green grasses. "Maiden" is likely a corruption of the word for "Bag," as the ancient pronunciations of these words were similar. This explanation is correct, so the "Winter Cherry" of the *Classic*, the "Lantern Grass" of the *Tang Herbal*, and the "Bitter Dallying" of the *Jiayou Herbal* are now merged into one entry.</gloss>
<insert>Collected Explanations</insert> The *Additional Records* say: Winter Cherry grows in the rivers and marshes of the Jing-Chu region <note>modern Hubei/Hunan</note> as well as in household gardens. Harvest in the fifth month and dry in the shade. Hongjing says: It is found everywhere. The sprouts look like Water Eggplant but are smaller; the leaves are edible. The seeds grow inside a "room" <note>the husk</note> and look like red cherries. The flavor is extremely sour. <gloss>Other editions</gloss> say the fruit is red and children eat it. Baosheng says: Winter Cherry is the Bitter Husk. The root is like Chinese Yam, white and extremely bitter. Yuxi says: Bitter Husk grows near old ruins and walls, reaching two to three feet high. The seeds grow in husks. <gloss>Yuxi</gloss> They are as large as plums and are yellow-red. <gloss>The fruit</gloss> is like a cinched pouch containing a pearl-like seed that turns red when ripe. <gloss>The people of the Guanzhong region call it the Goddess of the River Luo’s Pearl, the Queen Mother’s Pearl, or Leather Cap Grass.</gloss> There is a smaller type called Bitter Husk. <gloss>Illustrated Classic</gloss> Elegantly called the "Yellow Husk." <gloss>Gong says:</gloss> Lantern Grass is found everywhere, with stems three to four feet high. It has red flowers <note>referring to the husks</note> shaped like lanterns with red seeds inside that are edible. The roots, stems, flowers, and fruits are all used in medicine. Zongshi says: Winter Cherry is the Bitter Husk. <gloss>Jiayou Era</gloss> It was listed twice under Bitter Dallying. It grows everywhere. The sprouts are like Black Nightshade. It has small white flowers and green husks; when ripe, they turn deep red. The fruit inside is as large as a cherry and also red. Inside that are tiny seeds. Eating them tastes like green grass. Shizhen says: Black Nightshade and Winter Cherry are of one category but two species. Winter Cherry and Bitter Husk are one species but two varieties—the large one is Winter Cherry, and the small one is Bitter Husk. This is how they are distinguished. "Patrinia" <note>Baijiang</note> is also called Bitter Husk, but it is a different plant. The sprouts and leaves of Black Nightshade and Winter Cherry look the same, but the stem of Black Nightshade is smooth and hairless. It flowers in the fifth month through autumn; the flowers are small, white, with five petals and yellow stamens. It bears seeds without husks, hanging in clusters from the same branch like Gardenia seeds. They start green and ripen to purple. Winter Cherry flowers at the same time; the flowers are yellow-white with a purple center and white cover. The flower is cup-shaped without distinct petals but has five points. It forms a single bell-shaped husk per branch with five ridges, hanging down like a lantern. Inside is a single fruit like a Black Nightshade seed, green when raw and red when ripe. This distinction makes it clear. According to the *Jade Booklet of Geng and Xin*: Lantern Grass grows in all four directions, but the largest comes from Sichuan and Shaanxi. The leaves resemble Black Nightshade and are edible when young. It flowers and fruits in the fourth or fifth month; it has four leaves <note>referring to the husk structure</note> and looks like a lantern. It is called Winter Cherry. Based on this and Yang Shen’s words, the fact that Lantern Grass and Winter Cherry are the same is further proven. Yuxi followed the *Three-Leaved Sour Grass* entry and placed it after Winter Cherry, not knowing they were different plants with similar names. That plant is found under the "Wood Sorrel" entry in the eighth category of grasses.

## Seedlings, Leaves, Stems, and Roots
<insert>Nature and Flavor</insert> Sour, cold, and non-toxic. <insert>Yuxi says: Slightly toxic. <gloss>Gong says:</gloss> Very cold, non-toxic. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Sour and chilling.</insert>
<insert>Primary Indications</insert> Winter Cherry treats heat-related restlessness and fullness, stabilizes the mind, benefits the *qi*, and aids the urinary tract. <gloss>The Classic</gloss> Boiling the juice treats jaundice with great effect. <gloss>Hongjing</gloss> Lantern Grass treats "rebellious qi" <note>coughing or shortness of breath</note>, coughs, wind-heat, and clears the eyes. The roots, leaves, flowers, and fruits are all used. <gloss>Tang Herbal</gloss> Bitter Dallying treats "corpse-transmission" and "hidden-attachment" <note>ancient terms for infectious, wasting diseases like tuberculosis</note>, demonic influences, abdominal masses, yellowing of the eyes, loss of appetite, constipation, urinary blockage, "bone-stealing" heat <note>chronic low-grade fever</note>, cough, sleepiness, and fatigue. It drives away restlessness and pain, treats carbuncles, ulcers, scrofula, and thirst. It treats "Gu-poison" <note>wasting disease from parasites or toxins</note> in children, chills and fever, and abdominal swelling. It kills parasites, induces labor, and clears all toxins. One should drink the decocted juice or the pounded raw juice. It can be ground into a paste to treat "childhood stagnation" <note>nutritional or digestive issues</note>. <gloss>Jiayou Era</gloss> Jing <gloss>Zhenheng</gloss> says: Lantern Grass is bitter and can remove damp-heat. It is "light" in nature and can treat the Upper Jiao <note>the respiratory and circulatory region of the chest</note>, hence it is primary for heat-coughs and sore throats. This grass treats "heat-phlegm" coughs, whereas Gnaphalium <note>Buddha's Ear Grass</note> treats "cold-phlegm" coughs. It is even more effective when used with "Lung-Clearing Pills" containing Scutellaria.

Because it drains dampness, it can transform phlegm and treat ulcers. A person suffering from weakness, fatigue, and a phlegm-cough used this in a decoction, and the effect was divine. <gloss>Formulas</gloss> 3

# Shu Yang Quan
<gloss>Middle grade of the *Classic*</gloss> <gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Sheep’s Spring <gloss>Bielu</gloss>, Sheep’s Candy <gloss>Bielu</gloss>, Lacquer-Aunt Grass <gloss>Bielu</gloss>. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> The origins of these names are no longer understood. <gloss>Su Song and Tao Hongjing say:</gloss> These formulas are no longer used, and no one recognizes the plant. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It grows in flat marshes and damp, shaded areas. The stems and leaves are gathered in the third or fourth month and dried in the shade for storage. <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> In the notes on Cedarwood, it is said that Lacquer-Aunt Grass is fine-leaved and grows mostly by rocks; it can treat lacquer sores <note>allergic contact dermatitis from lacquer trees</note>. Su says Lacquer-Aunt is the same as Sheep’s Spring. Note: Sheep’s Spring is a large herb, while Lacquer-Aunt is as small as a mouse's footprint and grows in the shaded areas of walls and courtyards. Its scent is pungent and intense. Note: Applying it to lacquer sores also treats "stream toxins" <note>water-borne parasitic infections</note>, so they share the name. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Some say "Crow’s Eye Grass" <note>Black Nightshade</note> is actually Lacquer-Aunt, and Lacquer-Aunt is Shu Yang Quan, but people cannot decide for certain. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> There are two types of Lacquer-Aunt. What Su Gong described is Sheep’s Spring. What Tao and Chen described is the "Small Herb." What Su Song called "Crow’s Eye Grass" is actually Long Kui <note>Black Nightshade, *Solanum nigrum*</note>. Furthermore, the juice of the Lacquer-Aunt grass used by wasps to build the base of their nests is this herb. <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic. <gloss>Indications</gloss> Treats skin sores, malignant boils, swelling, scabies, itching, and infantile convulsions. <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss>. Treats tooth decay, internal injuries in the female genitalia, and hard accumulations under the skin. <gloss>From the *Bielu*</gloss>.

**Indications** Infantile convulsions and lacquer sores. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> For those suffering from the vapors of lacquer, crush the herb, mix it with lead red <note>original: "huangdan"</note>, and apply it in layers. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> See the attached formula.

**Jaundice**
> Take a handful of Lacquer-Aunt, crush it for its juice, and take it with wine. It will be cured after no more than three to five doses. — *Zhaoxuan Fang*

# Deer-Hoof Grass
<gloss>Compendium</gloss> <gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Little King of Qin’s Herb <gloss>Compendium</gloss>, King of Qin’s Sword-Testing Herb. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> The leaves of the Deer-Hoof Grass can heal metal wounds <note>wounds from blades</note>, hence the name "Sword-Testing." <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> According to Xuanyuan’s *Baozang Lun*, Deer-Hoof grows mostly in the Jianghuai and Guangdong regions. It is also called Mountain Ci Gu, but that is a different plant. It grows in fields and near abandoned temples. It is extremely rare in Northern Huai, but found in Sichuan and Shaanxi. The sprouts resemble violets, but the leaves are quite large and purple on the underside. In spring, it produces purple flowers and fruits that look like small eggplants <note>Solanum melongena</note>. It can be used in the processing of orpiment and cinnabar. <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> [Missing]. <gloss>Indications</gloss> For bleeding from metal wounds, crush and apply to stop it immediately. It is also applied to treat the venom from snake, insect, and dog bites. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

# Rancid Sauce Herb
<gloss>Middle grade of the *Classic*</gloss> <gloss>Explanatory Names</gloss> Bitter Herb <gloss>Compendium</gloss>, Jian-zu <gloss>Compendium</gloss>, Ze-bai <gloss>Bielu</gloss>, Deer Intestines <gloss>Classic</gloss>, Deer Head <gloss>Bielu</gloss>, Horse Herb <gloss>Bielu</gloss>. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Tao Hongjing noted that the root smells like old, rancid bean sauce, which is why it is so named. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Southerners pick the tender parts, steam them, and dry them to eat as a vegetable. <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>The *Bielu* says:</gloss> Rancid Sauce Herb grows in the river valleys of Jiangxia. Gather the roots in the eighth month and dry them in the sun. <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> It comes from nearby areas. The leaves resemble Xi Xian <note>Siegesbeckia</note> and the root shape is like Bupleurum. <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> This medicine does not come from nearby areas; it mostly grows among hills and ridges. The leaves are different from Water [Rancid Sauce]. <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> The stems and leaves produce yellow flowers. The roots are purple and have the color of old sauce. The leaves do not resemble Xi Xian at all. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is also found in Jiangdong, shaped as Su Gong described. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> It is found everywhere in the plains and wilderness, commonly known as Bitter [Herb].

Wild people eat this herb. People east of the Yangtze River gather and store it. In early spring, the seedlings sprout; they do not wither until late winter. Initially, the leaves spread across the ground, resembling pine needles <note>original: "songye," likely referring to the narrow, divided shape</note>, but the stalks are long with saw-toothed edges. The surface is green and the underside is pale. In summer and autumn, the stalks grow two to three feet high, though they are soft and weak. Every few inches there is a node, and from these nodes, leaves grow outward in four directions like a tiered collar. It bears clusters of white flowers shaped like tiny flakes. The seeds form in clusters of small fruit. The root is white-purple and quite similar to Bupleurum <term>Bupleurum: a medicinal root used to harmonize the body's internal systems</term>. Past claims that the root resembles Balloon Flower <note>Platycodon grandiflorus</note>, or Chen Ziming’s claim that it resembles Snake Berry roots, are both incorrect.

**Root** <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> Whenever you harvest it, pound it coarsely and mix it with Licorice leaves. <gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss> Bitter, flat, and non-toxic. <gloss>The *Bielu* says:</gloss> Salty and slightly cold. <gloss>Quan says:</gloss> Pungent, bitter, and slightly cold. <gloss>Zhen says:</gloss> Sour. Steam it from the hour of the Snake to the hour of the Goat <note>9:00 AM to 3:00 PM</note>, then remove the Licorice and bake until dry for use. <gloss>Daming says:</gloss> Sour. Shizhen says: Slightly bitter with a hint of sweetness. <term>Indications</term> Sudden heat, fire-induced sores, "red qi" <note>likely erysipelas or inflammatory skin redness</note>, scabies, itching, carbuncles, hemorrhoids, and "saddle heat" <note>chafing or sores from riding</note>.

**Qi** <gloss>From the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss> Primarily removes abscesses and swelling, edema, knotted heat, and "wind-dampness" <term>wind-dampness: a condition causing joint pain and stiffness, similar to arthritis</term> deficiency. Treats postpartum pain. <gloss>The *Bielu* says</gloss> It treats toxic wind-sores that have been open for many years. It can turn congealed blood and pus into water. For various postpartum ailments, it stops abdominal pain, residual rashes, and irritability/thirst. Zhen says it treats blood-qi disorders, pain in the heart and abdomen, breaks up "knotted" masses, hastens labor, aids in the delivery of the placenta, treats dizziness, nosebleeds, vomiting blood, vaginal discharge, red eyes with cloudy vision, polyps, ear sores, abscesses, scabies, and "red-skin" toxins <note>erysipelas</note>. It discharges pus and tonifies deficiencies. <gloss>Daming says:</gloss> It treats deafness. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Patrinia <note>original: "Baijiang," literally 'rancid sauce,' named for its smell</note> is a medicine for the Hand and Foot Yangming and Jueyin channels; it is excellent at discharging pus.

It is an easy substance to obtain, yet later generations... <insert>Attached Formulas</insert> <gloss>Three old, two new</gloss> For abdominal abscesses containing pus: <gloss>Patrinia and Aconite Decoction: Use ten parts Coix seed, two parts Aconite, and five parts Patrinia. Grind into a powder. For each dose, take a square-inch spoonful in two liters of water, boil down to one liter, and drink at once. Healing occurs when the patient urinates.</gloss> From Zhang Zhongjing’s *Golden Chamber and Jade Vessel*. <gloss>For postpartum lochia that does not stop after seven or eight days:</gloss> <gloss>Six parts each of Patrinia and Angelica, eight parts each of Teasel root and Peony, four parts each of Chuanxiong and Bamboo shavings, and twelve parts of fried Rehmannia. Boil in two liters of water until eight-tenths of a liter remains. Take on an empty stomach.</gloss> <gloss>From the *Waitai Miyao*</gloss>. For postpartum waist pain where blood and qi have stagnated, making it impossible to turn the waist or knees: eight parts each of Patrinia and Angelica, six parts of Cinnamon heart. Boil in two liters of water until eight-tenths remains. Divide into two doses. Avoid onions. <gloss>From the *Guangji Fang*</gloss>. For "earwig urine" sores <note>a traditional term for a circular, spreading skin rash</note> that wrap around the waist: boil Patrinia into a juice and apply it; it is very effective. From Yang’s *Postpartum Care*. <gloss>From the *Guangji Fang*</gloss>. For postpartum abdominal pain that feels like a needle prick: use Patrinia.

## Winter Jasmine <gloss>From the *Compendium*</gloss> <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> People everywhere plant this. It grows in clusters to a height of two or three feet. It has square stems and thick leaves. The leaves resemble newly sprouted Sichuan pepper leaves but lack teeth; they are green on top and pale underneath. Small branches grow opposite each other at the nodes. One branch has three leaves. In the first lunar month, it opens small yellow flowers shaped like Daphne flowers. it does not produce fruit.

**Leaves** Nature and Flavor: Bitter, astringent, flat, and non-toxic. <term>Indications</term> Swelling toxins and malignant sores. Dry in the shade, grind into powder, and take two to three mace <note>approximately 8-11 grams</note> with wine. Recovery follows after sweating. <gloss>From the *Weisheng Yijian Fang*</gloss>

## Coltsfoot <gloss>Middle Grade of the *Classic*</gloss> <gloss>Explanations of Names</gloss> Kuan-dong. <gloss>Guo Pu’s commentary:</gloss> Ke-dong. <gloss>From the *Erya*:</gloss> Tu-xi. <gloss>The *Bielu* says:</gloss> Dong-xing. <gloss>From the *Jianming Yuan*:</gloss> Tiger’s Whiskers. <gloss>The *Classic*, Shizhen says:</gloss> According to the *Shuzheng Ji*, near the end of the year when the Luo River freezes intensely, Coltsfoot grows amidst the ice and water. It flowers in winter. <gloss>Note:</gloss> Jia says that among all herbs, only this one disregards ice and snow; it is the very first to greet spring. Thus, the world calls it "Ice-Driller" <note>original: "zuandong"</note>. Even beneath the ice and snow, it grows when its time comes. <gloss>The *Cloud Collection Bielu* says:</gloss> Coltsfoot grows in the valleys of Mount Changshan. People harvest the sprouts in spring to use as a vegetable. For medicine, it is best when the flowers are just barely visible. If the fragrance has already been released, its strength is gone. People today often use buds that look like bamboo shoots; these are the ones where the flower has not yet opened. <gloss>Xu’s Illustrated Classic:</gloss> Gather the flowers by the Li River in the eleventh month and dry them. Tao Hongjing.

It is said that the best variety comes from Hebei; those with a shape like a flower bud that has not yet opened are superior. Inside the "belly" of the bud, there are silky threads. The next best varieties come from the ancient Korean kingdoms of Goryeo and Baekje; their flowers resemble small chrysanthemums. Another variety comes from Dangchang in the northern commanderies of Shu <note>modern-day Sichuan</note>, but these are not as high in quality. In the winter months, this plant grows even beneath the ice. 

It is harvested on the first day of the first or twelfth lunar months. Su <note>referring to the Tang dynasty scholar Su Gong</note> says it is now found along the mountain streams of Nanshan in Yongzhou and the valleys of Huazhou. Its leaves resemble those of the mallow but are larger and grow in clusters. The flowers emerge from the base of the root. Song <note>Su Song</note> notes that it is also found in the Guanzhong region today. The root is purple, and the leaves resemble those of the *Bixie* <term>Bixie: Seven-lobed Yam, used to expel "dampness" from the body</term>. Between the twelfth and first lunar months, it produces buds with yellow or purple fuzz. One should dig one or two inches into the soil to find them. When they first emerge, they are straight and fleshy, like *Jingjie* <note>Schizonepeta</note>. They have no seeds. The varieties Tao <note>Tao Hongjing</note> described as coming from Goryeo and Baekje belong to this class. There is also a red-flowered variety with leaves like a lotus but smaller; the larger leaves can hold a liter of liquid, while smaller ones hold a few deciliters. Locals call this "Bee Bucket Leaf" or "Water Bucket Leaf." This is the variety Su described as being "as large as a mallow and growing in clusters." In the "Ode to Coltsfoot," Bo Xian writes in his preface: "I once chased a bird up the North Mountain in the middle of winter. The ice filled the valleys and snow covered the cliffs, yet the Coltsfoot was blooming brilliantly." 

When harvesting, one must remove the inner flower cores and the outer husks, as well as the parts that look like silk or millet husks, along with the stems. 
<margin>Zhen Quan says: Coltsfoot shines brightly when it first flowers.</margin> 
Although this is its nature, it should be soaked in Licorice water for one night, then wrapped in its own leaves for another night, dried in the sun, and the leaves removed before use.

**Nature and Flavor:** Pungent, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Xu Zhicai says: This herb belongs to the Hand Great Yin Lung Meridian.</gloss>

**Primary Health Benefits:** Treats "rebellious" coughing and upward rushing of Qi, settles asthma, and clears throat blockages. It is effective for various types of convulsions, epilepsy, and "evil" chills or fevers. <gloss>From the *Divine Farmer’s Classic*</gloss>. It treats "Wasting and Thirst" <note>a condition similar to diabetes</note>, shortness of breath, and respiratory distress. <gloss>From the *Collected Records*</gloss>. It relieves lung and heart tightness, exhaustion from labor, incessant coughing, thick and sticky phlegm, and lung atrophy or abscesses containing pus and blood. <gloss>According to Zhen Quan</gloss>. It moistens the heart and lungs, benefits the five internal organs, eliminates irritability, and clears the liver to improve eyesight. It also treats conditions such as wind-stroke. <gloss>From the *Daming Materia Medica*</gloss>. <gloss>Zhen Quan says: The *Classic* lists it for coughing. In ancient formulas, it is the most reliable "supreme standard" for warming the lungs and curing coughs.</gloss>

<insert>Treating Chronic Cough</insert> 
A powerful method: Every morning, take an amount of Coltsfoot flowers about the size of a chicken egg. Mix with a little honey to moisten them and place them in a one-liter iron pan. Cover it with a clay basin that has a small hole drilled in it. Insert a small bamboo tube into the hole and seal the edges with paper and mud so no air leaks out. Place charcoal fire under the pan. After a short while, smoke will come out of the tube. Place the tube in the mouth, inhale the smoke, and swallow it. If the chest feels slightly tight, lift the head, and use a finger to plug the tube to prevent smoke from escaping. Continue until the smoke is exhausted. Do this for five days. On the sixth day, eat a full meal of thin mutton noodles, and the ailment will be cured forever. <gloss>One source says to take only three to five breaths.</gloss> 
Alternatively, for someone who has coughed for many days: Burn three taels <note>about 110 grams</note> of Coltsfoot in a windless place and use a tube to inhale the smoke, filling the mouth and swallowing. It will show results in a few days.

<insert>Attached Formulas</insert> 
1. **Phlegm-cough with blood:** <gloss>Take equal parts Coltsfoot flowers and Lily bulbs. Steam and bake them, then grind into a powder. Mix with honey to form pills the size of a longan fruit. Chew one pill at bedtime and wash down with ginger tea. From the *Jisheng Fang*.</gloss>
2. **Mouth sores and ulcers:** <gloss>Take equal parts Coltsfoot and Coptis (*Huanglian*). Grind into a fine powder and mix with saliva to form small cakes. First, rinse the mouth with a decoction of Cnidium seeds (*Shechuangzi*), then apply the cake to the sore. In a short time, it will be much better, and the sore will vanish. From *Yang’s Experienced Formulas*.</gloss>

## Cudweed <gloss>Revised: Now includes the varieties previously listed as "Mouse Ear" and "Buddha Ear"</gloss>
<gloss>Other names: Mouse Ear <gloss>from the *Collected Records*</gloss>, Buddha Ear Herb <gloss>from the *Medicinal Nature*</gloss>, No-Heart Herb, etc.</gloss>

<margin>Li Dongyuan’s method classifies this as "Buddha Ear Herb."</margin>
<gloss>Li Shizhen says: The name refers to the flowers being yellow like "Ju" <note>a ball or cereal</note>, and it can also be mixed with rice flour for food.</gloss>
The "Mouse Ear" name comes from the white fuzz and purple flowers that resemble it. Northerners call it "Fuzzy Mother." "Buddha Ear" is a corruption of "Mouse Ear." People in the Huai region call it "Fuzzy Ear" or "Fragrant Fuzz." 
<gloss>Note: "Mao" (hair) was likely written as "Mao" (cogon grass). According to the *Miscellany of Duan Chengshi*, the "Serpent Wine Herb" is the Mouse Ear. Another name is No-Heart Herb. Perhaps serpents eat this, hence the name?</gloss>
It grows over a foot tall with white-fuzzed leaves and yellow flowers. The *Jingchu Almanac* records: "On the third day of the third month, take the juice of Cudweed and mix it with honey and flour to make 'Dragon Tongue Cakes' <note>interpreted as flat rice cakes</note>." People south of the mountains call it "Fragrant Fuzz" and use the flowers in a pressing process for bark. People south of the Yangtze call it "Mouse Ear Herb." Wang Ji says: "Buddha Ear" is called "Yellow Mugwort" by the people of Huizhou. In the third month, the seedlings grow a foot long with leaves like leek-mallows but thinner with fine white fuzz. The flowers are yellow. Locals gather the stems and leaves, pound them with rice flour, and make cakes. Shizhen notes: The *Rihua Materia Medica* states that "Shuqu" is the "Mouse Ear" of the *Collected Records*. Various scholars did not realize this and moved "Mouse Ear" into the category of "Names Known but Unused." Li Tang’s collection also used "Buddha Ear" without realizing it was the same as "Mouse Ear." It is very common in fields. In the second month, it sprouts soft stems and leaves about an inch long, with white fuzz like a mouse's ear. It produces small yellow flowers in spikes with fine seeds. The people of Chu call it "Rice Koji" <note>referring to fermentation starter</note>, and the people of Hubei call it "Fuzz."

Deng Guizi (also known as Yitian) remarked: "In the north, during the Cold Food Festival <note>A traditional holiday where no fire is lit and only cold food is eaten</note>, people harvest the downy shoots of **Cudweed** <note>original: "Rongmucao" (茸母草), likely *Gnaphalium affine*</note> and mix them with flour to eat. This is the same plant mentioned in the poem by Emperor Huizong of the Song Dynasty: 'Cudweed begins to grow as the smoke-free days are recognized.'"

<gloss>Its flavor is sweet and its nature is balanced; it is non-toxic. The *Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians* <note>original: "Bielu"</note> states it is also called 'Mouse-ear' (Shuer); it is sour and non-toxic. Li Shizhen says 'Buddha-ear Herb' (Fuercao) is sour and warm. When the plant is in full bloom, it should be consumed sparingly, as excessive use can damage the eyesight.</gloss>

**Main Indications:** "Mouse-ear" is primarily used for numbness, chills and fever, and to stop coughing. <gloss>From the *Bielu*</gloss>

**It regulates the "middle" (the digestive system), tonifies the vital energy (Qi), stops diarrhea, eliminates phlegm, and treats seasonal illnesses and "heat" coughs. It can be mixed with rice flour to make cakes, which are sweet and delicious.**

<gloss>Rihua says: "Buddha-ear" treats "cold" coughs and phlegm, removing cold from the lungs and significantly raising the lung energy. Zhu Danxi <note>original: "Zhenheng"</note> notes: For "cold" phlegm coughs, use Buddha-ear; for "heat" coughs, use Groundcherry <note>original: "Denglongcao"</note>. Li Shizhen explains: The *Bielu* says it treats chills, fever, and stops coughing. Li Dongyuan says it treats "cold" coughs, which addresses the symptoms (the "branches"). Rihua says it treats "heat" coughs, which addresses the root cause. Generally, "cold" coughs occur when fire is trapped inside and cold covers the exterior. According to Master Chen’s *Proven Formulas*, the "Three Wonders Powder" (Sanqi San) treats all coughs regardless of how long they have lasted or whether they occur day or night. It uses 50 stalks of Buddha-ear, 200 units of Coltsfoot flower, and two taels of Prepared Rehmannia. These are roasted and ground into a powder. One mace of the powder is burned in a brazier, and the smoke is inhaled through a tube. Any excess saliva should be spat out. A servant girl in Yuanzhou once used this method only twice to cure a chronic illness that other doctors could not treat.</gloss>

# Cassia
## Superior Grade — Explanation of Names
<gloss>Li Shizhen says: This is the "Horse-hoof Cassia" (Matixue Jueming). It is named "Jueming" (Clear Eyes) because of its efficacy in improving vision. There is also a "Wild Cassia" (Caojueming) with similar properties; this is actually the Celosia seed (Qingxiangzi), which Tao Hongjing called "Linghao."</gloss>

<gloss>Collection of Commentaries: The *Bielu* states that Cassia seeds grow in the rivers and marshes of Longmen. They are harvested on the 10th day of the 10th lunar month and dried in the shade for 100 days. Tao Hongjing notes that Longmen is north of Chang'an, but the plant is now found everywhere. Its leaves resemble those of the *Mangzi*, and the seeds are shaped like horse hooves, hence the name "Horse-hoof Cassia." They should be crushed before use. There is another variety of Wild Cassia, a creeping vine. Su Song notes that it is now planted in gardens everywhere. In early summer, the seedlings grow three to four feet tall. The roots are purplish, and the leaves resemble alfalfa but are larger. In the 7th or 8th month, it produces yellow flowers and pods. The seeds look like green beans but are pointed. According to the *Erya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note>, it treats vision loss. Guo Pu explained that the leaves are yellowish and pointed, and the fruit resembles Cornelian Cherry (Shanzhuyu). Some call it "Ling," but descriptions from the west call it "Xiezhai," which seems to be a different species. There is also a variety of Horse-hoof Cassia with leaves like cowpeas and seeds shaped like hooves. The seedlings grow four to five feet tall and are eaten as vegetables in spring. In late autumn, it pods, and the seeds inside look like sheep kidneys. It is widely grown in Hunan and Hubei, sometimes in wild patches. The *Illustrated Classic of the Shu Kingdom* says the variety with wide alfalfa-like leaves is the authentic one. Li Shizhen adds: There are two types. One is Horse-hoof Cassia, three to four feet tall with leaves larger than alfalfa that close at night. It has pale yellow flowers and pods five to six inches long containing green, horse-hoof-shaped seeds; this is the best for eye medicine. The other is "Mangmang Cassia" (Sicklepod), also called "Mountain Flat-bean." Its leaves are pointed like Locust tree leaves and do not close at night. It has deep yellow flowers and small pods with flat, brown seeds. Both can be used to make fermentation starters for wine, but only the tender shoots and flowers of the "Mangmang" variety are edible as vegetables or tea; the Horse-hoof variety is too bitter to eat. Su Song's mention of "Bixie" being the same as Cassia is likely an error.</gloss>

# The Seed
<gloss>Flavor is salty and nature is balanced; non-toxic. The *Bielu* says it is bitter, sweet, and slightly cold. It should be used with "Huo-xiang" (Agastache) as its guide; it dislikes hemp seeds.</gloss>

**Main Indications:** Treats "green blindness" <note>likely glaucoma or internal ocular disorders</note>, inflammation of the eyes, redness, white film over the eye, and excessive tearing. Long-term use strengthens the eyes' ability to perceive light and makes the body feel light. <gloss>From the *Benjing*</gloss>. It treats bluish discoloration of the lips, assists the Liver Qi, and benefits the "essence" (vitality). Mixed with water as a powder, it is applied to toxic swellings. When applied to the temples, it treats headaches. It can also be applied to the chest. It is used in pillows to treat "head-wind" <note>migraines or chronic dizziness</note>; it is even better than black beans for clearing the eyes. <gloss>For liver heat and red, tearing eyes: take one spoonful daily, clean it, and swallow on an empty stomach. After 100 days, one will be able to see clearly even at night.</gloss> It treats blue lips.
<gloss>Zhen Quan says: This information is based on the original texts. Wang Min’s *Record of Mountain Living* says that in spring, one can harvest and eat the young leaves, and the flowers can be dried in the shade and eaten as well.</gloss>

## The Leaf
**Main Indications:** Eaten as a vegetable, it benefits the five internal organs and is excellent for clearing the eyes. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>
<gloss>Li Shizhen says: The *Record of Mutual Influences* states that if Cassia is planted in a garden, snakes will not dare to enter. Zhu Danxi also notes that Cassia can neutralize snake venom.</gloss>
<gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>
<gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>

One must strictly avoid brewing this as tea and consuming it in excess, or they will surely suffer from "wind" <note>In traditional medicine, "wind" (feng) refers to a broad category of symptoms including tremors, dizziness, or erratic pains</note>. **Appendix:** Jiangmang
<gloss>Zangqi's *Supplement to the Materia Medica* states: Tao Hongjing said the leaves of Cassia look like *Jiangmang*. Note: *Jiangmang* grows by the roadside; its leaves are smaller than Cassia. It is neutral in nature and non-toxic. Char three *sheng* of the plant and boil it down to one *sheng*. Divide into two doses. Generally, it is used when blood stagnation causes sores. The *Prescriptions Behind My Elbow* <note>A famous emergency manual by Ge Hong</note> notes it makes a very fragrant drink that eliminates phlegm and stops thirst. It keeps one from sleeping and regulates the "middle" (digestion). The Zen Master Sui Chou used to rub the leaves to make a drink to present to Emperor Yang of the Sui Dynasty. It harmonizes the liver energy without damaging the "Original Qi" (vitality). In Master Xu's *Book of Essential Knowledge*, the entry for *Jiangmang* uses a character pronounced "tu." Another name is *Jianglizi*. This plant resembles a bulrush and grows by the sea, where it can be woven into mats; it is not truly similar to Cassia leaves. Li Shizhen notes: *Jiangmang* is indeed a species of Cassia, which is why folk tradition still calls it "The Lone Occupant." The explanation for this can be found under the entry for mats.</gloss>

**Joint Harmony Grass (Hemingcao)**
<gloss>Zangqi's *Supplement* states: Its flavor is sweet and its nature is cold; it is non-toxic. It is primarily used for sudden "heat strangury" <note>painful, urgent urination associated with internal heat</note> where the urine is red and difficult to pass. It also treats childhood convulsions (seizures), improves eyesight, promotes water drainage, and stops bloody dysentery. Grind it to extract the juice for consumption. It grows in low, damp places. The leaves look like a four-petaled flower; they close together at night (hence the name "Joint Harmony").</gloss>

# Broom Cypress (Difu) <gloss>Upper Grade in the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss>

**Exegesis of Names:** Earth Mallow <gloss>*Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss>, Lu <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Qi <gloss>Guo Pu</gloss>, Lone Broom <gloss>*Illustrated Classic*</gloss>, Dung Broom <gloss>Guo's Commentary</gloss>, Sweeping Broom <gloss>Tao Hongjing</gloss>, Benefit to Eyesight, Joy <gloss>*Tang Materia Medica*</gloss>, White Earth Grass <gloss>*Compendium*</gloss>, Duck-Tongue Grass <gloss>*Illustrated Classic*</gloss>, Prostitute of a Thousand Hearts <gloss>*Alchemical Materia Medica*</gloss>.
<gloss>Li Shizhen says: It is called "Earth Mallow" because the shoots taste like mallow. It is called "Duck-Tongue" because of its shape. It is called "Prostitute" because its branches are prolific and its seeds are numerous. It is called "Benefit to Eyesight" because the seeds function to improve vision. When the plant wilts and grows old, it can be made into a broom, hence the various names involving "Broom."</gloss>

**Collected Explanations:** <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* state:</gloss> Kochia seeds (*Difuzi*) grow in the plains, marshes, and fields of Jingzhou. Harvest the fruit in the eighth and tenth months and dry in the shade.
<gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> It is common in the fields now. People use the stems and shoots to make brooms. The seeds are very fine and are used in tonifying pills and powders. Alchemical texts do not use it much.
<gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> Country folk call it "Earth Zero." Northerners call it "Trailing Robe Herb." Its leaves are fine and the stems are red. It grows in ripe fields. The shoots are extremely weak and cannot stand upright. The claim that it can be made into a broom suggests the author did not actually recognize the plant.
<gloss>Daming says:</gloss> *Difu* is simply the seed of the "Falling Broom" plant. Its color is green and it looks like silkworm droppings after their first sleep.
<gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is found everywhere near the ground in Sichuan. When young, it is five or six inches tall. The root is shaped like mugwort. The stem is red and resembles catnip. In the third month, it opens yellowish-white flowers and produces greenish-white seeds. Harvest the fruit in the eighth or ninth month. The *Seven Spirit Powder of the Immortals* says Kochia seed is the "Essence of the Stars." Some say the shoots are the "Lone Broom," also called "Duck-Tongue Grass." Regarding the disagreement between Tao Hongjing (who says it makes brooms) and Su Gong (who says the stems are too weak), current physicians all agree it is the "Lone Broom." The illustration from Mizhou shows the roots growing in clumps, with twenty to thirty stems per cluster. The stems are red or yellow. It flowers in the seventh month. This is indeed the Broom Cypress.
<gloss>Kou Zongshi says:</gloss> In the eighth month, it withers and the dry stems can be harvested; this matches the description of the "Lone Broom." I suspect the plants in the northwest are shorter and weaker, which led to Su Gong's description.
<gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> The tender shoots of Broom Cypress can be eaten as a vegetable. A single plant has dozens of branches that cluster together in a round, upright shape. Its nature is very supple and weak, so when it is about to grow old, it can be tied into a durable broom. Su Gong's claim that it cannot be used for brooms only refers to the tender shoots. The seeds are the most essential part. The *Erya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> refers to it as *Jian* or "King's Broom." Guo Pu's commentary says it looks like goosefoot and can be used for sweeping. People in the Jiangdong region call it "Falling Broom." This explanation is correct.</gloss>

<summary>This page concludes the medicinal applications of Cassia seeds (Juemingzi) for eye health and skin ailments, then introduces Broom Cypress (Difu), detailing its botanical identification, its use in making household brooms, and its role as a "Superior Grade" medicinal herb for the liver and eyes.</summary>

<keywords>Cassia seeds, Juemingzi, eyesight, liver health, Su Dongpo, Broom Cypress, Difu, Kochia scoparia, traditional medicine, botanical history, broom-making</keywords>

Collect it during the Autumn Equinox and dry in the shade. Tao Hongjing says: It now grows near roadsides. One stem produces thin leaves and reddish-purple flowers.</gloss>

All varieties use the smaller types. There is another kind with similar leaves and stems but with hairy parts; its flowers bloom late and are deep red. According to the *Classic*, the seeds should be harvested when the plant is dry and hot, at which point they will naturally fall off. Su Song <note>original: "颂曰"; a Song Dynasty scholar-official and naturalist</note> says: It is found everywhere today. The sprouts grow to about a foot tall. The leaves resemble those of the small Green-blue plant <note>original: "小青"; likely a species of Indigo or Malabar nut</note>.
The roots are purplish-black and shaped like thin Chinese yams. The flowers are reddish-purple or crimson, resembling the Flame Azalea <note>original: "映山紅"</note>. They bloom from the second to the fifth month and bear fruit in the seventh month, forming spikes. The grains resemble wheat. The plants from Heyang and Hezhong prefectures are used for their sprouts, while those from the Huai River region have thin roots. The wild variety found in villages and fields has flowers as large as coins and is reddish-purple. The cultivated variety in gardens has slightly smaller, delicate flowers that are quite elegant, with fine white powder and a vibrant mix of reddish-purple and crimson spots. Commonly called the "Cut-flower of Luoyang" <note>original: "剪洛陽花"</note>, its fruit resembles wild oats and contains small black seeds.
Once washed, these can be eaten. The tender sprouts can be blanched in water and cooked.

**Medicinal Use of the Spikes** Zhen Quan says: When using this, avoid any specimens without grains; do not use the stems or leaves. If all parts are used together at once, taking it on an empty stomach may cause a choking sensation in the *qi* <note>vital energy</note> and urinary incontinence. When preparing, soak the herb in ginger juice for one full day <note>original: "一伏時"; approximately 24 hours</note>, then drain and dry in the sun. **Flavor and Nature:** Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic. The *Records of Famous Physicians* <note>original: "別錄"</note> says: Sweet, slightly cold, and non-toxic. Red Sage (*Danshen*) acts as its messenger; it is inhibited by the mole cricket and can subdue Cinnabar <note>original: "伏丹砂"; a term from alchemy suggesting it stabilizes or alters the mineral</note>. **Primary Indications:** Tao Hongjing <note>original: "陶隱居"; a famous 5th-century alchemist and physician</note> says it treats various fistulas, urinary
obstruction, and extracts thorns. It resolves abscesses and swellings, brightens the eyes and removes opacities <note>cataracts or films over the eye</note>, breaks up stagnant blood to induce labor or expel a dead fetus, and clears blocked menses. It nourishes the Kidney *qi*, expels pathogens from the Bladder path, stops sudden turmoil <note>original: "霍亂"; refers to acute vomiting and diarrhea</note>, and promotes the growth of hair. Other masters state: It treats the "Five Stranguries" <note>painful urinary disorders</note>, unblocks menstruation, breaks up blood clots, and expels large amounts of pus.

**Medicinal Use of the Leaves** Treats hemorrhoidal fistulas and clears heat from food consumption. It also treats intestinal worms in children and poisoning from mineral drugs <note>original: "丹石藥毒"</note>.
Also used for red, painful swelling of the eyes and toxic swellings. Pound it into a paste to treat spreading sores and vaginal sores in women. Jing says: Fringed Pink is excellent for facilitating the Small
Intestine. Su Song says: Formulas from ancient and modern times consider it the most essential medicine for clearing the Heart Meridian and facilitating the Small Intestine. Zhen Quan says: The "Eight-Ingredient Rectification Powder" <note>original: "八正散"</note> uses Fringed Pink; modern people consider it a vital medicine. However, if there is heat in the Heart Meridian but the Small Intestine is "deficient" <note>weakened or lacking energy</note>, taking it will not resolve the Heart heat and will instead cause a separate illness in the Small Intestine. This is because the Small Intestine and Heart are paired in a "transmission" relationship <note>referring to the TCM concept of paired organs</note>. <header>Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 16, Herb Division</header>

# Cowherb Seed <gloss>Wang Bu Liu Xing</gloss> <gloss>Listed as a Superior Grade herb in the *Classic of Supplementary Records* <note>original: "別錄"; the *Bielu*</note></gloss> <gloss>Forbidden Palace Flower <gloss>According to Rihua</gloss></gloss> <gloss>Golden-Cut Flower <gloss>According to Rihua</gloss></gloss> <gloss>Golden Cup on a Silver Stand <gloss>Shizhen says: The nature of this substance is to move without stopping. Even if there were a Royal Command (Wangming), one could not stay (liu) its movement (xing); hence the name. The Liang and Han versions of the *Materia Medica* call it "Unstoppable Movement," which is likely an error.</gloss></gloss>

## Collected Explanations
<gloss>The *Bielu* states:</gloss> Cowherb Seed grows in the valleys of Mount Tai. It is harvested in the second and eighth months. <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> It is found everywhere today. Its leaves resemble those of the Ground Cherry <note>original: "酸漿"; *Physalis alkekengi*</note> and the seeds resemble pine nuts. Some say it is a type of smartweed, but that is not so. It is frequently used in prescriptions for carbuncles and fistula. <gloss>Han Baosheng says:</gloss> It grows in many places. The leaves resemble Woad <note>original: "菘藍"; *Isatis tinctoria*</note>. Its flowers are reddish-white. The seed pod resembles the Ground Cherry; inside, the fruit is round and black, like turnip seeds and about the size of broomcorn millet. The sprouts are gathered in the third month and the seeds in the fifth. The roots, sprouts, flowers, and seeds are all used medicinally. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Today it is found in the Jiang-Zhe region and near rivers. The sprouts and stems are both green, reaching about seven or eight inches in height. The roots are yellow, like those of Shepherd's Purse. The leaves resemble small spearheads or sometimes locust tree leaves. In the fourth month, it blooms with varied yellow and purple flowers, appearing alongside the grass like pine nuts or Pig’s Tooth Flowers. In the fifth month, the sprouts and stems are harvested and dried in the sun. Common folk call it "Golden-Cut Flower." The variety growing north of the Yellow River has rounder leaves and red flowers, which is a slight variation. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> It mostly grows in wheat fields. The sprouts reach one or two feet. In the third or fourth months, small flowers bloom like little bells, reddish-white in color. The fruit forms like the Lantern Plant <note>original: "燈籠草"; another name for Ground Cherry</note>; the seed pod has five ridges. Inside the pod is a fruit the size of a pea, containing fine seeds like turnip seeds. They are white when raw and black when ripe, perfectly round like tiny pearls. They are edible. Tao Hongjing’s claim that the leaves resemble Ground Cherry and Su Song’s claim that the flowers resemble pine nuts were not carefully observed; they were likely describing the seeds as if they were flowers or leaves. <gloss>The Lantern Plant is the Ground Cherry. Both its sprouts and seeds are used in medicine.</gloss>

## The Seeds <gloss>Miaoji</gloss>

### Preparation
<gloss>Lei Xiao says:</gloss> After harvesting, mix them with moisture and steam from the hour of the Snake to the hour of the Sheep <note>9 AM to 3 PM</note>. Soak them in rice-washing water overnight, then bake dry for use.

### Flavor and Nature
<gloss>Bitter, neutral (flat), and non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Wu Pu says:</gloss> Shennong says it is bitter and neutral. Qibo and Leigong say it is sweet. <gloss>Li Gao says:</gloss> Bitter and neutral. It is the "Yin within Yang" <note>meaning it has a cooling, descending nature but possesses some active, rising qualities</note>.

### Main Cures
Incised wounds, stopping bleeding, expelling pain, extracting thorns, removing "wind-dampness" numbness and internal blockages. It stops palpitations, nosebleeds, carbuncles, malignant sores, and fistula. Helps with difficult labor in women. Taken long-term, it lightens the body, prevents aging, and increases longevity. <gloss>From the *Bielu*</gloss> Treats wind-toxins and clears the blood vessels. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss> Expels wind-damp numbness, treats irregular menstruation in women, and carbuncles on the back. <gloss>Rihua</gloss> Promotes the flow of breast milk. <gloss>Li Gao</gloss> Benefits urination and extracts bamboo or wood splinters. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>

### Inventions
<gloss>Li Gao says:</gloss> Cowherb Seed is used to guide breast milk downward because of its ability to benefit the blood vessels. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Cowherb Seed can move the blood division. It is a medicine for the Yangming <note>Stomach</note> and the Penetrating and Conception vessels <note>Chong and Ren vessels, essential for female reproductive health</note>. There is a folk saying: "If a woman takes Pangolin scales and Cowherb Seed, her milk will flow forever." This illustrates its nature—it moves and never stays. According to Wang Zhizhong’s *Classic of Nourishing Life*, a woman suffered from painful urination (strangury) and stayed in bed for a long time; no medicine worked. Her husband consulted me at night. Following an effective recipe for all types of strangury, I told him to decoct ten or so leaves of the Golden-Cut Flower. The next morning he said the illness was eighty percent gone. Another dose cured her. Golden-Cut Flower is another name for Cowherb Seed. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Zhang Zhongjing treated incised wounds with "Cowherb Seed Powder," and the *Zhenyuan Guangli Fang* treated various "wind-infestations" with "Cowherb Seed Decoction." These are both highly effective.

### Attached Formulas <gloss>1 old, 8 new</gloss>

#### Unceasing Nosebleeds
Take Golden-Cut Flower (Cowherb Seed), including stems and leaves, dry in the shade, and make a strong decoction. Drink warm. <gloss>From *Zhixiao Zhinan Fang*</gloss>

#### Blood in Stool
Take Cowherb Seed powder, one teaspoon <note>approx. 1 gram</note>, with water. <gloss>From *Shengji Zonglu*</gloss>

#### Blood Loss from Wounds
"Cowherb Seed Powder" for treating wounds from knives or axes. Use 10 parts Cowherb Seed <gloss>harvested Aug. 8th</gloss>, 10 parts fine Sambucus leaves <gloss>harvested July 7th</gloss>, 10 parts White Root Bark of Southeast-facing Mulberry <gloss>harvested Aug. 3rd</gloss>, 3 parts Sichuan Pepper, 10 parts Licorice, and 2 parts each of Scutellaria, Dried Ginger, Peony, and Magnolia Bark. Burn the first three ingredients to retain their properties, then grind the remaining six into powder and mix. For large wounds, take a large spoonful with a drink. For small wounds, simply apply the powder. This can also be taken after childbirth. <gloss>From Zhang Zhongjing's *Essential Prescriptions from the Golden Cabinet*</gloss>

#### Insufficient Breast Milk
For milk deficiency caused by Qi stagnation: "Gushing Spring Powder" <note>Yongquan San</note>. Equal parts Cowherb Seed, Pangolin scales <gloss>roasted</gloss>, Dragon Bone, Fringed Pink spikes, and Ophiopogon. Grind into powder. Take one teaspoon with warm wine, followed by pig’s trotter soup. Comb the breasts with a wooden comb three times a day. <gloss>From *Xianfeng Huipian*</gloss>

#### Cold Pain from Head-Wind
Equal parts Cowherb Seed and Fragrant Angelica <note>Baizhi</note>. Grind into powder. Apply dry to the hair overnight, then comb out. <gloss>From *Shenghui Weisheng Baojian*</gloss>

#### Carbuncles and Various Sores

# Cut Spring Silk <gloss>From the *Compendium* <note>original: "綱目"; the *Bencao Gangmu*</note></gloss>

<gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Cut Red Gauze Flower <gloss>From a poem by Han Qi</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> The Cut Spring Silk <note>original: "剪春羅"; *Lychnis coronata*</note> sprouts in the second month. The stalks grow over a foot tall and are supple. The green leaves grow in opposite pairs, clasping the stem. In summer, it blooms with deep red flowers as large as coins. Each flower has six petals, and the edges are serrated as if cut by scissors, making them quite lovely. The fruit is the size of a bean and contains fine seeds. Many people plant it for its ornamental value. There is also the "Cut Red Gauze Flower," which has stalks three feet high and overlapping leaves; it blooms in summer and autumn. Its flowers resemble the Fringed Pink <note>original: "石竹"; *Dianthus chinensis*</note> but are slightly larger, with four sides appearing as if clipped, and are red in color. The seed head is like that of the Fringed Pink and contains fine seeds.

## Properties: Sweet, Cold, Non-toxic

## Primary Indications: For "Fire-belt" sores <note>original: "火帶瘡"; likely referring to Shingles (Herpes Zoster)</note> that wrap around the waist. Harvest the flowers or leaves, crush them, and apply as a poultice. It may also be used in powdered form. <gloss>Shizhen says: This herb does not appear in older medical formula books. Based on its properties, it should also promote urination and treat swellings and pus.</gloss>

# Pot Marigold <gloss>From *Relief of Famine*</gloss> <gloss>Corrected Edition</gloss> <gloss>Incorporated from the *Illustrated Classic* of the Song Dynasty; also called "Little Golden Cup" or "Ever-spring Flower"</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> The Pot Marigold <note>original: "金盞草"; *Calendula officinalis*</note> is named because the flower is shaped like a golden wine cup.

<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Pot Marigold grows in Changzhou, trailing along the base of fences. The leaves grow in opposite pairs. In autumn... <gloss>Prince Xuan of Zhou says:</gloss> The sprouts of the Little Golden Cup grow four to five inches high. The leaves resemble young lettuce but are thicker and narrower, growing from the stem. The leaves are tender and brittle. The flowers at the tip of the stem are the size of a fingertip, golden-yellow, and shaped like a small lid. It blooms through all four seasons. The leaves have a sour taste; they can be blanched, soaked in water, and eaten with oil and salt. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> In summer it bears fruit. Inside the calyx, there are several seeds huddled together like coiled "measuring worms" <note>original: "尺蠖"; inchworms or geometer moth larvae</note>. Therefore, Su Song’s claim that they "transform into insects" is incorrect; they are merely seeds that look like insects.

## Properties: Sour, Cold, Non-toxic

# Draba <gloss>Inferior Grade in the *Divine Farmer’s Classic* <note>original: "本經"; the *Shennong Bencao Jing*</note></gloss>

<gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Lijing <gloss>Pronunciation by Guo</gloss>, Dashishi <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss>, Dashi <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss>, Dog's Shepherd's Purse <gloss>From the *Supplementary Records*</gloss>. <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> The etymology of the name "Tingli" <note>original: "葶藶"; *Draba nemorosa* or *Descurainia sophia* (Tansy Mustard)</note> cannot be easily explained.

<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* say:</gloss> Draba grows in the plains and fields of Gaocheng. Harvest the seeds after the Start of Summer <note>term: "立夏"; a solar term beginning around May 5th</note> and dry them in the shade. <gloss>Tao Hongjing says:</gloss> It can be found everywhere. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> It is found today in the prefectures east of Kaifeng and north of Shaanxi. Those from Caozhou are the finest. In early spring, it sprouts leaves six to seven inches high, resembling shepherd's purse. The root is white, and the stalks are green. In the third month, it blooms with tiny yellow flowers and produces flat pods with tiny seeds like yellow broomcorn millet. The *Monthly Ordinances* <note>original: "月令"; a classic ritual text</note> state that in the first month of summer, "the Mi-grass dies." Commentators Xu Shen and Zheng Xuan both state that Mi-grass refers to Draba and its relatives. Another theory says Mi-grass is a climbing vine. There is also "Dog's Mustard," whose leaves grow near the root and whose sprouts are thin and long; one must distinguish between these two. <gloss>Lei Xiao says:</gloss> Do not use the "Red-beard" seeds; they look similar but have a slightly sweet and bitter taste. The bitterness of true Draba seeds "enters the crown of the head." <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> According to the *Er Ya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note>, "Li" is Draba. Guo Pu's commentary says the seeds and leaves both resemble mustard. One name is "Dog's Shepherd's Purse." Thus, Dog's Mustard is indeed Draba. There are sweet and bitter varieties. Dog's Mustard has a slightly sweet flavor and is the Sweet Draba. Some say Sweet Draba is actually the seed of the Fringed Water Lily, but judging by its effects, this is likely incorrect.

# The Seed <gloss>Lei Xiao says:</gloss> When using Draba, combine it with glutinous rice...

## Properties: Pungent, Cold, Non-toxic. <gloss>The *Supplementary Records* say: Bitter, Very Cold; works well with wine.</gloss> <gloss>Zhen Quan says: Sour, slightly toxic; should be roasted for medicinal use.</gloss> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says: It is a "sinking" herb, Yang within Yin.</gloss> <gloss>Zhang Zhongjing says: Place it on the stove and lightly roast it until the rice is cooked, then remove the rice and pound the seeds for use.</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> Draba benefits from wine, which carries its Qi to the brain... It dislikes Silkworm Slough and *Ranunculus sceleratus*.

# Primary Indications: Abdominal masses, accumulated Qi, and fluid retention. Treats chills and fevers, breaks up hardness, expels pathogens, and opens the water passages. <gloss>From the *Classic*</gloss>. Lowers Qi in the bladder, treats heat trapped in the skin and edema of the face and eyes. For sudden heat-stroke or abdominal fullness. Best used with Large Jujubes. <gloss>From the *Supplementary Records*</gloss>.

# Draba <gloss>Tansy Mustard</gloss>
<margin>11</margin>
**Herbs Category**

Long-term use causes a person to become deficient <note>original: "虛"; "Xu" refers to a state of depletion in the body's vital energy or substance.</note>. <gloss>From the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> It treats lung congestion, ascending Qi <note>reversal of the natural downward flow of energy</note>, coughing, and rapid wheezing; it also removes masses and fluid accumulations in the chest. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss> It opens the menstrual flow. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Gao stated that Draba strongly descends Qi; it should be used with pungent or sour substances to guide out the "swelling Qi." The *Ten Categories of Materia Medica* states that "draining can remove congestion." Its flavor and energy are both intense, no less than that of Rhubarb <note>original: "大黃"; a potent purgative</note>. Furthermore, its nature surpasses other medicines in its ability to drain the blockage of the Yang portion of the Lungs. It can also purge the bowels. Because its physical form is light, it represents Yang. <gloss>Zongshi says:</gloss> There are two types of Draba: sweet and bitter. Their appearance is the same. The Classics state the flavor is pungent and bitter; therefore, the sweet variety is no longer included in medicine. Generally, its therapeutic essence is used to move water and drain fluids. Thus, it is said that "long-term use causes deficiency," as it utilizes the principle of bitter draining. <gloss>Records on the Nature of Medicinals</gloss> should not state that the flavor is sour. It says Draba belongs to the element of Fire and is urgent in nature, excelling at chasing out water. Patients who are even slightly deficient should avoid it. It is very effective at "killing" <note>meaning it is highly potent/toxic if misused</note>; why wait for long-term use to become deficient? <gloss>Wang Haogu says:</gloss> Their primary treatments differ. Master Zhongjing used the "Bitter" variety for his Lung-Draining Decoction, while other formulas might use the "Sweet" variety or not specify. Generally, the bitter type drains downward, while the sweet type is more gradual. One must carefully examine whether the patient's condition is "Excess" or "Deficient." Although the *Materia Medica* says their treatments are the same, how can the sweet and bitter flavors not differ? <gloss>Shizhen says:</gloss> The two types, sweet and bitter, are just like the black and white colors of Morning Glory seeds <note>original: "牽牛"; *Ipomoea nil*</note>—their speed of action differs. It is also like the sweet and bitter varieties of Gourd; their medicinal and toxic properties vary. Generally, the sweet type's draining nature is slow; while it drains the Lungs, it does not harm the Stomach. The bitter type's draining nature is urgent; as it drains the Lungs, it easily damages the Stomach. Therefore, Jujubes <note>original: "大棗"; Chinese dates</note> are used as an adjuvant to protect the body. However, for urgent cases of water-Qi and swelling in the Lungs, nothing but this herb can remove it. Once the water is gone, one should stop; it must not be over-prescribed. If not taken for a long time, how could it "kill" a person? *Huainanzi* says: "Great Euphorbia removes water, and Draba heals bloating." If used without moderation, it will instead result in... <insert>**Attached Formulas** <gloss>14 old, 6 new</gloss></insert>

# Plantain
<gloss>Top Grade in the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss>

### Name Explanations
**Fuyi** <insert>pronounced *fú-yǐ*</insert>, **Xi** <insert>pronounced *xī*</insert>, **Ma-xi** <insert>pronounced *mǎ-xī*</insert>, **Cartwheel Herb**, **Xia** <insert>pronounced *xiá*</insert>, **Wei** <insert>pronounced *wěi*</insert>, **Earth Clothing** <note>from the *Compendium*</note>, **Toad's Coat** <note>from the *Miscellaneous Records*</note>, **Cow's Tongue** <note>from the *Poetry Commentary*</note>.

> The names *Xi*, *Ma-xi*, and "Cow’s Droppings" all refer to things trodden underfoot. People of Youzhou call it "Cow’s Tongue." Because the herb's runners spread and hide low to the ground, people east of the Yangtze River call it "Plant-in-front-of-the-Cart" <note>Cheqian</note>. It grows in wild fields. Lu Ji's *Poetry Commentary* states: This herb loves to grow by the roadsides and within the tracks of cattle and horses, hence the name "Plantain" (In-front-of-the-Cart). Regarding the names "Toad's Coat" and the claims in the *Outer Tradition of Han Poetry* that the straight stems are called *Cheqian* while the drooping ones are *Fuyi*—I fear these are forced explanations. Luo Yuan says: It grows on both sides of the road. Tao Hongjing says: The variety currently coming from Kaizhou is superior. Su Song says: It is found everywhere near the Bian River in the north and the Huai River valley. In early spring, the seedlings sprout with leaves spreading on the ground like the surface of a spoon. Older plants grow over a foot long. From the center, several stalks rise like rat tails, bearing very tiny flowers. Su Song describes the color as slightly reddish, with seeds like Draba but black. Today, people harvest the seedlings in the fifth month and the seeds in the seventh and eighth months. Some grow it in gardens; it is especially prized in Sichuan. Northerners sometimes take the roots, sun-dry them, and mistakenly sell them as "Purple Flower." Lu Ji mentioned that the tender seedlings make a very slippery potherb, though people today no longer eat them. Shizhen notes: Wang Man’s *Records of Mountain Living* contains a method for pruning and eating the seedlings, showing that the ancients frequently used it as a vegetable. Wilderness dwellers still gather and eat it today.

### Seeds
<gloss>From *Emergency Formulas* and the *Compendium*. Li Shizhen notes: For all uses, they must be washed in water to remove sand, sun-dried, and stir-fried before use in decoctions. For pills or powders, soak in wine overnight, steam until cooked, mash into a pulp to make cakes, sun-dry, and then roast and grind.</gloss>

**Aroma and Flavor:** Sweet, Cold, Non-toxic.
<gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* say: Salty, slightly cold. Tao Hongjing says: Slightly cold. Kou Zongshi says: Neutral. Daiming says: Constantia <note>Changshan</note> serves as its messenger herb.</gloss>

### Primary Locations
Treats urinary blockage and stops pain, benefits the water pathways and urination, and eliminates "damp-numbness." Long-term use makes the body feel light and resists aging. <gloss>From the *Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss>
Treats internal injury in men and supplements essence. It helps people have children and brightens the eyes while treating redness and pain. <gloss>From the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>
Stops cholera, benefits the liver against "wind-heat" toxins, treats red eyes and pain from wind-blown irritation, cataracts, headaches, and excessive tearing. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>
Nourishes the liver and lungs; treats difficult labor in women. <gloss>Tao Hongjing</gloss>
Conducts heat out of the small intestine and stops diarrhea or dysentery caused by summer dampness. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>

<margin>Cited in *Evidence-Based Materia Medica* and the *Compendium*</margin>
Tao Hongjing states: Plantain seed is cooling by nature. The *Classic of the Immortals* suggests taking it as a supplement, saying it makes the body light. A famous ancient formula for longevity, "Jingwan," uses Plantain and Cuscuta <note>Dodder seed</note> mixed with honey into pills. Wang Haogu states: Plantain seed can facilitate urination without draining the body's Qi, sharing similar merits with Poria <note>Fuling</note>. Li Shizhen states: According to the *Classic of Divine Consumption*, Plantain is also called "Earth Clothing" and is the essence of the spirits; consuming it can transform one's form. It says to harvest in the eighth month. Today, Plantain seeds are mature by the fifth month; the mention of the seventh or eighth month is simply due to differences in regional climates. A poem by Zhang Ji of the Tang Dynasty says: "In the fifth month in Kaizhou, the Plantain seeds / Are called divine by all who use them as medicine. / I feel for Wenjun's ailing eyes / Sending them from three thousand miles away." This shows that the fifth-month harvest from Kaizhou was considered best. It also demonstrates its power in treating the eyes. Generally, for tonic use, it must be paired with other herbs, much like how Alisma is used in the "Six-Ingredient Rehmannia Pill." If used alone, its draining effect is too strong and perhaps not suitable for long-term use. The statesman Ouyang Xiu once suffered from a sudden, severe bout of diarrhea that the imperial physicians could not cure. His wife bought a packet of medicine from a street vendor, and he recovered instantly. When he asked for the formula, it was simply powdered Plantain seed taken with rice water. The logic was that the medicine cleared the water pathways without disturbing the Qi; once the water was flowing correctly, the "pure" and "turbid" elements of the body were separated, and the diarrhea stopped naturally.

# Plantain

<gloss>Preparation</gloss> Lei Xiao says: When using this herb, one must find a specimen with a central spike, which can be one or two inches long. Steam the spikes, leaves, and roots together. # Compendium of Materia Medica
### Volume 16: Vervain

This is a name given to various types of "Dragon's Teeth" <note>original: "Longya"; often used for Agrimony, but here discussed in the context of Vervain</note>. <gloss>【Collected Explanations】</gloss> **Hongjing** <note>Tao Hongjing, 5th-century physician</note> says: It is very common in villages and along paths. The leaves resemble Wild Ginger (*Asarum*), and the flowers are purple, slightly resembling those of Lotus-leaf Wormwood. **Gong** says: The leaves resemble Wolf’s Teeth or Motherwort. It produces three or four spikes, with flowers like those of Plantain, resembling the tip of a whip. Tao's previous descriptions are unreliable and cause confusion. **Song** says: It generally looks like Mugwort. **Baosheng** says: The flowers are white. Harvest the seedlings and leaves in the seventh or eighth month and dry them in the sun for use. **Su Song** says: Today it is found in the prefectures of Mount Heng, Mount Lu, and the Yangtze-Huai region. The seedlings resemble Motherwort, but the stems are round, growing two to three feet high. He also says: "Dragon’s Teeth Herb" grows in Shi Province; it is about two feet tall, with seedlings and leaves in spring that wither in autumn and winter. The roots are washed clean for use. **Shizhen** <note>Li Shizhen, the author</note> says: Vervain <note>literally "Horse-whip Herb"</note> grows in many places. It sprouts in spring with square stems and leaves like Motherwort growing in opposite pairs. In summer and autumn, it blooms with purple flowers on spikes, similar to Plantain spikes. Its seeds are like lotus seeds but taller and thinner. Its roots are white and small. Tao’s claim that the flowers resemble wormwood, Han’s claim that the flowers are white, and Su’s claim that the stems are round are all incorrect.

# Compendium of Materia Medica: Volume 16, Herbs

### Snake-mouth Herb <note>original: "Shehan" (蛇銜); likely *Potentilla kleiniana*</note>

**Song** <note>Su Song, 11th-century scholar</note> says: This herb originates in Xing Province, though it now grows nearby in rocky soil or damp lowlands. People in Sichuan also cultivate it. It consists of a single stem with five or seven leaves and two stalks. The roots are harvested in the eighth month and dried in the shade. **Rihua** says: It has no leaves; the whole plant is harvested in the fifth month. It is also called "Purple-backed Dragon's Teeth" <note>original: "Zibei Longya"</note> and grows in Sichuan. It can be harvested during the spring and summer at any time. **Shizhen** <note>Li Shizhen, the author</note> says: There are two varieties. The one with fine leaves is called **Snake-mouth** (*Shehan*), and the one with large leaves is called **Dragon-mouth** (*Longhan*). Dragon-mouth is also used in ointments for scrofula <note>tuberculosis of the lymph nodes</note>. For Snake-mouth, use the leaves dried in the sun; do not expose them to fire. The roots and stems are not used, so do not use them by mistake. There is another herb with the same name, but its properties are different. <gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic. <gloss>Quan says: It is toxic.</gloss> **Song** says: Purple-backed Dragon's Teeth is pungent, cold, and non-toxic.

**Main Indications**
Seizures and epilepsy, chills and fevers, "evil qi" <note>pathogenic factors</note>, and clearing heat. It treats metal-inflicted wounds <note>cuts from blades</note>, malignant sores, hemorrhoids, scrofula, and carbuncles on the head. <gloss>From the Classic of Materia Medica</gloss> It treats evil qi in the chest and abdomen, abdominal pain, dampness-related numbness, and stabilizes the fetus. It is beneficial for children’s ailments, specifically treating childhood fevers, "cinnabar toxins" <note>erysipelas, a skin infection</note>, and swelling. It stops bleeding and kills "ghost toxins" <note>hidden pathogens or infections</note>. The juice can be applied to red and swollen eyes. For bites from snakes, vipers, or stings from bees and scorpions, rub the area with Purple-backed Dragon's Teeth mixed with vinegar; it neutralizes all snake venoms. For throat pain, gargle and swallow the juice for immediate effect. <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> **Zhangqi** says: Snake-mouth treats snake bites. Today, if the herb is placed in a snake’s mouth, even if it bites a person, the venom will not take effect. Planting it also keeps snakes away. **Song** says: Ancient and modern formulas for skin infections and scrofula commonly use it. <gloss>From Record of Proven Experiments</gloss> To treat scrofula, pound Snake-mouth herb into a pulp and apply it; it will heal. This condition often arises from cold-dampness in the muscles, which then turns to heat and becomes red. It worsens in hot weather and subsides in the cold.

**Shizhen** says: According to Ge Hong’s *Master Who Embraces Simplicity*, **Snake-mouth Ointment** can reconnect severed fingers. I have investigated this. Ge Hong’s *Handy Prescriptions for Emergencies* records this ointment for treating carbuncles, swelling, blood stasis, postpartum blood accumulation, and various eye and ear diseases, as well as sores on the necks of oxen and horses. Use Snake-mouth, Rhubarb, Aconite, Peony, Spurge, Asarum, Lovage, Scutellaria, Angelica, Mangle-plant, and Sichuan Pepper—one tael each—and fourteen pieces of Realgar. Grind these into a powder, soak in bitter wine overnight, then add two catties of pig fat. Boil over a "seven-star fire" until it becomes an ointment. Store it. For internal illness, take a pill the size of a bullet with warm wine twice a day. For external illness, rub and apply it. For ear issues, plug the ear with a cotton ball soaked in it. <insert>Attached Prescriptions</insert> <gloss>Two old, one new.</gloss> For postpartum thirst and diarrhea: take a handful of Small Dragon-tooth roots, decoct them thickly, and drink; it is very effective. **For bleeding from metal wounds:** apply the juice of the herb. If one tael of "Dragon-mouth Vine" is added, it is called **Dragon-mouth Ointment**. I do not know if this is the same ointment said to reconnect fingers. <gloss>If effective, it is the Snake-mouth formula.</gloss> From the *Doumen Prescriptions*: Pound the herb and apply it. **Spirit-of-the-Body Medicine:** For skin ailments, grind Purple-backed herb with raw alum and apply. **Centipede and Scorpion Stings:** Pound Snake-mouth and apply it. From *Handy Prescriptions for Emergencies*: Spirit-of-the-Body Medicine using three new roots of thorny caltrop. From *Record of Proven Experiments*.

# Female Azure
<gloss>Classic of Materia Medica: Middle Grade</gloss> <gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> <insert>Sparrow Gourd</insert> <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> The *Additional Records* say Female Azure <note>original: "Nvqing"</note> is the root of the Snake-mouth herb. It grows in Zhuya and is harvested in the eighth month and dried in the shade. **Hongjing** says: If it were simply the root of Snake-mouth, it should not grow only in Zhuya. The plant commonly used by the people has different leaves and is a separate entity; it is unclear which is correct. A master says: carrying one tael of this prevents plague and pestilence, but one must recognize the true plant. Another says: merchants use a root shaped like "Japanese Teasel" <note>*Dipsacus*</note> with very bitter leaves, claiming it is Female Azure root from Jingzhou. **Gong** says: This herb is actually "Sparrow Gourd" <note>original: "Quepiao"</note>. It grows in level marshes. The leaves resemble *Metaplexis* and grow in opposite pairs. The fruit is shaped like a gourd and is the size of a date, hence the name Sparrow Gourd. The root resembles *Cynanchum atratum*. Both the leaves and flowers are the true Female Azure. It is not the same category as Snake-mouth. Furthermore, the *Additional Records* state the young leaves resemble *Metaplexis*, round at the ends and large, with black stems and yellow-white sap. This matches the previous description. If it were the root of Snake-mouth, how could the seedlings grow in Yi Province while the roots are in Zhuya, ten thousand miles apart? Because *Metaplexis* leaves resemble Female Azure, it is also called Sparrow Gourd. **Zhangqi** says: *Metaplexis* is "White-ring Vine," and Sparrow Gourd is Female Azure. The two are similar and hard to distinguish, but they are not the same thing. **Ji** says: *Metaplexis* refers to the seeds, Female Azure to the root, and Snake-mouth to the seedlings. These three differ greatly in nature and function. Various commentators suspected they were one thing because they share the name Sparrow Gourd, or suspected they were two things because they come from different regions. The *Materia Medica* clearly states Female Azure is the root of Snake-mouth; why doubt this just because the root and seedling are harvested in different places? Just as the production sites of *Miwu* and *Chuanxiong* <note>lovage</note> differ, should we split them into two plants? Or like how *Chijian* and *Xuchangqing* are both called "Ghost-Supervisor," should they be combined into one? **Shizhen** says: There are two types of Female Azure. One is a vine, which is the *Metaplexis*-like plant described by Su Gong. The other is a herb, which is the root of the Snake-mouth herb. Snake-mouth has two types, large and small. The fine-leaved one is Snake-mouth; the large-leaved one is Dragon-mouth, and its root is used. Thus, in Wang Tao’s *Arcane Essentials from the Imperial Library*, the "Dragon-mouth Ointment" used for carbuncles and metal wounds uses the root of Dragon-mouth, which is this Female Azure. Chen Zhangqi said Female Azure and *Metaplexis* cannot be distinguished, and Zhang Yi's *Expanded Encyclopedia* said Female Azure is a type of Kudzu; both refer to the vining Female Azure, not this one. The *Additional Records* clearly state Female Azure is the root of Snake-mouth—this single statement is our evidence. Other schools are wrong to doubt it based only on its growth in Zhuya. Local traditions vary, and perhaps they did not know there are two types of Female Azure. Furthermore, the *Records of Mount Luofu* mention a "Male Azure" that resembles Female Azure on that mountain...
