### Root

**Flavor and Nature:** Pungent, balanced, and toxic. <gloss>Quan says: Bitter and non-toxic. Snake-mouth Herb <note>original: "Shehan" (蛇銜)</note> acts as its catalyst.</gloss>

**Main Indications:** Poisoning from "Gu" parasites <note>original: "Gudu" (蠱毒); refers to toxins derived from venomous creatures or dark magic</note>, expelling evil and malignant "qi" <note>pathogenic energy</note>, killing demons, treating "warm malaria" <note>a type of malaria with more heat than chills</note>, and warding off ill omens. <gloss>Prescriptions: 2 old, 1 new.</gloss>

> Sudden death: <gloss>Grind **Female Azure** <note>original: "Nvqing" (女青); possibly *Cynanchum atratum*</note> into a fine powder. > Vomiting and diarrhea: <gloss>Also for adults or children whose abdominal skin suddenly turns blue-black and who cannot breathe. Use **Magnolia flower** <note>original: "Xinyi"</note>, **wild soybean** <note>original: "Ludou"</note>, bark, and **celosia seed** <note>original: "Qingxiangzi"</note>, one *liang* <note>approx. 30-40 grams</note> each. Grind these on a *Yin* day <note>the third day in the 12-day Chinese calendar cycle, often associated with ritual power</note> along with **Female Azure** powder. Place in a triangular crimson bag. For emergencies, put the **Female Azure** powder in the mouth and wash down with wine.</gloss> Source: *Secrets of Mother and Child*.

> Warding off epidemics: <gloss>On the first *Yin* day of the first lunar month, grind **Female Azure** into a powder and place it in a triangular crimson bag. Hang this inside the bed canopy for great fortune.</gloss> Source: *Handbook of Prescriptions for Emergencies*.

### Mouse-tail Herb <gloss>From the *Bielu* (Supplementary Records), Lower Grade</gloss>

**Explanatory Names:** *Quchu*, *Shanlingqiao* (Mountain Ridge Beauty), and what the people of Wu <note>modern-day Jiangsu/Zhejiang area</note> call **Mouse-tail Herb** <note>original: "Shuweicao" (鼠尾草); likely *Salvia japonica* or a related sage</note>. <gloss>Shizhen says: It is named "Mouse-tail" because the shape of its flower spike resembles one. The *Erya* <note>the oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> states that *Quchu* is the Mouse-tail herb. It can be used to dye things black <note>original: "zao" (皂)</note>, hence the name. It is also called "Water Azure." Su Song’s *Illustrated Materia Medica* calls it *Lingshi*, but this is a mistake for *Lingqiao*.</gloss>

**Collected Explanations:** <gloss>The *Bielu* says: Mouse-tail grows in flat marshes. Gather the leaves in the fourth month and the flowers in the seventh, then dry in the shade. Tao Hongjing says: It is very common in the fields; people gather it to produce dyes. Wu Baosheng says: It is found everywhere in low, damp ground, but only the people of Qianzhong <note>modern Guizhou</note> gather it for medicine. Its leaves resemble mugwort, and the end of the stem produces four or five spikes in summer. These spikes look like plantain. There are two varieties of flowers: red and white. Chen Zangqi says: The purple-flowered variety has leaves that can be used to dye fabrics black.</gloss>

### Flower and Leaf <gloss>Flavor and Nature: Bitter, slightly cold, and non-toxic.</gloss>

**Main Indications:** Scrofula <note>tuberculosis of the lymph nodes</note>, alternating chills and fever, and persistent dysentery with pus and blood. The white-flowered variety is used for white discharge, and the red-flowered for red discharge. <gloss>From the *Bielu*.</gloss> Also treats malaria and abdominal swelling from "water Gu" <note>parasitic bloating</note>. <gloss>Shizhen says: Quoting Tao Hongjing, ancient formulas frequently used this for malaria. It should be boiled into a thick decoction and made into pills, or simmered until it reaches a maltose-like consistency for ingestion. Modern people also drink it as a tea or take it in powder form. Prescriptions: 1 old, 3 new.</gloss>

> Abdominal swelling from water parasites: <gloss>Formula found under the entry for **Vervain** <note>original: "Mabiancao"</note>.</gloss>

> Chronic and intermittent dysentery: <gloss>Where the illness stops and starts. Grind **Mouse-tail Herb** flowers into a powder and take one *qian* with a drink.</gloss> Source: *Sagely Benevolence Prescriptions*.

> Persistent blood in stool for years: <gloss>Take two *liang* each of **Mouse-tail Herb** and **Sanguisorba** <note>original: "Diyu"</note>. Boil in two *sheng* of water until one *sheng* remains; take all at once. Even for a condition lasting twenty years, it should take no more than two doses.</gloss> Source: *Essential Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold*.

> Malignant sores with protruding flesh: <gloss>Where the flesh grows like grains of rice; if broken, it bleeds and regrows, protruding outward. Cut **Mouse-tail Herb** roots and pound them with pig lard to apply as a poultice.</gloss> Source: *General Record of Sagely Benefaction*.

---

### Fierce-Grasp Herb <gloss>From the Song Dynasty *Kaibao* era</gloss>

**Correction:** Now combined with the entries from the *Supplements* <note>original: "Shiyi"</note>.

**Explanatory Names:** *Langyecao* (Young Gentleman Herb). <gloss>Shizhen says: This is the same as the *Langyecao* mentioned in Chen Zangqi’s Materia Medica. In Fujian, the herb *Xixian* <note>Siegesbeckia</note> is called *Langye* or *Langba*, which are related names. Some alchemists claim this is the same as Mouse-tail Herb because their functions are similar, but there is no definitive proof.</gloss>

**Collected Explanations:** <gloss>Chen Zangqi says: **Fierce-Grasp Herb** <note>original: "Henbacao" (狠把草); likely *Bidens* species or "Bur-marigold"</note> grows by mountain paths. Like the "autumn spike" plant, its seeds can be used to dye things black. He also says: *Langyecao* grows in mountains and marshes to a height of three or four feet. The leaves have jagged edges like goose teeth, resembling "Ghost Needle" <note>original: "Guizhen"</note>. The seedlings are like "Ghost Hairpin" <note>original: "Guichai"</note>, with leaves shaped like the tines of a hairpin. Su Yuxi says: This herb is found on common roads, but I have not seen it used in ancient formulas. Only Chen Zangqi mentions it, and not in great detail. Note: The Yellow Emperor’s records mention it treats scrofula and blood dysentery with great efficacy. I have carefully included it here at the beginning of the "External Species" section of the *Illustrated Materia Medica*.</gloss>

**Flavor and Nature:** Bitter, balanced, and non-toxic.

**Main Indications:** Scrofula, and it can be used on a man’s beard to prevent aging. It is also said that *Langyecao* treats red and white dysentery, abdominal fullness in children, and erysipelas <note>a skin infection</note>. For fever, take the juice of the root, stem, and leaves.

> Treatment using **Fierce-Grasp Herb**: <gloss>For chronic blood dysentery in men or long-term childhood parasitic dysentery in women. Take three *jin* <note>approx. 1.5 kg</note> of the herb, pound it to extract one small *sheng* of juice. Mix with a portion of white maltose about the size of half a chicken egg. Drink on an empty stomach. For severe cases, no more than three doses are needed. Alternatively, dry the seedlings in the shade, grind to a powder, and take two spoonfuls with half a cup of honey water.</gloss> Source: *Illustrated Materia Medica*. Can also be used to dye the beard.

# Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 16, Herb Section
<note>Sixteen</note>

<margin>For chronic internal masses <note>original: "pi" (癖); a localized accumulation or lump in the abdomen</note> that itch whenever the weather turns overcast, and which discharge yellow fluid when scratched: pound [this herb] into a fine powder and sprinkle it over the area. —Shizhen</margin>

### Green Bristlegrass
<note>Commonly known as Dog-tail Grass; Latin: *Setaria viridis*</note>
<gloss>Compendium: Explanation of Names: Weed <note>original: "You" (莠)</note>, Bright Light Herb, Arhat Herb.</gloss>
<gloss>Shizhen says: This weed looks elegant <note>original: "xiu" (秀)</note> but does not bear grain, which is why its name contains the character for "elegant." The seed head is shaped like a dog's tail, hence the common name. Shizhen also notes: It grows abundantly in wilderness fields and along walls. The seedlings and leaves resemble millet but are smaller. Its spikes also resemble millet—yellowish-white and without edible grain. One can take the hollow stem and use it to treat eye diseases.</gloss>
<gloss>The saying "I detest the weed for fear it be confused with the sprout" <note>A reference to the Analects of Confucius, warning against things that look genuine but are false</note> refers to this plant.</gloss>

---

### Snakehead-Intestine Herb
<note>Commonly known as Eclipta or False Daisy; Latin: *Eclipta prostrata*</note>
<gloss>Tang Materia Medica: Explanation of Names: Lotus Seed Herb, Dry Lotus Herb, Golden Spirit Herb, Ink Smoke Herb, Ink Head Herb, Ink Vegetable, Monkey Head Herb, Pig-Tooth Herb. Shizhen says: "Li" <note>original: "鳢"</note> refers to the snakehead fish, which has a black head; this herb's "intestines" (internal juice) are also black. The stems are soft, and when broken, an ink-like juice flows out, which is why it is commonly called "Ink Vegetable." The small fruit clusters resemble a miniature lotus pod.</gloss>
<margin>Collected Explanations</margin> [Su] Gong says: Snakehead-Intestine Herb grows in low, damp places and is frequently found in ditches and trenches. The seedlings resemble the *Inula* flower <note>original: "Xuanfu"</note>. It should be harvested in the second and eighth months and dried in the shade. [Su] Song says: It is found everywhere, especially in the south. There are two varieties. One has leaves like a willow, which is why it earned the "Lotus" name. Its fruit is smooth and glossy, and its stem resembles purslane, growing one to two feet tall. It opens small white flowers, and its fruit looks like a tiny lotus pod; this is the variety Su Gong described as resembling *Inula*. The other variety has withered, thin seedlings, somewhat resembling the lotus but with yellow flowers; its fruit also forms a round pod. Southerners call this variety "Transporting Forsythia" <note>original: "Yunqiao" (運翹)</note>. When the stems of either variety are broken, juice flows out and turns black within a moment. Locally, it is called "Dry Lotus Seed" or "Golden Spirit Herb." Shizhen says: There are indeed two kinds of Dry Lotus. One has seedlings like *Inula* and small white flowers; this is the true Snakehead-Intestine Herb. The other has yellow-purple flowers and forms a pod like a lotus; this is actually "Small Forsythia" <note>original: "Xiao Lianqiao"; likely *Hypericum*</note>. Those who work with smoke and fire also use it; see the entry for Forsythia.

---

### Dry Lotus Herb
<gloss>Nature and Flavor: Sweet, sour, balanced, and non-toxic.</gloss>
Primary indications include bloody dysentery and acupuncture wounds or sores that bleed profusely and uncontrollably; applying this herb stops the bleeding immediately. Smearing the juice on eyebrows and hair makes them grow quickly and thickly. <gloss>Tang Materia Medica: For yellow or white beard and hair. Shizhen: It stops bleeding, expels pus, benefits the small intestine, and can be applied to all types of sores, silkworm bites, and skin irritations caused by lacquer.</gloss>

<margin>Prescriptions: 1 old, 9 new</margin>
**Golden Spirit Decoction:** To benefit the beard and hair and turn white hair to black. After the sixth month, collect "Golden Spirit Herb" (Eclipta). Choose young, green plants without soil. Do not wash them. Remove yellow leaves, pound them to extract one large *sheng* <note>approx. 1 liter</note> of juice. Combine with one *jin* <note>approx. 500-600 grams</note> of white honey. Simmer in the sun, stirring constantly with a willow spatula. Once it reaches the consistency of thin maltose, the medicine is ready. Take one spoonful every morning and afternoon, dissolved in a cup of warm wine.

**Blackening the Beard and Strengthening Teeth:** From the *Wondrous Uses for Preserving Life*. Collect the herb in the seventh month. If you wish to make pills, simmer the juice in the sun until it can be rolled into pellets the size of a parasol tree seed. Take 30 pills per dose. It is best to prepare a large batch when in season; the effects are very rapid. From *Sun Simiao's Thousand Golden Monthly Ordinances*: Take one *jin* of Dry Lotus Herb with roots, wash clean with "ashless" wine <note>pure wine without additives</note>. Soak for three nights with four *liang* <note>approx. 150 grams</note> of blue salt. Fry the mixture (including juice) in an oil pan until it retains its properties but is charred <note>original: "cunjing" (存性); a pharmaceutical technique of charring the outside while keeping the inside medicinal</note>. Grind into a powder. Use daily to rub the teeth, swallowing the saliva. Another method: Take the juice of Dry Lotus and refine it with salt until dry, then grind to rub the teeth.

**Dry Lotus Powder:** From the *Book of Longevity and Filial Piety*. For blackening hair and strengthening teeth. Master Wenwei says: Minister Nahe used this formula; at age seventy, his beard and hair were not white. I obtained this after earnest requests, and later Master Zhang Jingshi also obtained the proportions. Dry Lotus Herb (1.5 *liang*), three pieces of Magu cake, blue salt (3.5 *liang*), 20 Chebulic Myrobalan fruits <note>original: "Hezi"</note> including pits, 3 stalks of Gleditsia <note>original: "Zaojiao"</note>, and "Dawn Hermitage Sand" (2 *liang*). Grind into powder, mix with thin vinegar paste into balls the size of a bullet. Dry in the sun. Place in a clay jar and heat over a fire until smoke emerges (retaining properties). Remove and grind to a powder. Rub on the teeth daily.

**One-Sided or General Headaches:** Drip the juice of Snakehead-Intestine Herb into the nose. From the *Comprehensive Record of Divine Assistance*.

**All Eye Diseases:** For opaque membranes covering the eyes <note>original: "yimo"</note>. It cools the brain, treats headaches, and can stimulate hair growth. On the fifth day of the fifth month, at dawn, prepare Lotus Seed Herb...

Take one handful of Eclipta leaves and soak them in one catty <note>approximately 600 grams</note> of oil. Seal the container tightly for forty-nine days. Every night before sleeping, use an iron spoon to take some of the medicine and rub the top of the head forty-nine times. Pound them to extract the natural juice. <gloss>For ceaseless blood in the stool:</gloss> Take Eclipta, roast it on a roof tile, and grind it into a fine powder. Dry it in the shade and leave it out overnight in the dew. When an illness strikes, chew a piece.</gloss> Place the chewed herb in the palm and rub the affected area. <gloss>Apply the leaf to the boil and cover it with a toxin-removing plaster. # Forsythia
<note>Latin: *Forsythia suspensa*; widely used in traditional medicine to clear heat and detoxify.</note>
<gloss>Listed in the Upper Grade of the Classic</gloss> <gloss>Revised and included among named herbs previously lacking specific uses</gloss>

<margin>Explanation of Names</margin> **Lian** <gloss>from the Er Ya dictionary</gloss> **Yi** <gloss>from the Er Ya dictionary</gloss> **Dry Lotus Seed** <gloss>from the Treatise on Medicinal Properties</gloss> **Three-Ridged** <gloss>Wu Pu’s Materia Medica</gloss> **Also named Middle Bamboo Root** <gloss>from the Miscellaneous Records</gloss>. It is said that the fruit resembles a lotus pod <note>original: "lian" (蓮)</note> but has segments that point or "soar" <note>original: "qiao" (翹)</note> above other herbs, hence the name. Zong Lin says: Forsythia does not actually soar above all other herbs. It is abundant in the valleys of Mount Tai. When the seeds are broken, the pieces align like the feathers of a bird's wing <note>original: "qiao" (翹) can also mean long tail feathers</note>; the name likely comes from this resemblance. Shizhen says: According to the *Er Ya*, the names are *Lian* and *Yi-qiao*. People eventually combined them into "Lianqiao." The name is also written as "Lian-shao," which corresponds to the "Qiao Root" listed in the Lower Grade of the *Classic*. During the Tang Dynasty, Su Gong revised the Materia Medica and moved it to the category of "Named but Unused" herbs. Now they are combined into one entry. "Dry Lotus" is actually a smaller variety of Forsythia, though some people mistake it for Eclipta <note>Snakehead-Intestine Herb</note> because they share the same common name.

<margin>Collection and Preparation</margin> <gloss>The Miscellaneous Records state:</gloss> Forsythia grows in the valleys of Mount Tai. Gather it in the eighth month and dry it in the shade. <gloss>Jing says:</gloss> It is found everywhere. Nowadays, the stems, flowers, and fruits are all used together. <gloss>Su Gong says:</gloss> There are two types: the Large Forsythia and the Small Forsythia. The Large variety grows in low, damp lands. Its leaves are narrow and long, resembling Water Mint. Its yellow flowers are lovely. The seed pods, before opening, look like lotus pods and stand out above other herbs. The Small variety grows on hills and plains. Its leaves, flowers, and fruits all resemble the large type but are smaller and finer. People south of the mountains use both. Currently, in Chang'an, only the Large variety is used, and they do not use the stems or flowers. <gloss>Song says:</gloss> It is now found near the capital <note>Kaifeng</note>, as well as in the marshy areas between the rivers and the Huai region. It is also found in Jia, Yue, Li, and Nankang. There are large and small types. The Large grows in low damp ground or on hills. Its stems are green, and its leaves are narrow and long like Elm or Water Mint. The stems can also be reddish, reaching three or four feet in height. A single stem opens with yellow flowers at the tip. In autumn, it bears fruit like lotus seeds in a pod. The roots are yellow, like those of wormwood. The pods are gathered in the eighth month. The Small variety grows on hills; its flowers, leaves, and fruits are like the Large but finer. Those growing in the south have narrower, smaller leaves and shorter stems, only one or two feet high. The flowers are also yellow. The seed pods are yellowish-black and contain black seeds like millet grains; this is also called "Dry Lotus." Southerners use the flowers and leaves. Southern physicians say there are two kinds: one resembles the fruit of the Toona tree <note>Chinese Mahogany</note> before it opens; its shell is small and hard without outer sepals. When split, the inside is fragrant. When mature and dry, the fruit falls off the stem. The other kind resembles a grain or lotus bud with sepals embracing it. It lacks internal divisions and has no fragrance; even when dry, it remains attached to the stem. These two are very similar. The latter is extremely common in the marshes of Jiangnan. The variety resembling the Toona fruit comes from Sichuan and is superior for medical use compared to the Jiangnan variety. According to the Materia Medica, the Sichuan variety is best, though I have not yet seen its stems or leaves.

<margin>Property and Flavor</margin> **Bitter, neutral, and non-toxic.** <gloss>Element says: Its nature is cooling, and its flavor is bitter. Both its qi and flavor are thin, allowing it to be light, floating, and ascending in the body. It belongs to Yang. It is used for the Hand Minor Yang <note>Triple Burner</note> channel. Haogu says: It is the Yang within Yin. It enters the Hand and Foot Minor Yang <note>Triple Burner and Gallbladder</note> and the Hand Bright Yang <note>Large Intestine</note> channels, as well as the Hand Lesser Yin <note>Heart</note> channel.</gloss>

<margin>Primary Indications</margin> **Chills and fever, scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes</note>, tuberculous neck lumps, carbuncles and swellings, malignant sores, goiters and tumors, and knotted heat.** <gloss>The Classic</gloss> **Expels white worms.** <gloss>Miscellaneous Records</gloss> **Promotes urination for the five types of strangury <note>painful urinary syndromes</note> and urinary blockage; removes "guest heat" <note>external pathogenic heat</note> from the Heart.** <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss> **Opens the Small Intestine, expels pus, treats fistulas, stops pain, and regulates menstruation. Powerfully disperses blood stasis and qi stagnation in various channels and reduces swelling.** <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss> **Drains fire from the Heart, removes damp-heat from the Spleen and Stomach, and serves as an "envoy" <note>guiding herb</note> for treating blood-related diseases.** <gloss>Zhenheng</gloss> **Treats deafness and clouded or roaring sounds in the ears.**

# Forsythia <gloss>The stalk; Shizhen says</gloss>
<note>original: 苙 Li; an ancient name for Forsythia suspensa</note>
Mainly used to treat accumulated heat in the heart and lungs. <gloss>Yuansu says</gloss> <note>Zhang Yuansu, a famous Jin dynasty physician</note> Forsythia has three primary uses: first, to purge "guest heat" <note>external pathogenic heat</note> from the Heart Channel; second, to remove various heats from the Upper Burner <note>the chest and head area</note>; and third, as the "holy medicine" for those suffering from sores and ulcers. <gloss>Gao says</gloss> <note>Li Gao, founder of the Earth-Reinforcing school</note> Among medications for sores across the twelve channels, one cannot do without this; its purpose is to disperse masses. <gloss>Haogu says</gloss> <note>Wang Haogu</note> This is a medicine for the Hand and Foot Lesser Yang channels. It has a miraculous effect on treating ulcers, tumors, goiters, and scrofula <note>lymph node swelling</note>. It shares similar merits with Bupleurum, though they differ in their effects on the Qi and Blood levels. Furthermore, when used alongside Great Burdock Achene <term>Shuzianzi; Arctium lappa</term>, it shows divine efficacy in treating sores. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss> The Forsythia fruit is shaped like a human heart with two halves joined together; the seed inside is very fragrant. It is the primary medicine for the Qi level of the Lesser Yin Heart Channel and the Absolute Yin Pericardium Channel. Since all pain, itching, and sores belong to Heart Fire, this is the holy medicine for sores in all twelve channels, while also treating heat in the Qi level of the Hand and Foot Lesser Yang channels.

**Attached Formulas** <gloss>New</gloss>
**For scrofula and nodules:** <gloss>Forsythia and Sesame in equal parts</gloss>. Grind into a powder and eat it regularly.
**For "Horse-Knife" swellings:** <note>A term for scrofula that spreads in a line along the neck or armpit</note> which belong to the Lesser Yang channel. Use one catty <note>approx. 600g</note> of Forsythia, one catty of Pink Herb <term>Qumai; Dianthus</term>, three taels of Rhubarb, and half a tael of Licorice. For each dose, use one tael of the mixture in one and a half cups of water. Boil down to one cup. <gloss>Drink warm after meals. After ten days, perform moxibustion on the Linqi acupoint with fourteen cones. A certain cure is expected in sixty days. From Zhang Jiegu’s "Essentials of the Living Method."</gloss>
**For painful swellings of sores:** Boil Forsythia to make a decoction and wash the area repeatedly. Afterward, apply "Fragrant Paste" to it. <gloss>From "Collection of Proven Formulas"</gloss>

# Forsythia Root
**Flavor and Nature:** <gloss>Bitter, cold, balanced, and slightly toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Pu says</gloss> <note>Guo Pu</note> Shennong and Lei Gong say it is sweet and toxic. <gloss>Li Dangzhi says</gloss> it is bitter. <gloss>Haogu says</gloss> it is bitter and cold.
**Main Indications:** <gloss>Dispels downward heat-Qi, benefits the Yin essence, and makes the complexion pleasant, clear, and bright. Long-term consumption lightens the body and resists aging.</gloss> <gloss>From the "Divine Husbandman's Classic"</gloss>
<gloss>Used for patients who have overindulged in steamed wine</gloss>; treats heat-Qi from typhoid fever. <gloss>Fu Shen says</gloss> as does Shizhen: <gloss>The "Classic" says the root grows in the plains and marshes of Mount Song; harvest in the second and eighth lunar months. Hongjing says: Modern doctors do not recognize it. Haogu says: This is simply the root of the Forsythia plant.</gloss>

# Chinese Elder
<note>Latin: Sambucus chinensis</note>
<gloss>From the Divine Husbandman’s Classic</gloss>
<gloss>Lower Class</gloss>
**Explanation of Names:** <gloss>See below for explanation.</gloss>
<gloss>The "Records of Famous Physicians" says</gloss> Chinese Elder (Luying) grows in the valleys of Bear Ear Mountain and in Yuanju. Harvest at the Beginning of Autumn. <gloss>Su says</gloss> This is actually the same as the "Bone-Knitting" herb <term>Shuodiao</term>. Ancient formulas did not use the name Shuodiao, only Luying. Later people did not realize this and mistakenly created a separate entry for Shuodiao. This plant, along with the "Water Elder" <term>Suiying</term> and the "Wood Elder" <term>Muying</term>, are of the same category. Thus, the water variety is called Water Elder, this variety is called Chinese Elder (Land Elder), and the bone-knitting variety is called Wood Elder. Their flowers and leaves are all similar. <gloss>Kou says</gloss> Su Gong considers Luying and Shuodiao to be the same thing. However, looking closely, Luying is bitter, cold, and non-toxic, while Shuodiao is sour, warm, and toxic. Since these properties differ, even if they are related, they are likely different species. <gloss>Zongshi says</gloss> The nature, flavor, and habitat of Shuodiao and Luying are different, and their treatments are distinct. They are definitely two different things. <gloss>Song says</gloss> The "Materia Medica" says Luying grows in Bear Ear Mountain, while for Shuodiao, it does not list a specific region, only that it grows in fields everywhere. In spring it sprouts; the stalks have joints with branches in between. The leaves resemble water celery. Harvest leaves in spring/summer and roots in autumn/winter. Tao and Su both thought they were one thing. Ma Zhi doubted this due to the differing medicinal properties. However, the "Erya" dictionary calls the flower "Rong" and the flower that does not fruit "Ying." Since this plant has "Ying" in its name, it likely refers to its flowers. The "Classic" says to harvest at the Beginning of Autumn, which is exactly when it flowers. <gloss>Shizhen says</gloss> The "Erya," the "Materia Medica," and the "Treatise on Medicinal Properties" all state that Luying is Shuodiao. There must be a basis for this. Although Ma Zhi and Kou Zongshi challenged this view, they had no solid proof. It should still be considered one plant, with the roots, stalks, flowers, and leaves used differently, as Su Song suggested.
**Flavor and Nature:** <gloss>Bitter, cold, and non-toxic.</gloss> <gloss>Quan says</gloss> Chinese Elder, also known as Shuodiao, is bitter and acrid, and slightly toxic.
**Main Indications:** <gloss>All types of numbness and blockage at the "Anus Gate" <note>possibly referring to the pelvic floor or lower orifices</note>, contracture of the four limbs, aching, cold pain, impotence, shortness of breath, and swelling of the feet.</gloss> <gloss>From the "Classic"</gloss>
Can treat wind-toxins and "Foot Qi" <note>Beriberi/edema</note> that rushes upward toward the heart, causing irritability and distress. Treats edema, wind-related itching, and malignant skin conditions. Boil into a decoction, add a little wine, and let it cool before use; it is wonderful. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>

# Chinese Elder <gloss>Pronounced *shuo-diao*</gloss>
<gloss>Also known as Bone-Knitting Herb <margin>from the *Separate Records*</margin>, Land Hero <margin>from the *Separate Records*</margin>, and Land Successor <margin>from the *Rihua Materia Medica*</margin></gloss>

<gloss>Chinese Elder <note>original: 蒴藋 Shuodiao; *Sambucus chinensis*</note> grows in fields and wilds. Gather the leaves in spring and summer, and the stems and roots in autumn and winter. <margin>Hongjing says</margin> <note>Tao Hongjing, 5th-century polymath</note> It is very common in fields and village ruins. <margin>Su says</margin> <note>Su Gong, lead editor of the Tang dynasty pharmacopoeia</note> This is the same as the "Land Hero" herb, though it was listed separately in the "Lower Category" of the *Separate Records*. <margin>Su says</margin> Land Hero is indeed this plant. In the *Erya* <note>the oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note>, it is mentioned alongside reed-grasses, and Guo Pu’s commentary notes it as the sprout of the plant. However, checking the names of the "three herbs" reveals no such entry; the *Separate Records* says one name for it is "Stalk Herb," but its origin is unknown. <margin>Zongshi says</margin> <note>Kou Zongshi, Song dynasty medic</note> The flowers are white, and the berries are initially green like mung beans. Each cluster is as large as a lid, and a single plant can produce one or two hundred berries. They ripen in the tenth month and turn red. <margin>Shizhen says</margin> Each branch has five leaves; further details can be found under the entry for "Land Hero."</gloss>

<term>Nature and Flavor</term> Sour, warm, and toxic. <margin>The Rihua Materia Medica says</margin> Bitter, cool, and non-toxic.

**[Primary Indications]** Wind-induced rashes, hives, generalized itching, and damp-related numbness <term>shibi</term>; it can be used to prepare a medicinal bath. <margin>from the *Separate Records*</margin>

## Leprosy and Wind-Paralysis <gloss>from the *Rihua Materia Medica*</gloss> **Prescriptions** <gloss>12 old, 7 new</gloss>

**Leprosy and paralysis of the hands and feet:** <gloss>Lightly scorch Chinese Elder leaves over a fire and spread them thickly on a bed. Lie on them while they are hot. Replace them once they cool. In winter, use the roots; pound them until crushed and heat them for use. From the *Secret Essentials of the Outer Treasury*</gloss>

From the *Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold*</gloss>

From the *Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold*</gloss>

# Water Dropwort <gloss>From the *Song Illustrated Pharmacopoeia* and *Separate Records*</gloss>
<gloss>**[Names]** Water Violet Herb</gloss>

<gloss><margin>Song says</margin> <note>Su Song, 11th-century scholar</note> The *Illustrated Guide to Simple Formulas of the Tianbao Era* states: This herb originally grows in the ponds and marshes of Yongyang and along the seacoasts. Local people call it "Cattle-Red Herb." People in Xindu, Hebei call it "Water Node." In Neihuang, people call it "Water Thorn." In Suining and other prefectures of Jiannan, it is called "Dragon-Shift Herb." In the prefectures of Huainan, it is called "Sea Perilla." It also grows in Lingnan, where the soil makes the leaves particularly lush and large; there it is called "Sea Essence Wood" or "Fish Ford Herb."</gloss>

<gloss><margin>Song says</margin> Brave men call this "Bone-Wind." This illness should not be treated with needles, moxibustion, or internal medicine. # Indigo
<gloss>An essential item from the *Classic* <note>The *Shennong Bencao Jing*, China's oldest herbal manual.</note></gloss>

**Shizhen says:** According to Lu Dian’s *Piya*, the "Monthly Ordinances" <note>a chapter in the *Book of Rites*</note> commanded that in the middle of summer, the people were not to harvest indigo for dyeing. Zheng Xuan commented that this was to avoid harming the "Energy of Spring" <note>the vital growth force associated with the season</note>. This is why the character for Indigo (藍 *lan*) contains the element for "Supervision" (監 *jian*), as the ancient kings placed a prohibition on it.

<gloss>Collecting Explanations</gloss>
The *Separate Records* says indigo seeds are produced in the marshes of the Henan region. Its stems and leaves can be used to dye things blue. **Hongjing says:** This is the plant used today to make blue and green dyes; those with six leaves are considered the best. **Gong says:** There are three types of indigo. One has round leaves about two inches wide and nearly half an inch thick; it is suitable for dyeing blue and comes from south of the mountains. The Court of Imperial Sacrifices calls it "Wood Indigo" <note>original: *mulan*; likely *Indigofera tinctoria*</note>. The variety described by Master Tao [Hongjing] is "Woad" <note>original: *songlan*; *Isatis tinctoria*</note>; its juice is beaten into a paste to make indigo dye. The variety used in the *Classic* is "Polygonum Indigo" <note>original: *liaolan*; *Persicaria tinctoria*</note>; its sprouts look like water-pepper but are not spicy. When used for dye, it only produces a blue-green color. **Song says:** Indigo is found everywhere; people plant it in garden beds. In the third or fourth month, the sprouts grow two to three feet high. The leaves resemble water-pepper, the flowers are reddish-white, and the seeds are like water-pepper seeds but larger and black. The seeds are harvested in the fifth and sixth months; they can only dye things blue-green and are not suitable for making indigo paste. This is the "Polygonum Indigo" used in medical formulas. There is also "Wood Indigo" from south of the mountains, which is not used in medicine. "Woad" can be made into indigo paste and is also called "Horse Indigo" <note>original: *malan*</note>. This is the plant referred to as *fan* or *malan* in the *Erya* <note>the oldest Chinese dictionary</note>. Additionally, there is a type of Horse Indigo in Yangzhou that exists in all four seasons; its stems resemble bitter-chicory. Locals harvest the entire plant, including the roots, to treat "exhausted blood" <note>blood stasis, often post-partum</note>. There is also a "Leaf Indigo" from Jiangbin that sprouts in the second month; its leaves resemble wormwood, and it has white flowers. It also clears heat-toxins. Although these two types are different, they both bear the name "Indigo." Ancient formulas often used "Wu Indigo" <note>original: *wulan*; indigo from the Wu region</note>, which might be these varieties, so I have included them here. **Zongshi says:** Indigo seeds are the seeds of the "Great Indigo" <note>large-leafed variety</note>. Calling them "Polygonum Indigo" is incorrect. The "Horse Indigo" mentioned in the *Erya* is essential for treating various drug poisonings. Both the seeds and leaves are used, but earlier commentaries failed to fully explain the seeds. **Shizhen says:** There are five types of indigo, each with its own therapeutic uses. When taking the seeds, one specifically uses those of the "Polygonum Indigo." Its leaves are like water-pepper, and it blooms in the fifth or sixth month with small, pale red flower spikes. Its seeds are also like water-pepper. It can be harvested three times a year, which is why the ancient kings restricted its harvest. "Woad" has leaves like white cabbage. "Horse Indigo" has leaves like bitter-chicory; this is what Guo Pu called the "Large-leafed Winter Indigo," commonly known as "Plate Indigo" <note>original: *banlan*; the source of *Ban Lan Gen*</note>. Its flowers and seeds are like those of the Polygonum Indigo. "Wu Indigo" has long stems like wormwood and white flowers; it is grown by the people of the Wu region. "Wood Indigo" has long stems like sickle-pod <note>original: *jueming*</note>, growing three to four feet high with spreading branches and leaves like sickle-pod. Su Gong's claim that its seeds resemble sickle-pod but are smaller makes it quite different from the other indigos, though they are all used to make dye. Su Gong's identification of Horse Indigo as Wood Indigo, Su Song's identification of Woad as Horse Indigo, and Zongshi's identification of Indigo seeds as the seeds of the Large-leafed Indigo are all incorrect. I have listed them correctly below.

This may refer to a specific source or a corruption of the text regarding marrow benefits.</note> Fills the bone marrow, brightens the ears and eyes, benefits the five viscera, regulates the six organs, clears the joints, and treats "stagnant qi" in the meridians. Makes one require less sleep and increases mental strength. <gloss>Zhen Quan</gloss>

Treats traumatic injuries, nosebleeds, vomiting of blood, discharge of pus, postpartum blood fainting, high fever in children; detoxifies mineral and "stone" drug poisoning, monkey poison, and aconite-tipped arrow poison. <gloss>Daming <note>Refers to the *Rihua Bencao*, a 10th-century herbal.</note></gloss>

# Indigo Paste
<margin>Materia Medica</margin>

**[Nomenclature]** <gloss>Shizhen says: The "paste" (*dian*) refers to the sediment of stone-like indigo; the dregs settle and remain at the bottom. It is also written with a different character for "sediment" and is commonly called *dian* (indigo dye). Southerners dig pits in the ground to soak indigo in water overnight, then add lime and stir it a thousand times. Once the water is drained, a blue-black paste remains. It can be dried and stored for dyeing fabrics blue or green. The foam skimmed from the surface and dried in the shade is called "Indigo Flower," which is the variety often seen in herbal manuals.</gloss>

**[Aroma and Nature]** <gloss>Bitter, cold, and non-toxic. Primarily used to treat various heat-toxins, red sores, childhood baldness/scabs, and hot, swollen pain. It stops bleeding, kills parasites, and treats esophageal constriction (difficulty swallowing).</gloss>

<gloss>Shizhen says: Indigo paste is more potent than the indigo plant itself. According to the *Extensive Records of the Five Elements*: during the Yonghui era of the Tang Dynasty, there was a monk who suffered from esophageal constriction and could not eat for several years. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the medicinal properties of indigo, transitioning from the fresh juice to the processed dye-paste and the refined pigment known as Indigo Naturalis (Qingdai). It begins with a legendary account explaining the origin of using indigo dye-water for swallowing disorders.</meta>

...After death, my chest and throat may be opened to see what kind of creature has been possessing me so. When he died, his disciples followed his orders and opened him up. Inside the chest, they found an object shaped like a fish with two heads; its entire body was covered in fleshy scales. They placed it in a bowl, where it jumped and leaped without stopping. They playfully tossed various seasonings toward it; although it did not appear to eat them, the seasonings all turned into water. They then tossed in various poisonous substances, which also dissolved. A monk happened to be making blue indigo dye <note>Indigo dye at this stage is a fermented slurry or paste.</note>; when he threw a small amount of this dye-paste into the bowl, the creature became terrified and tried to run away. In a short moment, it dissolved into water. Traditional lore says that indigo dye-water can treat "choking disease" <note>likely referring to esophageal cancer or severe dysphagia</note>, and this is the origin of that belief. Today, some medical prescriptions use the water from dyeing vats for patients to drink.

From the *Formulas of Secret Records*.

### Indigo Naturalis (Qingdai)
<gloss>Kou Zongshi says</gloss> <gloss>From the Compendium</gloss> <gloss>Li Shizhen says</gloss>

<gloss>Alternative Names</gloss> Indigo Flower <gloss>From the Materia Medica Network</gloss>, Blue Clam Powder. <gloss>Li Shizhen says: "Dai" refers to the color of eyebrows. Liu Xi's *Explanation of Names* says: "Dai" means "to substitute." Ancient records state that Indigo Naturalis came from Persia. Today, it is made from the purple-tinged foam that forms on the surface of indigo dye vats in places like Taiyuan, Luling, and Nankang. Since it was used to substitute for real eyebrows, it is called "Dai" <note>Literally "eyebrow-blackener" or "substitute".</note>.</gloss>

<gloss>Collection</gloss> <gloss>Li Shizhen says: Persian Indigo Naturalis is simply the "Indigo Flower" from foreign countries. If it cannot be obtained, the Chinese "Indigo Flower" <note>the foam from the dye-making process</note> can be used. If that is unavailable, one may soak blue-dyed cloth in water and use the resulting juice as a substitute.</gloss>

<gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Salty, cold, non-toxic. <gloss>Zhen Quan says: Sweet and balanced.</gloss>

<gloss>Primary Indications</gloss> Neutralizes various drug poisons. Treats all pediatric heat-related illnesses, convulsions, spasms, external heat, and epidemic headaches with alternating chills and fever; grind into water and take orally. It is also ground and applied to heat-sores, malignant swellings, metal wounds, bloody stools, and bites from snakes or dogs. <gloss>Daming says: Relieves pediatric "wasting heat" <note>malnutrition-related fever</note> and kills parasites.</gloss> <gloss>Zhen Quan says: Treats "red-pill" heat in children when taken with water. Mix with egg white and rhubarb powder to apply to abscesses and bites from snakes or vipers.</gloss> <gloss>Meng Shen says: Purges the liver, disperses suppressed fire in the five internal organs, neutralizes heat toxins, and dissolves food stagnation.</gloss> <gloss>Zhu Zhenheng says: Removes persistent irritability, treats vomiting of blood, skin rashes, genital sores, and kills harmful parasites.</gloss> <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>

<gloss>Exposition</gloss> <gloss>Kou Zongshi says: Indigo Naturalis is made from the indigo plant. There was a woman who suffered from "moist sores" below the navel and across the abdomen, extending to her private parts. They looked like "horse mange" <note>likely a severe, crusty fungal or bacterial infection</note> and were extremely itchy. She had no sores elsewhere, but the area was both itchy and painful. Her urination and bowel movements were difficult, she discharged yellow fluid, and her appetite decreased. Her body and face were slightly swollen. Doctors treated it as a malignant sore, using ointments made of eel, pine resin, and red lead, but the burning pain only intensified. Upon inquiry, I learned she loved alcohol and enjoyed eating fish, crab, and other "wind-inducing" foods <note>foods thought in TCM to trigger inflammation or skin reactions</note>. I immediately ordered the ointments washed off. We took four ounces of purslane, crushed it into a pulp, added one ounce of Indigo Naturalis, and ground them together until smooth. After applying this, the heat immediately diminished, and both pain and itching vanished. She was also given "Eight-Herb Rectification Powder" three times a day to clear the external heat. When the topical medicine dried, we reapplied it. After two days, the condition was reduced by one-third; after five days, by two-thirds; and after twenty days, she was cured. This was due to "wind-heat" and toxic qi accumulating in the middle and lower burners <note>the abdominal and pelvic cavities</note>. If it had not been drawn out through the skin, it would have turned into an internal intestinal abscess or internal hemorrhoids.</gloss>

<column-break/>

She still needed to abstain from alcohol, sexual activity, and "wind-inducing" foods. However, she could not maintain these restrictions, and later she did indeed develop internal hemorrhoids.

# Cabbage <gloss>Supplemented and corrected</gloss> <gloss>Moved here from the Vegetable section</gloss> <gloss>Also known as Blue Cabbage</gloss> <note>original: "Ganlan" (甘藍). While translated as cabbage, this refers to a variety of colewort or kale-like greens known for their blue-green hue.</note>

**Appendix:** The *Old Records of Famous Physicians* <note>original: "Jiu Bielu"</note> lists this as a known but rarely used herb. It says: The flavor is salty, it has a neutral "Qi" <note>In Chinese medicine, "Qi" or nature refers to the thermal effect on the body; "neutral" means it neither heats nor cools significantly</note>, and it brightens the eyes. It grows among indigo plants. Its leaves are fine and yellow, its stamens are red, and it has thorns. In the fourth month it fruits, looking yellow on the outside and black on the inside. Harvested in the fifth month and dried in the shade. One name is "Mother-Remover," another is "Regenerator."

**Chen Cangqi says:** This is the "Blue" of the Western Territories. The leaves are wide and edible. **Shizhen says:** This belongs to the same category as the "Large-Leaf Winter Blue." According to the lay scholar Hu Qia, the peoples of the Hedong and Longxi regions <note>historical regions in Northern and Western China</note> as well as the Qiang and Hu tribes plant and eat this extensively. It is rarely found in the central Han lands. Its leaves are long, large, and thick; when boiled and eaten, they are sweet and delicious. The plant does not die in winter. In spring, it produces sprouts; its flowers are yellow and grow in pods that produce seeds. Its medicinal power is close to that of the indigo plant.

**Nature and Flavor:** Sweet, balanced, and non-toxic.

**Main Treatments:** Long-term consumption greatly benefits the kidneys and fills the marrow and the brain. It benefits the five viscera and six bowels <note>the fundamental organ systems in traditional medicine</note>, clears the joints, and opens the meridians and collaterals. It disperses knotted Qi in the chest and "hidden Qi" beneath the heart. It brightens the eyes and sharpens the hearing. It makes one alert and requires less sleep, benefits the strength of the heart, and strengthens the muscles and bones. It can be made into pickled vegetables <note>original: "Zū"</note>.

If pickled overnight until the color turns yellow and eaten with salt, it treats chronic cold syndromes. <gloss>From the appendix of Chen Cangqi</gloss>

# Smartweed <gloss>Middle Class of the Classic; Corrected</gloss> <gloss>Moved here from the Vegetable section</gloss> <gloss>Shizhen says: Smartweed varieties all grow high and lofty, hence the character is derived from "Liao," which means the appearance of flying high.</gloss> <note>original: "Liao" (蓼), referring to plants of the Polygonum genus, such as water pepper or knotweed.</note>

The *Jiayou Herbal* <gloss>Appendix says: Smartweed seeds grow in the rivers and marshes of Leize.</gloss> **Tao Hongjing says:** There are three kinds that people frequently eat. One is "Green Smartweed," which households commonly use; its leaves are not very pungent and are good for eating. **Han Baosheng says:** There are many types of Smartweed, including Green, Fragrant, Water, Horse, Purple, Red, and Wood—seven types in total. The Purple and Red varieties have small, narrow, thick leaves. Green and Fragrant varieties have similar leaves, but both are thin. Horse and Water varieties are both wide and large with black spots on them. Water Smartweed is also called "Heavenly Smartweed"; it grows as a vine and its leaves resemble those of the Zhe tree <note>Cudrania tricuspidata</note>. The flowers of six of these varieties are red or white, and the seeds are as large as sesame seeds, reddish-black, pointed, and flat. Only the Wood Smartweed has yellow-white flowers and seeds with a green, smooth skin. All Smartweeds die in winter, except for the Fragrant Smartweed, which regrows from its old roots and can be eaten as a fresh vegetable. **Su Song says:** Wood Smartweed also has large and small varieties, both of which are vines. Master Tao used Green Smartweed in medicine, while the others were not used. The *Biographies of the Three Mao Lords* mentions a recipe for "White Smartweed Sauce," but since the *Pharmacopoeia* lists no "White Smartweed," I suspect it is actually Green Smartweed. **Su Gong says:** Smartweed seeds <note>original: "Liaoshi"</note> are the seeds of the "Water Smartweed" listed in the Lower Class of this book. That entry discusses using the stalks, while this entry discusses the use of the seeds. In early spring, people fill a gourd with water, soak the seeds, and hang it over a fire to keep it warm day and night until red sprouts emerge. These are taken as vegetables to prepare the "Five Pungent Herbs Platter" <note>A traditional dish eaten on the Beginning of Spring to stimulate the Qi</note>. **Shizhen says:** What Han Baosheng described clarifies that the ancients grew Smartweed as a vegetable and harvested the seeds for medicine. Thus, the *Book of Rites* notes that when cooking chicken, pig, fish, or turtle, one should stuff Smartweed into the belly. When making broths or sliced meat, one must also shred Smartweed into it. Later generations stopped using it in food, and people no longer cultivate it. Today, only those making wine-starter <note>yeast or fermenting cakes known as "Qu"</note> use its juice. Currently, the Fragrant, Green, and Purple varieties found in flat marshes are considered the best.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the "Liao" (Smartweed/Knotweed) family from Volume 16, moving from the common garden and marsh varieties to larger species like Water Red and specialized varieties like Hairy Smartweed and Sea Root.</meta>

Compendium of Materia Medica, Volume 16

Chen Zangqi explains that Sky Smartweed <note>original: "Tianliao" (天蓼)</note> is actually Water Red <note>original: "Shuihong" (水紅), likely Polygonum orientale, also known as Prince's Feather</note>, also known as Wandering Dragon <note>Youlong</note> or Great Smartweed <note>Daliao</note>. Based on this, the <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> in the <gloss>Miscellaneous Records</gloss> state: "Water Red grows by the water, resembling common smartweed but larger. Harvest the fruit in the fifth month." <gloss>Hongjing</gloss> states: "It grows in low, damp places today. It is very similar to common smartweed but its leaves and stems are extremely long and large." *The Book of Odes* mentions "Wandering Dragons in the marshlands." <gloss>Guo Pu</gloss> notes that this refers to the *Longgu* plant. <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> "Water Red is indeed the same as 'Water Red' smartweed. It resembles smartweed but has larger leaves that are red and white in color. It grows over ten feet tall." The *Er Ya* <note>the oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> calls it *Honglonggu*; the larger ones are called *Jing* (though this is a phonetic error for *Long*). <gloss>Lu Ji</gloss> says: "Wandering Dragon is another name for Horse Smartweed <note>Maliao</note>." However, Horse Smartweed is actually a distinct species. <gloss>Li Shizhen states:</gloss> "The stem is as thick as a thumb and covered in fine hairs. The leaves are as large as those of the Indian Poke <note>Shanglu</note>. The flowers are light red and form spikes. In late autumn, the seeds mature; they are flat like sour date pits but smaller, reddish-black in color with white flesh. They are not very pungent. When roasted over a candle, they are edible."

# The Fruit
<gloss>Flavor and Nature</gloss> Salty, slightly cold, and non-toxic. <gloss>Primary Treatment</gloss> Treats "wasting and thirsting" <note>Xiaoke, a condition resembling diabetes</note>, clears internal heat, improves eyesight, and benefits the vital energy <note>Qi</note>. <gloss>Miscellaneous Records</gloss> <insert>Attached Prescriptions</insert> <gloss>New</gloss>: 1. For scrofula <note>original: "Luluo" (瘰癧), tuberculosis of the neck lymph nodes</note>: Take any amount of Water Red seeds. Lightly roast one half and use the other half raw. Grind them together into a fine powder. Take with good wine after meals.
2. For <term>Abdominal Masses</term> <note>original: "Jiapizheng" (瘕痞), referring to hard masses or obstructive tumors in the abdomen</note>: Take one pound of Water Red seeds and three liters of water. Boil down into a thick paste. <gloss>Records</gloss> Take two qian <note>approx. 7.5 grams</note> three times a day. It works even if the mass has ruptured; long-term use is effective. Stop once cured. <gloss>Kou Zongshi's</gloss> *Augmented Materia Medica* for <term>Hard Tumors</term> <note>original: "Zhengpi" (癓痞)</note>: For abdominal swelling and hardness as firm as a cup, use one sheng <note>approx. 1 liter</note> of Water Red seeds (ground separately), thirty cloves of garlic (peeled), one portion of fresh dog fat, and four liang <note>approx. 150 grams</note> of Glauber's salt <note>Pixiao</note>. Pound these together and spread over the affected area. Cover with oil paper and bind with a long silk cloth. Apply during the day and remove the next morning at the hour of the Dragon <note>7-9 AM</note>. If not cured, repeat two or three times. Do not be alarmed if pus forms. Assess the patient's strength; daily use of Mr. Qian's "White Wafer" or "Purple Frost Pills" can break up stagnant Qi. Generally, use accumulation-dissolving pills to purge and wear down the mass for half a month—or a month for severe cases—and it will surely be cured. Those with shortness of breath and fullness are considered to have "excess" conditions; those without are "deficient." From *Master Jian’s Proven Prescriptions*.

# Chinese Knotweed <gloss>Standard Illustration</gloss>
<gloss>Su Song says: It grows in the wild fields of Enzhou. The stems are reddish and flexible, resembling a delicate smartweed. The leaves are pointed at the tips and somewhat square near the stem. It produces white flowers in summer and fruit in autumn that looks like Sichuan pepper, turning a bluish-black. It has a sweet taste and is edible.</gloss>
**Flavor and Nature:** Sour, neutral, and toxic. **Main Indications:** Eliminates "wind-heat" <note>a traditional Chinese medicine category for symptoms like fever or rashes</note> from the skin and treats swelling and pain in the joints. Harvest at any time, pound the herb into a paste in an earthenware vessel, sauté it with salt and wine, and apply it to the painful area. Change the dressing after one night. <gloss>Su Song</gloss>

# Three-White Grass <gloss>Tang Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> <gloss>Hongjing says: The name comes from the three white leaves on top. [Su] Gong says: It grows by the banks of ponds and marshes, about one foot tall. The leaves resemble water-smartweed or the E-plant. He claims that if you pluck the leaves, there are three black spots on top, not white. He believes the ancients mistook the spots for white and named it accordingly. See more below.</gloss> <gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> <gloss>Secret lore refers to it as the "Hidden Grass." Its roots are like the Bian-root, yellowish-white, thick, and large. [Chen] Zangqi says: When this grass first sprouts, it has no white. In summer, the upper half of the leaf turns white, appearing as if dusted with powder. Farmers watch it to time their planting; when three leaves turn white, the grass is in full bloom <note>original: "xiu" (秀), meaning flowering or peak growth</note>, hence the name "Three-White." To say it has three black spots is a sign of not knowing the plant. Its leaves resemble sweet potato vines and water-smartweed. Xu Sheng says: It is now found in Xiangzhou; harvest the roots in the second and eighth months. [Li] Shizhen says: Three-White Grass grows by the edges of fields and marshes. In the eighth month, it sprouts to a height of two or three feet. The stem is like that of the Arrowhead plant <note>original: "ci" (慈), likely referring to Cigu (Sagittaria trifolia)</note>, and the leaves resemble Indian Poke or Green Celosia. In the fourth month, the top three leaves turn white on the upper three-tenths of their surface, while the remaining leaves stay green. Folklore says: if one leaf is white, it is time to eat wheat; two leaves white, eat plums and apricots; three leaves white, eat broomcorn millet. In the fifth month, it flowers in spikes like smartweed, white and faintly fragrant. It bears small, fine fruit. The roots are long, white, hollow, and segmented, resembling the roots of the Mud Sweet-Flag.</gloss> **Flavor and Nature:** Sweet, pungent, and cold. The *Guide to Creation* states: Harvest the flowers and roots in the fifth month; they can be used to process realgar. [Su] Gong’s claim that it has three black spots refers to the "Horse Smartweed" <note>Maliao</note>, not Three-White Grass. Although Chen Zangqi’s description is accurate, the leaves do not actually resemble sweet potato vines. It is slightly toxic. **Main Indications:** Edema and beriberi <note>leg swelling and weakness caused by vitamin deficiency</note>. It facilitates urination and bowel movements, dissolves phlegm, breaks up stubborn skin diseases, removes internal accumulations, and dissipates boils. <gloss>Tang Materia Medica</gloss> Pound and squeeze for juice to induce vomiting to clear malaria and heat-phlegm in the chest and diaphragm, or to treat "fright fullness" <note>acute digestive or nervous distress</note> in children. Zangqi says the root treats the wind-toxins of beriberi and swelling from spasms; take as a decoction in wine for great effect. It can also be boiled into a wash for leprosy-like skin conditions. <gloss>Shizhen</gloss>

# Tiger Cane <term>Huzhang; Giant Knotweed</term>

It grows to a height of over ten feet. The stems are reddish, and the roots are yellow. Harvest the roots in the second or third months and dry them in the sun. <gloss>Su Song says: Today it is found in Fenzhou, Yuezhou, and Chuzhou, and indeed in many places. In the third month, the shoots emerge looking like bamboo shoots with red spots. As they grow, they branch out. The leaves resemble small apricot leaves. It flowers in the seventh or eighth month and bears fruit in the ninth. Those found in the southern regions do not flower; their root bark is black, but when broken open, the inside is yellow like willow roots. Some also grow over ten feet tall. The *Erya* <note>the oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note> refers to it as "Kang-Tiger Cane." Guo Pu's commentary says it resembles red-grass but is thicker and larger with fine prickles and can be used to dye things red. Kou Zongshi says: This is a medicinal herb. The *Shu Materia Medica* claim that it is a tree growing over ten feet tall is incorrect. In the Taiping region, it resembles a winter chrysanthemum; the flowers and pistils are slightly larger and taller. The stems and leaves have pale yellow spots. It flowers gradually from the sixth or seventh month until the ninth. The flowers have four petals and look like peach blossoms, but are slightly larger and a deeper shade. It is very common at the foot of mountains and by the water in Shaanxi.</gloss>
<margin>Fu says: Whenever using this, do not mistakenly use "Sky Blue" or "Spotted Axis" roots. These two roots are similar in shape and taste.</margin>
<gloss>Wang Ji says: Various commentaries suggest it resembles red-grass or red-knotweed, but these descriptions don't match. Perhaps it is because they grow in different regions? Li Shizhen says: Its stem resembles knotweed, its leaves are round like an apricot, its branches are yellow like a willow, and its flowers look like chrysanthemums while the color resembles peach blossoms. When viewed as a whole, these descriptions are actually consistent.</gloss>

**The Root**

【Preparation】 <gloss>Lei Xiao says: After harvesting, chop the roots finely, wrap them in a handful of leaves overnight, and then sun-dry for use.</gloss>

【Nature and Flavor】 Slightly warm. <gloss>Zhen Quan says: Sweet and neutral, non-toxic. Kou Zongshi says: The taste is slightly bitter. Today, during the hot summer months, many people decoct the root juice to make a drink; however, without licorice, it is undrinkable. The original text does not mention the taste. The *Treatise on Medicinal Nature* says it is "sweet," but that refers to the flavor of the licorice added to it, not the flavor of the Tiger Cane itself.</gloss>

【Main Indications】 Promotes menstruation and breaks up stagnant blood and abdominal masses <term>Zheng-结; internal blockages</term>. <gloss>The *Additional Records* say: Soaked in wine, it treats sudden abdominal masses. Tao Hongjing says: If "wind" <note>referring to wandering pain or inflammation</note> is between the joints or if there is blood stasis, boil it to make a medicinal wine. Chen Zangqi says: It treats intense heat, restlessness, and thirst; it promotes urination and suppresses all types of heat toxins. Zhen Quan says: It treats postpartum blood fainting, retained lochia, and fullness and distension in the heart and abdomen. It discharges pus, treats sores and boils, heals bruising from injuries, and breaks up "wind-toxins" and stagnant Qi. Da Ming says: Burn it to ash to apply to malignant sores. Or grind it into powder, mix with honey into pills, and take with stale rice water to treat bleeding hemorrhoids. Su Song says: Taken as a powder with wine, it is effective for postpartum convulsions, blood-related pain, and dizziness from falls or injuries. Li Shizhen says: In the summer, decocting the root with licorice produces a drink with a lovely amber color. It is sweet and delicious. If the bottle is placed in a well to make it ice-cold, people call it a "Cold Drink." Sipping it is more refreshing than tea, and it effectively relieves heat exhaustion. Its juice can also be used to dye rice to make porridges or cakes, both of which are excellent. Pounded into powder and soaked in wine for regular consumption, it breaks through menstrual blockages in women; however, pregnant women must not take it. Li Shizhen continues: Sun Simiao's *Thousand Golden Formulae* uses it to treat women with blocked menstruation, abdominal accumulation, distension, "thunderous" bowel sounds, and heavy limbs. It also treats accumulations in men. This "Tiger Cane Decoction" involves taking two bushels of chopped root from a high-altitude location, boiling it in twenty-five bushels of water until only one and a half bushels remain. Remove the dregs, add five bushels of refined wine, and boil until it reaches a syrup-like consistency. Take one small cup per dose, adjusting based on effectiveness. Furthermore, Xu Xueshi’s *Effective Formulas* treats all types of urinary strangury <note>painful or difficult urination, often due to stones</note> in men and women: wash and chop one small cup's worth of Tiger Cane root, boil it in five parts water until one cup remains, remove the dregs, add a little frankincense and musk, and drink it. The wife of Geng Mengde, a military official in Yinxian, had suffered from "sand and stone" strangury for thirteen years. Every time she urinated, the pain was unbearable, and one could hear the sound of the stones hitting the ceramic chamber pot. A hundred prescriptions had failed, but she happened upon this formula and was cured in a single night. This is something I witnessed with my own eyes.</gloss>

【Prescriptions】 <gloss>Three new, three old.</gloss>

**Urinary Disorders (The Five Stranguries):** <gloss>Grind Tiger Cane into a powder. Take two mace per dose with rice water.</gloss>

**Irregular Menstruation:** <gloss>Three taels of Tiger Cane and one tael of Trumpet Creeper flower. Grind into powder. Take one mace per dose with hot wine.</gloss>

**Another Formula for Blocked Menstruation (where the abdomen is as large as a jar and the patient is short of breath and feels near death):** <gloss>One pound of Tiger Cane (remove the tips and chop coarsely). Use two bushels each of juice from Earth-Melon root and Achyranthes root. Soak the Tiger Cane in one bushel of water overnight. Boil until two bushels remain, then add the other two juices and boil together until it reaches a syrup-like consistency. Take one small cup with wine twice a day and once at night. The blood should then pass. From the *Sage's General Benevolence Formulas*.</gloss>

**Epidemic Toxins (where hands and feet are so swollen and painful they feel as if they might break off):** <gloss>Chop Tiger Cane root and boil it to make a juice; soak the affected limbs in it. From *Formulas Behind the Elbow*.</gloss>

**Sudden Abdominal Masses (hard as stone with stabbing pain; if untreated, death occurs within a hundred days):** <gloss>Take Tiger Cane roots and slice them. Near a water source, you can obtain about one 'dan' <note>a large volume unit</note>. Wash and grind them. Take one bushel and five liters of the powder, cook it with rice, and place it in a vat. Soak it with five bushels of good wine. Seal it and wait for the "Qi to rush" <note>a sensation of the medicine working</note>. If the person suddenly feels a strange, throbbing pain all over the body under the skin, like waves or a bubbling sound, or an unbearable itch that causes bleeding when scratched, do not be alarmed—this is the "rushing Qi." Once the sediment settles, one can drink one and a half liters. Do not eat salmon or salt. Or, simply take one liter of the dried root, pound it thinly, soak it, and drink. Taking three doses a day starting from a small amount is also good. The mass should then pass. This formula is far superior to all other medicines for treating masses.</gloss>

**Secret Formulas from the External Station:** <gloss>Take equal parts of charred Tiger Cane, pumice stone, cuttlefish bone, and cinnabar. Grind into a powder. When thirsty, take two mace with Ophiopogon decoction, three times a day.</gloss>

## Crabgrass
<term>Matang; Digitaria sanguinalis</term>
<gloss>From the *Supplement to the Materia Medica*</gloss> <gloss>Revised and corrected</gloss> <gloss>Includes entries from the *Miscellaneous Records of Famous Physicians* for unnamed but useful plants</gloss> <gloss>**Names:** Crabgrass <gloss>called *Matang* in the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Horse-Rice <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Sheep-Hemp <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Sheep-Millet <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, Creeping Grass <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>, and *Wei* in the *Erya Dictionary*.</gloss>
<gloss>The *Erya Dictionary* calls it *Wei*.</gloss> <gloss>Chen Zangqi <note>an 8th-century pharmacologist</note> says: Horses eat it as if it were sugar or rice, hence the names "Horse-Sugar" (Matang) and "Horse-Rice" (Mafan). Li Shizhen says: Sheep also eat it, so it is called "Sheep-Hemp" or "Sheep-Millet." Its scent is thin and foul, so it is called *You*, which implies something lean or sickly, like rotting wood. This grass has a stem like an onion but smells bad. This is why the *Zuo Zhuan* <note>an ancient Chinese narrative history</note> says: "One fragrant *Hui* plant and one foul *You* plant—after ten years, the smell of the *You* still remains."</gloss> <gloss>Master Sun’s *Collected Explanations*: The *Miscellaneous Records* say Crabgrass grows in low, damp places. The stems have joints that take root. Harvest in the fifth month. Chen Zangqi says: It grows in abandoned rice fields in the south. The joints rise up. The *Tan Pu* <note>a Song Dynasty miscellany</note> mistakenly identified this as Fragrant Shepherd's Purse, but it is actually the Crabgrass from the *Miscellaneous Records*. They are now combined into one entry. <gloss>Explanations:</gloss> The roots cling to the soil like Bermuda grass; it is suitable for feeding horses. It is also said that it grows in fields, looks like Bermuda grass but with longer leaves, and horses love to eat it.</gloss>
<gloss>Chen Zangqi says:</gloss> **Flavor is sweet, property is cold, and it is non-toxic.** <gloss>Extremely cold.</gloss>
**Primary Treatments:** Crabgrass regulates the "middle" <note>the digestive system</note> and clears the hearing and vision. <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> Decocted into a juice, it brightens the eyes and lubricates the lungs. It is also said to eliminate water-energy, "damp-collapse" <term>shibi; a form of arthritis</term>, beriberi, stubborn numbness, and empty swelling. For tightness in the lower abdomen and painful, red, or difficult urination, boil it with adzuki beans and eat; do not add salt or soy sauce. The squeezed juice stops "wasting-thirst" <term>xiaoke; often corresponding to diabetes</term>. Yang’s *Collected Traditions* notes it treats toxic swellings. <gloss>Chen Zangqi</gloss>

## Knotgrass
<term>Bianxu; Polygonum aviculare</term>
<gloss>Pronounced *Fù-Xù*</gloss> <gloss>**Names:** Knotgrass <gloss>*Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss>, Flat Bamboo <gloss>Tao Hongjing</gloss>, Creeping Knotgrass <gloss>Wu Pu</gloss>, Bamboo-Joint Grass <gloss>*Materia Medica Index*</gloss>, Road-Born Grass <gloss>*Compendium of Materia Medica*</gloss>.</gloss>
<gloss>Li Shizhen says: Xu Shen's *Shuowen Jiezi* <note>an ancient dictionary</note> writes it as *Bianzhu* <note>Flat Bamboo</note>, which sounds like "bamboo." There is a white powder at the joints. Because it grows mostly by the roadside, Daoist alchemists call it "Powder-Joint Grass" or "Road-Born Grass."</gloss>
<gloss>**Explanations:** The *Miscellaneous Records* say Knotgrass grows in the valleys of Mount Donglai. Harvest in the fifth month and dry in the shade. Tao Hongjing says:</gloss>
It is found everywhere, spreading across the ground. The flowers are white and the leaves are fine and green. People call it "Flat Bamboo." <gloss>Su Song says: In mid-spring, it spreads across the ground by roadsides. The sprouts look like Pink-gentian, with fine green leaves like bamboo. The stems are red like hairpin legs. Very tiny blue-yellow flowers emerge from the joints. The roots resemble mugwort roots. Harvest the sprouts in the fourth or fifth month and dry in the shade. The *Illustrated Classic of Sichuan* says: Harvest and dry in the second month. Guo Pu’s commentary on the *Erya* says it looks like small goosefoot with red stems and joints, grows well by the road, is edible, and kills parasites. Some say the "King’s Fodder" mentioned in the *Erya* is this plant. Li Shizhen says: Its leaves look like Broom-Cypress but are not pointed. The weak stems creep with short joints. In the third month, it blooms with tiny red flowers the size of millet grains.</gloss>
<gloss>*Compendium of Materia Medica*:</gloss> The blue flowers produce tiny seeds. Alchemists burn it for ash to refine "frost" <note>chemical precipitates</note>. There is a water-based variety called *Ti*, mentioned in the *Shuowen*. <gloss>Seeds.</gloss>
**Energy and Flavor:** Bitter, neutral, non-toxic. <gloss>The *Compendium* also notes: Sweet and warm.</gloss>
**Primary Treatments:** Spreading skin sores, itchy scabs, necrotic ulcers, and hemorrhoids; kills the "three worms" <note>internal parasites</note>. <gloss>*Divine Husbandman's Classic*</gloss> Treats "vaginal erosion" in women. Drink the decocted juice for childhood convulsions and toxic heat. <gloss>*Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> Treats cholera, jaundice, and promotes urination; treats pinworms in children. <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>
<margin>Attached Formulas</margin> <gloss>6 old, 3 new</gloss>
**Painful Urination from Heat:** Drink a decoction of Knotgrass frequently. <gloss>*Sheng Sheng Bian*</gloss>
**Jaundice from Heat:** Pound Knotgrass for juice; drink more than one liter. <gloss>*Thousand Golden Formulas*</gloss>
**Cholera with Vomiting/Diarrhea:** Cook Flat Bamboo in fermented black bean juice with five spices. <gloss>*Dietary Materia Medica*</gloss>
**Toxicity from Alchemical Minerals:** <gloss>*Mirror of the Heart of Medicine*</gloss> When taking mineral elixirs leads to toxic heat attacking the eyes with swelling and pain, pound Flat Bamboo roots <gloss>*Dietary Materia Medica*</gloss> and take the juice. <gloss>*Mirror of the Heart of Medicine*</gloss> Take one handful, wash, pound for juice, and drink. <gloss>*Dietary Materia Medica*</gloss>
**Parasites Causing Heart Pain:** For children with pinworms causing heart pain, a blue face, and foaming at the mouth near death: Take ten pounds of Flat Bamboo, chop it, and decoct in one *dan* <note>approx. 100 liters</note> of water until reduced to one *dou* <note>approx. 10 liters</note>. Remove the dregs and boil down to a syrup. Do not eat the night before; take one liter on an empty stomach. The worms will pass. One may also regularly cook the juice with rice. A *Maritime Song* <note>a rhyming folk remedy</note> says: "When sudden heart pain is too much to bear, I have an immortal's remedy from the sea. Decoct Knotgrass in vinegar and swallow; it will bring peace and comfort in an instant."
**Parasites Attacking the Lower Body:** For worms that look like maggots causing itching in the lower regions: Take one handful of Flat Bamboo, boil in two liters of water. For a five-year-old child, give three to five portions. <gloss>Yang’s *Childbirth and Nursing*</gloss>
**Swelling and Pain from Hemorrhoids:** Pound Flat Bamboo for juice and take one liter. If not cured after one or two doses, take more. The juice can also be mixed with vinegar for washing itchy scabs on bad sores. For pain, apply Flat Bamboo as a poultice; once the scab falls off, it is healed. <gloss>*Handy Formulas for Emergencies*</gloss>
**Make into cakes or boil for food three times a day.** <gloss>*Treatise on Medicinal Properties*</gloss>

# Lü Grass <gloss>pronounced *lu*</gloss>
<gloss>Lower category in the Classic <note>Referring to the *Shennong Ben Cao Jing*, the oldest Chinese herbology text</note></gloss>

<term>Explanations of Names</term> Lü Grass <gloss>from the *Tang Materia Medica*</gloss>, Yellow Goose <gloss>from *Master Pu’s Materia Medica*, the *Materia Medica of Herbs*, and the *Outline of Herbs*</gloss>, Lü <gloss>pronounced *li*</gloss>
<insert>Li</insert> <gloss>from the *Erya* <note>The oldest surviving Chinese dictionary</note></gloss> <gloss>This is the same as the character for *Lü*, just a variation in pronunciation. In ancient times, this grass was offered to the "Bath People" <note>officials in charge of royal ceremonies</note>, which is how it got its name. Those who offered "King’s Hay" were considered loyal subjects, and *Lü* also means "official." The *Book of Odes* says: "All morning I gather the Lü grass, yet it does not fill a single handful." Xu Shen’s *Shuowen Jiezi* <note>an early 2nd-century dictionary</note> states: "Lü grass can be used to dye things yellow." The *Book of Han* mentions "Princes' Scabbard-Hemp," and the commentator Jin Zhuo notes: "Scabbard grass comes from Langya; it looks like mugwort and can dye materials a golden color." Jin states: It grows in the valleys of Mount Tai. Su Gong says: It is found in Qingyi County in Yizhou. Today, it grows everywhere in flat, damp areas and by hillsides. Its leaves resemble bamboo but are thinner and smaller; the stems are round. People in the Jing and Xiang regions boil it to produce a very bright and beautiful yellow dye. It is commonly called "Crimson Grass." Shizhen notes: This grass is green but can dye yellow, so it is called "Yellow" or "Green." *Lü* is simply the northern pronunciation for green.</gloss>

<term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* state: Lü grass grows in the valleys of Mount Qingyi. Harvest in the ninth or tenth month. It can...</gloss>

<term>Properties</term> Bitter, balanced, non-toxic. <gloss>Zhen Quan says: According to Shennong and Lei Gong, it is bitter. Li Zhicai says: It is inhibited by the woodlouse <note>meaning they should not be used together</note>.</gloss>

<term>Therapeutic Uses</term> For coughs, rebellious Qi <note>disrupted energy flow</note>, wheezing, panting, chills, palpitations, scabies, itchy skin, "white baldness" <note>fungal scalp infections</note>, sores, tumors, and for killing small parasites on the skin. <gloss>Master Pu says it treats body heat, malevolent energy, fever in children, and is effective when used as a wash for all types of malignant sores.</gloss>
