# Caltrop <gloss>Top category in the Classic</gloss>

<term>Explanations of Names</term> Ci <gloss>Thorn</gloss> <gloss>from the *Classic*</gloss>, Pangtong <gloss>Passer-by</gloss> <gloss>from the *Erya*</gloss>, Quren <gloss>Stopper of Men</gloss> <gloss>from the *Classic*</gloss>, Zhixing <gloss>Stop Walking</gloss> <gloss>from the *Classic*</gloss>, Yutui <gloss>Feather-Pusher</gloss> <gloss>from the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss>

<term>Collected Explanations</term> <gloss>Tao Hongjing says: It grows mostly on roadsides and walls. The leaves spread across the ground. The seeds have thorns and look like water caltrops but are smaller. They are most abundant in Chang’an. When people walk, the thorns often stick to their wooden shoes. These thorns cannot be swept away easily. They are used in formulas under the name Lü. Li Shizhen says: The name *Jili* (Caltrop) implies "haste" and "sharpness." The thorns injure people very quickly and are very sharp. The names "Stopper of Men" and "Stop Walking" both come from the way it injures travelers. The *Miscellaneous Records* state: Caltrop seeds grow in the flat marshes or roadsides of Fengyi. Harvest the fruit in the seventh or eighth month and dry in the sun. Tao says: They are also planted in winter. The "White Caltrop" currently grows in the horse pastures of Tongzhou and Sha-yuan. It is found near roads as well. It has green leaves and thin vines that spread across the sand. In the seventh month, it blooms with small yellow flowers, exactly like pea flowers but smaller. In the ninth month, it bears fruit like Gorgon nuts, which can then be harvested. The seeds taste sweet and have a slightly fishy smell. They are brownish-green and look like silkworm seeds but are slightly larger. They also closely resemble Malan seeds, but Malan seeds are a bit larger and are not suitable for medicine; one must distinguish them carefully. Kou Zongshi says: There are two grades of White Caltrop. The "Du Caltrop" is the one that grows along roadsides today, with yellow flowers and prickly thorns. The other type is the "White Caltrop" from the Sha-yuan pastures in Tongzhou. Its seeds look like a sheep’s kidney and are as small as lacquer grains. This is a medicine for tonifying the kidneys and is widely used today. For "Wind" ailments <note>such as itching or stroke</note>, only the Spiny Caltrop is used. Li Shizhen says: The Caltrop leaves look like newly sprouted locust tree leaves; they are neat and lovely. The Spiny Caltrop looks like a small water caltrop with three or four spikes. There is a kernel inside the fruit. The White Caltrop <note>Flatstem Milkvetch</note> produces pods about an inch long, with seeds inside that are fatty and shaped like green sheep kidneys. People today call this "Sha-yuan Caltrop" to tell them apart.</gloss>

### Seeds

<gloss>Preparation</gloss> <gloss>Lei Xiao says: To use them, clean and steam them from noon until evening (the hours of the Horse to the Rooster), then dry in the sun. Master Mu says: In spring, remove all thorns before use. Mix with wine, steam, and sun-dry. Then steam again from noon to evening and dry on a clear, bright day. These can then be used in pills or powders. Generally, they are dry-fried to remove the thorns before being added to medicine.</gloss>

<term>Properties</term> Bitter, warm, non-toxic. <gloss>The *Miscellaneous Records* say: Sweet, slightly warm. Zhen Quan says: Sweet, slightly toxic. Ri Hua says: Its nature is to circulate and penetrate. If taken for a long time, it does not cause coldness nor does it cause stagnant heat. It is correct to consider its nature warm. Li Zhicai says: Aconite serves as its "envoy" <note>an assisting herb</note>.</gloss>

<term>Therapeutic Uses</term> For "bad blood" <note>stagnant blood</note>, breaking up tumors and internal masses, throat blockage, difficulty in lactation; if taken long-term, it builds muscle, clears the eyes, and makes the body feel light. <gloss>from the *Classic*</gloss> <gloss>For itchy skin rashes, headaches, rebellious coughing, lung injuries, lung atrophy, stopping irritability, lowering Qi, childhood head sores, swellings, and impotence. It can be ground into a rubbing powder. From the *Miscellaneous Records*</gloss> <gloss>Treats all "Wind" disorders, vitiligo, and sores. For coughing up pus. Clears dry heat and rebellious coughing. Treats "Running Piglet" Qi <note>a sensation of gas rushing up from the abdomen</note>, kidney Qi, lung Qi, and fullness in the chest and ribs. It hastens childbirth, induces abortion, benefits the "essence" <note>vitality/semen</note>, treats scrofula <note>neck swellings</note>, stops urinary incontinence, frequent urination, dribbling, bloody urine, and lower back pain. It is excellent for hemorrhoids, scrotal sweating, and women’s...</gloss>

# White Caltrop <note>scientific name: *Tribulus terrestris*; also known as Puncture Vine</note>

<gloss>Nature and Flavor</gloss> Sweet, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Main Indications</gloss> Tonifies the kidneys and treats lower back pain, nocturnal emission, deficiency, and physical exhaustion. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> <gloss>On the development of its use:</gloss> <gloss>Su Song says:</gloss> Ancient prescriptions all used the spiked variety. It is excellent for dispelling "wind" <note>in Chinese medicine, "wind" refers to conditions like tremors, itching, or sudden onset illnesses</note> and improving eyesight. The Taoist immortals also had a method for taking Caltrop alone, stating that regardless of color, one should simply choose firm seeds. In spring, remove the spikes before use. <gloss>Li Shizhen says:</gloss> Ancient formulas for tonifying the kidneys and treating "wind" used the Spiked Caltrop. Later generations mostly used the Sha-yuan Caltrop <note>*Astragalus complanatus*</note> for kidney tonification, or made it into a medicinal paste; I suspect their efficacy is not far apart. Spiked Caltrop can be stir-fried until yellow, the spikes removed, and ground into flour to make cakes or steamed for food to survive during times of famine.

---

<insert>Appended Prescriptions <gloss>nine from old sources, eight newly added</gloss></insert>

<margin>Method for general consumption</margin> Collect Caltrop seeds in the 7th or 8th month when ripe. Dry them in the sun. In spring, remove the spikes and grind into a powder. Take two *qian* <note>about 7.5 grams</note> per dose, mixed with freshly drawn water, three times a day. Do not interrupt the treatment. This "grain-cutting" <note>a practice of avoiding common grains for spiritual or health reasons</note> method leads to longevity. After one year of use, the body will not feel the winter's cold or the summer's heat. After two years, the elderly will regain their youth; white hair will turn black, and lost teeth will grow back. After three years, the body will feel light. <gloss>From the *Secret Instructions of the Immortals for Longevity*</gloss>

<margin>Radiating pain in the lower back</margin> Pound Caltrop seeds into a powder and mix with honey to form pills the size of a lablab bean. Take with wine twice a day for nine days. <gloss>From *Secret Essentials from the Outer Terrace*</gloss>

<margin>Full-body swelling (Edema)</margin> Use "Earth Caltrop" <note>another name for the plant</note> to make a decoction and bathe in it daily. <gloss>From *Prescriptions of the Sage’s Benevolence*</gloss>

<margin>Sudden collapse from the "Five Corpses"</margin> <note>An ancient term for sudden, severe ailments believed to be caused by malevolent spirits or internal parasites</note> Pound Caltrop seeds into a powder, mix with honey into pills the size of a lablab bean. Take two pills per dose, three times a day for nine days. <gloss>From *Prescriptions for Emergencies*</gloss>

<margin>Constipation due to "Wind"</margin> Stir-fry one *liang* <note>approx. 37g</note> of Caltrop seeds. Take five *qian* <note>approx. 18g</note> of Gleditsia pods (remove skin and toast with butter). Grind into powder. Take one *qian* per dose with salt tea. <gloss>From *Prescriptions for Universal Relief*</gloss>

<margin>Absence of menstruation</margin> Use equal parts "Earth Caltrop" and Angelica root. Grind into powder. Take three *qian* per dose with rice water. <gloss>From *Confucians' Duties to Their Parents*</gloss>

<margin>Expelling the placenta and difficult labor</margin> For difficult labor, a fetus remaining in the womb, or a retained placenta, and even for stillbirths: Use two *liang* each of Caltrop seeds and Fritillaria. Grind into powder. Take three *qian* with rice water. If it does not come out shortly, take another dose. <gloss>From *Master Mei’s Prescriptions*</gloss>

<margin>Vomiting clear fluid</margin> Collect Caltrop seeds on the 7th day of the 7th lunar month. Dry in the shade. Take one "square-inch spoon" <note>an ancient measurement, roughly 1.5–2 grams</note> three times a day. <gloss>From *Secret Essentials from the Outer Terrace*</gloss>

<margin>Chronic masses and accumulations</margin> Collect Caltrop seeds in the 7th or 8th month. Boil in water until cooked, then sun-dry. Mix with honey into pills the size of a Firmiana seed. Take with wine, starting with ten pills and increasing until effective. The leftover decoction can be boiled down into a syrup to be consumed.

<margin>Blindness of thirty years</margin> Use "Liver-Supplementing Powder." Collect Caltrop seeds on the 7th day of the 7th lunar month and dry in the shade. Pound into powder. Every morning after eating, take one "square-inch spoon" with water, twice a day. <gloss>From *Secret Essentials from the Outer Terrace*</gloss>

<margin>Loose or shaky teeth</margin> For teeth that are shaky due to sores, itching, or injury: Take five *qian* of raw, ground "Earth Caltrop" (with horns removed). Dip into half a cup of boiling water, add a little salt, and use as a warm mouthwash. This is very effective. Alternatively, burn the root to ash and apply to the teeth to make them firm. <gloss>From *Prescriptions of the Imperial Pharmacy*</gloss>

<margin>Uncontrolled gum bleeding</margin> Or for loose teeth.

<margin>Worms emerging from teeth</margin> <note>Ancient explanation for dental cavities</note> Use White Caltrop powder every morning for painful, loose teeth. <gloss>From the *Taoist Canon*</gloss>

<margin>Toothache</margin> Use Caltrop seeds or roots ground into powder and apply to the area daily. <gloss>From *Prescriptions of the Hall of Auspicious Bamboo*</gloss>

<margin>Nasal congestion and discharge</margin> For those who haven't smelled fragrance or foulness for many years: Take a handful of Caltrop and crush it (as if by a wagon on a road). Boil it in a large cup of water until half a cup remains. Lie on your back, first hold a mouthful of rice, then pour one *he* <note>about 100ml</note> of the juice into the nose. After two applications, you will sneeze out one or two polyps that look like red silkworm pupae, and you will be cured. <gloss>From *Prescriptions of the Sage’s Benevolence*</gloss>

<margin>Facial scarring</margin> Take one *he* each of Caltrop seeds and Gardenia seeds. Grind into powder and mix with vinegar. Apply at night and wash off in the morning. <gloss>From *Prescriptions for Emergencies*</gloss>

<margin>Vitiligo and skin disorders</margin> Take six *liang* of White Caltrop seeds, pound raw into powder. Take two *qian* per dose with soup, twice a day. After one month, the root of the disease will be gone. After half a month, red spots will appear in the white areas, which is a sign of effectiveness. <gloss>From *Master Sun’s Dietary Taboos*</gloss>

<margin>All types of swellings</margin> Roast one *sheng* <note>approx. 1 liter</note> of Caltrop seeds, then pour into vinegar. Apply the mixture to the head of the swelling to draw out the "root." <gloss>From *Secret Essentials from the Outer Terrace*</gloss>

# Pipewort <note>original: 穀精草 Gu Jing Cao; scientific name: *Eriocaulon buergerianum*</note> <gloss>From the Song Dynasty "Kaibao" era records</gloss>

## Names and Explanations: Star-Wearing Herb <gloss>from the "Kaibao" records</gloss>, Literary Star Herb <gloss>from the "Materia Medica" Compendium</gloss>, Shooting Star Herb <gloss>Li Shizhen says: It grows from the residual vital energy of grain fields, hence the name "Grain Essence" (Gu Jing). Its flowers are white and resemble stars, leading to the various "star" names. Another record says: The white flowers resemble stars, hence the name "Star-Wearing."</gloss>

## Collected Explanations <gloss>Su Song says: It is found everywhere. In spring, it grows in grain fields. The leaves resemble those of the Celosia (Feather Cockscomb), and the roots look like horse-whisks. It grows best in rich soil. There is also a variety with long, jointed stems and tiny roots found in the Qin and Long regions (modern Shaanxi and Gansu). Li Shizhen says: This herb grows in fallow fields after the grain harvest. It is common north and south of the Yangtze River. It grows in clumps with leaves like tender rice seedlings. It sends up thin stems four to five inches high, topped with tiny white flowers like scattered stars. The flowers are gathered in the ninth lunar month and dried in the shade. It is a mistake to gather them in the first, second, or third months.</gloss>

## Nature and Flavor <gloss>The flower</gloss> Pungent, warm, and non-toxic. <gloss>Chen Zangqi says: Sweet and neutral. It is highly clarifying and can be used by alchemists to bind mercury into cinnabar beads.</gloss>

## Main Indications Sore throat <term>Throat Bi: a condition involving swelling and blockage of the throat</term>, toothache caused by "wind," various sores and scabies <gloss>Kaibao records</gloss>. "Wind" headaches, blindness or membranes over the eyes <term>Yimo: cataracts or pterygium</term>, eye membranes forming after smallpox, and to stop bleeding <gloss>Li Shizhen</gloss>.

<margin>Li Shizhen says: Pipewort is light and airy in nature, allowing it to "float" upward to the "Yang Brightness" <note>Yangming: a meridian system associated with the stomach and large intestine that reaches the face and eyes</note> regions of the body. It is extremely effective when added to formulas for treating various eye diseases. Its power to clear the vision seems to surpass even that of the Chrysanthemum flower.</margin>

## Appended Prescriptions <gloss>One from older sources, seven newly added</gloss>
Headache and eyebrow pain: <gloss>Take two mace <term>Mace: a traditional unit of weight, approx. 3.75 grams</term> of Pipewort, three mace of earthworm, and one mace of frankincense. Grind into a powder. Use half a mace each time; burn it and draw the smoke into the nostrils through a tube, alternating sides. From the "Sagely Universal Relief" records.</gloss>
Migraines or general headaches: <gloss>From the "Collection of Proven Formulas": Use one tael <note>approx. 37.5 grams</note> of Pipewort powder. Mix with egg white into a paste and spread on a cloth. Apply to the painful area and change when dry.</gloss>
<gloss>Note: The "Sagely Universal Formulas" suggest using Pipewort powder and wrapping it with copper wire. For unstoppable nosebleeds: take two mace of Pipewort powder with flour soup. From the "Divine Benefit Formulas."</gloss>
Membranes over the eyes: <gloss>Equal parts Pipewort and Sililer (Fangfeng). Grind into powder. Soak pig liver in rice-wash water, coat it with the powder, and roast it. Eat daily. Another formula can be found under "Bat Droppings" (Ye Ming Sha).</gloss>
Night blindness: <gloss>Grind Pipewort and clam shell powder in equal parts. Insert into pig liver and boil until cooked. For childhood night blindness. From "Divine Benefit Formulas."</gloss>
Obstruction by eye membranes: <gloss>Grind Pipewort into powder. Eat by dipping dried persimmons or slices of pig liver into it. Another formula is listed under "Bat Droppings" in the "Taoist Master Lang’s Emergency Formulas."</gloss>
For childhood night blindness: <gloss>When a child suddenly cannot see at dusk: take one set of ram lungs, do not wash with water, split open with a bamboo knife, and insert a pinch of Pipewort powder. Tie tightly and boil until cooked. Eat daily for great effect. Avoid using iron utensils. If the child refuses to eat it, roast the mixture, pound it, and form into pills the size of mung beans. Take thirty pills with tea. From "Household Treasures for Health."</gloss>
Heatstroke in children: <gloss>For vomiting, diarrhea, and excessive thirst: Burn Pipewort but retain its properties <note>carbonizing the herb</note>. Covering it with lacquer is effective. When cold, grind to powder. Take half a mace with cold rice water. From the "Complete Book of Child Protection."</gloss>

# Japanese Fern Spores <note>original: 海金沙 Hai Jin Sha; "Sea Gold Sand"</note> <gloss>From the Song Dynasty "Jiayou" era records</gloss>

## Names and Explanations: Bamboo Garden Coriander <gloss>Li Shizhen says: Its color is yellow like fine sand. It is called "Sea" (Hai) to signify its miraculous properties. The common name "Bamboo Garden Coriander" refers to the shape of its leaves.</gloss>

## Collected Explanations <gloss>Zhang Yuxi says: It comes from the Qianzhong prefecture, and also grows in Hunan. It grows in small clusters one to two feet high. In the seventh or eighth months, the "gold powder" is collected by drying the plants in the sun. Place paper underneath and strike the plants with a staff so the fine sand falls onto the paper. Continue drying and striking until finished. Li Shizhen says: It is found in Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Hunan, Hubei, Sichuan, and Shaanxi. It grows under trees in mountain forests. The stems are as thin as thread and climb up bamboo or wood to about a foot high. The leaves are small like coriander, thin, and green on both sides. They are wrinkled, and within the wrinkles are spores like cattail pollen, colored yellow-red. It does not flower. The small roots are strong. Both the spores and the herb itself can be used in medicine. Alchemists collect the fuzz and juice to boil and transform cinnabar.</gloss>

## Nature and Flavor <gloss>The taste is</gloss> Sweet, cold, and non-toxic.

## Main Indications Promotes the flow of the small intestine. When combined with "E-zi" <note>possibly a type of seed or mineral</note>, Glauber’s salt, or borax, it treats the frantic fever of typhoid. Used in pills or powders to treat edema from damp-heat, painful or hot urination, "fatty" urination <term>Gaolin: chyluria, where urine looks like oil or cream</term>, bloody urination, or urinary stones. It relieves pain in the urethra and treats toxic heat.

<margin>Li Shizhen says: Japanese Fern Spores act on the "blood level" of the Small Intestine and Bladder meridians. It is suitable for those with heat in the blood.</margin>

## Appended Prescriptions <gloss>One from older sources, five newly added</gloss>
Urgent pain from hot urinary disorders: <gloss>Dry the Fern Spore herb in the shade and grind into powder. Take two mace mixed with a decoction of raw licorice. This is Commander Chen's formula. One variation adds talcum. From "Records of the Resolute."</gloss>
Inability to urinate: <gloss>With fullness and discomfort below the navel: One tael of Japanese Fern Spores and half a tael of "Wax-South" tea. Crush together. For each dose, take three mace with a decoction of ginger and licorice twice a day. Can also be taken as a powder.</gloss>
Fatty urination (resembling oil): <gloss>One tael each of Japanese Fern Spores and talcum, with two and a half mace of licorice tips. Grind into powder. Take two mace with a decoction of Ophiopogon (Mai Men Dong) twice a day. From "Benevolence Preservative Formulas."</gloss>
Bloody urination with sharp pain: <gloss>If the water passage is opened, the clear and turbid will separate naturally. Use Japanese Fern Spore powder. Wrap in fatty pork... <note>text cuts off</note> or take one mace with sugar water. From "Formulas for Universal Relief."</gloss>
Edema from splenic dampness: <gloss>Abdominal swelling like a drum with such breathlessness that one cannot lie down. Japanese Fern Spore powder <unclear>...</unclear></gloss>

# Water Avens <note>original: 水楊梅 Shui Yang Mei; likely *Geum japonicum* or *Adina pilulifera*</note>
<term>Compendium</term> <term>Explanation of Names</term> <term>Details</term>

# Centipede Grass <note>original: 地蜈蚣草 Di Wu Gong Cao; likely *Helminthostachys zeylanica* or similar trailing herbs</note>
<term>Compendium</term> <term>Details</term>

<margin>
<term>Collected Explanations</term> <note>Li Shizhen says:</note> It grows in villages and open wilds. The vines crawl from left to right and right to left. Its leaves are dense and grow in opposite pairs, resembling the shape of a centipede. Its flower spikes are also long. Common folk call it "Path-Crossing Centipede." The variety that climbs trees is called "Flying Heaven Centipede." Both the roots and sprouts can be used medicinally.
</margin>

**Nature and Flavor:** Bitter, cold, and non-toxic. <term>Primary Indications:</term> To detoxify and treat constipation. Crush for juice to treat abscesses, swellings, and burns. It can also treat eye ailments by removing toxins and draining pus. For centipede bites, crush the plant with a little salt and apply to the wound, or apply as a dry powder. <note>From Li Shizhen’s records</note>

<term>Attached Formulas</term> <insert>One new</insert> For all types of abscesses, intestinal abscesses, and breast abscesses that are swollen but not yet broken, or have broken but the pus and blood will not disperse, accompanied by fever and pain in patients who can still eat. Use the "Pus-Draining and Interior-Supporting Powder."

Centipede Grass is also known as "Happy Angelica." Mix equal parts of the herb and licorice, grind into powder. Take two mace per dose with warm wine. <note>From the *Formulas of the Bureau of People's Welfare Pharmacies*</note>

# Lobelia <note>original: 半邊蓮 Ban Bian Lian; scientific name: *Lobelia chinensis*</note>
<term>Compendium</term> <term>Details</term> <term>Collected Explanations</term>

<margin>
<term>Collected Explanations</term> <note>Li Shizhen says:</note> Lobelia is a small herb. It grows in shaded, damp open fields. It hugs the ground with thin stalks that spread as vines, rooting at every node. It has tiny leaves. In autumn, it opens small, pale reddish-purple flowers. Each flower only has "half a side," resembling half a lotus flower, hence the name. It is also called "Quick Detoxifier" <note>original: 急解素 Ji Jie Su</note>.
</margin>

**Nature and Flavor:** Pungent, neutral, and non-toxic. <term>Primary Indications:</term> For snake and scorpion venom. Drink the crushed juice and apply the dregs as a poultice around the wound. It also treats "Cold-Heat" asthma and malaria. For malaria with alternating chills and fever, crush equal parts of the herb and realgar <note>original: 雄黃 Xiong Huang; arsenic sulfide</note> into a paste. Place in a basin and cover it until the color turns green. Form into pills the size of a parasol tree seed. Take nine pills on an empty stomach with salt water. <note>From Li Shizhen and the *Formulas of the Beneficial Regions*</note>

# Chinese Violet <note>original: 紫花地丁 Zi Hua Di Ding; scientific name: *Viola philippica*</note>
<term>Compendium</term> <term>Explanation of Names</term> Arrowhead Herb <term>Compendium</term> Solitary Tiger <term>Secret Records</term> Goat Horns <term>Details</term> <term>Collected Explanations</term>

<margin>
<term>Collected Explanations</term> <note>Li Shizhen says:</note> It is found everywhere. Its leaves resemble willow leaves but are finer. In summer, it opens purple flowers and produces horn-like seed pods. Those growing on level ground have upright stems, while those in gullies crawl as vines. The *Formulas for Universal Relief* says: The variety growing on village fences has small white flowers in summer and autumn that hang down like little bells, with leaves slightly resembling Woody Rose <note>original: 木香 Mu Xiang</note>. This is related to the purple variety but might be a different species.
</margin>

**Nature and Flavor:** Pungent, cold, and non-toxic. <term>Primary Indications:</term> All types of abscesses, carbuncles, scrofula <note>swollen lymph nodes</note>, nameless swellings, and malignant sores. <note>From Li Shizhen’s records</note>

<term>Attached Formulas</term> <insert>Eight new</insert>

<margin>
**For painful boils and swellings:** Take Chinese Violet (with roots) and Cocklebur leaves in equal parts. Crush them together. Mix one cup of wine into the mash, strain the juice and drink. <note>From Yang Cheng’s *Proven Formulas*</note>
</margin>

<margin>
**For boils:** Burn Chinese Violet into ash and take three mace with wine. <note>From *Secret Treasures of Heaven and Earth*</note>
</margin>

<margin>

**For carbuncles on the back and nameless swellings:** Applying this is like a divine miracle. Gather Chinese Violet during the hottest "Three Dog Days" of summer. Mix with white lotus root, salt, and vinegar. Soak overnight and apply as a poultice. Long ago, a nun had a carbuncle on her back; she used this formula and was cured within a few days.

**Scrofula** <note>original: 瘰癧 luoli; chronic swelling of the lymph nodes, often tubercular</note>. For all malignant scrofula: take the roots of **Purple-flower Earth Nail** <note>original: 紫花地丁 Zihua Diding; *Viola yedoensis*</note>. Dry them in the sun. Store in a jar and calcine with fire. Use the smoke to treat the sores. — From *Formulas from the Collection of Benevolence*.

For all scrofula: boil it and use the steam to fumigate the area. Yellow fluid will be discharged; when the fluid is exhausted, the patient is healed. — From *Easy and Simple Formulas for Health*.

For scrofula, carbuncles on the back, and various swellings: take **Purple-flower Earth Nail** roots. Remove the coarse outer skin and use with white <unclear>root</unclear> for effectiveness. 

Another method from **Yang’s Formulas**: Use the stems of **Purple-flower Earth Nail**. For boils <note>original: 疔 ding; small, hard, deep-rooted sores</note> and scrofula with swelling and pain: decoct the leaves and add a small amount of soy sauce. Grind and apply.

Take the herb in clusters and grind into a powder. Mix with oil and apply. It has divine efficacy. — From *Secret Treasures of Heaven and Earth*.

For boils and carbuncles: the *Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold* <note>original: 千金方 Qianjin Fang</note> uses **Purple-flower Earth Nail** grass. Pound to extract the juice and drink. Even in extreme cases, it works.

Mix with honey, pound it, and paste it on the site. For tumors, add fresh black cow dung. — From *Formulas for Universal Relief*.

For boils and scrofula: Use the fresh herb, ingest it, and induce vomiting. — From *Formulas for Universal Relief*.

# Ghost Needle Grass <note>original: 鬼針草 Guizhen Cao; *Bidens bipinnata*</note>
<gloss>Supplement</gloss> <gloss>Chen Zangqi says:</gloss> It grows by the banks of ponds. It has square stems. The seeds are very small and shaped like hairpin legs <note>original: 釵腳 chaijiao</note>. They cling to people's clothes like needles. Northerners call it **Ghost Needle**, while Southerners call it **Ghost Hairpin**.

<term>Nature and Flavor</term> Bitter, flat, and non-toxic.

<term>Primary Indications</term> Used to treat spider and snake bites. Pound the herb to extract the juice for oral consumption, and also apply the mash topically. <note>From Chen Zangqi's records</note>. For cholera <note>original: 藿亂 huoluan</note>. <note>From Li Shizhen's records</note>.

<gloss>Appendix of Formulas</gloss> (New)
1. **For split fingernails or wounds where the flesh does not heal:** Take the sprouts of **Ghost Needle Grass** and the roots of **Burdock** <note>original: 鼠粘子 shunanzi</note>. Pound for juice and mix with winter lard. Apply to the wound. — From *Formulas Worth a Thousand Gold*.

# Single-Use General <note>original: 獨用將軍 Duyong Jiangjun; likely *Sarcandra glabra*</note> <gloss>Tang Materia Medica</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> Su Gong says: It grows in forests and wilds. The leaves emerge at every node, and the heart of the plant produces sprouts. Its foliage resembles the **Phoebe tree** <note>original: 楠 nan</note>. It can be harvested at any time. Both roots and leaves are used.

<term>Nature and Flavor</term> Pungent and non-toxic.

<term>Primary Indications</term> For toxic swellings and breast abscesses. It crushes toxins and breaks up stagnant or "evil" blood. <note>According to Su Gong</note>.

<gloss>Appendix of Formulas</gloss> (New)
1. **For dysentery with inability to eat:** Take the root of the **Single-Use General** herb. Choose those with bead-like nodules the size of beans. Take the beads and pound for juice. Take three spoonfuls, mix with half a cup of white wine, and consume. — From *Simple and Convenient Formulas*.

<gloss>Supplement</gloss> Su Gong says: It grows in the valleys of Cizhou. The leaves are like those of the Phoebe tree but are thinner and longer. Harvest at any time. Flavor is pungent, temperature is warm, and it is non-toxic. It primarily treats wind-pain in the joints, injuries from falls, internal bruising, and cramping pains of the five viscera.

# Swelling Disappears <note>original: 見腫消 Jianzhong Xiao; likely a species of *Isodon* or *Plectranthus*</note> <gloss>Song Illustrated Manual</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> Su Song says: It grows in Yunzhou. In spring, it produces sprouts. The stems and leaves are purple. It grows to a height of one or two feet. The leaves resemble mulberry leaves but are glossy; the front is green while the back is purple-red. Harvest at any time.

<term>Nature and Flavor</term> Sour, astringent, and slightly toxic.

<term>Primary Indications</term> Treats carbuncles, swellings, and dog bites. Pound the leaves and apply them topically. <note>According to Su Song</note>.

<gloss>Appendix of Formulas</gloss> (New)
1. **For all toxic swellings and injuries:** For toxins emerging at the front or back of the ears or under the neck with hard swelling. Use fresh **Swelling Disappears** grass, fresh **Bletilla** <note>original: 白及 baiji</note>, fresh **Ampelopsis** <note>original: 白歛 bailian</note>, **Local Rhubarb** <note>original: 土大黄 tudahuang</note>, fresh **Thistle** root <note>original: 大薊 daji</note>, and **Wild Ramie** root <note>original: 野苧麻 ye zhuma</note>. Pound these together to form a "cake." Mix in one mace <note>approx. 3.7g</note> of **Glauber's Salt** <note>original: 芒硝 mangxiao</note> and apply. Leave the "head" of the swelling exposed. Change the dressing once it dries. If you add **Paris polyphylla** <note>original: 金線重樓 jinxian chonglou</note> and **Cremastra** <note>original: 山慈姑 shancigu</note>, the effect is even more wonderful. — From *Essentials of Typhoid Disorders*.

# Overturning the Steamer <note>original: 攀倒甑 Pandaozeng; *Patrinia villosa*</note> <gloss>Illustrated Manual</gloss>
<gloss>Explanation of Names</gloss> Su Song says: It grows in the countryside of Jizhou. Stems and leaves resemble **Mint**. One name is **Spotted Staff** <note>original: 斑杖 banzhang</note>; another is **Bone-knitter** <note>original: 接骨 jiegu</note>.

Li Shizhen says: The name "Spotted Staff" is shared with **Giant Knotweed** <note>original: 虎杖 huzhang</note>, and "Bone-knitter" is shared with **Elderberry** <note>original: 蒴藋 suozhuo</note>. I do not know if they are of the same genus.

<term>Nature and Flavor</term> Bitter, cold, and non-toxic.

<term>Primary Indications</term> To ward off dysentery, wind-heat, restlessness, thirst, and mania. Pound the juice and consume; it is very effective. <note>According to Su Song</note>.

# Water Licorice <note>original: 水甘草 Shui Gancao; likely *Saururus chinensis*</note> <gloss>Illustrated Manual</gloss>
<gloss>Collected Explanations</gloss> Su Song says: It grows in Yunzhou, mostly by the water. In spring, it produces sprouts. The stems are green and the leaves resemble **Willow**. It has no flowers. Locals harvest it in the eighth or tenth lunar month. It is used alone and is not typically mixed with other medicines.

<term>Nature and Flavor</term> Sweet, cold, and non-toxic.

<term>Primary Indications</term> For pediatric wind-heat and "Red Cloud" <note>original: 丹毒 dandu; erysipelas or skin rashes</note>. Decoct with **Licorice** <note>original: 甘草 gancao</note> and drink. <note>According to Su Song</note>.

<term>**Compendium (Gangmu):** This refers to the "Principles and Details" style of organization. Li Shizhen rejected the disorganized lists of earlier eras, instead creating a rigorous taxonomy where "Principles" (*gang*) represent broad biological or physical classes and "Details" (*mu*) provide the specific descriptions, history, and medical uses for each item. This structured approach is often compared to the modern biological classification systems developed later in the West.</term>

# Expanded Compendium of Materia Medica
<note>original: "增廣本草綱目" (Zengguang Bencao Gangmu)</note>

<term>**Expanded (*Zengguang*):** <note>original: "增廣"</note> This prefix tells the reader that the publisher has added extra material to the original text. During the 17th and 18th centuries, publishers often "expanded" famous works like this one by including new medical formulas, more detailed woodblock illustrations, or scholarly commentary to make the book more competitive and useful for practicing physicians.</term>

<term>**Compendium of Materia Medica (*Bencao Gangmu*):** <note>original: "本草綱目"</note> Authored by Li Shizhen and first published in the late 16th century, this is the most famous work in the history of Chinese medicine. It is a massive encyclopedia of natural history, categorizing plants, animals, and minerals used in healing. The title literally means "The Outline and Details of Roots and Herbs," reflecting the rigorous taxonomic system the author used to organize nearly 1,900 different substances.</term>
